en: The Kāvyamālā:
The *Haravijaya*, composed by the great poet, the noble Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara.
Accompanied by the commentary titled *Viṣamapadodyota* composed by Rājānaka Śrīmad Alaka.
First Canto.
[He whose] neck’s splendor was as beautiful as a cluster of blue water-lilies—

May Dhūrjaṭi grant you happiness— he who bears the formidable Kālakūṭa poison, which resembles the color of a rope, appearing as if soiled by the smoke rising from the incense consumed as an offering. ||1||
May that form of the Teacher, which has a mouth opened wide in a yawn, which reveals a reflected face within the mirror of its claws,
and which is pregnant with the destruction of the enemy host, purify you.
May the fulfillment of Hari’s slaying of the Daitya Mudvṛtta bring you prosperity. ||2||
May the circle of lotus buds, which serve as his seat upon a lotus throne and possess rows of petals pale at their edges,
purify you— bearing the grace of the divine mountain encircled by the spray of waves from the surging Ocean of Milk. 3.
On the lofty peak of Mount Mandara, which possesses the luster of the rising sun and whose surface is washed by the waters of the celestial river,
there exists a city named Jyotsnāvatī, the sole ornament of the three worlds.
Her ornament is like a crescent moon upon the head of the Lord whose mark is the bull.
In those nights, when the sky had its center reddened by the luster of the palace of fresh rubies, with the crescent moon situated therein—
[just as] the chest of the lord of the Asuras was marked by the claws of the Man-Lion.
It shines with an unevenly split expression, accompanied by a streak of blood. ||5||

The courtyard of the palace made of jyotīrasa stone, with its milky ocean overflowing with the abundant and lofty waves of shimmering rays, [is surpassed by] the orb of the moon-like faces of the women stationed at the windows— Please note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available. If you have the complete verse or passage, please provide it for a full rendering.
In which [city], it seems as though [the moon] shines incessantly from the mere sight of it.
Their cheeks, drenched with thick perspiration during lovemaking and with the tips of filaments fallen from the flowers of their ear-ornaments clinging to them,
resembled the feathers on the shafts of Cupid’s arrows as they flew toward them.
And in that [city], the women appeared as if their eyelashes were disheveled.

Raising up Madana— who, though long ago consumed by the fire of wrath that shattered the meditative absorption of the moon-crested Lord within the minds of women— by means of his rays, he shines forth.
In which the moon hangs suspended within the lattice-work of its path.

In her, during acts of love, the beauty of her broad and full orb-like hips and her slender body with its shimmering row of teeth appeared like the tortoise of the Flower-Bowed God (Kāmadeva) upon the tips of her lover’s fingernails.
The sound of the women’s sweet singing was interrupted by their hands striking the corners [of the instruments]. ||9||
Where the palace of Bāṇāsura, made of sapphire, shines with large ruby windows situated on both sides—
[the palace] whose arms were severed by the discus of Hari.
His body was as if covered with root-wounds, moistened by splashes of blood. ||10||
Where the waves of the celestial river flowing nearby, having entered the path of the windows of the ruby palaces, dispel the exhaustion born at the end of amorous play.
The breezes, cooled by following the waves, [caused] the women [to shiver]. ||11||
In that city, during the nights, the white crescent moon— marked with its spot and reflected upon the cheeks of beautiful women—
was rendered variegated by the calluses formed from the striking of bowstrings upon the fish-bannered god of love.
It appeared as if it were the surface of a polished jewel laid down [as a foundation]. ||12||
Upon which the hosts of gods suspected that the moon upon Śaṅkara’s crest had approached out of eagerness to behold her—
she who was radiant, kissing the sky, and built of bricks of the essence of light.
And the ocean of milk [shines] as if with the mass of light from its embankments. ||13||
Lakṣmī does not dwell in that house, which is filled with women whose gait possesses the brilliance of playful grace like that of female swans on Lake Mānasa,
and who are adorned with the tinkling sound of jeweled anklets.
He caused [the quarters] to resound with the cymbals of the fish-bannered god [Kāma]. ||14||
In whose nights the orb of the moon’s rays was mottled by the smoke of burning aguru incense,
as it struck against the silvered panels of the latticed windows.
He attains prosperity as if it were a scar-line left by being caught in a pair of tongs. ||15||

The bedchamber, where the limbs of women crushed by the friction of amorous play, have scattered fragments of petals from blossoming blue lotuses that served as their ear-ornaments— [fragments] belonging to the flower-arrowed god who was being torn asunder there.
It was strewn with fragments [of the chariot] like shattered pieces of a sword. ||16||
From the openings of the windows of which palace, the dark columns of smoke from playful incense of black aloe-wood flowed forth,
as if out of fear of being broken by the rays of the nearby moon.
Like hands with fingers that are long and quivering tips. ||17||
With the creepers of the wish-fulfilling tree— those fresh sprouts of youth that are delightful yet devoid of reflection upon the stages of transformation bound by passion—
the groves of the Golden Mountain [are filled].
It shone like a street frequented by the city's foremost women.
Where, even with its doors closed, it possesses a splendor such that at night they appear as if their openings were wide open from afar, being fashioned with spokes of lapis lazuli.
The rows of jeweled mansions reach toward the sky in every direction. ||19||
In which city, even though the moon-crested Lord Śiva dwells ever-present, the God of Love resides within the bodies of the city’s matrons,
having cast off all fear and mounted the arrows of their sidelong glances.
Having performed self-protection with a thousand earth-arrows. ||20||
In the pleasure-lotus-pools, they do not grow poor; rather, being suffused with the brilliance of dense masses of moonbeams,
they bear a luster like the ivory tusks of the elephant of Love.
In which [city] the blue lotuses corresponded to the lilies during the nights. ||21||
Where, for a moment, the rays from the bodies of the horses on the poles of the sun’s chariot— hanging not far from the ruby archway—
make it appear as if fashioned from green sprouts.
It shines as if not empty because of the garlands of salutations. ||22||
In which [city], by the weight of the overflowing cascade of the nectar-poison of the beauty and splendor of the moon-like faces of young women—
[a stream] whose broad basin is the circle of the watchtowers and palaces— ...
It mimics the playful sport [of the sun] as it kisses the orb of the sun. ||23||
The deer-eyed women captivate the heart with their forms, beautiful like the crescent moon whose parts are fully revealed,
wherein there unfolds a sweet, charming, and clever coquetry.
They are the smiles of the palace of the Flower-Armed God (Kāmadeva), which cling to all beings. ||24||
In whose dwelling-lotuses the interiors were suffused with the luster of ruby stair-treads,
and where the lotuses of slow radiance shone with beauty for their beloved.
Like clusters of lotuses whose moonbeams have been captured as prisoners. ||25||
In that city, the peaks of the divine temples, inlaid with fragments of rubies,
shine forth as they embrace the clouds split apart by the very tips of their summits, with the pale-red luster of those gems.
Like flashes of lightning, they appeared as golden flagstaffs. ||26||
At the dead of night, he goes to his beloved’s house,
holding in his lotus-like hand a blooming lotus taken for sport,
while the impetuous darkness of the evening provides him with cover.
The world of women stood as if seeking a hand to hold. ||27||
With a sweet sound from the water-machines of the lotus-pools where they sported, possessing the beauty of the Kaiśika and Madhyama scales following their sequence,
with necks uplifted and wings fluttering as their feet remained still—
In which [city] it is heard by the flocks of swans dwelling in the palace-lakes.
Where, upon the banks of the palace lotus-pools, the long-enjoyed and ripening mango fruits— darkened by the radiance of the rays of emerald light—
captivate the heart.
Like flocks of swans [leaving] the tasteless masses of moss. ||29||
In which city, at night, the clusters of stars in every direction have their bellies licked by the rays from the palaces constructed of emeralds,
as if they were clinging to the tips of freshly sprouted, tender *kuśa* grass blades.
They embraced the beauty of a mass of dewdrops at night. ||30||
In that city, the moon, its luster eclipsed by the faces of women overflowing with loveliness,
bore a turbidness of heart as it was reflected in the jeweled pavements during the nights.
It seems to enter the depths of the netherworld under the guise of its physical form. ||31||
At dawn, the interiors of the houses shine forth, strewn with heaps of jewel-like flowers scattered upon their paved floors,
as they are struck by the impact of the rising rays of the sun.
Where the streets are as variegated as the constellations and the zodiac signs. ||32||
She shone as she stood, her posture fashioned with the care of an embrace,
her broad hips like spreading *sāla* trees,
her girdle-line like a blooming moat, as she turned about.
Wearing a girdle of rays from the jewels of the stars— (thus ends the description of the city)— he,
who had destroyed the circle of his enemies and assumed a constructed body out of a desire to favor the world, dwelt within that city.
Like a wheel-bearer, the Lord, whose crown is adorned with a digit of the cool-rayed moon, assumed the form of the King of Serpents, white as a palace. ||34||
He whose body, marked by the calluses from prostrating at the footstools of his lotus feet for the sake of the multitude of those who have sought refuge,
will become radiant with the splendor of the Rudra-form.
His forehead appeared as if its pupils were turned upward. ||35||
As the three cities were being scorched, the serpent, distressed by the fatigue of his loosened matted locks,
seemed to hiss forth wind with its flickering, upward-flaring flames as if to provide assistance.
The fire of whose arrows was suddenly kindled. ||36||

The submarine fire first arose from the hissing of the multitude of serpent hoods that served as the bowstring for the staff-like bow of Mount Mandara when it was whirled around; thereafter, the fire [of Śiva’s eye] blazed forth.
The arrow, matted with a mass of flames, [pierced] Tripura. ||37||
Upon his head, the Mandākinī shines forth, its mass of waves shattered by their collision with the crown and the skull-band;
from which the crescent moon is leaped upon by the fire of his upward-turned eye.
Possessing the beauty of a cascading torrent of cool, flowing nectar. ||38||
Seeing Gaṅgā, who— under the guise of the dark hue of manifest *kālakūṭa* poison— had her playful tresses seized by him out of the power of passion, was defiled by a continuous surge of jealousy;
Embraced as it were by the Yamunā, his neck shines forth. ||39||
He whose crown-jewel, pressed down by the serpent of his topknot, shines as it seeks to ascend to the sky out of a persistent resentment and anger toward the daughter of the Snowy Mountain.
Like the Gaṅgā rising from its source and heading toward the opposite bank. ||40||

By him, who formerly beheld the ancient skull-crowned [Śiva] laughing as he shook his head— [the head] of Pūṣan, who had sought refuge out of fear of being crushed, while the others remained as mere remnants— [that same Śiva was now seen].
The row of teeth, loosened from their bonds, was falling downward. ||41||
He whose slow-moving moon was effortlessly defeated in the beauty and splendor of the lotus-face of the Daughter of the Mountain King,
and who, like a captive, has his mass of matted hair loosened at its tip—
For a long time, Khaṇḍa was held in the hand by Bandhacyuta. ||42||

Even today, upon whose head the Goddess Śrī has taken up residence, there arises from the deep caverns of his belly— filled to the brim with the waters of the Mandākinī— a loud roar that remains unappeased.
Like the sound of the Vedas emerging from the skull of the Supreme Creator.
In the grand displays of his *tāṇḍava* dance at the onset of the night of cosmic dissolution,
the mountains, struck by the winds from his staff-like arms,
gradually recede before him as he performs his circumambulation.
The lords of mountains [have gathered] as if for the purpose of providing space for her divine play. ||44||
The foremost line of whose circle was formed by the impact of the tips of his ankles and feet as they rose with the impetuosity of his imitation,
while the sharp edges of the mountains were shattered and cast down.
The moon attains the splendor of a foot-ornament made of rubies.

Whose mountain ranges, tossed by the wind of his staff-like arms and loosened from their foundations upon the surface of the earth by the grace of his various movements, whirl even in the path of the sky.
As if terrified of falling into the underworld during their frantic dances. ||46||

Whose crown-light, as it shines upon his neck, seems to circumambulate it sportively— that neck which is darkened by the hue of the Kālakūṭa poison and possesses a body as black as the clouds of universal destruction.
Having approached the moon, the night took its beloved as its established dwelling place. ||47||
Upon his throbbing head, the crescent moon of his crest-jewel clings to the cavity of his ear that trembles like a wave of the Gaṅgā; meanwhile,
the tips of lotus stalks are held in his slightly opened beak.
He carries a white skull that bears the beauty of a swan. 48.
The serpent of his necklace seemed to imitate him as he closed his eyes in the meditative absorption of twilight,
while the mass of ash-powder smeared upon him from the ritual smearing was stirred up.
His timid eyes were narrowed by the weight of overwhelming fear. ||49||
In this heart of mine, which has been flooded by the nectar of love centered upon the Daughter of the Mountain King, there is no room for anyone else—
she who fixed her gaze upon his neck as if it were "excessive."
The flood of poison has its flames like those of the fire of the three worlds kindled.
Stationed in the middle of his flower-bow, which was turned to powder by the dust from the blossoms drawn back to his ear,
he was like the fire of wrath arising even before the transformation of the mind's prior state.
His passion became as if enveloped in flames. ||51||
When the bow was drawn by the Flower-Armed One (Kāmadeva), who had shattered his intense meditative absorption, [the Lord] frowned with a knitting of his brows;
and as he was being overwhelmed by the impetuosity born of that agitation—
The eyes of him who was filled with wrath became closed like buds. ||52||
He, whose fierce and distorted form was caused by the fury of burning the body of the flower-arrowed god (Kāma), was seen before them by the gods who were terrified;
he was one whose throat and belly were the abode of an unrestrained fire of his own "hum" sounds.
As if vomiting the Kālakūṭa poison under the guise of smoke. ||53||

When he became enraged and his meditative absorption was broken, the god of love took his stand upon the very corner of his eye, becoming fuel for the mass of flame-like sparks from his upward-glancing gaze.
[This is] the playful grace of the eyebrows of charming women. ||54||
The face of him who, assuming the illusory form of a Kirāta, was gazing with wrath upon Arjuna—
his complexion turning deep crimson by the fire of the eye blazing from his radiant forehead— was beheld by Arjuna.
As if by the power of the transformation of a mass of flames, [it arises] in an instant. ||55||

He whose eyes wandered excessively to behold the Daughter of the Mountain, who was adorned with the plumage of peacocks as ear-ornaments and whose breasts were embraced by garlands of *guñjā* berries; Please provide the full passage for translation. You have provided a fragment ending with "yasyekṣituṃ girisutāmadhikābhrāma-", which appears to be part of a longer verse. Once you provide the complete text, I will translate it for you.
She gazed intently at his form, which was like water hidden by fire. ||56||
The mind of him who had assumed the form of a Kirāta was deeply pierced by the daughter of the Mountain as she became a Śabarī woman,
with the beautiful peacock feathers adorning her ears—
By the casting of the shadows of their long, prominent eye-sockets. ||57||
As he held the Kirāta by the body, a multitude of sweat-drops suddenly formed upon his hand from the wrath of his crown, as if caused by the hidden heat of the [Kirāta’s] eyes.
Having wiped away [the sweat] from his forehead, which caused the quarters of the sky to appear as if dappled with spray. ||58||
He who, with his face slightly bent in playful grace, beheld the crescent moon of the crest-jewel resting upon the surface of the reflection on the side of his breast,
[He displayed] the grace of one who has leaped over the jar of nectar with his great waves—
by whom [the ocean] was made to bear his lotus-hand placed upon the surface of the breasts of the Daughter of the Mountain King.
His chest was as rugged as a rock from the Himalayas,
appearing like a lute with its gourd and strings during the graceful movements of his whirling dance.

He who, after a long time, casts off his handfuls of water at twilight, his slender body trembling with horripilation and covered in beads of perspiration, [and who beholds] the moon-like face of the Daughter of the Mountain situated upon half of his own body— [The rest of the verse follows: ...that very person, O King, attains the state of being a lord of the earth. || 10 || (Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly; the full verse describes the reward for one who performs the twilight ritual with such intense devotion that their body reacts physically.)
The splendor of his eyes was fixed in stillness by the bliss of beholding her form. ||61||
As if eager to examine whether or not there would be a seam between these two halves of a body joined together,
his eye seemed to move with impetuosity toward one side.
It issued forth from the forehead-plate of Nārīśvara.
Those whose eastern slopes were illuminated by the rays from the nails of the branches of his pair of feet— his gaze being not excessively wrathful—
and who possess white-lotuses with pale roots and reddish-pink petals, [attain liberation].
The flames of the fire, tawny like the crest of a peacock, bear the splendor of lotus petals.

Day after day, throngs of Siddhas, Sādhyas, and gods attended upon him— their faces resonant with hymns of praise, their jeweled earrings swaying, and their evening rites rendered fruitful by the worship of his steadfast feet.
Their radiant crowns are touched by the tips of their clearly visible palms.

Thus ends the first canto, titled "Description of the Enemy of Puras' City," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked with the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
The Second Canto:
Then, once upon a time, on a mountain peak, he [Śiva], out of a passion for play...
With the fingertips of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain resting upon him in playful sport,
he adorned the pleasure-pavilion of the Stone-abode, which was graced by the arrangement of fresh golden creepers. ||1||
There, having accepted the seat offered by him, he was skilled in discourse steeped in the sentiment favorable to the Daughter of the Mountain King; meanwhile,
the joints of his gem-studded belt were being rubbed and polished by their mutual friction.
The gods, adorned with golden armlets, approached him.
[She who has] a mass of matted hair like mossy tendrils,
whose great lotus-stalks are curved like the crescent moon on her crest,
[and who possesses] the sky-ocean with its skull-adornments as her swans—
Seeing him from afar, they gazed upon him as he wore a smile. ||3||
[The world] was emptied by the masses of sparks from the eyes of the peacock, which were struck by the wind from the hissing of the hooded serpents fashioned as ear-ornaments,
yet [the peacock] remained full of joy.
He who bears upon his head the celestial river beheld by Gaurī.
By the dull-rayed moon, having reached the crest of his head and become slender, as it was about to enter [the sky] with haste from nearby—
the orb of the sun on the surface of the navel of his radiant forehead—
He bore an upward gaze, as if about to swallow the very center of the sky.

"How is it that even a mere crescent of the moon-like face of the Daughter of the Mountain is not equal to the full moon? Alas, with my eyes upturned as if by a crest of fire arising from grief, I feel as though I am about to fall."
[It was] near the vicinity of the high forehead-plate, which had been occupied by [him]. ||6||
In some places, his head was rendered crimson by the sprinkling of blood dripping from the hide of an elephant,
appearing as if it were stained by the deep red hue of betel.
In a row, [he saw] the fragments of crowns and skull-bowls that had been stripped away.
Having placed upon his crown the moon— which acts as a beloved, bestowing a pure sky radiant with the luster of its moonlight—
he [Śiva] appears as if bearing a mass of thick *kālakūṭa* poison in the form of the moon's dark spot.
Bearing [the moon] clinging to her broad neck under the guise of a shadow. ||8||
She who swallowed the seven worlds at the time of universal dissolution,
who is dark blue like a cloud heavy with the weight of the ocean,
and in whose throat the yellowed smoke [of the funeral pyre] revolves—
And bearing a curved line of poison that possessed a shimmering luster. ||9||
The ocean whose circular waves are curved by the hoods of the lord of serpents, who wears necklaces shimmering with thousands of trembling, formidable jeweled conchs,
and whose throat holds the fierce and vast Kālakūṭa poison—
Carrying a tortoise-shell house formed by a mass of deceptive radiance.
White with ashes for body-unguent, his shoulders were crowded with the hoods of serpents whose color matched the plumage of cuckoos;
the waves of his [the ocean's] ripples were darkened by the smoke of the submarine fire.
Resorting to a splendor resembling a garland of milk-ocean waves.
With the fresh smearing of ashes rising from his forehead— struck by the breaths of the serpents upon his armlets—
the orb of the moon whirls above like a whirling wheel.
It shone brilliantly, having attained a state of perfect correspondence.
His chest, as broad as a slab from the snowy mountain, bears a necklace of serpents darkened by the radiance issuing from the *kālakūṭa* poison residing within the depths of his deep throat.
...bearing [it] like a garland of blue lotuses hanging down. ||13||
To the daughter of the Snowy Mountain, whose body was beautiful with a complexion as tawny as the fracture of lovely gold resting upon his lap,
[he gave] the Kālakūṭa poison, blackened by collyrium—
Once again, she was surrounded on all sides by the radiance from her throat, which made her appear dark.
Fanned repeatedly, resting upon the pillow of his hump with his two long, upraised arms doubled over it,
he was [awakened] by the breezes from the tips of the chowries of his tail.
As if with a mountain possessing a mind full of devotion, [he approached] from afar. ||15||
Your pair of feet is rendered fragrant by the *pārijāta* flowers from the ear-ornaments of the lords of the divine hosts who have come for service;
it bears the mark of the reflections of bees following the scent [of those flowers].
bearing a multitude of moon-like nails that were as white as the interior of a cloudless sky. ||16||
Of the one who possesses the form of an elephant-faced deity, whose shadow— the darkness of the poison in his throat— is dispelled by the luster of his teeth,
and who dwells in close proximity [to you], there is the radiance of the fire from his upward-gazing eyes, like thick Chinese pigment.
[He was] as if depositing clouds of dust upon his face.
(17) (A Kulaka) Having bowed to him, [the king], whose golden footstool resounded with the strikes from the tips of the peaks of the jeweled crests [of the prostrating gods],...
When Śailādi had bowed his head and presented them, they were comforted by taking their appropriate seats. ||18||

They struck [the instruments], delightful with specific tonal pitches, diverse melodic paths, varied movements, rhythmic beats, and hand-beats; their methods of instrumental performance were clearly manifest, accompanied by the *karaṇas*.
The drums were sounded in succession, clearly marked by their cleansing strokes. (19) [This is a pair of verses.
Here is an alternative reading:
Then the drums were struck, displaying a manifold variety of rhythmic patterns, diverse movements, and tempos through the distinct application of the hands.
The arrangements for sweeping, the application of yoga, the paths divided according to their functions, and the prescribed methods for playing the beloved musical instruments that captivate the mind.
While the *mujara* drums, struck mercilessly by the hands of Nandīśa,
resounded with deep tones, Taṇḍu divided [the performance] into the *āsārita* sections,
which are conceived as having seven varieties.
Then he sang the Tāṇḍava dance, which was perfectly beautiful.

O Mothers, who have embraced the Daughter of the Mountain, whose crowns perform praise for the one with the crescent moon upon his head, and who are the expansion of graceful gestures, the essence of divine play— Please provide the full passage you would like me to translate. You have provided only a fragment of the verse. Once I have the complete text, I will provide the translation.
They performed with graceful movements, their glances revealing the aesthetic flavors (rasas) and emotional states (bhāvas). ||21||
With bodies as fair as jasmine, yet possessing a complexion that was neither yellow, nor pale-red, nor white,
the lords of the Gaṇas wandered amidst the expressive gestures of graceful dancing.
They were like the aesthetic sentiments (rasas) incarnate, upon the well-adorned stage-platforms. ||22||
As the Enemy of the Cities himself rose up before them with the impetuosity of teaching the dance of uneven movements,
the surface of the earth became a hollow pit leading to the underworld.
It was strewn with fragments of the jewels from the hoods that had been crushed to pieces.
Having arisen, he threw the world into agitation—
a world where the swans had fled in terror at the clearly visible darkness—
as the playful Boar did when his crest of smoke-like matted hair was raised.
Moistened by a gloomy downpour of spray from the water of his quivering arms.
As his arms, white with the application of ashes,
streaked the sky with the whirling of his sword,
they were mistaken for a mass of bright clouds by those who were gathering together—
The peacocks fled, their bodies adorned with tails and crests. ||25||

Of that mountain, whose opposite slopes had their masses of darkness shattered by the radiance from the jewels on the hoods of the snakes coiled tightly upon its arms, and which served as the limit for the rays of the sun— his...
Instantly, the heaps of stones were shattered by the trees [hurled] from his arms. ||26||
As he laughed, his multitude of arms flung out in all directions, his head trembling through the sequence of his *aṅgahāra* movements,
the celestial river with its waters falling in front [of him] reached—
The splendor of a curtain shimmering with fine Chinese silk. ||27||
O Agni, let your flames indeed dance forth,
swiftly turning the peripheries of the quarters golden-yellow,
their movement bound to the rim of the sun’s orb.
With its rays, it dispelled the sun's parasol-canopy.
As if for the purpose of displaying a continuous series of various dramatic gestures being enacted before all directions,
his long arms were clearly extended and agitated.
He made the paths appear like heaps of ground peaks from the mountain ridges. ||29||
Of those two [arms], whose bodies were bent by the movements of their limbs, whose hands performed the dance, and whose high, fleshy arms were white with the ash of the fire of passion;
[like] a thousand masses of waves, terrible with whirling eddies and circles—
It bore the likeness of an ocean of milk mixed together. ||30||
When the thousand-petaled wheel of the golden mountain Meru— the seed-vessel of the expansive universe— twists in its dance,
the surface of the world-lotus becomes as red as a blooming *japā* flower.
With his hands, he acts as the leaf-sheath for this treasure-trove. ||31||
Formed upon his thick, rounded shoulders, it was as if it had approached to follow the shadows of the *kālakūṭa* poison on his neck;
by him, with the loosening of his crown-bindings through the shaking of his head—
She bore a loosened crescent moon. ||32||
Before him, who possessed upward-turning rays of vision and whose tawny luster had long since faded away, there appeared—
due to its continuous circling— a terrifyingly gaping [form] that was expanding.
With clusters of petals that are reddened fingers, [he is] adorned with fragments of lotus-hands.
The waves of the milk-ocean, tossed by the force of the wind from his tree-like arms smeared with white ash and dust,
spread for a moment through the sky as if they were clouds.
[They were] embraced by the celestial Gaṅgā, whose waves were exceedingly thin.
As if wishing to behold their kinsmen who had gone to the chambers of the netherworld (pātāla),
the serpents, with their circular hoods released from the binding of their jeweled joints, spread themselves out and performed [their dance] for him.
The oceans, whose waters were shattered by the wind of his breath.
By means of his outstretched arms, which formed a circle as they were cast about in a sequence of distinct *aṅgahāra* movements,
he bore the likeness of a world-destroying wind shaking the *kalpavṛkṣa* trees.
The moon-crested Lord [bestowed] a splendor resembling Mount Kailāsa. ||36||
By him, with the rows of bright ashes from his staff-like arms whose tips were swaying, it was as if he performed an even more intense dance,
out of the exertion of his desire to create his own future cosmic dance.
The laying of the foundation-line for the intermediate spaces between the yogis and the intermediate worlds. ||37||
The clear surface of his [mirror], marked by the tips of rays emitted from the ends of his fingers as he began to dance,
became like a polished slab inscribed with thousands of shimmering figures.
The sky was like the mark of a bud from the moon’s light when it is obscured. ||38||
The ocean of the perfected ones (siddhas) is agitated by the continuous churning of the hands of Uddāmara-recaka, filled with droplets like bubbles;
it is bound by the state of Kirāta, who has not abandoned Lakṣmī.
His matted hair shone like the slough of a lordly serpent. ||39||
Terrified by the falling tips of his claws— which were like the edges of a diamond that shatter the points of a lion’s skin tossing and rolling with the movement of his arms—
the elephants of the quarters quickly bent their knees.
He was distressed by the surfaces of his massive frontal globes as they became shriveled.
Suddenly, the skin of the king of lions, serving as the resting place for the severed fragments of his trunk-like arms which were agitated by the performance of various dance postures,
was torn away with claws by Tārā, who was fierce and tawny.
Desiring to perform a service for the moon, as if for a beloved wearing a crest-jewel. ||41||
The heat of the sun was obscured by the masses of dust rising from the peaks of mountains shattered by the wind of his staff-like arms—
dust that resembled the ash-powder smeared upon him as he performed the ritual smearing.
As if to wipe away the quarters of the sky from the surface of his reflection.
Like the sun of the Lord of Lakṣmī, whose rays are formed by the tips of the branches of his unrestrained staff-like feet, the hot-rayed one shone for a moment against the sky,
which was like a garment clinging to the water of sin.
The beauty of her lotus-seat and her other jewel water-pot. ||43||
As she traversed the sky in various new dramatic gestures,
her head— facing toward the path of the ocean and covering the expanse of the atmosphere on all sides of the circle of the quarters— [was like the moon].
His staff-like arms were like the flowing currents of rivers. ||44||
By him was beheld that which had been scattered by the impact of the fierce wind from his whirling staff-like arms,
fallen from the surface of the sky like a head severed from its body.
With the thought that it was a skull from which the crest-jewel had fallen away, [he mistook] the orb of the moon. ||45||
Upon the lotus-throne of Brahmā, which causes all the worlds to tremble,
the dust of the ashes from the rubbing of his outstretched arms resembles the cold season in its appearance.
The beauty of its petals was crushed by the falling of frost. ||46||

Like the night at the time of universal dissolution, it shrouded the circle of the quarters, variegated by stars reddened by twilight and by the circular array of jewels on the hoods of the serpents serving as necklaces.
The radiance from her throat, shimmering with a dark-blue luster like that of the night, [shines forth]. ||47||
Even the moonlight from his crest-jewel, having long found its dwelling place within the bower of matted locks upon his head,
reached out in every direction as it was struck by the wind from his hands raised for the commencement of his dance.
The joys of the embrace of Śambhu with his celestial consort Tārā.

From him, whose head was shaken in sport, there issued forth the essence of a fierce *tāṇḍava* dance from the tip of his matted locks, which was drenched with thick water dripping as it remained motionless while he was awake.
Like the Mandākinī river from the foot of Viṣṇu when he took up his staff. ||49||
At that moment, the mountains, distressed by the blows of his massive, staff-like arms, vomited forth what appeared to be their own blood—
mineral dust raised by the force of the winds from their upheaval.
The ripples and breaks of the mountain streams were reddened by the spray of falling dust. ||50||
By him were created [arrows] tawny with the glow of the jewels on the hoods of black serpents bound to his arms, forearms, and wrists—
[arrows] resembling columns of smoke rising with fury at the time of universal destruction.
The quarters of the sky were as if stained by the flames of a variegated fire. ||51||
As the gamblers’ wrists were targeted by his glances, which were not excessively fierce,
they were seen turning them about due to the distress caused by that heat.
With their bellies distended from drinking, they attained the splendor of molten gold. ||52||
Delighted by the sound of the anklets on his charming calves as they struck the tips of his lotus-like hands in joy,
and thrilled by the resonance of his breasts,
he began to perform the rhythmic movements of the *recaka* breath-control.
He, with his dark-blue throat and the beauty of distinct moon-spots, performed his divine play.
Bearing the grace of charming movements of her limbs with whirling navel-circles on all sides,
and possessing a delightful gait, that beloved woman, heart-stealing through her sentiments and emotional expressions, captivated the mind.
The form and action of the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva) are seen with auspicious hands. ||54||

Anticipating the extreme narrowness resulting from the twisting of his staff-like arms, they did not place themselves in front of the directions; instead, he strode about with his feet set down slowly.
"The circle of the earth is splitting asunder" because of his persistence in compassion. ||55||
The staff and the foot were not fashioned above the point where the shell of the cosmic egg was clearly bursting;
thus, the dance of the one adorned with the cool-rayed moon did not remain graceful due to the weakness of its support. (56) [A pair of waves]

The row of human skulls on his head, with their loud and piercing "jhāṃkāra" sounds from the waves of the celestial river that has entered his belly, seems to offer a continuous and intense cry of "well done! amidst his dancing movements. 57.
Glancing with a smile at the enemy of Smara, who had drawn away the crescent moon from the crest of the Snowy Mountain’s daughter,
he, whose banner bears the enemy of serpents, danced upon the stage of Vidūṣaka.
In front of him, he placed a crooked, elevated wooden staff.
These are those captivating techniques, such as the *talapuṣpapuṭa* and others, belonging to the leaders of the Gaṇas;
thus are the methods of the *aṅgahāra*, with their manifest elaboration—
Maintaining a posture graced by yoga, they were foremost among those with steady hands. ||59||
Thus, as he led him through the throngs of the assembly circles, performing this threefold transformation while they sat in the hall,
his eyelashes— providing the pleasure of a full gaze— remained unblinking.
A thousand eyes appeared upon the face of Indrāṇī, clearly visible. ||60||
Being torn asunder by the tips of the trunks raised in play by the elephant-faced [Ganesha], whose movements manifest a mimicry of the playful agitation [of the clouds],
the water-bearing clouds release a multitude of cool droplets of spray.
They offered him the sequence born of dramatic representation, which flows forth with continuous grace. ||61||
Having thus performed a dance characterized by graceful movements and the clear manifestation of the functions of the dramatic sentiments (*bhāva-rasa*), the Lord,
together with his attendants, returned as he had been addressed by Aṅga.
His fatigue was dispelled by the accumulation of droplets from the waves of the Gaṅgā. ||62||
The mountain Mandara, struck by the harsh hooves of the aged bull being dragged by Śiva— who had conquered the hosts of the Mountain-Daughter’s father—
had its moon-like crest-jewel seized and cast aside.
Once, Khaṇḍa became distracted by the allure of the gambling table. ||63||
Thus, performing various gestures there, he who was unacquainted with separation from the Daughter of the Mountain brought them to an agreement;
for the lords of the gods repeatedly [honored him] with jeweled footstools and silk bands.
He was being served by those whose golden crowns were shimmering with rolling jewels.

Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Description of the Tāṇḍava Dance," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—whose pen-name is Vāgīśvara and whose other name is Vidyādhipati, and who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
The Third Canto:
Then, on Mount Manthara, he [Śiva], together with all the seasons, through his own splendor radiant with their blossoms...
Once, the conqueror of his enemies, whose tree-like arms were sinless, served and took refuge with Girijā equally. ||1||

The world bore the fragrant beauty of the flowers of the hearts of proud women, which had been conquered by the swarm of honey; it possessed the splendor of blooming copper-red lotus groves, and was filled with a multitude of water-lilies that had been prevented from perishing.
Swiftly abandoning the direction frequented by Yama, as if out of a fresh longing, the sun took refuge in the quarter of Aiḍaviḍa,
establishing stability for those of good intellect among living beings.

The mountain valleys possess a beauty created by their union with the forest; they hold in their hands clusters of blossoms as sweet as honey and sprouts like mirrors, and they are radiant with tilaka trees and leafy creepers.
With their beauty enhanced by resting upon lotuses and moving with a languid gait due to contact with honey,
the bees and the days alike made the young women— who had descended into the power of the god of love— subject to another's will.

Constantly partaking of food of many flavors, her mind—well-established through the mastery of alchemy (rasāyana)—attained a state of ease like that of bees; having transcended worldly existence, she remained firm in her composure.
With their sweet voices like those of cuckoos, the spring glories slowly approached as if meeting their own kin;
thus, the fawns-eyed women were united with their beloveds, bestowing joy that was enchanting through its sweetness.

In the *campaka* flower, which possesses fragrance and is accompanied by bees, its luster enhanced by fresh honey, the bee—having taken up his station as if in a pleasure palace—experienced the state of wearing new, choice garments. (8)

The mountain forest grounds were in full bloom; there, the cuckoos—eager to peck at the lips of young women with their tender shoots—were believed by the bees to be lovers themselves, filled with passion as they were tormented by the god of love. 9.

Let the dark bees, intoxicated by drinking the sweet nectar-liquor of the Madhavī creeper in its state of sweet blossoming, disturb the women who are the very breath of the laughter of Love’s power. 10.
The cluster of *kurabaka* flowers, awakened by spring, possesses a formidable beauty due to its upward-pointing filaments;
yet this is a source of distress for women separated from their lovers, because it causes them anxiety even through its purity. 11.

"Having said that, O sweet-spoken one, bring him here quickly!"—at these words of their friend, the women, who were intent on the sentiment [of love], became eager for the arrival of their beloveds. (The Tilaka verse) In separation, the bees, possessing a luster like that of the seeds of a mature lotus, ventured forth to drink the honey;
while the women, having placed obstacles in every direction, were intent on the act of killing [their own lives].
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, though sometimes abandoned by coolness and possessed of fresh childishness,
the lotus-pools became exceedingly steady and full of passion for their lovers, even among those who were otherwise tranquil.
In the springtime, the lotus pond, with its bees hovering eagerly over the gently swaying red lotuses,
possessed a splendor even more vividly radiant than that of the goddess of the ocean.
With the hollows of its wings greyed by the mass of dust-particles shaken up by its final steps,
the swarm of bees, its heart full of joy, settled upon the lotus-beds along the mountain slopes amidst a humming sound.

Even when the dust of pride had been instantly swept away by the Malaya breeze, those fawn-eyed women, longing for the vehicle of sexual union, became enraged with their lovers due to the intensity of their passion. 17.

With her hands like copper-colored, trembling leaves, the creeper—bending and swaying as she plucked a fruit from the tree—shone as if to offer a lotus with bees hovering over it in the honey, like a flower-bud. 18.

In the springtime, amidst hundreds of banners of blossoming filaments that spread wide upon the grounds of lotuses— banners manifesting the destruction of pride— the frown of the high-minded women fell away like a swarm of bees.
When the moon, the bearer of cool light, arrived after a long time having caused an obstacle to the union with the beauty of day,
even the turbidity on her face was not bestowed by the night, which had been deprived of its splendor through contact with spring.

Having alighted with impetuosity upon the breast of the lotus— which possessed the luster of a bedspread— and remaining silent there together with his kinsmen, the bees, pungent from drinking honey, settled as if on a couch.
At the time of dalliance, the young wife captivated her husband’s mind intensely with her playful coquetry;
she surpassed the shimmering blue water-lilies with her tremulous eyes and was adorned with a series of bracelets. 22.
Bearing breasts like those of Surabhi, she bowed down equally to the feet of the friend of Smara,
her beauty enhanced by the ornaments on every limb shimmering as they rested upon the region of her hair.

The noble Navamālinī trees, possessing unassailable banks, acted as auxiliary causes for the God of Love— who was increasing his own power to bring about the destruction of travelers— by accompanying him on the ninth day of the month of Madhava.
When the breeze, fragrant and enveloped by clouds of collyrium-stained pollen as if armored by the forces of Love, began to blow, who were not overcome by the passion of amorous play? 25.
Captivated by the golden powder of the fragrant beauty of the blossoming lotus petals,
they rejoiced as the fatigue from their bodies being shaken by their wives— who were sighing with the joy of their embrace— was dispelled.

Beholding the pair of bees entering the lotus without restraint—like a couple entering Śivapura, which possesses the beautiful splendor of moss—alas, what young women did not attain union with their beloveds? 28.

The *atimuktaka* creepers, radiant with ornaments of manifest leafy tendrils as beautiful as bees and collyrium drops, did not attain the splendor of fragrance, for their beauty lay in the excellence of their pervasive union. ||29||
The sun, as if enamored, did not pluck with the tips of its rays the lotus-bud breast of the day-lotus, whose nipple was a bee clinging to its face. (30)
In the coral-like expanse of the forest-ocean formed by the spray from the ichor of the elephant of Love,
a swarm of bees appeared, possessing the beauty of flickering flames upon a palāśa tree.

In the springtime, those whose minds were restless with passion fell swiftly and helplessly under the power of the *navamālikā* jasmine—whose playful glances were cast from unblinking eyes and who was fragrant like a celestial nymph—upon beholding it. (32)

With golden earrings, shimmering with jewels, set against his well-polished cheeks, the intoxicated man indeed experienced in spring the playful grace of unevenly swaying [his head], O timid one. (33)

Beholding that blooming aśoka tree, which— tawny like fire— kindled the god of love in her upward-turned eyes just as the enemy of the cities (Śiva) kindles his upward-flaming eye tawny with fire, the bride was not at all eager for her lover.

The lotus-faced beauty of the woman held the hearts of the multitude of men with her thick nectar, like a lotus-pond possessing a shimmering swarm of bees with dust-free wings and a charming tilaka-mark. ||35||
Thus Spring made the days of the bright fortnight cool with bathing, laden with the paste of fresh sandalwood,
and adorned with jasmine flowers— like beloved female friends whose breasts are slightly weary from the intensity of new vows. ||36||
When the sun touched the quarters with its rays,
the beautiful splendor of day remained for a long time like a beloved woman, her heat having increased as she stood firm in the embrace of intense indignation.
Anointed with the moist paste of fresh sandalwood and bearing a body drenched in water, she—
though separated from her beloved— maintained the state of a woman in exile through a most excellent discourse consisting of words that were exceedingly long.

As the Lord of Day was scorching the earth, the people were overcome with exhaustion, harboring the delusion: "What is this brilliance that is trickling down, struck by the violent blows from his rugged horns? (39)
The circle of mountain forests, illuminated by the lamp of love, assumed a far greater splendor through Rucirā;
for there, Mallikā took her stand during the rainy season, and the birds did not fail to frequent the thick clouds.

The wind, spreading with the fragrance of fresh and charming [flowers] and possessing the power to burst open the caskets of the clusters of trumpet-flowers (pāṭalā) filled with swarms of bees, clearly bore that scent. ||4||
"Desiring to rival this very delicate Śirīṣa flower, she looked at it as if wishing to conquer it;
yet, as if with great anger, that flower bestowed upon her—a woman separated from her lover—a grief characterized by fresh laughter and petals. [Thus ends the description of Summer.
Where the rows of clouds, slow-moving like elephants, bear the luster of the throat of the Lord of Mountains (Śiva).
That season, which consists of the essence of passion and causes the trembling of the wives of travelers, was unfolding. ||43||

The torrent of clouds over the earth quenched with its waters the long-accumulated stain of pride even in the mind of a woman; how much more so, then, the dust raised by the powerful thundering of the drums?

The fragrant breezes, laden with the world-conquering ashes from their own bodies and with particles of the pollen from *kuṭaja* filaments, brought about the blossoming of amorous passion in the hearts of women. (45)
Assuming a splendor marked by the crescent of the new moon, which imitated the body of the enemy of Smara (Śiva),
he stood with his arms like serpents, as the Lord, addicted to the great Tandava dance at that time, remained amidst the thundering sounds.
With the brilliance of their manifest forms and bodies, the forest grounds,
where swarms of bees were wheeling about to swallow the showers of falling drops of nectar, assumed the beauty of the path leading through the interior of the woods.

The beautiful radiance of the solitary golden vine situated on the rugged mountain peak was instantly eclipsed by the lightning flashing from the water-laden clouds, as she was repeatedly gazed upon by the assembly of high-minded women who had bowed down before her.

By means of breezes— like sighs from the fatigue of drawing his own bow— Smṛtibhū brought about a *tāṇḍava* dance of the throbbing horripilation upon the foreheads of the deer-eyed women near their beloveds.

Who indeed among your tributary kings have not been brought under your sway by this mass of clouds—which rivals the bow of Indra, displays the splendor of a fourfold army, and possesses formidable mountains? (50)

At the time of the lightning flashes, when the clouds thundered and the dust of the earth was incessantly swept away, the people gazed upon the ground covered with centipedes, like a cow-pen where the plowmen have bent down their plows.
In the sky, bright with the moon and ketaka petals, the blossoming mass of *kuṭaja* flowers acts as a multitude of stars white as frost, eclipsing the splendor of the moon. (52)
"Scatter the water, flash the lightnings, thunder in the sky, and obscure the horizons!"—
thus the cloud acted toward his wife, who was not yet pacified and remained averse to peace.

Wandering through the trees with its sounds at the opportune moment, the cloud—though soiled by dust—seemed to proclaim to the young men that even one who is impure can be helpful in certain circumstances;
for it stood there, concealing the city women who were terrified by its thundering.

Even the charming *kadamba* flower, resplendent with its two sets of nine petals like an ornament for the glory of arriving wealth, and abiding upon the ears of women, became the abode of arrows humming with the sound of love. 55.

The lightning, appearing with its streaks now sparse and now dense, became like those women in this world whom Samavartin (Yama) had not seen while they were still powerful in the thickest darkness, but who have since been withered by separation.

The forest ranges, variegated by *urvaka*, *sadgiri*, and *mallikā* flowers, and possessing the exquisite beauty of clearly blossoming *kandala* buds, shone like lotus-pools in every direction, swarming with bees. (57)

The sea breeze, bearing the fragrance of the *kuṭaja*, *kandala*, *nīpa*, and *śilīndhra* flowers, caused the young women—whose passion had departed—to be neither truly brides nor non-brides, as they were cast out by the spreading dust of their anger. 58.
In the absence of Smṛtibhū, the young women struck [the trees] with the mallets of fresh *mālatī* buds;
clearly, the bees—intoxicated by honey and humming with longing—were rendered unconscious by that final blow.

With buds appearing like the tips of Hari’s teeth, as the sky stood filled with the fading of the *mānatama* (the pride of women), what desired object indeed did that creeper-like arm not bring to its beloved? [Thus ends the description of the rains.
With the beauty of dense clouds shimmering most charmingly, and with a lovely attire that delights the heart—
Resorting to the autumn as if to a beloved wife, the people experienced pure joy and practiced the complete destruction of their impurities.
Like horses prone to swift movement yet burdened by fatigue, the days, with their necks (the sun) lowered,
bore the splendor of the autumn season, which possessed hands as tender as the buds of lotuses.
"This spear is now falling upon me; it no longer yearns to bask in the heat of the sun"—thinking thus for a long time, the noble lotus, filled with joy, seemed to attain full bloom. (63)

When the night of the rainy season had passed, a beautiful radiance was nowhere to be found by the peacocks, who were rendered lusterless by the rays of the exceedingly clear and pure moon shining forth.
Like the sky filled by the waters of rain-clouds through a continuous succession of pouring,
the moon, being free from blemish, bore a complete splendor together with its fullness.

In autumn, the clouds— pale as if from the distinct state of their existence being overturned by the destruction of the world's heat— surely laughed a great, incomparable laugh with the groves of their feathers of rays.

The rays of the moon—cool as waterless ice and residing in great lakes, removing the distress of the people—destroyed the confinement of the honey-drinking bees dwelling within the beds of night-lotuses. 67.
The mass of winds from the forest, joyfully bringing the pollen of lotuses, was unable to conceal the glances of separated lovers that were turned away in aversion, despite its intense praise.
The banks of the lovely river, with their water trickling after being struck by the feet of birds, were obscured by a dense mass of clouds,
as if by the bare and beautiful hips of women marked with nail-scratches.
In the forest, where the bees established their dwellings amidst the blossoms of the spring season,
there was no languor whatsoever among those radiant drinkers of honey who had taken up their fresh state.

Indeed, the powerful heat produced by the multitude of arrows—which bore the splendor of a drawn bow and whose name was not in vain—did not merely cause the burning of the hearts of women separated from their lovers; it brought about their very destruction. ||71||

And her stability was attained through the action of the aesthetic essence (rasa), as if by the splendor of autumn— whose stars were clearly purified by the arrival [of the season], which dispelled the darkness of the moon's light, and in which the lotuses blossomed.

The entire circle of the earth was, for a long time as it were, filled with the deep and sweet sound of ripening rice, which resembled the victorious war-cry of arrows whistling through the gentle force of the spreading breeze.

In autumn, after a very long time, the opportunity arose for the female swan to bathe in the newly formed lake— its waters unclouded and pure— with the desire to sport, now that her mate had provided her with lotus stalks.

Resounding with the cries of swans intoxicated by the water, that season—possessing a splendor like the moon at its peak—was exceedingly enchanting, like the path to a palace, and bore the lofty beauty of a pleasure garden. 75.
A creeper, having reached old age, loudly caused her young son, the bee, who was rolling about on her lap, to drink from her cluster of blossoms— which emitted an indistinct humming sound—
just as a woman whose youth has passed causes her son to drink from her breast, which flows with her own milk.
The lake, filled with the cries of cranes leaping with impetuous joy toward their mates, and possessing the beauty of its lotus filaments,
bestowed upon the impassioned women a state of intense aesthetic rapture.

With its clear rhythmic beat and tempo, the song of the female cowherds— sweetly sung by the parrots and elephants and heard by the herds of deer— captivated the minds of those who were eager to devour the abundant, succulent crops.

On the paths through the mountain forests, which are thick with clusters of *karīra* shoots, the wind—laden with the fragrance of even-numbered petals—counteracts the pride of the elephant by agitating the bees that have spread over his temples. [Thus ends the description of Autumn.
In the winter season, the lotus pond bears the beauty of the lotus-faced one, possessing delightful pericarps that have assumed the splendor of her face.
It bore a state of being purified and freed from blemish by the disturbances caused by the reddish hue of frost-dust. ||80||
From fear of being overwhelmed by intense cold, the garden tree shone as if embraced by a clever, trembling creeper shaken by the snowy wind.

As the wind blew, thick with droplets of frost, the young woman—her graceful gasps of "sīt" uttered for her lover—turned toward him, trembling and waving her quivering palms in her longing for union. [Thus ends the description of Hemanta.
Even the season itself becomes a virtue when it serves the beloved woman’s desire for an embrace.
The weight of the heat from her pair of breasts caused the moon, the lord of night, to lose his coolness at the onset of winter.
The peerless young *rodhra* tree sprinkled the faces of all directions with dense clusters of pollen from blossoming flowers, as if with thick masses of autumn clouds. (84)
The bee abandoned its departure from the lotus-pond, submerged as it was in golden pollen that veiled the quarters of the sky;
for what person, even if stained by sin, would suddenly forsake a benefactor when in distress? (85)

Seeing that the other flowers had withered and the kunda flower had risen up in dejection, the humming bee, darkened by its swarm of black companions, spoke as if laughing: "I am the kunda in asceticism. (86)

Though their necks were pressed against the throats of their lovers, the women— struck by the cool breezes from the fresh *lavaṅga* trees and longing for the winter season— panted with their lower lips and hips, which were marked by the impressions of their girdles.
Shaken by the cool breezes together with the hearts of women separated from their lovers,
the flowering branches of the *phalinī* trees shone like bees seeking the sweet nectar of honey.

Unperturbed by the disturbances caused by the countless other blossoms, the bee took delight in a fresh sprig of clove—a manifest fragrance that was the fruit of great asceticism—within the mountain thicket. (89)

The goddess Rati bestowed her grace upon the fair-eyed women, for it was considered that a moment’s respite would render them capable of the festival of love, as their chests were firmly pressed by their lovers’ bosoms, which held the orb of the breasts heavy with perspiration. 90.
When the thorn of memory is driven into the heart, it takes firm root even more deeply than in a khadira tree;
for what woman in this world, separated from her lover, did not feel that very same pain? 91.

The vine-like bodies of the deer-eyed women, together with their beloveds, attained the beauty of *tāla* trees; likewise, the female bees, having drunk the honey, possessed the great essence of the *rasa* (sap) of the *lava-lī-latā* (creepers). 92.
"What anger can there possibly be toward a beloved? You have gone to Māli, whose nature is like the peak of the fresh Mandara mountain; once he has returned, that woman shall be brought to grace."
Thus she embraced the slope of the fresh Mandara mountain. ||93||
To behold the mountain bearing Lakṣmī through the seasons, with its pure saffron-colored filaments blooming upon the radiant jeweled ground,
the Lord went forth gracefully to the shore of the agitated sea.
Slightly visible and tinged with passion upon the tresses of the Daughter of the Mountain.

Thus ends the third canto, titled "Description of the Seasons," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara— who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
The Fourth Canto.
Having emerged [from the city], he reached a bower of celestial wish-fulfilling creepers within an inner garden, fit for the enjoyment of the pleasure of the women of the sky-dwellers,
its slopes adorned with clusters of radiant jewels.
He gazed upon that place where the chariot of the sun had come to rest.
He who has crushed the entire ocean with his base, whose splendor is jagged with the mass of rays from the clusters of shimmering, clear stars,
and who has struck down the maker of frost (the moon).
And by its peak, elevated with delight, the path to heaven was reached. ||2||
When the host of gods and demons had suddenly placed the back of the door-panel upon the ocean for the purpose of churning it,
the Lord of Tortoises called to mind the foot of the Primordial Boar.
It was surely made into a seat for that exceedingly great burden. ||3||
By him, whose encircling flames— whose fuel was the waters of the ocean as it underwent incessant revolutions and transformations—
sustained the path of the sky, which is otherwise without support, within the milk-ocean.
It possesses the quality of imitating a dissolving halo around the sun. ||4||
Having established her seat upon the back of a tortoise, with her cheeks and face washed by the warm water of perspiration flowing from her melting sweat-glands,
she appears agitated as if displaying the playful movements of a man in the role of a woman.
Her form captivated the heart with the swaying of her hips. ||5||
Whose [height] was so great that, fearing the crushing pressure of the churning as if it were falling upon him, the ocean simultaneously with its waters deeply raised its neck,
while the uneven gasping of the tortoise was cast aside—
The waves of the mountain torrents flowed backward.
Because the ocean was encircled by the sloughs of the lord of serpents as they slipped from his coils due to the force of being dragged,
it appeared as if [the ocean] were quickly seeking to alleviate the pain of the churning.
Mandākinī long encircled the soles of his feet.
Suddenly turning his gaze toward the broad middle region of the earth, he was seen from afar by the circles of sky-dwellers as he whirled playfully like the circular Milky Ocean.
The moon, with its cooling orb as its body and the deer as its crest-ornament.
By her form, which bore the agitation of turning her hips with the graceful movement of shifting her eyes and glances,
she [caused] a dense mass of incessant waves to arise swiftly.
He churned my agitated heart like the ocean. ||9||
By whose waves, during the manifestation of the churning,
the Ocean of Milk— having cast aside the Kaustubha gem—
deposited [the jewels] as a trust for the gods and demons to be seized by force.
As if out of fear, the masses of jewels have taken refuge in every house.
The waters of the pure Sindhu river, encircled by swans and bound by lotuses with formidable petals crowded with bees;
where the Siddhas have occupied the jeweled caves for intense *rāsa* dances.
It was as beautiful as a dense cloud, yet as fierce as a lion in its fury. (The blending of vernaculars:
He beheld upon the broad back of the tortoise-shell door-panel a circle of reflections formed by the breaking of the waves.

The world of the gods and demons, as if dividing their lofty bodies into many parts, wandered about for the sake of churning the ocean. (A pair of verses) In which [ocean], the world was afflicted by the distress of constant whirling and tossing as it revolved.

The lusterlessness of the hoods of the serpent king, whose darkness in the depths of the netherworld had been dispelled, was suddenly overtaken by fragments of jewels extracted from the claws of the sovereign tortoise.

Whose gaping mouth, with its tongue made terrifying by the lightning of thousands of clouds opening and closing like a mass of clouds at the dissolution of the world, and which was moistened by the waters of the shore during the churning of the ocean—
by that serpent [was he swallowed].
From exhaustion, the winds from the openings of the mountain caves ceased to blow.
Whose banks shine with dark-hued rocky cliffs that steal away the splendor of the sun with their own luster,
as if they were the Kālakūṭa poison produced during the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
Like lumps of food scattered by the tossing of violent waves. ||15||
But the water-bearing clouds, having entered the multitude of caves and mountain clefts,
[pour forth] droplets of nectar risen from the ocean of milk into the clearly visible leaf-cup basins.
They displayed their playful grace as they set foot upon the valleys of the Yadu land.
In whose mountain ranges the grounds of pure sapphire jewels create the illusion of the ocean being churned,
as its peaks, swaying in their rotation, tear apart [the clouds].
It resembled fragments of the path of the stars fallen and shattered.

He washed away with the trickling water from the mountain springs that [dust] which had been swallowed by the falling glances of the terrified earth-dwellers, who were thrown about in great agitation as they were seized by his fangs.
The primordial boar [took] upon his body the mud-stained mire of the netherworld.
The center of that [mountain], obstructed by the moon, shines as if reflected in the thick bracelets of sapphire,
like the back of the Lord Tortoise resting upon the waters of the Milky Ocean.
The orb of the moon was rendered powerless by his foot being planted upon it. ||19||

Seeing the jewels upon the slopes of whose ridges— jewels that scatter their mass of light across the quarters of the sky, thereby piercing the thicket of darkness— the mind of the moon becomes utterly infatuated during the nights.
The external [perception] alone quickly causes the vision to shift. ||20||
He who, as if sowing [seeds], appears like the moon— exhausted by wandering through the empty sky— seated upon his chariot on the mountain slopes,
with the wind from the deep caverns and chasms following him from afar.
With palm-leaf fans in the form of clouds whirling as they were cast down. ||21||
The orb of the moon, for a moment resting upon the slopes of the swaying, formidable kuruvinda-stones,
attained a likeness that was accepted as true by its own radiance.
Having established themselves upon the ridges that were shimmering with heat. ||22||

With its clearly visible and lovely growth of *kuśa* grass, its splendor established as the dwelling place of sages, and its mountain ridges standing firm, it was like the daughter of King Janaka— resplendent, with her auspicious signs manifest, her beauty delightful, and her lineage unimpeded.
He attains splendor through the state of being like a fresh *daṅkolla* leaf. ||23||
At night,

by the clusters of flowers bending down and exhaling fragrance— their own forms inferred from the abundance of scent that was difficult to perceive due to the halo of white planets clinging to them— [the garden appeared].
In whose fortress the silver creepers shine. ||24||
Upon whose ridges, as it plays upon the rugged jeweled rocks, the sun— possessing a pole like a chariot-shaft— fills the quarters of space with the piercing sound of its wheels.
Truly, the Vālakhilyas have rendered your words futile. ||25||
The lake, whose banks were lined with stairs formed by masses of dark stones resembling the bodies of nearby serpents, was filled with herds of elephants bending down toward the lotuses;
it was like a fresh, dark-blue māla-creeper that had climbed up from heaven.
Having bound [the mountain] whose ridges and groves are dense with darkness— (an immersion in the language of the Piśācas)—
[he beheld] the mountain-peak of stones, its vast and formidable summits bursting open by the fire blown forth from the multitude of hoods of the coiled Vāsuki.
The moon-crested Lord, having taken up that bow capable of bearing his own weight, it is said,
shattered the cities of the Dānavas.
(A pair of verses) In former times, the Supreme Lord [used] it to destroy the cities of the Asuras.
With his body serving as a bow,
he spreads his splendor even today, appearing as if beautiful with the binding of a bowstring formed by the long coils of the lord of serpents, from which the water of mountain torrents flows.
Like the string of his bow, curved and beautiful with the binding of the bowstring, the water of the cascading waterfall flowed down from the half-moon crest-adornment upon his head.
Of him whose arrow was the Lord of Serpents, who held the hand of the Daughter of the Mountain— whose ear was adorned by the crescent moon— as his fist rested upon her lotus-face,
the dense mass [of the enemy] was struck down by that very cord.
Its surface was covered by rows of conch shells that extended like a floor-covering. ||29||

Even though she was terrified by the hissing of the lord of serpents, whose hoods were fainting from the intense pressure as he coiled tightly around the body of her husband standing upon his half-form,
the daughter of the mountain did not loosen her grip on him with her fists.
What indeed will one whose heart is colored by devotion not accomplish? ||30||
Heated by thousands of flames from the fire, harsh with the fury expanding at the time of universal dissolution,
he shines as if extinguishing the slopes of the mountain ridges.
He who even today [is refreshed] by the winds issuing from the mouths of mountain caves. ||31||
Whose regions possess a delightful quality, with the luster of teeth clearly visible, the beauty of broad mountain-like cheeks, and extremely formidable, lofty bamboo thickets.
And the leaders of the elephant herds, dwelling in the thickets of the Sañjā forest, were also present.

Whose lofty peak, ever increasing in height, could not be surpassed even by the daily rising [of the sun], though it was being drawn upward by the exerted rays of Aruṇa; [The remainder of the verse: ...being pulled up by the upward-stretched hands of Aruṇa, [the mountain] appeared as if it were being weighed on a scale by the Creator. (Note: The provided fragment appears to be the first half of a verse from Māgha’s *Śiśupālavadha*, describing Mount Meru.)
The sun-god Vivasvat arrived with his chariot drawn by horses whose mouths were adorned with shimmering bits. ||33||
Upon whom even today the circles of clouds, dark as swarms of bees wandering profusely under the weight of unrestrained water, shine forth—
[those clouds that were the fuel] for the fire of the ten-fold destruction of the world-cycle.
The openings of the mountain caves and dwellings appeared as if filled with smoke. ||34||
Upon its pure lap, which is filled with the clamor of the playful sport of swaying, sweet-voiced birds, and whose thickets of nests are agitated by their cries;
and where there are *kakkola*, *kanda*, plantain, *lavalī*, and clove trees—
On the banks and marshes, charming with garlands of *lalamaja* flowers— (this is the convergence of six languages)—
wherein the elephant-like dark and lofty *gaṇḍaśaila* rocks sportively brandish their terrifying trunks out of indignation.

[This is] the crest of the tree of day, which reaches to the clouds, possessing a peak of intense ruby [red], [and] having a circular basin for the solar orb [filled with] the breaking of fresh sprouts of crimson sunlight. (A yugma.
[He who... the sky-scraping peak of intense rubies...
It bears a stalk that is the blue cloud-lotus of the sky, with petals of dark clouds, a filament of golden lightning, and a pericarp made rosy by the mass of the sun's protective radiance. (37)
The beauty of women was surpassed by her breasts,
which were adorned with jewels, possessed nipples as large as radiant pearls, and whose middles were made beautiful by three folds that were as praiseworthy as the faces of the three-faced god.
And the virtuous dwelling of the sages within the mountain ranges. ||38||
For those gazing at the western quarter, the mark of the moon's orb, being enveloped by its spotless purity,
attains the state of a deer resting upon its lap.
For those who have made their dwelling upon his lofty peaks. ||39||
He who bears one whose mind is captivated by the clusters of filaments arranged within the petals of the true lotuses of unsurpassed longing,
as if with blue lotuses worn as a crest-ornament.
She was like Lakṣmī with her hips encircled by girdles resembling wheels of Palāśa flowers. ||40||
The orb of the cool-rayed moon, having reached the vicinity of that mountain at night,
assumed the beauty of lotus petals through the spreading streaks of its dark stone-like rays upon the jeweled slopes; thus, the forest lands were graced by the luster of the crest-moon.
The matted locks of Śiva are heavy with bees, while the shadows of the groves of lotuses have vanished due to their contraction. ||41||

Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Description of Mount Mandara," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who is known by the pen-name Vāgīśvarāṅka and also by the name Vidyādhipati—and who is a dependent of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
The Fifth Canto:
Then, with eyes wide with joy, gazing respectfully upon the Lord of Mountains...
With a mind filled with wonder, Śailādi addressed the Moon-crested Lord in this manner: ||1||

This mountain, whose beauty was weighed against the essence of the lake of Lake Mānasa, which possessed the essence of golden-hued lotuses, and which contained the essence of tireless cranes, attained the highest excellence; thus it flowed forth with its waters. 2.
Behold, this mountain shines, adorned with a pavilion of golden creepers variegated by the crests of peacocks engaged in their dance;
it imitates the roar of clouds— its own thunder.
Resounding with the loud, tinkling sound of cascading waterfalls like cymbals. ||3||

Its ground is a fresh forest, yet it is not a forest that has attained a transient beauty; oh, how the bees, delighting in the rhythmic swaying of the graceful *tālī* trees, captivate the mind there where they cling to the creepers! 4.

Here, in this celestial realm, the Lord bears for his eyes the luster of a fresh lotus grove—a place possessing the beauty of crushed *nalada* grass and abounding in the fruit of the *atibala* plant. (This is an example of the *samapratilomānulomārdhapāda* meter.
Here, the frontal globes of the divine elephant are shaken by the wind blowing from the flapping of his ears.
The river of passion, red with pollen, carries a supreme splendor like the wall of a pleasure-chamber. ||11||
Having approached this forest, the bee steals away the darkness from my heart by virtue of its newly formed wings;
the sun is capable of dispelling it within the depths of the thickets.
Because its wings have been fully developed, the mind does not sink into the darkness.

Who would not take delight upon beholding this lord of mountains—its slopes shimmering with the girdle of the serpent king, its vast surface covered by the skins of elephants—as they behold you, the beloved of the worlds? 13.

Adorned with lovely ornaments of *tālī* and *atālī* trees, where birds are intent upon the essence and the non-essence [of their food], this mountain bears a slope frequented by intoxicated bees; it possesses the splendor of peaks joined with low-lying plateaus. (14)
From afar, he drinks the waters of this very waterfall, which are shattered by the tossing of boulders, whose circular ripples are filled with loud sounds that pervade the quarters of the sky,
and which flow without ceasing.
Like the sun distressed by the fatigue of the summer heat, [he scorched] with the tips of his rays.
The multitude of its branches, bent repeatedly by various fruits, possesses an exceedingly abundant splendor. ||16||

O son, the face of the fair-browed woman attains a beauty like that of a riverbank path—lovely with its prominent chin, possessing a radiant complexion darkened by *malikā* flowers, and featuring a clearly visible, pale-red lower lip of noble appearance. (17)
Whom does it not delight—

this ground of meditation, which possesses the beloved quality of purity and the enemy of impurity, appearing like a dense mass of clouds as dark as a blooming *tāpiñcha* flower in a mountain fastness?
And what wealth has not gone to the Tāpiñcha tree? ||18||

In this place, during the union with beloved men, the amorous gestures of women—whose soft lotus-hands mimic the gentle ploughshare—are radiant, possessing a beauty as charming as clearly trembling creepers. 19.

Behold, O Lord, this king of mountains, which is not crowded with elephants nor devoid of ascetics; it is not aged by the splendor of celestial palaces, but is adorned with groves of hibiscus and surrounded by forests of *kuñja* trees that purify. 20.
Thrown by the palm of a woman whose garment had been snatched away by her lover, its stalk crushed,
it was like a jeweled lamp with a blue lotus for a handle.
Here, the bee shines upon the tip of a fresh campaka flower.
Shining with splendor, she makes the people of Mānasa full of passion, bringing delight to the minds of the lovers;
here, the golden palm tree (hematālī) cries out with its upward-reaching playfulness, as if it were a gathering of birds through its graceful movement. 22.

Bearing the beauty of breasts facing their navels, with their girdles constantly hanging upon their well-rounded hips, and having dispelled the light of the moon, the women here shine like the rainy seasons. 23.
Those high ridges bear a circle of jewels;
let them be terrified by your female elephants,
for from their very wrinkles there falls before them a rain of nectar.
There, [the bees] were drawn from the clusters of flowers that were terrifying due to the ichor flowing from the temples of the elephants. ||24||
Fearing lest these children should suffer from fear while held upon his lap out of parental affection,
the Mountain bestows gems as protective threads, under the pretext of the canopy formed by their rays.

The livelihood of those who provide delight through lotuses does not depend on the multitude of bees; here, the musk of the celestial beings shines, belonging to those who have taken refuge in the abundant musk-patches of the deer.
Her courtyard ground is never still, its position crowded by the wheel of unbridled constellations that eclipses the sun; there,
amorous women are engaged in playful dalliance and amorous agitation.
It bears a splendor fashioned by the maker of the night, like the night itself. ||27||
Here, the guild of hunters— whose strength lies in shattering the frontal globes of elephants, who are devoted to their craft, and who possess a charming display of pearls—
shines forth among women in their elaborate seductions, appearing like the goddess Kālī, manifest in her undertakings and red with passion.
(Verse with inverted and regular feet:
