Here, by the swiftness of their glances and the shimmering play of their clearly white pupils, young women possess a beauty like that of lotus ponds, which are made lovely by bees and by the presence of the cakora birds within them. 29.
The herd of deer, having placed their trust here, bears a multitude of horns with minds free from fear, while the curved tails of the intoxicated bees—
due to the weight of the honey-nectar they have surely attained— assume a state of restlessness.
The bees were not at all agitated by the creepers. ||30||
In this world, those who are unable to endure trees that have descended from the path of their vision abandon them;
yet those standing above cause the trees to cast their circle of eyes wide upon the surface of the earth. 31.
This earth shines, its borders brightened by clusters of jewels from the ponds where many hosts of gods wander;
here she possesses the abundant splendor of the Sādhyas, who are worthy of being served and whose dust has been laid by the waters of their meditation. 32.
Spreading his delight upon the jeweled banks, where the rows of bees are like braided locks of hair fragrant with the scent of blooming flowers, he makes the multitude of women—
adorned with beautiful folds of skin— his city.
The "Climbing Tree" (vṛkṣādhirūḍhaka) attains supreme beauty. ||33||
In this place, the people, their passion for women newly dulled by the dust they carry away, do not bear the swarm of bees;
for this forest row has its nectar untouched, its fresh pollen not yet greyed.
Having encountered this dense battle, which is like a thicket of reeds and is strewn with hundreds of sharp arrows,
these throngs of monkey troops leap in every direction, intent upon devouring various shields.
With its peaks piercing the sky, it bears a likeness to the lotus-bed of the enemy of Mura; by means of the sweet whirling of its attraction, it draws the earth upward toward heaven,
and having approached this place, it offers worship with *pāṭala* and sandalwood.
He performed the drawing-in, the going-forth, the charming whirling, and the irreproachable [concluding] descent. ||36||
In this place, these women with arched brows— whose splendor is as bright as refined gold and whose cheeks are touched by golden palm leaves— do not fail to captivate the mind in every direction.
And they were joining together the ground of the slopes of the circles of pure jewels. ||37||
The planets above no longer remain far removed from him, having abandoned their distance due to his state of extinguished heat;
and ascetics, free from possessions and with their fever of passion extinguished, resort to the forested slopes of the celestial mountains.
In this [place], where peacocks are made to dance by the deep and shrill cries of circles of clouds sluggish from the heavy burden of water,
what small portion of similarity can there be with the ground far removed from the path of the chariot-rims?
The moon moves by means of its jewel-tipped finger of light. ||39||
Here, a radiant beauty unfolds, a playful lover who repeatedly performs the dance of passion for the fawn-eyed women;
O singer, let unsurpassed delight be fully produced!
And by Madhupa, they attained unsurpassed peace. ||40||
Pushed aside by the surfaces of her massive jeweled ramparts, this celestial maiden holds within the hollows of her gem-studded caves the mountains, which are devoid of any space to remain;
they stand there like those who have sought refuge in the very quarters of the sky.
Look, this mountain, beautiful with its green slopes, is being thoroughly drenched by the currents of the Mandākinī’s waters;
it is fully capable of enduring the arrival of autumn,
bearing upon its forested ridges the onset of the season.
Repeatedly bathed with the red hue of a lotus stalk, he [acted] with ease. ||42||

O Lord, this mountain slope bears your very own illusion—wonderful to the people and consisting of a multitude of Arjuna’s arrows joined together—which is made beautiful by the Kirātas who possess a splendor like that of wealth. 43.
Having attained this mountain, which through its loveliness becomes the abode of the first pangs of love for separated lovers, what passionate woman would not find delight in its beauty? (44)
From the mud of the elephant of the Mind-born God, who had emerged victorious and whose ichor was dripping as drops of nectar,
[there arose] a lotus-pond with the buds of fresh lotuses for its tusks.
The circle of bees clinging here spreads forth beauty.

In this world, what woman, possessing the passion of intense arousal, would not bestow delight upon her beloved while standing in a bower of wish-fulfilling creepers, pure in her intent and having commenced love-play with ease? (46)
(Verse in reverse and forward order:

Here, upon the slopes of the western hills that have attained a station transcending the world, possessing intense and abundant luster and bearing a grace that reaches the hearts of night-lilies, they bear a beauty fashioned by the moon.

(47) The moon, having reached a state beyond the world upon the slopes of the western hills, possessing intense and abundant luster and bearing a grace that reaches the hearts of night-lilies, bears a beauty fashioned by the moon. (47)
Behold Miśrakeśī dancing before you to songs, her arms encircled by formidable bracelets,
as she moves in perfect rhythm with the breezes from the ichor of lordly elephants on this bank.
What are these spray-drops, shimmering as they are encircled by clusters of lavalī flowers? ||48||
As this mountain pervades the entire upper portion of the world-egg with its hundreds of long and vast jeweled peaks,
the possibility of space for anything else has vanished; thus, it rests upon the ground of the mountain range.
Like a celestial nymph, the Śabara woman frequents the mountain peaks. ||49||
Here, this perfected couple approaches from afar, possessing a flavorful charm that deludes even the virtuous;
and here is the peak of this mountain, which dispels the darkness of ignorance with its mass of rays. (50)
Bearing the splendor of a multitude of yak-tail fans with long,
shaggy tails shaken off, these elephants, together with their female companions, sport gracefully here in the waters of the mountain torrents, imitating the city of Rājagṛha.
The Nāgas on the mountain had their formidable frontal globes entirely washed clean. ||51||

Agitated by their wandering, those celestial maidens here, with their shimmering and boundless flight unimpeded, no longer sport now with their lovers, who are as fickle as great fires, despite their arts of charming smiles. (52)

O Lord, upon the wheel of formidable seven-petaled lotuses joined together, which is a creeping vine upon the path of wealth, the Siddhas and Sādhyas take their station here, desiring to engage in union;
likewise, the Siddhas and Sādhyas reside upon the mountain peak and its ridges.
The celestial nymphs, dancing with expressive hands according to the melodies of the musical scales (*grāmarāga*), do not reach satiety;
nor do people, together with their kinsmen, tire of moving about in this praiseworthy place.
[He was] free from the passion for the village and devoid of the agitation of the senses. ||54||
I see this peak of the lord of mountains nearby, frequented by kinnaras overflowing with intense love;
it possesses a preeminent beauty through its minerals of unaltered form, as if it were performing a lute concert of many kinds.
The bank of this river shines forth, free from all flocks of birds, devoid of passion, immeasurable, incomparable, and possessing trees with branches that provide refuge for birds;
it gleams with the radiance of shimmering jewels and is beneficial to him. 56.
Behold his face, which, like the dawn, is characterized by self-restraint; it possesses half-closed pupils that have dispelled the subtle darkness and clearly perceive reality.
This circle of sages has ascended the ridges of the mountain.
The ascetic, his strength exhausted by old age, has gone [to the next world], taking as his support that which was given by the female ascetic and you.
In this mountain, he sometimes maintains a steady course, while at other times he moves about with passion;
in one place he ascends and in another he descends, like a deer of variegated and beautiful hue, worthy of trust. (59)
Here, the lion does not subdue any lordly elephant by force with his blows from the trunk, nor even with his effortless playfulness;
yet even by day, he is not overcome by the herds of buffaloes.
Even by those longing for sport, [the elephants] were not led from the reed-beds into the mud.
The lions, provoked by the sight of the elephants, seize them even as they stand upon their palms;
it is clear that this brings about the fame of the king, under the guise of the pure pearls fallen from the frontal globes onto the earth.
In this place, the creeper, sweet as fresh nectar and frequented by honey-bees with the nectar of its flowers, shone most brilliantly;
the mountain slopes, strewn with various jewels, did not shine so brightly as the sweetness of the earth. 62.
Scented by the special fragrance of the women's breath, which was inhaled at the same moment as the wine rinsing their mouths,
they seemed to exhale a sweet perfume that overwhelmed [all others].
Behold here the clusters of filaments within the midst of the flowers.
In this place, there are elephants whose great trunks are fragrant with the scent of ichor-drops;
and at the end of the night, these elephants laugh together with flowers that possess a charming splendor.
O Lord, here the young bride, overwhelmed by the intoxication of honey-wine, speaks aloud with a voice that conveys a sense of incompleteness;
she shines like the very splendor of the lotus-hand of her husband, appearing in the guise of a deceitful woman. 65.
Pervading the interior of the Golden Peak and the sky, this mountain shines like you, O Lord, with its mass of matted hair adorned with rugged rocks, bestowing joy upon all.
He does not shine like one who is marked by a harsh stone and is thus rendered unsightly. ||66||

From here, the wielder of the plow draws toward himself this Yamunā— her waters dark with the beauty of falling mud, her entire expanse filled with the clamor of birds, and her banks lined with rows of cranes— as if she were a braid of water from the Yamunā.
Here, because of its grasping at the water, the expanse of golden peaks shines forth as the clouds bow down;
and what woman would not be delighted by a lover who, in his love, causes her to rejoice with ever-new advances? (68)
Its slopes of shimmering blue stone were variegated by the circle of planets possessing stainless luster as they reached the reflection [of the mountain],
and it bore the pale hide of a young deer with its eight tufts of hair clearly visible.
This [mountain] shines at night as if its center were wrapped in a garment. ||69||
These dense masses of clouds, not long-stretched like rivers, do not leave the sky;
what great lake-like stability of lotuses is perceived here in this great lake of the atmosphere? (70)
Though never before seen even by the throngs of sky-dwellers, these mountain caves— adorned with golden girdles and occupied by chamberlains—
bear the likeness of the ladies of the harem.
The assembly of gods and asuras, along with Lakṣmī— the essence of all excellence— flowed toward him;
and the lotus-ponds bear his resplendent path at their forefront.
In these [verses] which possess the essence of the essential and the non-essential, there is true aesthetic flavor (rasa) that is the very core of rasa.
In this place, the breeze has been perfumed on all sides by flowers that have shed their sleep;
it is delightful with the multitude of Vedic mantras and possesses the splendor of the fresh *vauṣaṭ* syllable.
The gait of those fair-browed women there possesses a supreme charm through its languid grace;
it spreads a far-reaching splendor that is unsurpassed in its delight, characterized by a slow and steady movement. (74)
The formidable camp of this lord of the earth, crowded with Pīlu trees and filled with hundreds of enemy armies being crushed,
brings about the manifestation of prosperity for him who has cast aside [all obstacles].
His splendor is victorious through various supreme and final Magadhan [teachings]. ||75||
Here, the female bee, intoxicated by the nectar, does not abandon the fresh cluster-vine;
likewise, this [king], through his cries, now causes the vine-like line of the gods—who are themselves clusters of nectar—to fall, as if breaking their fixed posture.
O Lord of the Gods, this youth, wearing a dense forest garland that displays the splendor of manifest intoxication,
captivates the mind like Balarāma, who bears the mark of a high plow-handle and possesses the beauty of a clearly visible plow.
Standing here pervading the sky with peaks that possess the luster of the nine gems,
as if with outstretched arms,
the mountain sported with the Kirātas who, mistaking them for elephants, struck at the deer.
With their forearms serving as assistants for their bows, they rained down arrows. ||78||

With its passion undiminished, its excellence fully manifested, its clarity of color and brilliance, and its many paths, this circle of souls here attains glory like a song that relies on the *jātis*, possessing a tone sweet to the ear. 79.
This mountain, which pervades and abides amidst the rivers rich with waterfalls,
robs the humming of the female bees of their nasal resonance through its own resonant echoes.
On its plateau, bearing the appearance of being distressed by the distant fall of its exceedingly high peak rising upward,
it possesses the shimmering light of a multitude of far-reaching jewels swaying to and fro.
Under the pretext [of modesty], she clung to the edge of her hip with her garment. ||81||

Satiated by the pollen of the filaments of the lotuses in the lake, resounding with the humming of bees, and bearing a single fresh cosmetic paste made from the pollen of the filaments, O friend, sport here in this lake! (82)
In this very place, the female bee, her sweet humming as charming to the ear as that of a honey-bee, speaks thus;
she dwells throughout the forest, delighted by the wine-like essence of the flower nectar.
(A pair of verses) She is not surpassed by the flowering plateaus.

Who here on the mountain has been released by circles of arrows that were accompanied by *kośātaki* juice and *āmalakī* fruits? And who has been released by which [arrows] that were accompanied by *kośātaki* juice and *āmalakī* fruits? (84)
As he wanders among the lotus ponds, this tiny fragment of eyelash—moist with honey-paste and clinging deeply to his heart—attains the beauty of a slender shaft of Cupid, like a bee-sting. (85)
Therefore, O mountain, covered here by dust and with its birds turned brown by clusters of blossoms, you ward off calamity;
for your beloved, possessing a noble mind, does not carry away your wealth—by whom could your wealth be carried away? 86.
Upon your peak, they attain a state of supreme excellence.
The two dark-complexioned ones had arms raised from their chariots,
their manes rendered tawny by the mass of pollen hanging down from the celestial trees shaken by the wind. ||87||
O Lord, behold how this pair of perfected beings shines intensely, engaged in amorous play within the most beautiful groves of jujube trees;
even the multitude of leaves here, O Master, is busily occupied with the most lovely jujube fruits.

Bearing a night that captivates the eyes with the dark-blue gaze of swarms of bees and is adorned by circles of peacocks as lustrous as clouds, he steals the hearts of those in the forest groves of Kaṭaka. (89)
O Lord of the Gods, when this mountain attained the reputation of being a forest land,
it did not assume the status of a lake because of its splendor illuminated by lotuses,
for that glory had already found its home in the groves.
What was that which they bore, shining like a lotus of the essence? ||90||

For those yogis who constantly practice self-restraint with respect to various objects of focus, whether internal or external, specific distinctions of that particular perfection clearly arise for them as they occupy the seat of yoga. (91)
Even those who dwelt upon the Golden Mountain (Meru) for the sake of their ascetic vows found no peace;
O noble one, we consider that the affection of fair-browed women here on earth is far superior to that of the mountain-dwellers. 92.

The horse-faced one (Aśvavaktra), whose middle is gracefully curved by hundreds of arrangements, possesses a posture that is more beautiful due to its slight Gāndhāra [intervals] in both direct and reverse order.
Singing here this pure Ṣāḍava melody, which possesses a middle *vaikāra* [note] not far removed [from the tonic], he does not experience fatigue. 93.
For people here, whose expectations have vanished because they have requested what they desired, who are filled with the joy of amorous play,
and who are united with their beloveds, every season is a time of beauty.
This bee, its dark-hued body adorned with the luster of flower clusters, drinks the honey with impetuosity;
like a cluster of blossoms from a fragrant tree, it is filled with sweet sounds as it encounters the fresh fragrance.

O friend, having beheld this lake here, which possesses a swarm of bees that are the axes for cutting down the pride of lovers, the woman does not even look at her beloved, who has the luster of full-blown campaka flowers.
[He was] like one whose axe is surrounded by a swarm of bees shimmering with gold. ||96||

The Goddess Śrī, who cannot endure the destruction of her abode, did not emerge from the ocean in any way by means of this [king], even though she appeared holding a lotus from which the bees had departed and whose petals were slightly opened, as if she were laughing with a gentle smile. ||97||
A bee does not grow weary of a sweet and exceedingly beautiful flower;
nor does a woman, though far away, fail to torment the mind of a traveler because she is new. (98)
While the lover was applying a tilaka-mark upon the forehead of the graceful-limbed woman, she felt a surge of longing;
for here, in this assembly of all, there was a joy arising from the gathering of blossoming coconuts. 99.
Here on this earth, which grants happiness like Mount Meru, the desires of the lords of the gods do not find a dwelling;
yet the earth, possessing abundant fruits, trembles with their juices, while the latent impressions of the monkeys (or: the senses) are no longer devoid of desire. 100.
The tall *palāśa* bud, resounding with bees, finds full satisfaction here by raining down its nectar;
and yonder, the army of Indra sports with the waters that bear...
The fickleness of desire is the cause of the impurities of the sparks [of passion]. ||101||

Here, the multitude of trees, with the fragrance of their flowers, has perfumed the sense of smell; with various lovely bees engaged in new activities, it shines from afar with its branches bent down by the weight of those lovely bees in their ceaseless tasks. ||102||
The arrows of the God of Love, tipped with flowers, rest upon this mountain which is like a mango tree with bees clinging to its blossoms;
what woman separated from her lover could endure union with him, who is like a mango tree with bees clinging to it, in the presence of the beauty of spring? ||103||

O Lord, in the month of spring, the riverbanks were surely abandoned by women, who could not rival the beauty of his creeper-like arms and flower-like hands with their own canopies of vines and well-proportioned forms.
Cultivated for a month by those of equal status upon their natural creepers. ||104||
In this place, the forest attains a singular splendor through its connection with the intense heat of the sun;
yet the multitude of bees, clinging to the lotuses, abandons their desire for the water that flows from the obstructed rays of the sun. 105.
The flocks of birds have taken up residence upon this mountain; the deer, sporting here, bestow delight with their sprout-like arrows.
These very places, born of memory, flash before me; may this mountain, where the deer sport, grant you pleasure for your minds. 106.
Out of love, as he was thus seated by his female friends within the thickets of trees and creepers upon the grounds shrouded in fresh darkness,
he shines forth, bearing a shower of falling flowers.
By the heat of the midday sun, this season [summer] does not depart from the earth. (Thus ends Spring.

In the forests, having dwelt upon the petals of the *śirīṣa*—which are sweet with the exudation from the interior of yellow lotuses—which swarm of bees would not be captivated here by that which is sweet and delighted by contact with the petals of the *śirīṣa*? (108)

Mallikā finds no pleasure here for Madana, whose mind is ever pure; and the pleasure-chamber, though adorned with sandalwood, shines as one whose lord is ever pure-minded and free from passion. ||109||

In this world, what woman—possessing a voice as sweet and soft as a lute, yet distressed by love and devoid of essence—is she who has attained incessant amorous play, delighting in passion, gestures, emotions, laughter, and pleasure? (This is a verse with words in both direct and reverse order.
What woman here, in the groves of Mandāra trees, does not feel pride?

Women who have been led to union with lovers inferior to themselves are considered base; yet, when those same women are led by their fortune to the shores of the ocean, what excellence does their firmness not surpass? 111.
The river, with its flavorful waters, as it flows over hundreds of rocks, shines forth having met with breaking;
and the girl with arched brows, having been led to the house of her beloved, shines forth having been brought to a state resembling the flavorful waters. 112.

Having come from the slopes of the hills, the buffaloes stand affectionately here by the lakes, which resemble fresh wine; they are not seen by the joyful swans, nor are the lakes seen by the buffaloes. (Thus ends Summer.
The bee does not leave the blossoms of the *asamaṃsalāṅgalī* plants that are blooming all around.
Even a cloud, though it holds lightning, cannot encompass those [trees] with their thick trunks on all sides.
Covering his body with the rays of jewels,
this peacock has taken refuge out of a desire for proximity to the moon-like face; thus possessing a bestowed splendor, he is sought after by the women of heaven.
This [place], being near the forest, is inhabited by peacocks due to its proximity to the woods. ||115||
By that god, whose mind was captivated by this [king], who surpassed even Mount Kailāsa with his wonderful splendor,
and who was accompanied by the gods, no dwelling-place was made that surpassed the abundance of Kailāsa or was equal to the assembly of the gods.

May you, who bestow the god of love upon the trees of those separated from their lovers, who are like a forest fire to the summer heat, and who wear garments as fresh as a ploughshare’s furrow, bring us the desired monsoon rich with nectar. 117.

Thus, as if proclaiming with its sounds that "Who here, possessing wealth in the form of a beautiful woman, would not fear the vastness of the unsurpassed state [of death]?", it repeatedly cries out to the bee. Who indeed, having a beautiful wife and being intent on pleasure, would not fear the vast abyss of the unsurpassed state in this world when separated from her? (Yugalaka) Bearing the splendor of its slopes, this mountain approaches... with flowers.
The quarters of the sky, possessing the luster of jewels and filled with the joy of Rāma, conceal themselves with their waters— easily accessible for descent— and are reddened by the rays of the sun.

O fair-browed one, upon obtaining you, my most beloved, this earth surely provides me with joy—a place where there is no standing for the heavy roar of sin, where various goals are easily attained, and where the crow-like harshness of unattainable things has vanished. (This is a verse with feet that read both forward and backward.
Separated from you, she is emulated by her tears and droplets, and by her burden of hips that surpasses the highest mountain peaks.
There, that woman was like a mass of clouds; she, who was bowed down by her breasts, bore the highest water and thunder.
The sight of him distresses people here—
him who bears a form possessing a mass of jewel-like rays, like a circle of serpents whose venomous fangs have been removed and whose poison has vanished.
[He was] like a circle of intoxicated serpents whose passion was undisturbed. ||122||

Who here has crossed the river whose waters are swollen by the rains and filled with waves— a river where the people are afflicted by the grit and pebbles— while the grove of *ketakī* trees puts forth its buds all the more intensely?
It is a state of continuous delight for the wise who possess refined taste. ||123||
This mountain bears the splendor of a royal camp, surpassing the dark beauty of the earth with its golden peaks that shed nectar;
bringing sweet joy to the ears here, it bestows delight.
"O lake, you whose lotuses surpass the nectar of the cries of my cranes! (Thus [speaks] the rainy season.
Seeing this, the young woman, though full of various playful charms, ceases her indignation toward her beloved; for here, the two of them together enjoy the moonlight upon the lake.
Attending to their lineage during lovemaking, they were not slow in passion, relishing various amorous sports, and remained joyful therein. ||125||

Even though the forest here in autumn strives to conceal itself with flowers so that it may not be subdued by the sound of peacock cries, O lady with arched brows, it was nevertheless subdued by him through his arrival, which was as charming as a kinsman. 126.

Here, during the act of love, this river is not resorted to by a fair-eyed woman, even though it is accompanied by cool breezes; for she is possessed by a bee that has become intoxicated by the pollen of fresh *tamatāla* flowers and, acting as a messenger of passion, instills amorous longing in people while remaining with her lotus-like consort.
Alas, not even by the body of Śiva, who was deluded by the thought that the sands on the banks of the Tāmala river were celestial damsels! ||127||
The lake at the edge of this mountain’s path, filled with large fish, desires to rival the celestial river as it flows through the forest-covered slopes;
yet in the sage’s grove, no one is inferior and none is superior.
The autumn season destroys that [delusion] for one who is surrounded by groves on the riverbanks. (Thus ends the description of Autumn.

Who here, deluded by intense passion, would not take delight after attaining the supreme state of the winter season, which is filled with the abundance of amorous play? O praised one, who would not rejoice, being deluded by passion? (129)
The forest floor attains splendor because of the cloves (*lavaṅga*) within its bursting buds;
it is frequented here by the deer-eyed women who have gone there, having reached a state where the impurity of the Kali age has been shattered and their passion has vanished.

Lakṣmī, seeing that the slopes of the golden mountain of the Lord of the Gods were being joyfully embraced by the peaks of the Nandana grove, laughed with delight as she beheld the immortals filled with love for their young wives.
In this season, the peaks are made smooth by those who have subdued their passion. (Thus ends Hemanta.

In this [winter], the fragrances of the kunda flower, which whiten the forest, provide anointment for the nose; who would not be filled with longing and rejoice in fresh sexual union? Who would not be filled with longing and rejoice in fresh sexual union? (Thus ends Śiśira.)
The earth bears his *kunda* flower, while the Lord of the gods, though obstructed by the immortals, carries away its cool essence;
and this mountain shines, bearing a circle of jewels as white as frost.
With his head bowed before the multitude of obstructed immortals, he was beautiful and cool. ||133||
In the essence of non-fear, O destroyer of unequal and inexhaustible sacrifice, you who possess the form of dense clouds with silent feet;

in the essence of non-fear, O you whose form is like dense clouds with silent feet, [you are] mine. (The Samudraka meter) O you who possess the essence of cool nectar, O you who are most constant in subduing the piercing pain of night, O you who shine with a victorious garland of excellence!
*Sasava-vasu-surārāma-madhv-adhvarārā-tata-lalada-darārāsa-atvat-varārā* (135). [This is a *āvali* (chain) verse.
O Lord, the forest ground, possessing the nectar of the *kunda* flowers and free from heat, attains the state of being beloved when it bears [the fruit of] its own self.
And here, for those who possess self-mastery, excellence has been attained,
which utterly dispels the lotuses of illusion even amidst the intense heat of the forest fire.
(The Tilaka) This mountain slope shines, having struck down the hosts of Dānavas and possessing a torrential flow that carries away the essence of the forests.
And the female elephant, with her constant flow of ichor, protects the herd most excellently from the forest fire.
(An example of *pādayamaka* with reverse and direct feet:
This row of trees does not exist on that mountain, which is always devoid of elephants due to the lightness of its fruit.

The spreading peaks of her husband [the mountain], slightly inferior to heaven, and the black creepers of the *akhila* trees, tawny with pollen, intoxicate the earth with the fragrance of mango trees. The destruction of the fallen... [is not even] a little less than the three heavens.
The rows of cuckoos were like creepers whose branches were tawny with the pollen of the *dūnā* flower. ||139||

O lady with a gait like that of a swan, you who possess the fragrance of wine, you who are adorned with *śārivā* flowers, you who possess an essence of dark luster like a mass of clouds, you whose splendor is the very essence of nectar—
what creeper in this forest of *sāla* and *tāla* trees would not be eager for you?
She was resplendent with supreme, unattainable glory, having taken refuge in a courtyard. (140) [This is a four-foot verse in direct and reverse order.

It possessed a body with heaps of gold, a forest of uninjured *tiniśa* trees, and the sound of bees; it had a multitude of white sandalwood trees whose trunks were split by the power of passion, and its strength was overcome by old age. (141)

With its golden heaps of flowers, its groves of *akṣata*, *tiniśa*, *asanāgata*, and *ālīsa* trees, and its beings made radiant by the dust from the bodies of rutting elephants torn apart by passion, it is like a forest of *añjana* trees;
O Lord, he bears such a self that is ever-increasing— (Mahāyamaka). 142.
He who is adorned with Dāmodara, who is free from all faults, and who consists of the three [qualities] that are stainless,
presides with reverence over the host of gods,
who is likewise adorned by Dāmodara, who is free from all faults, and who consists of the three [qualities] that are stainless. (Viśeṣaka)
With her heart broken by separation, she longs for the forests filled with bees and variegated with blossoming bakula trees, which now seem so far away to her deeply yearning brow-bent lady.
It is better to praise those of noble lineage than the trees of the forest. 144.

"Having approached her beloved, a friend says this: 'O lady with heavy hips, having beheld this mountain—its entire burden [of trees] bowed down by the head, its *ālā* trees crushed by the weight of its peaks—you too, with your head, have crushed the *ālā* tree of your own pride, for you bear the entire burden [of his love]. (A pair of verses.
"These elephants, having submerged themselves in the water, with the tips of their trunks—"
They cause terror by seizing the hands with their coils;
yet the mind of one who possesses meditative concentration becomes serene upon seeing them, for he dispels the unsurpassed fear of those who seize the hands with their coils day after day. 146.
On the riverbank, this flock of birds dwells for a moment,
intoxicated by the ever-fresh and clear nectar;
for what indeed is not made exceedingly beautiful in the heart?
Sporting with delight, she swiftly [attained] the most excellent and pure state. ||147||

O Lord, O dispeller of the misfortunes of the world, while this people remained on this mountain—which removes the afflictions of old age, disease, and death—there shone forth a cow that was free from the exhaustion of hunger and thirst;
yet even on the surface of heaven, such a cow is not easily obtained, even after long pursuit through hundreds of desires. Once attained, she is difficult to find.

By me, who am impetuous in burning the forest of enemies, the city of the Dānavas was suddenly destroyed during the third watch of the night. (This is a verse with feet in both direct and reverse order.
Here, upon the golden palaces of the divine mountain, Fortune has been shaken by those who are most excellent and beloved by women.
She has attained the secret of divine play through tireless virtues, and she is ever-new in her passion for her beloveds, the most excellent of men. 149.
The Malaya breeze blows, respectfully arranging the vidhuta, panasa, and māla trees for the women whose pride has been scorched;
here, amidst the assembly of sages, liberation shines with splendor.
She respectfully fastened her garment, shaking off the mass of dust.

Upon this mountain, whose jeweled rocks possess a shimmering and most pure luster, the sun shall make the foreheads of the Kinnarīs wet with droplets of their own perspiration, marked by the swaying locks of their hair;
and he shall cause their song to serve as a slender body-staff for the circle of women separated from their lovers.
Why does this high, heart-stealing sound, marked by the incessant clapping of cymbals, not cause the gods to melt with emotion? 151.

Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "Description of the Mountains and Seasons," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked with the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who bears the name Vāgīśvara and the secondary title Vidyādhipati, and who is a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
The Sixth Canto:
Then [the gods], overwhelmed by the humiliation caused by the demon Andhaka, approached him whose mind was gratified by their prior service...
The seasons, their own forms being the visible manifestations of their splendor, went for refuge, urged by the Lord of a Hundred Sacrifices. ||1||

Holding with their hands various clusters of flower-stalks followed by swarms of bees due to their intense fragrance, they stood with their knees pressed against the ground, having been presented with humility by Nandin. (A yugma) Then,
having prostrated before him, they offered their heads— crowns from which bees were released as they flew up, slipping from the golden ground.
By his permission, they occupied jeweled stone seats placed not far away.

Then the Lord of the World, his sprout-like lips bathed by the cascades of rays from his teeth, spoke to them with a voice as deep as the majestic thundering of clouds heavy with the weight of fresh rainwater. 4.
Why have you, who were once so full of vigor, suddenly fallen into a state of desolation as if the worlds themselves had undergone a reversal?
Your very complexions, now turned ashen, tell us that you are currently pained by the thorn of grief in your hearts. (5)

While the Lord of the Maruts stood there, his arms exceedingly radiant with a flashing thunderbolt as thick as the coils of the King of Serpents, by whom was this yawning displayed—a son of Diti desiring to bring ruin upon the worlds? (6)
The lotus-bud of the world has blossomed from the seat of Brahmā, who is as tender as a lotus-root and possesses faultless wings;
surely you alone are capable of protecting it, just as bees are able to guard a full-blown lotus. (7)

Like the poetic creation of Brahmā concerning the process of emanation—clear, with vividly unfolding meters, and neither too slow nor too hurried—the fame composed by the ancient poet is being spread far and wide by you all with great clarity. (8)
Then, when the Primordial Being had uttered these words with a voice as steady as a rain-cloud and remained silent,
he was slowly awakened by the glance of Śeṣa, the foremost of the pure ones, who embodies the entire circle of all the seasons.

With his mouth resonant with the continuous humming of bees wandering about, and possessing the beauty of fragrance enjoyed by those bees, he seemed to be emitting before him his own abundance of flowers, made formidable by the filaments of the rays of his teeth, as he uttered these words. (10)

When the third eye of the moon-crested Lord, which destroys the kinsman of Smara, blazed forth, his eyes were contracted by the impact of that fire; it was as if he had for a moment taken refuge within that eye out of envy.

Before him, as if his words were being carried away by the sweet humming of bees who had approached out of longing for the spray of nectar from fresh mango blossoms clinging to the tips of their ears, Madhurī spoke:
(Quintain) "O you who occupy the seat of the heart-lotus of the sole witness to the affairs of the three worlds..."
For you, whose consciousness is entirely devoid of aversion and misfortune, what is there that is not known by you, O Lord? 13.

O Sinless One, the fourfold group beginning with consciousness, which is innate to You, is well-known in the world as being such that, for this [group] which has attained a state surpassing all others, there is nothing else whatsoever that possesses even a degree of comparison. 14.

O Lord, for you who perceive the further shore, whose rays of unimpeded consciousness are spontaneously perfected, there is no possibility that the knowledge of the true nature of the entire circle of objects could ever be attained through the conventions of words. (15)
O Lord, just as the radiance of the sun, shining without distinction, unfolds throughout all things,
so too does your intellect— unobstructed, stainless, and free from the darkness of delusion— expand.
O Lord, although we have already comprehended the full extent of all things that exist, you ask us this today;
therefore, the moment of your sweet conversation with one another now brings about for us the supreme accumulation of merit. (17)

Having attained a state of being distinct from primordial nature (prakṛti) and devoid of transformation, and being inactive regarding the properties inherent in prohibited objects, you alone are indeed the Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth principle, as declared by the explicit words of the Sphuṭacūlikā. ||18||

Devoid of the nature of the well-known manifold of worldly pleasures, incapable of performing even the slightest act anywhere, and having descended to a state where the functions of the senses are void—oh, how you, O lover, resemble Prakṛti! 19.

O Protector, those skillful ones who follow the Sāṃkhya school of the elders—whose minds are purified and free from all disturbances by relying on the ten causes—declare that non-return (*anivṛtti*) is indeed your supreme state. (20)

Bestowing upon You—the knower of the reality of all objects, who is devoid of the experience of the fruits of karma—the status of a supreme person, the wise declare that the word "Lord" (Īśvara) is established as having no other referent. 21.

Those of pure vision have never, like other ascetics, perceived your sinless lordship—which is devoid of both positive and negative concomitance—as something to be grasped by the friction of the tips of firmly bound fingers. ||22||

In ancient times, when the lotus-born Brahmā had become intensely devoted to asceticism with the desire to create the worlds, there arose from him that which possesses five characteristics and is employed in all ritual acts, such as sacrifices and the like. (23)
O Blessed One, that which the Vedas declare to be the supreme state, that which is described as having many faces and feet,
and reaching which a person is not born again— that very sound *praṇava* is the designator of You alone.
(24) [A yugma] [It designates You] who possess the imperishable nature of being devoid of rebirth, and who have attained the unique status of being the sole preceptor to the leaders of the gods.
O Śarva, he who here does not cease from approaching you—having already consumed all things moving and unmoving—is never cut off anywhere. 25.
That which is perceived here through action, sequence, parts, number, and its own characteristic marks—
having tranquility as its beginning, middle, and end— it, by its own power, brings about Time itself, O Smaraka!
(Yugalaka) It is beyond thought, outside the sphere of discursive inquiry, devoid of the sensation of pleasure, and free from the succession of mental impressions.
Having attained the meditative absorption of Śaṃkara through your will, a person never again falls into delusion. ||27||

O Lord, the cultivation of detachment directed toward primordial nature (prakṛti)—which arises from the cessation of the contrary state of the power of consciousness—obstructs even that state of discriminative discernment by the will of Your mind, which restrains all masters. 28.

O Lord of the Gods, yogins who have practiced self-restraint within the various mandalas of splendor, such as the Tapoloka and others, become possessed of an unimpeded and variegated consciousness of their own self within the abodes beginning with the Bhuvana-loka. ||29||

By Your will, O Yogins who have entered the three states consisting of non-cognition and whose path of cessation has been brought face-to-face with the state of stability, there arises neither the realization of ten million stages nor that of sevenfold nature. ||30||

O Lord of the Thirty, for men whose minds are otherwise subject to unrestrained wandering, consciousness—consisting of you—becomes the foundation for an undisturbed state when it takes the objects of taste and so forth as its domain within the seats of the tongue and other senses. (31)
A person who possesses the notion "I am characterized by pure gold" is indeed called a "gold-man" from the tips of his nails to the crown of his head;
and he is said by the Upaniṣads to have attained a fivefold nature consisting of the experience of pleasure and so forth. (32)

O you who are white with virtues, it is you alone who are sung in this world by Brahmā as he chants the multi-pathed Sāman, which possesses the excellence of fivefold musical divisions (*bhakti*) beginning with the clear *hiṃ*-utterance and ending with the final *nidhana*. 33.

When those established in the steady recitation of the *aparāntaka* and other such refined compositions—well-settled in the sequence of syllables, the fixed order of the Vedas, and the modulation of accents—you alone resound as the ten-fold characteristic of sound. (34)

Having reached the state of being turned away from all literary compositions because they serve as causes for the cessation of every spiritual qualification, this atom (the individual soul), desiring to know your true nature, sings these profound Dravidian songs. 35.

O Lord, having attained the state of being the cause of eternal satisfaction—just as the drinkers of Soma regard you, the nectar—you are now, with great devotion, milking the supreme [cow] hidden in the cave for the sake of the vow of the sacrificial grass-strewn altar. 36.

When one is established in a steady and comfortable posture, endowed with the capacity for the various divisions of Sāṃkhya, the weighty Yoga, and Dhāraṇā, and when the mind has become serene, the eightfold sovereign power indeed manifests for the adept. (37)

Indeed, Sarasvatī herself, consisting of you, has arrived in her full majesty, sweet with the clear resonance of the Sāman chants, endowed with the excellence of the sequence of Vedic revelation through notes of two kinds and four musical modes. 38.
Those renowned as seers of the higher and the lower, who know the ancient truths, declare that which is praised by the universe as "not this, not this.
That alone is Your wondrous, supreme reality, devoid of all limiting adjuncts and means of apprehension. 39.

O Blessed One, those of pure vision declared you to be that very Puruṣa, consisting of earth, wind, fire, water, and so forth—highly exalted and possessing an unimpaired transformation of sensation—for men. 40.

Furthermore, those by whom this scripture—beginning with the syllable *praṇava*, culminating in the state of cessation (*virāma*), and expounding the seven categories of reality as determined by the Serpent [Śeṣa]—has indeed been studied here, O Blessed One, surely they too attain Your station. (41)
O Lord, though devoid of feet, You travel; though deprived of hands, You assume the state of a grasper;
though without eyes, You look; and though without ears, You hear everything and yet You do not know, and You do know. 42.
Thus, O Lord, for one who beholds you— the immutable one who bears a body of wondrous excellence, unique among all the worlds— indeed,
the entire consciousness of that virtuous person undergoes transformation.
(A pair of verses) Just as the orb of the moon reflected in a mass of water-waves in a lake, O Hara...
Just as a row of sunbeams, having taken refuge within the interior of a dwelling made of tree shoots, falls upon the earth when that shelter collapses. ||44||

Just as the sky, though clearly one and the sole abode of all wonders, assumes a manifold nature when reflected in various objects such as pestles and mortars, so too do you remain unchanged while appearing diverse through your reflection in different substrates. (A pair of verses) That Hari is of a single disposition, yet his partial manifestations are established through three, four, or many activities; [so it is with you].
To you, whose self is everything and who possess great majesty, this other [universe] stands as if it were a mere illusory transformation (vivarta). ||46||
O Lord, it is a marvel: he pierces the gem even though he has no eyes; he strings it even though he has no fingers, being so instructed by you;
he fastens it even though he has no neck; and he worships it even though he has no tongue. 47.
Though assuming manifold forms, you maintain a single nature; though having attained the state of stability, you are transitory.
Though situated in the sky, you do not transcend the earthly realm; though standing in close proximity, you are far removed.

Though beyond both consciousness and unconsciousness, He appears as neither yet assumes their very nature; though beyond both being and non-being, He abides as neither yet exists within them; and though devoid of many faces, feet, and limbs, He remains as such. (49)
Though situated within the orb of the thousand-rayed sun, the cool season dwells in the moon and yet maintains an abundance of heat;
whether you are thus of a dual nature or perhaps neither, you are profound and sufficiently wondrous.
(The Tilaka) O Blessed One, alas! You are indeed difficult to grasp by virtue of some renowned and magnificent form.
Or else, why is it that you, though possessing the nature of suchness, are not accepted anywhere by the wise? (51)
O Destroyer of Gods, you have no going and no coming; you are neither outside nor within, nor do you appear anywhere.
You appear only to those whose minds are not yet transformed, as you take as your object the suchness that is empty of dualistic appearance. //52//
Remaining indeed indivisible, you are established as the illuminator of the entire collection of objects in the world;
yet you have extensively entered into the state of being a benefactor for both words and sentences regarding the things to be expressed. (53)

Although you possess a single nature through that which is conceptually constructed, you are grasped by birth as manifold, having been divided by ignorance produced since beginningless time through the paths of agent, object, instrument, and so forth. (54)

That which indeed is the imperishable syllable (*akṣara*), without beginning, middle, or end, and which manifests as the embodiment of all objects—your very body, the indestructible reality of the word *Śiva*, the foundation of the world, they proclaim it to be such. (55)

O Lord, when the scope of conceptual construction and the turbulence [of the mind] are not yet complete, and when the two paths of worldly convention depend upon one another, the intellect and speech regarding this world attain their cessation once they reach the limit of being established through dependence on something else. (56)

O Bhava, you who have taken recourse to the supreme secret doctrine appear to no one as a dense and chaotic state of heterogeneity, characterized by a form that transcends both the high and the low upon which the world depends. 57.

O Lord of the Gods, you exist as a quality distinct from the qualities, yet you abide within them; you have taken recourse to the state of primordial nature (prakṛti) and have clearly attained both dissimilarity and similarity with the sixfold path of existence. 58.
Even though you abide beyond the range of the intellect, you are perceived by those whose vision is fixed within the interior of the syllable Om (praṇava),
by whom you— who possess no limiting adjuncts as your form or instrument— are somehow apprehended through the reversal of misconceptions.

The wise, having attained the state of the *suṣumṇā* nerve, reach Your station—the unassailable Self which bestows liberation and maintains the healthy existence of all living beings—thereby transcending the fourth stage of consciousness (*turiya-vṛtti*). ||60||

Having swiftly pierced through the four spheres, the skillful ones entered into you—who possess a form profound by virtue of having shaken off all conceptual construction, who are inexhaustible, unassailable, and wondrous—and who are yourself unobstructed. (61)
O Lord of the Gods, the fire of the body, agitated by its own flames, is struck by the mind impelled by you;
it then sends forth the five-fold wind that is the cause of the maintenance of the bodies of embodied beings, O Lord. (62)
Having mounted the chariot whose driver is the unimpeded mind and which has as its support the tenfold external organs,
the atom (the individual soul) wanders among the sense objects like a blue-throated [Śiva], and by your will, O Lord, it returns once again.
O Blessed One, you alone are worshipped by the wise as the Guru of all embodied beings, who abide in the ears and other seats of the entire host of presiding deities,
yet maintain a supportless existence within the ether of the heart.

O Blessed One, just as waters do not enter into a jar that is filled with dust and other impurities, so too, by Your will, the subtle atoms do not unite with pleasure and the other qualities within You, who are free from all affliction. (65)
With the graceful movement of the unfolding and turning of the interior of the petals of the lotus of the heart,
you have entered as the inner self of the world and bring about the two courses of existence based on the two solstices.
While the rays of the sun— whose essence is the three Vedas and whose nature is free from ailment— bear the splendor of the Ṛgveda as their beams,
you shine forth within that solar orb as the minute *yajus* formulas, appearing as the Puruṣa, profound with the various distinctions of its reflections.

Manifestly one alone, yet assuming various names, the form of Hari performs diverse actions for those who have taken refuge in him; you alone, like the sun, heat the earth and ordain the days, seasons, solstices, years, and so forth. (68)

O Lord of the Gods, through yoga, the state of embodied beings—whose bodies consist of all the atomic principles—is perceived as being free from affliction, like a triple staff, because it is mutually non-obstructive due to its being conditioned by You. (69)

O Lord, it is said that in former times, the deities Dhiṣaṇa and others, desiring to lead the world and wishing to show favor to those who were overwhelmed by mutual disputes, entered the minds of the knowers of the past, which consist of many aspects. (70)
By that Vidyā of yours— which has destroyed the delusion of ignorance, which has entered into those who know all that is to be known,
and which acts as a dense bolt upon the door of the path to liberation— the individual soul attains the state of Śiva.

O Lord, although the origin of all worlds—which are without beginning or end and remain as You alone—is indeed You, the progenitor who has abandoned all fixed states, and although qualities and other attributes exist in You, praise based on lineage or descent is not possible for You. (72)

Because the effects residing in dyads and other compounds—which are objects of a purity beyond the senses of ordinary people—are observed, the wise infer that you, though yourself a non-agent, are the cause, just as a potter is the cause of a jar. (73)

The wise have declared that your agency, O Lord, is devoid of any external instigator; for you, whose nature is utterly unrestrained, act through your own irresistible will, which is by its very nature unimpeded. (74)

Assuming the form of the abiding circle of powers, complete and unsurpassed, and manifesting the well-known transformations of existence, this world—composed of the three qualities—has indeed arisen from a mere fragment of Your power when it was stirred up. (75)

O Lord of the Worlds, from you—who are established in the glory of your own power beyond all stain, whose self is distinct from the circle of bound souls and their fetters—proceeds here this entire sphere of existence, characterized by the nature of both the conscious and the unconscious. (76)
O Lord, from you who have simultaneously dispelled the dense darkness with your rays, the various multitudes of objects have emerged like sparks from a blazing fire. (77)

O Lord, although Your state possesses a wondrous and supreme majesty that has attained permanence, Your activities do not exhibit any contradiction regarding the occurrence of successive or simultaneous action with respect to the accomplishment of all purposes. (78)
Presiding over the circle of your complete powers, you create, protect, and destroy the entire universe;
O Blessed One, you remain with a stable form composed of the five mantras, devoid of the two births.
When the state of being earth (the gross elements) is agitated, the primordial nature (prakṛti), having resided in the cave [of the heart], rises up like a blade of grass;
then, for the sake of the manifestation of the world, the gunas remain fixed in mutual dependence, like the strands of a rope.
You have fashioned this entire manifold circle of effects here, from dyads upward, as the domain of logical reasoning;
therefore, you are inferred by the wise as one endowed with extreme subtlety of vision, knowledge of all things, and omnipresence. (81)
Through your pervasive form you bring about the proximity of all things, and through your sovereign form you accomplish every purpose;
O Lord, by means of your power which has attained a twofold nature, you have manifested the state of all that is moving and unmoving. (82)

O Lord, by Your will, the manifestation of the world—composed of the faculties and qualities that are never impaired, and possessing a radiant and distinct form—has never at any time or place failed to attain its unfolding development. 83.
O Guha, this deep cave has been fashioned by you as a dwelling place, situated like the joined lids of a honeycomb;
it never undergoes any change of state, for it is the temple where the entire host of stainless attendants is bound together.
Just as the earth brings forth the stainless seed in the form of a sprout according to its capacity, so too, O Lord, do all your desired deeds bring about the entire circle of existence here. 85.

Others, however, declare that from the imperishable *prakṛti*-tattva—which is composed of a collection of renowned powers—there proceeds the entire array of effects beginning with intellect (*dhiṣaṇā*), which is non-different in form from it. (86)
For what insentient object indeed can assume the status of an agent in the performance of its own specific function?
Therefore, you proclaim the Lord—who consists of the activity of consciousness—to be the efficient cause of all living beings here in this world. (87)
O Lord, even at the time of universal dissolution, you remain with the splendor of your manifest consciousness undiminished;
like a spider, you are clearly the cause from which the collection of atoms emerges through the gathering of its rays.

O Lord, others indeed declare that you, the Sovereign, have attained a state of identity with the Puruṣa—the sole cause of the world, whose nature is causeless, all-pervading, immutable, devoid of the conditions of the guṇas, and who has reached the same essential nature as the Lord. 89.

Others, however, proclaim that the collection [of the three]—ascertained by the two means of valid cognition—is devoid of the world manifested by the activities of primordial matter (prakṛti), God (īśvara), or both, as well as consciousness (cit) and so forth, and is free from limiting adjuncts (anupādhika); furthermore, they declare it to be triadic in nature. (90)

Others, who maintain that liberation is natural, hold that for living beings, birth in existence consists merely of arising without regard for any other complete cause, like the spontaneous appearance of a peacock’s plumage. (91)
Others, however, know the pure essence of Sound (Śabdatattva) to be undisturbed by the fluctuations of dissolution and emergence;
it is this which appears here in the form of transformation as this entire sphere of existence, consisting of both the moving and the unmoving. (92)

O Lord of the Gods, others of profound intellect, who refute objects external to the three types of conceptual constructions that are untenable even within the interval between moments, maintain that the stability of the world is consciousness alone. (93)

Those whose minds are free from grasping at either [extreme] and who rely upon the position of the Madhyamaka view, their intellects firm in the certainty of reality, become colored by your virtue and consider themselves to have accomplished all that was to be done. (94)
Some, whose rays of consciousness have been awakened by Your grace, declare that the atom is indeed supersensible;
others, however, O Lord, know it to be non-sensory, consisting of that [consciousness], due to a misconception arising from delusion. (95)
"Consciousness is never observed here, even in the slightest degree, outside the body or anywhere else apart from its dimensions.
Having reached this certainty, those of perfected intellect have established your eternal nature as being free from all error. (96)
O Blessed One, those whose dense thicket of delusion has been cleared away by Your grace perceive You as one of pure vision;
yet others, such as Kaṇabhakṣa, Jaimini, and the Digambaras, describe the reality of the self in many ways. (97)
Others have mental activities that are unstable, bound by the nature of being both characterized and devoid of characteristics.
O Blessed One, those with nihilistic inclinations deny your existence by means of such reasons as "non-arising" and so forth. (98)

Some, whose minds had leaped forward, resolved upon the path to peace—meditating on the cessation of the cycle of existence that arises from the manifestation of various causes for conceptual construction; yet others, devoid of your grace, did not so resolve. 99.

When the Blessed One is averse to showing grace, even if one has entered that difficult path, the atom—remaining in the state of inversion—never attains anything at all within the five stable joints. (100)

Even a man who has attained the circle of reality through great effort, though it be as dense as the expansion of primordial nature, if he is excluded from the nectar of your scripture, falls into the extreme state of following the doctrines of the fettered. (101)

Those others, whose dense thicket of delusion remains unshattered by those of defiled soul who possess the lamp of the Smṛtis, undoubtedly possess a mass of atoms of darkness that has been thoroughly increased by the non-comprehension of Your scripture. 102.
O Lord of the Thirty-three, primordial nature (prakṛti) is not conscious of anything at all, and the Spirit (puruṣa) is likewise indifferent;
yet it is you alone, whose conscious activity is renowned, who bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation by means of your grace. (103)
Even those who mock the equality of even a mere fragment of Dharma remain in a state of non-difference between the individual soul and the Lord;
excluded from the nectar of your scripture, others do not become capable of discerning the distinction between them. 104.

For the multitude of words is twofold: that which loudly proclaims the teachings other than Śiva’s, and that which, led by you, O Bhava, attains the state of being the sole cause for the supreme and inferior fruits of the world. (105)

O Lord of the Gods, this fourfold consciousness proceeds here, resembling the natural light of Hari, Gopaka, Graha, Himāṃśu, and Bhāskara, and it partakes in degrees of excellence bestowed by your grace. (106)

Having clearly dispelled all doubt through the non-erroneous scriptures by means of the path of yoga, there are no discerning people here who, having conquered the qualities of worldly existence, would again resort to the cycle of birth and death. 107.
Seated upon the throne of the sky, having dispelled all darkness and established Your abode, You desired to manifest Your entire sovereign glory;
thus, with the pure rays of Your own powers, You became gracious and revealed the consciousness within the aggregate of atoms. 108.

O Lord of the Gods, by bestowing your grace upon the multitude of individual souls, you grant them a state of selfhood equal to your own—characterized by the power of consciousness through the cognition of all objects without distinction, and by agency through the capacity to accomplish every purpose. (109)

O Lord, that which indeed issued forth in the form of sound from Your imperishable self, who is both being and non-being, was the stainless scripture; by means of it, Sadāśiva has always understood the entire reality that rests upon You. 110.

Then Giriśa, with his four faces, gradually spoke that wondrous discourse, which contained the vast extent of the reality established in the eternal tradition of the infinite circles of Rudras, and which was a dense thicket of mantras of many varieties.

O Lord, from your mouth has emerged the lotus of the scriptures, which possesses a full-blown mass of filaments in the form of virtues, bears a pure essence as its clearly manifest stalk, showers honey, and reveals the true meaning of the six categories of existence. 112.

By means of syllables that have attained their own power to express every possible meaning, which possess specific functions conjoined with auxiliary factors, and which, when strung together, have reached a state in this world where they contain within them the entirety of all speech as if it were the universal form itself; ||113||

O Bhava, the Mātṛkā born from Your mouth is indeed Your Śakti; she is the embodiment of the eightfold classes of letters, naturally manifest as the maṇḍala of mantras that bring success to the practitioner, and her presence is firmly established in the three-fold divisions of reality. O Bhava, the various forms of mantras are composed of the syllables of the Mātṛkā that have arisen from Your mouth.
Having attained a state of detachment for the sake of liberation, those whose conduct is contrary [to this] bestow only the enjoyments of worldly existence. ||115||

O Blessed One, you alone, as a yogi, have fashioned for those desiring to ascend to the firm station situated above—the ladder that is the path of all things—relying upon a support constructed from the very wall of your own power. (116)

O Blessed One, even though You possess a form that is but a hundred-millionth part of a child, and although You have adopted a path characterized by the sixfold adjuncts—standing as the one and only, how does Your being not cause wonder in the minds of anyone? 117.
O Lord, we have heard that it was indeed Ananta, as you have clearly described, who first agitated the cave consisting of the qualities (guṇas);
from that, he then created the world, beginning with the white and black [sattva and tamas] and ending with the earth—so we have heard. 118.
O Lord of the Gods, those very Śiva-śaktis that constitute the essence of all things in this world perform their activities in succession;
by means of them alone, the Leader of all Mantras, through His will, has manifested this entire universe. (119)

O Lord, the leaders of mantra do not indeed ever waver from their duty of maintaining the stability and so forth of the worlds, which have come under the power of others and entered a state of cessation solely by Your will.

O Lord of the Gods, the sovereigns of the deities beginning with Kamalāsana, whom you have mentioned along with their attendants, have respectively become the causes of the arising, the maintenance, and the dissolution of the succession of worlds through their threefold states. ||121||
O Lord of the Gods, those renowned as Kṛśānu (Fire), Ṛṣabha (the Bull), and Bhānu (the Sun) have attained the state of being your own forms;
from them, indeed, the Threefold Veda (Trayī)—endowed with the excellence of all its limbs—has arisen here in a purifying sequence.
O Lord, that Dharma of Yours which is accomplished here through the path of hearing, having entered into the nature of the instruments of cognition from every side—
O Master, the wise desire that very Dharma of Yours to be eternally established and free from all affliction.

O Giver of Boons, by your will, the universal monarchs dwell in happiness, residing within various wonderful worlds contained inside the cavernous hollows of the mountain that grants all desires. 124.

O Lord, the agency of those things whose nature consists of primordial matter, inherent essence, atoms, and motion—being devoid of consciousness—is never possible, even when invoked by the oaths uttered by others. (125)

With the state of his consciousness stirred by a *kalā*, and perceiving objects through *vidyā*, this individual soul (*aṇu*), whose mind is colored by intense passion, becomes a partaker of the experiences of *prakṛti* by the will of Bhava. (126)

Those whose limbs are stained by the threefold impurity of the *kañcuka* and who fall into the caverns of worldly enjoyment—you, by your own will, draw these multitudes of individuals out from the hollow of the cave and lead them far toward purity. 127.

You liberate from the fivefold dharma those bound souls who, though powerless, have long remained with faces cast downward, longing for the circle of grass-like sense-objects; you do so by untying the mass of fetters through your grace.
The individual power of consciousness (*āṇavī citiśakti*), whose function is unimpeded, awakens the reality residing within the objects of experience;
yet it is your power, which possesses a wondrous state having attained a dual nature, that awakens that [individual power] in its entirety. 129.

O Lord, even this person, though established in the path of worldly existence by means of the firm noose of the subtle elements (aṇu), is nonetheless capable of enjoying what lies beyond the sphere of the self, having been impelled by a fraction of Your power. 130.
That which reveals the state of ultimate reality as it truly is—unfolding what was previously unmanifest—and yet veils even that which is manifest in appearance;
by such illusion of yours, he is not deceived, whose mind is bound by its very being to You. 131.
O Bhava, while your body is being consecrated by the waters of the immortal river of pleasant sensations according to your will,
the impurities inherent in your consciousness cease entirely.

O Blessed One, those individual souls (*aṇu*) whose power of consciousness has been long favored by you, who are gracious and have purified their vision of the intellect, do not become mere enjoyers of fruits within those various abodes of worldly existence (*upapatti-dhāma*). (133)
O Lord, while you have become a cloud of Dharma raining down nectar abundantly from your cave-dwelling heart,
the drop of the individual soul— having been refined by the oyster-shell of manifest power— gradually attains the nature of a pure pearl.
It is a marvel that when a wise man, whose internal self and senses have become steady—unagitated by other objects and withdrawn from them—beholds you alone, he becomes a seer of all things. (135)

O Lord, even a mere fragment of mindfulness is capable of severing the bonds of existence; yet, Your power alone is able to dispel the latent impressions of impurity that reside within the atoms of one's own self, as if to bring about their complete manifestation. 136.

Just as copper, having attained a state of gold through polishing, does not return here to its copperiness again, so too, O Lord, when the subtle reality (aṇutattva) has been purified by Your will, it does not fall back into its own latent impressions (vāsanā). 137.
O Lord of the Gods, these three—Prakṛti, Puruṣa, and Praṇava—are situated like a well, a jar, and a rope.
Standing above them, you, who are free from the manifold of the senses, wonderfully draw up the individual soul, O Aṇu. 138.
This transformation of the phonemes (kalā-pariṇati), assuming both internal and external forms, exists in two ways:
it proceeds in the natural order (anuloma) as the function of vowels and consonants, while in the reverse order (pratiloma), it is again negated by you. 139.

O Lord, by taking refuge in You, the atom becomes free from the qualities and marks of the physical body; it dwells within the created expanse of the heart, and its sphere of experience is devoid of past and future objects. 140.

Just as these visual qualities, O Lord, become manifest through contact with the rays of the sun, so too do the virtues residing in men become clarified through Your presence, O You of faultless conduct. 141.

O Lord, it is no wonder that when You are well-pleased, even a man who is incomplete and utterly helpless due to the exhaustion of all his powers proceeds alone upon the most difficult path to liberation. (142)

That stainless state which is indeed attained by those whose vows are sharpened by the practice of Amanaskayoga, and who maintain an untroubled stability within themselves—that is surely the very essence of divine grace. 143.
Through the grace born of the dharma of manifest yoga, the adept—whether his own self, another’s, or likewise the Self—is skillful;
by the intermingling of his subtle consciousness, he extends his awareness at will even toward other objects. (144)

That which is not described as the effect of egoism, which does not possess the quality of sound and is immutable, wherein the host of stars does not shimmer, and wherein there is no movement whatsoever from the nine [planets]—[that is the state]. 145.
Where the sky is marked by the unobstructed bow of the Thirty-three Gods, and where no rows of clouds wander—
beholding you stationed there in that firmament, the wise have entered into the midst of liberation.
(146) [A pair of verses] A man whose self-power has been gathered by you abandons the cycle of existence and non-existence through the fulfillment of his purpose.
Possessing stability and having defined five categories of objects, he attains a resemblance to your husband’s marvelous nature. (147)

O Lord, as you desire to show grace to the circle of atomic souls, your power proceeds in two forms—higher and lower—just as the stainless light of the sun proceeds forth; O Śiva, this power of yours, Śakti, manifests according to the distinction between the supreme and the non-supreme. 148.

O Lord, source of existence, abiding in both being and non-being, you who have realized the distinct majesty of the individual persons (pudgala); having attained a single-mindedness aided by spiritual power, the subtle one proceeds toward the domain of the fourfold objective.

"Indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever between the property and the possessor of the property; here, neither does there exist a separate subsistence, nor a substratum that possesses such subsistence.
Others, who abide in non-contradictory conduct, declare that the very absence of these two is the yoga of the mind. (150)

If this is indeed accepted, then surely everyone whose consciousness has ceased would clearly and effortlessly become a possessor of liberation here; yet, by your own wish, it is only that person who is stainless who becomes a possessor of liberation. 151.

O you who have gone to the mountain Vṛṣagiri, those atoms which were indeed made objects of your grace through your twofold self, they possess equality with you; for like the collyrium in the cave, those atoms have attained a state of birth distinct from ordinary beings.

O All-pervading Lord, that sovereignty—beginning with the power of atomization (aṇimā) and culminating in the state of the Supreme Creator—which resides among those born of the gods upon the earth and other realms, and which exists in ever-increasing degrees, has here manifested by Your will; oh, how marvelous! 153.
O Lord of the Gods, because you have approached and established the majesty of the conscious self as the very form of all dharma,
the entire circle of the world’s bonds now functions without obstruction in all its activities.

Your power, endowed with the sovereignty of unimpeded self-majesty and firmly established, never causes even your own atoms to waver in any of your duties concerning beings who are both supreme and non-supreme. 155.
O Blessed One, the entire circle of mantras and the assembly of gods consist of your very self;
indeed, in this threefold world composed of the three qualities, there is nothing whatsoever that is not permeated by you. (156)

O Lord, your powers are imperishable, possessing the consciousness of a fruit that is free from all obstructions and consists of both the supreme and the non-supreme; they pour forth an unimpeded stream of nectar and are the wish-fulfilling cows of the world. 157.
For those whose minds are graced by Your will—the leaders of the Rudras, headed by Śatarudra and Vīra, who enjoy the merits of Brahmā and the other gods—indeed enter the wondrous abode of Śiva. 158.

Just as the eye, though its nature consists of complete vision and action, does not see when covered by cataracts and the like, so too, O Lord, the atomic principle (aṇutattva) does not perceive anything when obstructed by impurities, except through Your grace. (159)

O Blessed One, a person whose entire nature has been delighted by Your qualities, who has swiftly and effortlessly polished away the dense impurities of the five sheaths, shatters the firm cage of worldly existence by taking refuge in You. 160.

Just as here, O Lord, the foliage of the banyan tree abandons its blueness and attains yellowness, so too, O Lord of the Gods, the subtle soul (aṇu), having cast off its state as a bound beast and established itself in Your teaching, indeed attains the state of Śiva. 161.

O Lord, when the bond of blinding darkness has been shattered by the rays of consciousness from Your heart, the skillful man, having realized the entire difference between the individual soul (kalā) and the Supreme Person (puruṣa), is liberated through disciplined practice. 162.

O Lord of the Gods, just as a reflection is not perceived with clarity in a mirror that has become soiled, so too are you—though naturally pure—not clearly discerned when the mind is overwhelmed by a flood of impurities. 163.

O Haṃsa, you destroy for men the dense mass of prosperity that spreads the blinding darkness of the bondage of worldly existence, while you yourself possess a form made manifest by the circle of your own powers, which are superior to fortune, authority, and innate strength, and which transcend the worlds of the senses. 164.
O Lord of the Gods, having transcended the sixfold path of the eightfold rays of consciousness belonging to the realm of manifestation,
those wise ones of tranquil mind, established in the proper time, enter your stainless state.
May [the Lord] bestow that which is the eternal, inconceivable, immortal reality dwelling in the cave of the heart, whose nature is consciousness free from all veils;
and may He grant the attainment of His own distinct powers, which have assumed the form of the stable, secondary, profound, and supreme sovereignty. 166.

It is the whole, yet devoid of parts; free from fluctuation, undisturbed, and situated beyond external disturbances; standing above the sixfold path, transcending it, peaceful, sinless, and the supreme Śiva. 167.
He has transcended the two types of creative intuition (pratibhā) and reached a state of ineffability that is free from clearly defined attributes such as objectivity;
He is the primordial God, both subtle and non-subtle, omnipresent, and all-pervading, with His face, hands, feet, and moments of time extending everywhere. 168.
He has assumed a form consisting of five stable faces, illuminated by his own limbs which remain in an undisturbed state;
he is a planet-like being who transcends the scope of all means of valid cognition, having reached the state of a profound self devoid of any objective apprehension.
O Śaṅkara, having taken refuge in you, the imperishable one, with a consciousness freed from pleasure, pain, and delusion,

and having transcended the eightfold bonds consisting of the threads [of karma], O Blessed One, I clearly become an atom [of liberation] like you. (A group of five verses) At the time of cosmic dissolution, your face, with its copper-red palate, was opened wide by your singular thirst to swallow the universe.
It attains splendor like the southern region, where the sun's orb shines upon the crimson petals of the hundred-petaled lotus. ||171||

Adorned by the rays of the young jewels on the circle of hoods of the lordly serpents bound in his broad topknot, this [crescent moon] resting upon your head bestows prosperity upon you, like the young moon bearing the glow of twilight. ||172||
Your forehead-eye shines, suffused by the circle of rays from the moon that serves as your crest-ornament;
it appears like the splendor fashioned from the remnants of Smara’s ashes, having found its seat within the uneven radiance [of your other eyes]. 173.

In ancient times, you consumed the three cities with an arrow whose brilliance was unshaken as it blazed like fire, which dried up the waters of the celestial river with its broad shaft, and which later became the upward-turning eye of Manmatha.

O Lord, your formidable mass of matted hair, entwined with newly sloughed, dark serpents, shines forth tawny like a circle of smoke from the fire blazing in the eye upon your brow, which is agitated by its constant rolling. (175)

Having assumed a body composed of the night of Kṛṣṇa, O Daughter of the Mountain, it does not for a moment abandon your broad neck, under the guise of a mass of luster ashen from the clearly manifest Kālakūṭa poison. 176.
O Lord, when you formerly set out to burn the cities, the orb of the moon was reduced by you to the state of being a mere wheel;
