it now appears as if its spot were a scar, its dark belly a stain, and its fissured navel a hole. 177.
O Lord of the Gods, the stainless circle of planets, accumulated over many successions of world-dissolutions, serves as the rosary-bead ring for you. 178.

O Lord, Kumāracandrakī dances before you as if out of an impetuous desire to offer instruction, appearing like a cloud heavy with a mass of water upon whose neck rests a peak of manifest Kālakūṭa poison. 179.

O Lord Śaṅkara, by performing dances throughout all the nights with elaborate procedures of hand gestures and rhythmic movements, you enact the likeness of yourself as you abide having pervaded the entire world of moving and unmoving beings. 180.

Having established the lineage of those who have entered the path and being firmly settled in the abode of your father along with your mother, O Blessed One, you are clearly celebrated as the beginningless dust and as the ancient Puruṣa. (181)

O Hara, even by the hosts of gods and demons who surpass all others, having bowed down and become small as they are reflected in the surface of the mirrors that are the nails of your lotus feet, your greatness is fully realized. 182.

The multitude of beings, having sought refuge in Your pair of lotus feet which are the shelter for the world including the gods and asuras, bows down even when prostrated somewhere; yet they certainly never fall downward by the flame of fire. 183.

Salutation to You, the Supreme Self, whose form transcends the sphere of thought, sound, and conceptualization, and who possesses the forms of earth, water, wind, fire, sun, sky, moon, and the sacrificer. 184.
O Lord, even the conceptual constructions of the wise, which fall within the range of intellect and speech, do not find a stable footing here in You;
therefore, having praised You with words that are but a mere atom of truth, I desist from this undertaking, even though I am filled with longing. 185.

By what cause does the favor of the Preceptor of the Gods manifest toward you when you are situated at a great distance, yet fail to manifest even when you are close at hand? And by what cause does its opposite occur? (186)
Or rather, let this wondrous deed of yours remain for now—you whose consciousness is devoid of resentment;
hear what we have undertaken by fixing it in our minds and taking refuge in you, the unborn and the imperishable. (187)
Once, while he was dwelling happily on the Himalayas, his face graced by the playful jests of smiles,
the Daughter of the Mountain approached him from behind and silently covered his eyes with her lotus-like hands as he turned to look.

O Lord, we have heard that in former times a primordial being arose from you, suddenly deprived of his eyesight, like the seed of a mass of darkness swelling at the onset of the night of the Ender at the time of universal destruction. (189) [Yugma] Then,
by the name "Andhaka"— a designation of clear meaning renowned throughout the three worlds— he was so designated.
At that time, you granted a son to the son of Diti, who was performing difficult austerities here for the sake of offspring.
Then, having witnessed his prosperity in the palace and being cherished by the embraces of Manorama,
he set out to perform unrestrained asceticism, which is exceedingly difficult to practice, as he was intent on destroying the blinding darkness [of ignorance].

Having obtained eyes from the Self-existent One through asceticism accumulated over a long time and performed with a serene mind, he attained the unshakeable sovereignty over the worlds—a dominion from which no rival gods or demons could dislodge him. ||192||
Having reached the chest of that [Vishnu], which dispels the mass of darkness with its rays and belongs to Vishnu,
even the discus lost its brilliance, like the shimmering orb of the sun upon the peak of the western mountain.
In battles, the spray of sweat-drops from the heat of Hari’s indignation— conquered by his intense valor—
wiped the face of [his opponent] whose fierce frown was broken into lines.
It flows down incessantly, as if stained by the darkness of her own shadow. ||194||
Thus, O our Lord, whose glorious sovereignty has its crest adorned by the Fortune of the World-Guardians who have been made to pay tribute,
he has taken the captives from the summit of the forest of his palace.
Because of the cause of bondage existing simultaneously with a constant succession. ||195||
Therefore, do now that which is appropriate for this moment; for here is Hari himself, accompanied by the world-protectors,
following you, as you clearly desire to cross even the ocean of worldly existence.
O sinless one, you are a raft; how much more so can you [endure] the suffering of distress? 196.
When he had uttered these words and remained silent with his face cast downward,
the playful onset of anger immediately took hold of the Ganas who had previously approached him.
By the clapping of her palms, the gems on her rings were crushed. ||197||

Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The Description of the Praise of the Blessed One," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked with the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—whose pen-name is Vāgīśvara and whose other name is Vidyādhipati—and who was a dependent of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
The Seventh Canto: Then, [the gods], their shoulders struck by their hands in fierce anger...
With furrowed brows and lips bitten by teeth,
their many kinds of terrible transformations and gestures, accompanied by a coppery glare, flashed forth in the assembly at that time. ||1||

As he entered the assembly hall, his anger was revealed by the loosening of his spotless crown-bands, caused by the friction against the floor as it shook under the weight of his placed feet; meanwhile, his armlet-tip remained caught upon the pillar.
The hem of the soft silk garment of the Enemy of Smara has slipped down.
On the chest of the enraged Gaṇapati,
the thick rows of pearls flying up from the snapping of his necklace produced the appearance of the Fortune of his enemies, who had previously fled and sought refuge in the mark of the elephant-goad.
She possesses a beauty as if sprinkled by a multitude of droplets of perspiration.
Kālamusala, casting a shadow that darkens the quarters of the sky and the directions, with a face made terrifying by the manifestation of a frown, [overwhelms] the entire host of enemies.
He desired to perform what was like the creation of the night of universal destruction.
With a mind heavy with wrath born of intense fury,
Vīrabhadra uttered a terrifying roar of "huṃ" in battle;
from the cavernous hollow of his gaping mouth, wide open in a yawn—
Lengthened by the echoes from the hollows between the mountain ridges.
The shouts of the warriors, thick with the sound of "huṃ" uttered without the terrifying constraint of intense and unrestrained fury,
and the sharp cries produced by the striking of their shoulders against one another;
He somehow perceived a connection between heaven and earth.
In his wrath, he tore from her neck with his lotus-like hand the garland that was dripping with thick nectar and clinging to it were bees;
[the garland] that had come from the Fortune of the enemy of Rati’s Lord.
Like a dark cloud, as if impetuously interrupting his play. ||7||
In the assembly of the Three-formed One, as he rubbed his forehead— which had become pale-red from the heat of fierce anger— with the palm of his hand,
the third eye was visible above it.
Like a cluster of blossoms on her brow, the new column of smoke rises upward. ||8||
With his face turned sideways, his gaze reddened by a frown that was being blunted, and made pale by the rays of his smile—
he who was renowned for the heat of his valor, which was both essential and unrestrained.
His arm was seen by the fire as if it were being reduced to ashes. ||9||
Bearing a face with his adamantine fist placed upon his lower lip— which, as if out of fear of being bitten by his own teeth, was trembling and agitated—
he struck the staff-like arm of the enemy of the gods with his hand.
With a continuous flow of horripilation blossoming from the passion of his agitation. ||10||
The winds of his breath, entering the openings in the earth revealed by the impact of his hands as he lowered his face,
caused the lotuses within the depths of the netherworld to bloom.
[She was] like a white lotus whose remaining petals had been gathered up.
A bee, turned tawny by the thick pollen of the fresh filaments of flowers in his crest, fell down,
struck by the honey-intoxicated [club] of Bhṛṅgiriṭi as he suddenly crushed it against his forehead.
With his face turned upward, he was like the pupil of an eye, tawny with the crest of a flame.
From the opening of his mouth, Naḍakūbara— his eyes reddened with rage— emitted a mass of smoke from his *huṃkāra* outbursts,
as if with eagerness to swallow the king of the Daityas.
The people gazed upon her as she suddenly leapt up, like a magical spell (kṛtyā).
The swarm of bees, languid with the confidence born of excessive drinking of the makaranda nectar hanging from his throat,
[rests] upon that elephant who is a lake for the waters of battle against arrogant enemies.
The lotus garland of Jiṣṇu shone like a chain. ||14||
Thinking that his own arm was his only sinless companion in battle— having performed its ablution in the flood of water consisting of the rays of his fingernails—
he stroked that tree-like arm with his palm.
Then, his form became difficult to behold, and he caused distress to all the worlds. ||15||

The orb of the sun, terrifying and difficult to behold, creates the delusion of a clinging headless trunk through its connection with the dense streaks of smoke arising from its friction against the moving forehead of the mountain.
The beautiful form, possessing unimpaired splendor, beheld [him]. ||16||
A mass of smoke from the wick, rising into the sky from the hollow of his cupped hands as they pressed firmly together,
shone like a white lotus with its petals slightly unfolded.
Like a row of bees emerging from the belly of Agnika’s treasury. ||17||
And by the touch of the mass of flame-tips from the upward-gazing eyes of Krodheśvara— [a touch] consisting of rows of skulls upon his crown—
the mountain peaks were scorched by the rays of the sun of universal destruction.
With a loud, sharp *ṭāṃkāra* sound, his head shattered.
With the stalks of the bodies of the remaining [beings] completely agitated,
and with fragments of vast cloud-leaves whirling about,
the lotus of the world— [the form] of Caṇḍeśvara— ...
She withered under the power of the heat from her hot, heavy sighs. ||19||
Tālaketu trembled, drenched with drops of sweat,
his mouth gaping with a terrifying yawn that reddened the surface of his palate;
he was like one who has conquered the Fortune of his enemy standing before him through mere thought.
Or perhaps due to the force of a tight embrace, or from the intensity of another's passion. ||20||
The arm of Lulāyaketu, whose face was turned sideways, shone like the trunk of a victorious elephant, variegated with the decorative patterns of white ashes from the flashes of his laughter.
His broad shoulders were like formidable, high-rising frontal globes upon a pedestal.
In that assembly, streams of dharma-water flowed forth from his anger, possessing the luster of a face ruddy with thick vermilion;
they were as pale as the sprouts of moonbeams, yet possessed stars of light that cast doubt upon them.
From the necklace of Sunandaka, clusters of water droplets [fell]. ||22||
And even when you were enraged, Śeṣa— distressed by the weight of your feet and raising his thick, long hoods—
did not display his thousand curved and formidable hoods.
The earth, becoming slack, was barely supported with great difficulty.

Beholding him enraged, whose banner bears the peacock’s tail and who, with his webbed rays, illuminates all twelve directions— resembling the day of universal destruction— though they [the gods] were attempting to do so.
They did not make their forms possess the radiance of a thousand eyes.
Anointed with the thick paste of saffron-like dust arising from the fragments of harsh stones crushed by her armlets,
she appears as if adorned, though she is a transformation brought about by the wrath of the Five-Eyed One.
It was like a pearl necklace formed from a multitude of droplets of perspiration. ||25||

How was it that the assembly of Dhūrjaṭi was not somehow scorched by the sparks scattered by the wrathful Diṇḍis, who were stained with smoke arising from the mutual clashing of their hands? For the submarine fire—though its flames were quenched by the water of the ocean—was not extinguished even when the gods, having obtained the nectar, drank it all. How could the fire of the wrath of Śiva, which had been kindled by the friction of his matted locks, be extinguished by the mere water of the ocean? Indeed, the submarine fire was not quenched by the water of the ocean; rather, it was the fire of Śiva’s anger that could not be extinguished. Furthermore, the submarine fire was not quenched by the water of the ocean, nor was it extinguished by the gods drinking the nectar; how then could the fire of Śiva’s wrath be extinguished by the water of the ocean? He brought about her utter confusion with his piercing glances.
The temple of Agni was strewn with thick, trickling drops of sweat and smeared with saffron paste that was beginning to dry;
its vast golden dome appeared like a wandering star.
His chest attained the splendor of the slopes of the king of mountains.
With the masses of dust from crushed necklaces—
resembling a scattering of ashes— that reddened the splendor of his eyes, he threw the circle of the earth into turmoil like a fever.
The three-headed one, whose transformation of anger was difficult to restrain, [appeared] in the assembly. ||28||

Like serpents emerging from the hollows of anthills, they issued from the openings of their mouths, which stained the expanse of the sky with the sparks of fire intensified by the brilliant jewels upon their hoods.
Then, with staffs of smoke produced by the sound "hum," they emerged from the fire-pits.

Even for Āmardaka, the crusher of the enemies of the gods, the mass of smoke from his "hum" sound— which serves as fresh, dark leaf-designs upon the faces of the women of the quarters— acts as a protective barrier for the lotus of the world.
The rows of bees hovering over her angry belly lent it great beauty. ||30||
The dust of him whose flame-tips were entwined with necklaces formed from the mass of moonbeams swallowed in his wrath,
and who was expanding through the quarters of the sky agitated by his fury—
It was like a spray of rodhra pollen upon the surface of Lakṣmī’s cheeks. ||31||
Possessing a luster terrifying with the contortions of fierce, crooked brows tawny like a mass of flame-tips,
it shone like a cloud adorned with a steady flash of lightning amidst a heavy downpour of water.
Beholding his face, she became afraid and sought to protect herself from fear. ||32||
As Tāra cast a sidelong glance, copper-red like fire, filled with wrath and emitting a piercing *huṃ* sound,
the delicate leaf-patterns on her body instantly melted away from the heat of that gaze.
His staff-like arm had the tips of his shoulders adorned with golden armlets. ||33||
With the skill of swallowing the three worlds in a single mouthful, as if in a fit of rage at death’s desire to devour them,
his mouth was wide open in a yawn, revealing a terrifying tongue.
Beholding him in the assembly, the worlds were struck with awe.
Spreading across the broad, copper-colored palate, which was strewn with sparks from the fire of fearless *huṃ* sounds,
it was touched by the rays of the sun as red as the unmingled twilight.
The blood-stained head was like the sky with a formidable face. ||35||
The mouth of Agnimukha, gaping wide in a yawn, with its copper-colored tongue and a row of formidable, bared teeth,
shone like a frying pan from which sparks of fire have burst forth.
Its interior was filled with parched grain, white like the belly of a serpent resting upon a row [of stones]. ||36||
When the three-peaked mountain, its eyes clearly reddened by the blossoms of the *tindukinī* tree, sighed deeply in anger,
the descent of the world's dissolution was indeed imminent.
The assembly of kings did not perceive that he was trembling uncontrollably—
[he who was] struck on the surface of his shoulder by the palm of the hand, from which a row of sapphire fragments splintered forth as his armlets were crushed.
The mass of bees, agitated by the fragrance of the offerings of lotuses upon the paved floor of Time, became like a display of shimmering beauty. ||38||
The quarters were filled with harsh cries arising from the shoulders of those whose arms and hands were crushed and struck;
the circle of gods and asuras was awakened and incensed.
By Antaka, whose prowess is difficult to restrain even at the time of universal dissolution. ||39||
The sound of the tinkling gems on the armlets being shattered by the blows of Caṇḍānana’s hands was heard; it was like the sound of the teeth of Yama,
who has increased his speed for the destruction of the Daityas.
It produced a sound resembling the terrifying roar of crashing thunderbolts. ||40||
With his neck and shoulders bearing gaping wounds shattered by blows,
and his fierce arms and bracelets loosened as they flailed upward,
he— like an image of Death himself— was filled with rage.
With the walls of his thick cheeks bristling with horripilation and trembling with agitation. ||41||
Beholding the wielder of the discus weapon, who had suddenly become enraged,
whose pair of hands had their waves crushed by the pressure of his towering shoulders,
and whose face was as difficult to gaze upon as the sun of universal destruction;
The hosts of gods, having become afraid, did not even remember themselves.

The circle of light from the teeth, gleaming with laughter that treated the battle with the sons of Diti as a mere trifle, turned the quarters of the sky into a spectacle where the expanding signs of the impending dissolution were made manifest.
Like a blue vajra amidst flowers growing on a tree trunk. ||43||
The pet parrot of the daughter of Śikhin (Agni) desired to devour the scattered succession of sparks from the fire of his *huṃkāra* uttered by the impetuous [peacock] before him—
sparks as ruddy as the ripening [fruit] of the peacock's own birthplace.
With a bewildered mind, he suspected even a ball of rice to be a grain of gold.
His forehead, furrowed by a knitting of the brows, assumed as it were a state of agitation born of fear from the burning of a meteoric fire, shimmering with the flickering rays of his tawny eyes.
Nandi struck the surface of the mosaic floor with his foot.
He bore a turbid radiance arising from the laughter and loud cackling issuing from the cavity of his upturned face—
a shimmering light emerging from the depths of the netherworld as it swayed unrestrainedly.
The splendor of his remaining body was white with the radiance of the moon. ||46||
A face with cheeks bristling and trembling from horripilation, eyes wide and bloodshot with lids rolling upward,
and a nose distorted by the gaping of the formidable, bitten lips.
The cloud-bannered god (Indra) assumed a reddish hue with a knitting of his eyebrows. ||47||
Having donned his armor with a deep-seated passion for battle, he suddenly manifested like wrath incarnate;
with a roar as deep as the caverns of Pātāla, he crushed [his foes].
He made the earth tremble, distressed by the blows of his heels.
Jayanta bore the scars of weapon wounds upon his body, where horripilation shimmered at the edges and thick drops of perspiration gathered;
he resembled a tree on the bank of a pond with but a little water remaining, where young sprouts have grown.
With his chest resembling a lake of young grass sprouts. ||49||
The rear portion [of the chariot] was strewn with stars— jewels from necklaces shattered by the force of its recoil—
and its floor was variegated by a multitude of loosened celestial bodies.
She became like a flash of lightning amidst the play of the winds of destruction. ||50||
The earth, distressed by the playful blows from the hands and heels of the attendants who were overwhelmed by a weight of indignation and joy, resounded;
while in the palate of the netherworld, the timid serpents were filled with agitation.
It possessed a terrible roar from the violent destruction of those who were arrogant regarding their embryos.
The jeweled floor of the ground shone with the heaps of armlets and bracelets of the lords of the thirty gods fallen from their shoulders as they were crushed,
like the impact of the thunderbolt hurled by the hand of Purandara.
Like the mountain ranges with their wings of ridges torn asunder. ||52||
As if to instantly extinguish the flames of the Daityas' prowess,
they sportively [discharged] showers of droplets of the water of righteousness from the broad surfaces of their foreheads.
Having dragged [him] forth with their fingertips, those of harsh wrath acted. ||53||
In an instant, the lords of the Gaṇas, filled with wrath, [assumed] faces formidable with yawning, gaping, and contortions, from the corners of which issued forth sparks of a subtle fire.
With its formidable fangs, it seemed as if it were about to devour the entire circle of the quarters.
By the weight of their turning back, as their armlets were shattered by the impact of their mutual shoulder-blades,
their weapons clattered upon the edge of the rugged pavement.
The necklaces, as if out of fear of being crushed by his wrathful hands, have become bonds. ||55||
The world-protectors, their armored coats bristling with horripilation as they were overwhelmed by the terrifying sword-blade playfully cast by his glance,
became powerless and grew enraged at his tawny cheeks.
By the portions [of the moon] in the assembly of the Kapālis, that is, by the lords of the Gaṇas. ||56||

As the assembly of Śiva drew near, it assumed the likeness of the moment of universal dissolution; it was terrible with the crashing sounds of mountain peaks tossed aside by the effortless breaths of his attendants, and its living beings were distressed.
With the tips of their tusks white with the pollen raised from the pearls of necklaces ground by the friction of their clearly clenched trunks,
they were like the gods at the end of the rainy season.
He was perceived as one whose stability was fashioned upon a foundation of firmness. ||58||
Brāhmī made the radiance of all the directions turn tawny at dawn with the particles of dust raised by the ruby-studded rings as their hands rubbed against one another.
She appeared like a blooming lotus with the masses of pollen on her hands. ||59||
With the casting of harsh side-glances, radiant with the outpouring of thousands of flames from the fire rising in his wrath,
he whose form was that of the Three-Eyed One illuminated the three worlds for a moment like a meteor.
Like staffs dispelling the agitation of the gods.
The discus, out of an impetuous desire to sever the circle of the enemy hosts, was made to whirl;
it was fierce, with the tips of its straight fingers (or spokes) being formidable.
It was clung to his hand like the abundant ear-ornament of the Goddess of Victory. ||61||
There, Vaiṣṇavī held her lotus-hand, which was filled with the fury and agitation of the circle of Asuras and whose lotus-fingers were stained by the dripping nectar from the tips of her ruby rings.
Under the guise of the dust that shook off the reddish-brown glow of its wounds. ||62||
Her copper-hued face assumed the guise of a swaying, playful braid of bees under the pretext of the graceful movement of her eyebrows, which were arched into a frown—
the very embodiment of the fury for crushing all adversaries.
Bhadrakālī possesses a lotus as playful as a sprout of the hand. ||63||
Thus, at that time, she— making the quarters of the sky variegated by the circles of light from the flood of bright pearls falling as her necklace was crushed—
was like the shore agitated by the uneven waves of a heap of jewels.
The assembly was filled with hundreds of shouting Gaṇapatis, like a mass of turbulent waves. ||64||

Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Description of the Disturbance in the Assembly," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who is adorned by Vāgīśvara, the servant of the illustrious Bāla-Bṛhaspati, and who also bears the name Vidyādhipati.
The Eighth Canto: In this manner, [the fire of] the anger of the Lord of the Gaṇas was pacified...
Like a cause,
the strings of moonstone necklaces on Śiva’s head released a shower of pure water by virtue of the falling rays from the jagged crescent moon upon his crown. ||1||
In those [palaces], whose interiors were whitened by the spreading glow of moonlight from the shimmering nets of rays of pearl-hanging necklaces,
[the swords] appeared like the white fame of the enemy faction, which had been drunk up and was now as bright as the moon.
While many staffs were held in the palms of the hands of numerous soldiers.
By the tossing of the tips of his palms, he bore the splendor of a ruby ball, Mount Mandara, and the lunar orb;
while his arm, like a celestial tree, was tethered— its arrangement...
as if bestowing a morsel of food upon the elephant of his own prowess. ||3||
His body was encircled by a serpent of dark hue, possessing the splendor of blackness and formidable due to its coiled posture;
its form was like a mass of crushed collyrium dust gathered at the edges.
The glory of the circle of the earth, with its moats formed by the ocean and its shadows provided by the trees. ||4||
Having playfully drawn his club, which was like the staff of Death (Kālamusala), with his upper garment slipping from the peak of his fleshy shoulders,
he uttered these unrestrained words with a voice like the roar of clouds:
[He beheld] the blue-throated Śiva (Nīlakaṇṭha), whose face was distressed as he performed a trembling dance out of apprehension. (A group of five verses.
Those [mental states] whose acquisition is famously said to be non-substantial, mutually produced, and of a fluctuating nature;
Having indeed transcended all those conceptual constructions as well as words, he has attained a state of being whose form is unmixed.
By him, through the unrestrained display of the *tāṇḍava* dance commenced at the onset of the night of the dissolution of the world,
another sky was as if lifted up, bearing the massed clouds of twilight.
He bore the passion like a cloud of the enemy's elephant-hide dripping with blood.
The moon on whose crown, its base overturned by the wind from the waves of the ocean of clouds,
appears as if it were the tip of a fingernail applied to cut it— [that moon] brings prosperity.
Even now, the skull of the Supreme Lord remains upon my head.
Upon whose [feet], when he sportively placed his fingernails— smeared with lac-dye by the Daughter of the Mountain King during their amorous encounters—
the stalks of the lotus-thrones were playfully severed.
It appeared as if wet with thick, trickling blood. ||9||
He whose thousand flames from the fire of his eyes part the darkness of the celestial path during the twilights,
while the submarine fire flickers within the waters surrounding it—
The playful ocean whose belly is tawny, illuminating the [hidden] arguments.
Upon whose upward gaze rested this mass of smoke without fuel— this very fire, whose mark of dust was disregarded, yet which remained unextinguished even as his head faltered.
The rays of which were both conducive to the pacification of one who has bathed in the Gaṅgā and otherwise [opposing]. ||11||

The bow of Hara, drawn upwards and aimed with a flaming arrow at the time of burning the city, was beheld by the gods as it rested upon the arms of Śarabha, whose nose was like a serpent clinging to a straight branch.
Terror-inspiring with the knitting of the eyebrows of his radiant third eye.
And the shadow of his body was seen by the throngs of forest-dwellers rushing toward him as he assumed the form of a Kirāta in sport—
the shadow that concealed within its throat the Kālakūṭa poison.
Possessing a dark splendor, as if resulting from the transformation of the radiance of a peak. ||13||
Even when the hunter’s body had been cast off,
the Daughter of the Mountain King stood facing him, wearing a pearl necklace whose strands were reddened by the luster of her three eyes.
Like the tips of her breasts embraced by a garland of *guñjā* berries. ||14||
Possessing sweetness with its qualities unimpaired,
agitating the entire circle of gods and asuras,
it remains entirely unbroken even before the eyes of the god whose banner is the sea-monster.
The fire of the Raurava hell was instantly consumed by that Lord.
Even the Lotus-born [Brahmā] cannot touch this Lord, by whose skill in splitting the panels of the door of illusion not even a trace of impurity remains in the three worlds.

Even the expectation [of victory] causes remorse toward others. (A group of eleven verses) Who indeed could endure this spear in battle, which leaves the waters of the ocean distressed by the heat of the fire from its branches?
He bears a terrifying appearance due to the knitting of his eyebrows, fierce with anger like the Night of Doom (Kālarātri) arisen from the devouring of the world. ||17||
The sparks of fire flickering within the branches made jagged by the tips of the swans' beaks that serve as its support—
these are released by this [fire], like the world-consuming fire at the end of an eon.
Scattering like showers of seeds throughout the ten directions. ||18||
While the lords of the gods watched, distressed with fear, [he],
out of anger, used a saw with sharp-edged teeth to sever his head—
even though he was a dweller in the lotus-abode— [with] no small...
What obstacle was there for him as he cut through [the bonds] in the assembly? ||19||
With a terrifying form that playfully tore asunder the elephant-demon with the tips of his millions of fang-like, jagged caverns,
this lion among gods possesses the sinless five-facedness.
He bears [the world] upon the mass of hair that resembles the crescent moon of his crest.

Upon his head rests the breaking of high waves, exceedingly cool from contact with the crescent moon of his crest-ornament, while the seven oceans have been dried up by the fierce radiance of his sun-like splendor.
The Gaṅgā does not go to dryness even at the dissolution of the world.
Upon the surface of the mirror-like golden bowl, which had burst open from the intense heat of the fire of her slightly squinted eyes during his destruction,
she clearly beheld the face of the Daughter of the Mountain.
He made the entire egg of the lotus-seated one fruitful. ||22||
This face of his, possessing the deep black luster of a swarm of bees, expanding like the night at the time of universal dissolution—
entering it, the entire world undergoes its final destruction within that darkness.
Seeding all around in the southern direction. ||23||

Or rather, let this one remain far off— devoid of the transformations of existence arising from the fire of suffering in the seven worlds that have been made his object; let him be one who stands beyond all things, from the unmanifest and the Great Principle down to the specific elements.
The sole cause for the states of the arising, subsistence, and destruction of the universe. ||24||
While the Dānava warriors look on, I shall now seize the Fortune of the Lord of Daityas, Bali, even before he has completed his three steps, just as the wielder of the Śārṅga bow did.
His thick, staff-like arms were tawny with the rays of his discus. (A pair of verses.
Crushing the enemy generals whose firm joints of bone were being shattered, I, devoid of pride, [advanced].
Why do I now bear the name Kāla (Time) after having assumed the nature of a mace? For in battle, that name possesses the true essence of human effort. ||26||

Holding the Sumeru mountain-staff in his hand, he [beheld] the circle of the earth, marked by the fluttering rags fashioned from the waves of the mass of waters at its edge, like silken Chinese garments.
Shall I suddenly lift it up like a playful parasol? ||27||

Let the soldiers now behold me, who am possessed of great splendor manifested here in the form of Diksundarī, as if with my glories that are like the essence of pure sandalwood, while [they] deliver firm blows with their heels.
It stood upon the shattered enemy of the gods (Rāhu), who resembled a toppled mountain of gold.
This single right arm of mine, smeared with the paste of fresh sandalwood, is capable of making women separated from their lovers tremble,
like the pervasive Malaya breeze.
The women are like creepers whose flowers are the falling streams of their tears. ||29||
Like the sun, I shall swiftly restore the splendor of day, which was obscured by the mass of darkness— the Daityas— who were bold enough to seize the circle of the quarters with violent haste.
The tip of his sword-blade was as crimson as blood, eclipsing the splendor of Arjuna.
The winds shall soon carry away to their destruction the smearings of blood-sandalwood paste and the dust of necklaces made of skulls ground wet with handfuls of sweat from my enemies.
Rising from the circles of fly-whisks shaken by female bards. ||31||

Though alone, he bore a brow tawny with rage, its surface bristling with horripilation as it struck the row of skulls of the many world-protectors who were trembling with agitation; he held aloft his sword.
With my hand, made wretched by compassion, I ward off the wheel of the enemy. ||32||
In these lotus-pools of battle, which abound in profundity,
what else remains clutched in the hand once one's virtues have been relinquished?
Like lotus stalks fouled by mud, [the virtues of] the King of Daityas—
O bull-bannered one, enter my army without hesitation as I shatter it. ||33||
For me, impetuous in battle amidst the throngs of the foremost Dānavas, whose shadows were like those of shaken tamāla groves,
my sword-blades were like the rays of the summer sun.
Now let splendor flash forth with even more intense majesty.
For she who constantly bears an exceeding delicacy is not even able to endure the wound caused by a thorn; let her,
who is a source of wonder, lay down her sharp sword—
Fortune does not falter in her step upon the path of the stream. ||35||
Let this staff-like arm of mine at the door now bring about the immobilization of Śrī during the combat,
as she strikes against the other door-panel with which she has formed a firm union.
The two settlements possessed excellent fences on both sides, like woven silk cloths.
Like the playful Varāha, this arm— with its broad, swelling shoulder-blade and shimmering, massive armlet—
destroys its enemies like the overturned Golden Mountain.
May my splendor, dark as a fresh rain-cloud, expand forth.

Like Upendra [Viṣṇu] pulling Mount Mandara, he draws forth Lakṣmī, who is being dragged by the gods and asuras whose arms— difficult to withstand due to mutual envy— are raised high in the surge of pride.
I shall make her alone, as if imprisoned within the cage of my arms;
may she soon bring forth for me a pure mass of glory that serves as a mirror for the playful reflections of the three worlds.
His hand was as if covered by the dust from the funeral pyres of his enemies—who were arrogant with pride—slain by the staff-like arms of that very [king] on the field of battle. ||39||
For a great and radiant being is able to repeatedly bestow favor or inflict harm upon another great being at the proper time;
just as the sun swiftly causes the moon to wane and then to wax full.
And it forcibly brings about a loss of luster at dawn. ||40||
Like a streak of the dark Kālakūṭa poison within the mass of clouds in the belly of the ocean, she was the boundary of the realm of Yama for the enemy of Manmatha;
[she who, on the path of battle, performed the embrace of the neck with the former gods...]
May the sword-blade of my Lord now perform its task for me. ||41||
With their throats cruelly sliced by the sharp-pointed, harsh, and dense thorns of the Kūṭaśālmalī trees,
they did not look up, O Lord, as if thinking, "The calamity of our master has not yet been seen."
Let headless trunks dance in the battle, filled with joy.
In the battle, let the rut-fluid— reddened by the dust of vermilion from the temples shaken by the slapping of ears—
be released like blood upon the circle of enemies.
The clouds over the temples of the elephants portend the destruction of the army.
May his body now become a mere collection of splinters, pulled from his frame by the gaping mouths of fierce jackals, which flash with excitement as they cling to their greed for flesh.
O Lord, it is like a flock of birds that has found its protector. ||44||
Or rather, what need have I for these— those forest fires that burn the boundaries of the world’s groves,
those lions among the camari-deer of the enemy armies,
who stand there as the glory of victory over the assembly of the sons of Diti?
O Lord, your warriors have hands eager to seize you by the hair. ||45||
Behold the peerless hero Bhadra in battle, amidst elephants formidable with deep and terrifying roars that dwarf the waters filling the depths of the mountains.
O Giver of Boons, [your power] is irresistible against the armies of your enemies. ||46||
From the circular trench of his sword-blade, which was constantly made more tender by the sprinkling of the blood-water gushing forth from the severed heads of his enemies,
and which was filled with a swarm of arrows like bees—
Shining forth for a long time upon the surface of the forest of battle. ||47||
Clinging to the tree of the hero’s arm, which has the pale luster of the moon, she bears a mass of flowers that is her fame;
she is the spreading cause for the production of a great abundance of fruit.
May the creeper of royal fortune surely attain immediate growth.
(A yugma) The radiant ones who have assembled here clearly illuminate this single task, which is the foremost support for all undertakings.
With a brilliance especially intense at the time of universal dissolution, they possess exceedingly hot rays; like the day at its rising, they are difficult to behold. ||49||
The royal swan in the temple on the sandy banks of the Mandākinī, bewildered by the dull roar of clouds agitated by the sound [of the battle],
while the circles of gods and asuras trembled with rage—
Having said this, Kālamuśala ceased speaking. ||50||
At that time, he was one whose great jewel of a mind was radiant with the intense brilliance manifested by the rubies of his speech; thus,
within the assembly of the lords of the Gaṇas, his inner desire to speak was revealed.
With his gaze fixed upon their faces, he beheld those whose lips were quivering.
Then the host of heroes, their limbs bristling with thrill upon hearing the full expansion of those powerful words, moved forward,
their shoulders struck by the resolve for the sport of battle that had approached them.
His arms were adorned with armlets that possessed the luster of radiant, polished jewels.

Thus ends the eighth canto, titled "The Description of the Utterance of the Staff of Kālamusala," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who is known by the name Vidyādhipati and bears the mark of Vāgīśvara, being a dependent of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
The Ninth Canto:
When the Lord of the Gaṇas had thus spoken these words, being solely intent on the task of waging war against the Daityas—
With the top of his shoulder quivering with the desire to speak, he, who was composed of light, spoke these peaceful words. ||1||
His policy, which utterly destroyed arrogant enemies through his warriors, was pursued by one who,
lacking the joy of the festival of battle, found his weight in the exertion of wisdom.
In battles where the quarters of the sky were shrouded in dense darkness by the swaying blades of swords brandished with graceful agility,
he alone roamed sportively, never experiencing fear.

Because his heart had become the abode of unfathomable being, even the sky could not equal it, for while the sky possesses only a minute fraction of its vastness, that heart was free from the defect of emptiness.
Having observed that Lakṣmī had established her residence upon his lotus-like face which was in full bloom, Sarasvatī,
as if out of rivalry with her, took up residence in his mouth, which possessed sufficient beauty and exquisite tenderness.
In his military expeditions, the dust born from the crushing of enemy armies flowed through the quarters of the sky,
as if to fill up the hollows and depressions of the earth so that it might become fit for the wandering of his fame.

He who, in battles, always bore his arm—intoxicated with the passion for crushing hosts of powerful enemies—as if its hair stood on end from the touch of royal fortune, which had forever taken up its residence there. (7)

By him, having granted fearlessness to his enemies who bowed down at the front of the battle, a beautiful fame was acquired—a fame that possessed the luster of Hara’s loud laughter and served as the silken sash for the goddesses of the quarters. (8)
The arrows released from his slender bow drawn back to his ear fell in battle, severing the lives, the bows, and the bodies of his enemies. (9)

The collyrium of envy belonging to the passionate women of his enemies was shattered— as if out of anger— by the moonlight of his fame, which had long cast darkness upon their eyes that now illuminate all directions.
As he spoke with a deep resonance, the radiance of his teeth, streaming forth from his face, adorned it like the moonlight adorning the full orb of the moon. (11) (A group of ten verses:
"Can the trembling of the mountain range be attributed to the impact of the cry of a sparrow? (12)
The third eye of the enraged Madana, blazing like a star, became a bringer of calamity when his bow was drawn into a circle by the string and his meditative concentration was broken. ||13||
He who bears the heavy yoke of the world in the tasks of creation, maintenance,
and dissolution— even though he stands here as the refuge for gods and demons— tell me, why is there such agitation among you?
(A pair of verses) I believe this lotus-like eye of the Lord, which is now closing, is his fifth face.
He meditates upon nothing other than the welfare of the world, contemplating the Self which is the moon-crested Lord. ||15||
This multitude of gods and demons, seized by destruction, shines with fragments of jewels from their necklaces and serpent-ornaments,
as if still not releasing their throats even now, while being liberated by living beings through successive incarnations.
As if knitting her brows because this [ocean] bore the streams flowing from all the joints of the limbs of the Nārāyaṇa-form, Gaṅgā seized him by the hair with her waves. 17.

The celestial river, falling from the vault of heaven into the hollows within the cavities of the garland of skulls, displays the splendor of a torrent of water released from clouds clinging to the tips of the hair at the parting of the head. (18)

With the reflection of Nārāyaṇa’s face resting upon one half of his body, which is dark as a rain-cloud, he attains a beauty as if touched by the dense shadow of smoke from the fire upon the altar of his forehead. 19.
The splendor of the throat’s interior shines forth, dark as collyrium and permeated by the hue of potent kālakūṭa poison;
it becomes dense, with its internal joints unmanifested and not harsh. 20.
As the snowy plateaus melt away, the weapon of the Snowy Mountain, fierce with its loud *ṭāṅkāra* and *tārā* sounds, somehow finds a way to gain passage in order to burn the forests. (30)

Intending to extinguish the rows of flames with the water from the sprouts of the jewel-creeper, he fiercely burns even the celestial trees, which are mistaken for smoke by the bees [hovering about them]. (31)
The skull, which serves as the dwelling for the moon-crested Lord within the bower of his matted locks, appears as if smeared with its shadow;
yet, obstructed by the mass of flames within, it utterly consumes the orb of the hot-rayed sun.
The moon’s orb, bearing the mark of the semblance of a streak of smoke first clinging to it,
is scorched by the overflowing flames, which offer oblations of streams of milk formed from thick, trickling nectar.

The host of stars, rendered tawny from afar by the copper-colored glow of his dense thousand crests, is utterly consumed, as if overwhelmed by a mass of sparks scattering through the quarters of the sky. 34.

With hundreds of crests that imitate a mass of chowries reddish-brown with the hue of madder, and which are shaken by the terrified winds, the fire, spreading with unceasing force, burns the Lord of the Gods as it clings to his sides at that very moment.
The flame, flickering at its edges from the tips of the slender whorls of the Four-Faced One’s ears,
reduces to ashes in an instant the lotus-seat whose petals are his eyelashes, radiant with their ash-like form.

Thus, at the arrivals of the cosmic dissolutions, Fire attended upon this triple world many times over by means of the application of the playful smearing of ashes— the very act of his own scattering— by gradually reducing the three worlds to ash. (Ten verses form a *kulaka*) With his feet firmly planted in the netherworld (*rasātala*), his neck slightly bent and his head held high...
The tortoise bears its back with great elegance, as if it were supporting Mount Mandara after it had been lifted up.

As Murāri whirled between his two staff-like arms, whose ring-fingers were interlaced like a circular rim, the mountain was shattered by the friction against his sides by the gem-studded ornaments on his forearms. (39)
The nectar-drenched peaks of the mountain, being dragged by the serpents bound to it, shine as if they were the waves of the ocean being churned under the guise of their trembling reflections. (40)

The mountain’s slopes alone were augmented by boulders that had fallen from its waist— boulders made thin by the intense friction of being dragged by venomous serpents— and which now lay nestled within its hollows.

The circle of flames rising from the hissing of the lord of serpents’ expanded hoods—his throat-pits being crushed by the queen of the Daityas—is swallowed up by the whirling waves like the orbs of the sun at the end of an aeon. 42.
The series of waves, shattered by the impact of Mount Mandara as it reeled from being dragged by the gods and demons, rushes with speed toward the four quarters like one seeking refuge. 43.
As if desiring to embrace from afar Lakṣmī as she rose from the ocean with the fluctuations of his mind,
the mountain Mandara itself is being firmly pressed by the arms of the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
Firmly embraced by the staff-like arms of Vaikuṇṭha, the form of Mount Mandara trembles,
its pure waterfalls falling down from its slopes which resemble silken garments.

The river Sarasvatī rises as the beloved of the lords of the gods, bringing forth the excellence of her virtues; she momentarily causes the disappointment of those who harbor the expectation of confidence born from the hope of attaining nectar.
For a moment, the pure crescent of the moon rises tall, entwined within the bowers of young sprouts,
as if preparing to dwell upon the tip of Śiva’s matted locks.
Bearing a playful redness upon its circles of coral creepers— as if it were the reflection of the tips of women's hair clinging to a cluster of ruby flowers—
the Pārijāta tree rises up gracefully.
The Mandara mountain, with its fragments of coral dust rising from the churning waters, having momentarily clung to the celestial elephant,
attains the state of being a tall golden pillar fixed to his hitching post.
Being scorched slightly here and there by the submarine fire as if by a physician's cauterization,
Uccaiḥśravas, with his thousand manes tossed upward, springs up impetuously from the midst of the waves.
Emerging from the milk-ocean, which is fairer than the moon, this mass of poison possesses a dark luster;

swallowed and remaining within his throat, it bears the playful charm of a garland of blue lotuses through its radiance. (A group of fourteen verses) It assumes the broad central cavity of both the sun and the moon as they form their circular discs.
It was as if proclaiming its terrifying nature, foretelling the imminent destruction of the lord of the Daityas by means of its surging portents. ||52||
Mounted upon their chariot, the horses, composed of the Vedas and drenched by the heat of the scorching sun,
pull the pole-bearing vehicle with their necks repeatedly bending and their flanks rolling as they turn.
The earth, with its mountain-pilings, has been turned into a chariot by the spreading mass of fire from the sun’s rays as they form a circle; thus heated, it attains a profound firmness.
In ancient times, while traveling with the desire to block the path of the sun, the Vindhya mountain—the banner of its lineage—had its excessive growth restrained by Agastya;
yet now, under another form, it once again obstructs the path of the sky.
The mountain, its middle portion thinned by the friction of the coils of Vāsuki and possessing a beauty of being grasped by a fist,
attains the state of a bow-staff with both its peaks bent down at their tips.
With the surface of his neck made uneven by the intense pressure of being bound with the cord from the bow of the Lord of Mountains,
the elephant performs, as it were, the preliminary rite for the act of burning with the fire of his sighs.

In due course, for the sake of the destruction of the lord of the Daityas, Janārdana—whose power remains unimpeded in the worlds—assumes the state of an arrow by means of his own illusory power, having contracted his body. 58.
Even before Śauri had made him an arrow, he became a barb, inflicting intense burning;
for the mass of fire was like a heap of embers to the young women of the circle of Asuras whom it sought to consume. (59)
With the speed of the destructive time that is capable of crushing the peaks of all the mountains drawn in,
he causes a trembling in the hearts of the great asuras by means of the rows of feathers on his wind-tufted arrows.

Thus, this very one alone— having mounted the foremost of chariots whose banner was Mount Sumeru and which was guided by Viriñci with the *praṇava* as his goad— reduced the triple city to ashes. (Ten verses in a *kulaka*) [He,] whose form was difficult to behold due to his uplifted wrath, [was like fire] tawny with the flames of blazing, terrible fire.
The rising frown seems to impel the third eye toward a fierce burning.
From the fire of his eyes, which clings to his body and is matted with fierce flames, streams of sweat-drops gush forth in haste, as if to extinguish it. (63)
Like lightning flashing from a twilight cloud from the multitude of stars in her forehead-eye, she—
brilliant with tawny radiance— was honored by the closing of eyes rather than being gazed upon.
When his passion had been thus consumed by the fire of his eyes, his anger and his grace both expanded in such a way that they found a footing in the limbs of women,
which were like lakes of the nectar of loveliness.
(Kalāpaka) Like oceans of water for the sake of extinguishing the conflagration of the seven worlds and the gods and asuras who were in agitation—
They clash with one another in a most terrible manner, driven by a wild and impetuous speed, as they strike against each other like a mass of ripples.
The orb of the hot-rayed sun grew dim, its heat exhausted by the forest fires whose flames licked upward;
it seemed as if it were being traversed by the limbs of the ocean’s waves, which had become intermingled with one another.
As the four-faced Brahmā was writhing in agitation, wondering "What is this?", a copious shower of nectar trickled from his lotus-mouth, which appeared as a mass of red luster. 68.
Thus, even his season, its command transgressed and fanned by the fire of his wrath,
bore the likeness of Mount Mekala ablaze and burning from a forest conflagration.
(Kalāpaka) [He was like] Kālakūṭa, possessing the dark hue of the clouds at the end of an aeon—
Under the guise of its shadow, at the times of the world's dissolution,
this [mountain] appears as if its throat were constricted by the darkness from the cavities of the seven worlds and the nether regions that it has swallowed. 70.
His pair of feet, with the surface of his toes reddened by the shadows of the leaf-patterns on the jewels of his shining crown,
[seems to be] under the guise of the tips of the rays of his glittering nails.
It shines like the radiance of wisdom, bestowing it upon the gods. ||71||

By means of this [treatise], the minds of even those whose intellects are free from the darkness [of ignorance] move about without doubt or delusion regarding difficult matters to be accomplished; for it is indeed said that their pure understandings range therein.
Above them, there are those characterized by various specific paintings. ||72||
Indeed, when the entire reality of effects is examined through the clarity arising from the power of superior wisdom,
it unfailingly nourishes the multitude of specific objects without obstruction.
Like fragrant wood being ground upon a grindstone. ||73||
And by means of the mantra which has attained a fivefold nature,
the elaborate composition of political science for men desiring victory [prevails] throughout the three worlds, following its sequence from the very beginning of transmigratory existence.
For the maintenance of the body is indeed brought to an end by the vital breath, as if by the wind. ||74||
Having thus abandoned all agitation, may you noble ones, who have now illuminated the path of policy by means of this [treatise], examine this matter with your delusions cast aside.
For those who possess discernment, there is nothing in this world that cannot be accomplished. ||75||
Having heard these words of him, the lords of the Gaṇas stood with their eyes fixed upon one another,
while the mountain peaks grew slackened by their playful movements.
Pure jewel necklaces rolled upon their broad, fleshy shoulders.

Thus ends the ninth canto, titled "The Illumination of the Method of the Radiance," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked with the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, whose mark is Vāgīśvara, and who also bore the name Vidyādhipati.
The Tenth Canto: He whose heat was indeed like the scorching sun of fierce majesty...
He caused the white lotus-fragments of his pale fame— which had grown in the lake of the three worlds— to wither, while causing the night-lotuses of the enemy clans' glory to close.
As if with the intention of resorting to the white lotus-clusters of the pale hoods of the serpent Śeṣa, which were left over from his breathing,
a flock of swans rose from the hollows and thickets of Mount Krauñca within the depths of the netherworld.
As if out of an eager desire to follow the path through the various quarters of the sky.
In heaven, his fame— by the power of its white wings— seems to long for the stalks of lotus fibers, which are like streaks of nectar-rays from the clearly visible moon.
Thus the female swan wanders through the three worlds with graceful charm. (A pair of verses.
The surface of his cheek shone, adorned with thick horripilation arising from the passion of crushing his rivals in battle.
It was as if kissed by Lakṣmī herself, who lay upon the bed of his arms—broad and raised as a pillow against the slope of his shoulders. ||4||

The earth, heavy with the burden of Balarāma, trembled violently upon the hoods of the king of serpents, which were like rafts upon the ocean whose waves were the crumbling ruins of the city of Paryantabaha.
In which [age], one who is distressed by exhaustion sets out for the conquest of the quarters.
By him, with his celestial elephant, the scattered hosts of the enemy's fortune— white as the moon— were shattered;
[he was like one] from whose upraised tip of the trunk issued forth fine threads.
Like the stalk-rings of a lotus plant. ||6||
He whose majesty, in battle, released as it were libations of milk— strewn with heaps of crest-jewels resembling pearls fallen from the frontal globes of rutting elephants he had shattered.
The sword [is like] a flame whose radiance is intensified by fuel in the fire. ||7||
When he set out, it was as if a second sky were rising to bear him, with the circle of the earth shaken loose from its dust;
the white parasols of the kings shone as they rose up.
Under the guise of its fragments, it was the thousand-fold hood of the vast Śeṣa. ||8||
Wearing a brilliant necklace of pure pearls set upon a pedestal of rubies fixed within its well-knit center,
it was fashioned for swaying, covering the very sky.
As if she were a forest deity with outstretched arms, [she held] the swing. ||9||
Bearing cheeks filled with a gaze whose pupils were wide and blossoming,
and a face beautified by a smile white as the moon; shaking his head, he loosened the serpent that had been bound [by him] in anger.
The matted locks were a mass of tawny hair disheveled upon his head. ||10||
He uttered speech that was composed like an ocean of profundity, possessing the white radiance of his teeth as its many paths, and having the charming words as its bright-colored swans.
Just as Jahnu [received] the daughter of Bhagīratha who bore Agni within her womb; (this is a *kulaka* of eleven verses).
Since you have thus spoken such exalted words full of splendor, I too am now inclined to speak.
The entire majesty of his breath’s power resounds through the flute, which brings exceeding pleasure to the ear. ||12||
Who else but you could utter such pure words as these, which are difficult even for eloquent men to speak?
Surely he must be some kind of jewel made of gold.
In this world, his doctrine is spat upon like saliva. ||13||
Those whose intellect— possessing innate purity like the flame of a lamp—
does not illuminate objects when the dense darkness of anger spreads abroad.
Indeed, they become blind even though their eyes are present. ||14||
Possessing an intellect that bears an exceeding purity, he dispels delusion and attains confidence;
his expanding [wisdom] obstructs the entire circle of the quarters.
The sun dispels even dense darkness by its very radiance.
Even at the rising of the moon, the ocean attains stillness;
even the creeper of lightning abandons its flickering nature;
and Rāhu does not swallow even the orb of the sun.
When this method is being expounded here by one possessed of wisdom. ||16||

Fortune, though fickle by nature, never abandons that conqueror who has remained steadfast upon the path of policy composed by those aged in the three Vedas, and who has eternally triumphed over his firm adversaries.
It was like the blazing splendor of the sun's orb. ||17||
I suspect that, having first dwelt within the hearts of the great until only a minute fraction of its atoms remained,
it has now settled into the depths of the oceans and the stability of the mountains.
And then the Creator fashioned its vastness within the sky. ||18||
Even for those who possess discernment, [the afflictions] are sharp when they repeatedly engage in activities that lack the application of appropriate means;
even for those with eyesight, [it is so] when they are devoid of attention toward their feet.
Indeed, sharp thorn-tips will surely pierce them. ||19||
For one desiring victory, the consideration of means such as time leads to the unimpeded attainment of one's goal;
however, for those whose minds are indifferent to such considerations, [success comes] through the treatises on policy.
The impetuous pride in one's staff-like arms is the cause of downfall. ||20||
The lords of the Daityas, their vision dimmed by the dense darkness of their long residence in the subterranean palace of Pātāla,
[beheld] his discus in battle, which was matted with the fire of its falling showers.
They were unable even to look at it, as if it were the orb of the sun itself.
At the head of the battle, that Pāñcajanya conch shell— which could not be clearly blown to its full extent even with great effort—
was [filled] by the seven worlds, which serve as the seat of his heart impelled by his breath.
The passage of his cavernous mouth was obstructed by its own physical form.
Bearing, as it were, the crookedness deposited by the *pāñcajanya* conch placed upon his mouth like a moonbeam of nectar,
whose naturally straight mind was solely for the purpose of deceiving the enemy—
It attains proficiency in the composition of the manifold display of effects. ||23||
The pair of jar-like breasts of that playful woman, whose body was assumed during the effort to carry away the nectar,
was observed as she rose impetuously from the surface of her chest, with her navel hidden.
It was beautified by two lotus buds that had grown there, [which were seized] by the Daityas. ||24||
Like a virtuous wife who, having been seen on the path by her husband, becomes overwhelmed with shame as she expands from the wound of being scratched by the sharp tips of a razor,
you did not stand before the Lord of the Daityas again.
Śrī, whose laughter is restrained and who is gazed upon by the circle of gods. ||25||
Beholding the earth raised up from a single corner of a mere fragment of the crescent moon of his fang,
he [the Boar] whirled the seven worlds within the cavernous hollow of his snout.
The splendor of whose form was augmented by the beauty of the arrangement of his playful boar-incarnation. ||26||
As he approached with an exceedingly slow gait for the sake of deceiving the guards, his body was seen covered in drops of perspiration,
its hair standing on end due to the cramped joints of his contracted limbs.
Like the waters of the ocean surging from within a well by means of Daityas. ||27||
As he strode through the three worlds to banish the royal fortune of King Bali, the beauty of his fresh,
playful ornaments was placed upon the cheeks of the wives of the gods and the Siddhas.
Upon his limbs, with the clusters of light from the rays of his toenails. ||28||
By him, having uprooted it from the Nandana grove and brought it here, a tree was planted upon the grounds of the palace garden;
even when merely looked upon, it causes that [Nandana] to lose its bloom and fade.
In the flower, with eyes wide open, there is beauty upon the face of the beloved. ||29||
He who, having attained the status of a cowherd, assumed another form as dark as a cloud,
while the Daughter of the Ocean, whose heart was bound to him at that very moment, remained hidden within his chest.
As if its essence were the joy of a firm embrace, [it was] the pair of arms. ||30||
Even now, the head of the serpent Kāliya, which was subdued by Him while He was still a child, acts as a thorn;
for when the weight of His foot was placed upon it, its crest-jewels were crushed and its circle of broad hoods, flashing with gems, quivered within.
Listen to the secret account of him who, having assumed the guise of a cowherd, was suddenly [embraced] by the beauties of Vraja;
his sound of song caused their hidden navels to quiver with their sighs.
His throat was stained by the pollen of the filaments of full-blown lotuses. ||32||
Upon his chest, which was as vast as a mountain rock— the heart of which bore the secret mark of a crest-jewel of deep passion firmly established there—
she [dwelt], along with sixteen thousand women of shapely hips.
Śrī was pressed by the force of a firm embrace. ||33||
In the course of time, Hari— who was like a revolving disc of bimba-fruits formed by the smiles from the lotus-faces of the women of many cities—
became intoxicated with the crushing of his enemies.
He struck down the sons of Diti, whose minds were arrogant because of their staff-like arms. (A group of fourteen verses.
Even though she is fickle, the Goddess Lakṣmī, having approached him who maintains a disposition consistent with the "Mace of Time" (Kālamusala) in all undertakings, remains for a long time.
She bore her feet, stained with red lac, as if they were carrying the nectar clinging from their movement within the interior of a cluster of lotuses. ||35||
This is indeed proper: that even during this present upheaval,
the noble ones do not cause the destruction of the world's stability,
remaining steadfast by their boundaries even at the onset of universal dissolution.
Or rather, what need is there to say that the oceans have not reached the end of this world? ||36||
Even though the mountain peak with its vast expanse of limbs was pursued by me, alas, there was no such pursuit of my heart’s misery.
As if seized by anxiety, the sky appears to be smiling.
[The world] was licked by rows of smoke-crests rising from this very [fire]. ||37||
Abandoning the elephants whose temples were washed by cascades of flowing ichor— the very touchstones for their unrestrained pride—
he placed upon his back the young fawn, whose [size] was like a wheel of hailstones.
Having leaped up, you wish to strike him down; you are not a lion. ||38||
Therefore, O Gaṇapati, let this impetuosity be abandoned— it is devoid of the subtleties of policy, despised by those who seek victory,
and observed to be both present and absent in other undertakings.
Those who are heavy with essence among all things do not fall into ruin. ||39||

O Lord of the Gaṇas, this wrath of yours, though it creates a dense darkness bound by the continuous knitting of your uplifted, curved eyebrows, nevertheless attains clarity within the orb of your moon-like face.
For whom would the vision of the stainless scripture not create a place of refuge? ||40||
Although the dark splendor of your sword-staff, O Lord of the Gaṇas, was beheld by the circle of gods and asuras who were seized with agitation,
it remained unimpeded.
This is the night of universal destruction at the end of time amidst the battles. ||41||
O Noble One, although I am currently devoid of the impetuosity and forceful resolve characteristic of agitation, I nevertheless desire to act now in accordance with right policy,
whether the task at hand be successful or even in its failure.
Otherwise, there would be no possibility for you to avoid being subject to refutation in some respect. ||42||
Why should he, who is like a cloud bearing rising lightning, exert his prowess— which results only in downfall— to strike at one who is merely roaring?
[He should rather strike] the frontal globes of the elephant whose temples are overflowing with rutting ichor.
Even a lion is like a saw that cuts through the joints of armor. ||43||
Like a fragment of cloud with its stream of water attempting to extinguish the strike of the cresting flame of the fire of universal destruction,
who could possess the harshness to forbid the impetuous onset of combat?
Or perhaps, O Lord of the Pramathas, it may be through your words that [the world] becomes mixed. 44.
Like the Lord [Śiva] who destroys the hosts of obstacles through his skill in incalculable numbers, the powerful one does not find rest;
for does not even the submarine fire remain for a single moment?
The orb of the earth became an ocean consisting not of water, but of ashes. 45.
At the front of the battle, the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu), having drawn his bow Śārṅga, and you, O wielder of the trident (Śiva), having swiftly drawn this trident with its scattered flames,
both became like those who hold the wheel in hand.
May those whose minds are proud of their staff-like arms crush the Daityas. ||46||
From his arm— which has the peak of its shoulders broad and high, which is like Mount Mandara that effortlessly churned the ocean of battle,
and from which a sword was whirled in circular motions— [the blood flowed].
Your turban bears the graceful charm of the coils of Vāsuki.

Without you, upon the borders of the forest of battle, by whom was this young woman led to bloom— her breasts being the full and high frontal globes of elephants— through the blows of the sword-blade creeper?
Fortune and glory, like a circular grove of *kurabaka* trees. ||48||
Only those who possess profundity can maintain such fortitude; he, being of vast courage, established his resolve in his heart,
having abandoned the abyss of the netherworld and taken his stand here.
Elsewhere, how could the water of the ocean be contained? ||49||

But I say this: O Lord of the Gaṇas, you who desire to conquer the next world, first abandon through delusion that which is the proper means for such a goal, while you remain subject to the sequence of punishment.
Success is certainly not found here as it is in another stage of life. ||50||
This straightforward path of policy, which follows worldly convention,
is designated by me as being "thus" for your sake;
beyond this, the Lord alone knows what is auspicious and what is inauspicious.
The Lord of Gaurī, the bridge across the ocean of the world's calamities. ||51||
Thus, from his mouth, there issued forth the speech of Bhārata— which dispels darkness by the unfolding of its shimmering garland of jewels and follows the path of right conduct—
just as moonlight streams forth from the orb of the moon.
The multitude of night-lotuses bloomed, and the assembly of kings rejoiced.

Thus ends the tenth canto, titled "The Composition on the Policy of the Fire-Womb," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by jewels, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
The Eleventh Canto:
Having heard these words of his, that [one] with a loud, boisterous laugh...

With his fangs like fire and his brows furrowed into a fierce, terrifying arch as formidable as a streak of *kālakūṭa* poison, he— spraying the horizons with froth— disturbed the assembly like the ocean. ||1||

With her eyebrows arched, which darkened the quarters of the sky with a formidable, deep-blue shadow like the massed clouds at the end of an aeon, and which were agitated by the fire of intense anger—
He bound it like the braid of hair of the Night of Doom.
In his anger, drops of perspiration flowed from him in that assembly, appearing like a circle of terrifying hailstones within the basin-like whorls of his hair.
They quickly bestow upon his body the splendor of a jeweled armor.
His anger likewise increased, his face with the surface of his forehead rippled by waves of furrowed brows,
just like that of a master who, though having received no haughty command, feels provoked.
He desired to swiftly withdraw the three worlds.
As he struck the formidable peak of his shoulder with his palm, the tips of the rays from his nails, shimmering in his rage,
bore the marks of being crushed within the cage of his powerful arms.
The playful mane of the lion of irresistible prowess.
The speech, endowed with propriety and beauty, of that one whose shoulders and peaks were unblemished, was a graceful manifestation of his intent;
like a presiding lady in an assembly who has ascended her throne, it revealed its true nature.
The face shone, with its curved, raised, and arched eyebrows. ||6||
Like a lotus-heart of the earth, through the path of the wound created by the wrathful kick of his foot,
the radiance of the jewel’s glow entered the cavernous belly of the netherworld.
Tawny, with a broad hood consisting of a thousand expanded hoods. ||7||
Wearing as an ear-ornament a crest-jewel-cluster from which swarms of bees were agitated by the weight of its fragrance,
he appeared as if his arm were resting upon a pillow formed by his own shoulder.
A full-blown lotus offered by Lakṣmī from her own hand. ||8||
Her splendor was like the roar of a most terrible sound produced by the clashing of masses of waves surging with pride as they rise;
she was bent low by the weight of her own body as it turned gracefully in play.
With his joints relaxed upon his jeweled throne, he spoke these words:
(this pair of verses) "O Lord of Gaṇas, by your truthful speech, the path of policy has indeed been adorned, even though it is naturally profound, O venerable one."
That very crescent moon arose from the ocean which adorned the matted locks of the blue-throated Lord Śiva.
There arises even this entire world as one alone, in whose words flashes that splendor which delights all;
he is another kind of wish-fulfilling tree, wherein the clusters of blossoms are jewels.
The wish-fulfilling gem becomes a mere cluster of flowers for him. ||11||
O Lord of the Gaṇas, that supreme speech of yours, which contains the essence of the reality of policy, never undergoes agitation;
it does not become like mud, for it is the cause of the stability of honey.
It is quite another matter that the pollen of the flower possesses accumulated qualities. ||12||
Even though I am possessed of a formidable appearance, my speech is strange, insignificant in form,
and unstable like the cotton-wool of a silk-cotton tree.
Being merely heard of, it will become an object of ridicule for you. ||13||
In battles, by his sword of blue luster, which was whirled in circles with ease as it struck down enemies,
[the sky] appeared like the stainless forehead-mark of the Enemy of Manmatha (Śiva).
Her fame spread through the worlds like a flash of laughter. ||14||

In the stormy onset of his battles, his sword-clouds, through the scattered sparks of fierce armor-fire leaping up from the blows of his thunderbolt-like fists, appeared as if filled with swarms of fireflies.
The stream carried away the splendor of the buds of the enemy's lotuses. ||15||
Whose fame, like a spreading garland of *bakula* flowers,
was repeatedly brought to full bloom by the playful drops of fresh red wine falling from the mouths of the wives of the multitude of slain enemy soldiers.
By means of the spreading sprays from mouthfuls of water, [he quenches the fires] in the forests of battle. ||16||

Even for you, O Immortal, having heard these words— profound with an intellect that has plumbed the depths of the truth of all treatises on worldly affairs and characterized by the path of ethics— it is indeed bold.
I suspect they possess a particular longing for ornaments. (Kalāpaka) Another surface of the earth’s expanse is fit for the intense clash of battle with the hosts of arrogant Dānavas.
Behold Hari, as if he were about to create [another world], with the masses of dust arising from the friction of his many jeweled armlets worn in his wrath.
Now these breaths of the wielder of the mace, heavy with the weight of his fury and resentment, cause the three worlds to tremble,
as they whirl the fierce-rayed sun into a state of instability.
The images placed therein are fixed according to specific locations, days, times, and years. ||19||
The mountain of the Lord of Wrath spreads terror, its brow-plate being the ridges of his forehead where the creepers of the rows of his formidable, quivering frowns grow;
he is the mountain of anger toward his adversaries.
Possessing an intense trembling induced by the winds at the end of the eon. ||20||
The body of this one, who has swallowed the form of Time, shines like the smoke-trail of the fire of his "huṃ" roar— an unshakable fury whose skin is as dark as the clouds at the end of an aeon.
Like a shadow emerging from the hollow of her mouth. ||21||
The more he frowns his brows, and the more he makes his eyes red with agitation,
and the more he crushes his handfuls of pearl necklaces; and as...
He will surely behold it for the asuras before long in that same manner. ||22||
The trident satisfies, as it were, the fire produced by the clashing of his teeth, which are firmly pressed together in a continuous fit of rage;
while the back of his own lip is bitten harshly by its tip.
With offerings of thick, flowing blood before him. ||23||
Kālī, whose thick flames are as dark as soot-stained ink, her arms formidable with a sword of blazing luster, her body like a fresh cloud at the time of universal dissolution— Durgā— [is here].
Like the Yamunā river, she bears the dark-tinted kālindī creeper as her companion. ||24||
This face of the elephant, with the fierce luster of its trunk-like tusks, possesses a beauty as white as a cluster of night-lotuses;
like the Mandākinī, it is one that has girded itself for a great battle.
This ewe kisses him on the face out of affection for her offspring. ||25||
By the downward turn of his face due to shame, he appears here as one whose arms are like trees for scratching the itching pride of those intoxicated by battle;
[he stands] amidst the water-like rays of the ruby-paved floor.
As if drinking this with a playful fragment of a lotus stalk. ||26||

Behold now the face of Guha, which, though exceedingly pure, has become darkened by the anger of Śiva upon hearing these words of yours— words uttered with ease in the assembly, yet so profound in their subversion of policy.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, the shadow bears a state of soiled darkness.

In battle, your fame will become one with the rays of laughter arising from the sight of the Lord of Asuras, who is perishing out of fear of blows from your sword— [laughter] that takes the form of flower-clusters.
White as the rays of the cool-rayed moon upon the branches of the *māśā* creepers.
Bearing a spear as heavy as a mountain shattered by my might, I shall uproot the fame of my adversary— who stands with his neck arched in the pride of his burden— making it as white as a lotus stalk.
Just as Kārttikeya [seized] the tusk-barrier of Gaṇapati. ||29||
What need have I for these followers of Kālakhañjana, who are like swelling Vātāpis, with their throbbing and fatal arrows of ill omen—
for those whose bodies are consumed by fate, what purpose is there other than battle?
Why do you not know this from the very beginning regarding one whose self is lost? 30.

O Lord of the Gods, may the Ganges— whose path through the sky was attained by Jahnu and who possesses the makara-sign of fresh sprouts— fill for us in an instant her course through even the three worlds with unimpeded flow.
Like a maiden [embracing] the waters of the Indus, so was that row of arrows in battle. ||31||
May the faces of the women belonging to the faction of your enemies turn pale during their separation from their husbands—
[faces] becoming like the dust of ashes from the fuel of hearts consumed by the fire of grief.
It was as if struck by heaps of breaths that had been exhaled and then cast away.
May the edge of the sword, like a skilled dancer, perform with great relish on the stage of the battlefield the expulsion of enemies by means of its exceedingly beautiful form.
Through the power of his valor, the Goddess of Victory attained her station. ||33||

The surface of the earth became visible, shimmering with rows of eyelashes in the form of rays of light from pearls released from the lofty frontal globes of herds of elephants crushed by his firm vajra-fists.
which rival the beauty of clusters of blossoms on the tree of heroism; ||34||
May the enemies of yours, who bear the agitation and confusion of battle and harbor wrath within,
discharge showers of cool drops from the water of dharma along with their forehead-crests.
By the floods of tears from the eyes of women with parted hair. ||35||
