May the sweet, piercing sound of the word "Victory!"— accompanied by the clashing of swords falling upon the frontal globes of elephants in the thick of battle amidst heaps of formidable bones— protect you.
There was a clamor in the sky from the throngs of sky-dwellers. ||36||
May the clouds that are the temples of elephants, radiant with the long-lasting glow of streaks of blood arising from wounds burst open by the force of the impact,
release a rain of ichor-water for the sake of the mindless one.
I am capable of destroying the host of the enemies of the gods. ||37||

O Nidāgha, may this battle quickly bestow fearlessness— its intense vigor arising from the crushing blows dealt to the ears of the elephants of the enemy of the gods, which were nearby, torn, scattered, pierced, and shattered.
It resembled a forest of trees with their leaves completely shattered and decayed. ||38||
He rendered the enemy of the gods one whose pair of eyes were crushed and whose head, with its mass of bones, was ground by a firm vajra-fist;
his mountain peaks and summits were shattered by the impact of the vajra.
It resembled a mountain of collyrium from which fragments of jewels had fallen away. ||39||
Having attained a repetition of actions reaching the very limit of excellence,
[they] violently crush the uprooted mountain peaks like the wind of universal destruction.
[He shattered] the mountains that were the enemies of the gods by his might on the battlefield.
The masses of my chowries, pale in luster and shaken by lotus-like hands agitated with confusion,
alas, produce for me a flood of tears born of grief and old age.
[This is] for one whose mental disposition has been defiled by the contemptuous treatment of a beloved. ||41||

When the wretched soldiers were engaged in battle by warriors who, with fierce intent, shattered the circular range of the mountain of Dāna with the blows of their thunderbolt-like fists and swords, [the earth]— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
Surely these silken cloths are before me. ||42||
Even if the entire burden of combat with all the asuras were placed upon this arm of mine, it would not be too heavy for it,
for it belongs to the one whose banner is the bird and who possesses the body of the Destroyer-Kāla.
The settlement of Ratnavatī was like the very tip of his fang. ||43||
I am one who crushes the frontal globes of herds of wild elephants,
and I am skilled in the arts of war;
[may I now] face that Fortune of Victory as if she were a heroine.
I lead myself alone, with my sole activity being the withdrawal of the senses from their objects. ||44||

May this battlefield, where the various silken banners serve as celestial wood for the fire of war, go today, O Lord, to the Himālaya mountains, bereft of Hari, whose wealth is Lakṣmī and who possesses inexhaustible treasures.
It was like a plateau on a mountain ridge, with its vast heaps of bamboo and karīra shoots. ||45||
O Lord, with Your foot You alone uprooted that enemy— full of many faults and loud with cries of intense agony— as one might uproot Mount Kailāsa by the strength of one's arms.
Having now squeezed [it], I shall imitate your graceful play.
O Lord, when the discus— though possessing the quality of being "Sudarśana" (beautiful to behold)— attained a terrifying state upon the path of battle,
Hari swiftly seized the head of Rāhu.
Where then were those sons of Diti, who were so fond of battle? ||47||
By this, what is gained by the head of Rāhu, which has swallowed the orbs of the sun and moon and throbs in the sky?
Why does Cāmuṇḍā carry this unbroken head?
Having cut off the flesh, it is no longer held in the hand even now. ||48||
Now that Bali has been bound by the powerful Madhusūdana, and Hiraṇyakaśipu along with his golden eyes has been torn asunder,
the pride of those staff-like arms has been cast far away.
May the pleasure of scratching away [the itch] in the battle against the Danavas bring you happiness. 49.
How could that submarine fire, whose abode is the mouth of the ocean-dweller who has swallowed all the rivers, dwell within the mere mouth of a frog, even if it were to possess great flames?
Of fierce brilliance, like the mouth of the enraged God of Death.
Even one who has attained brilliance remains gentle by nature;
indeed, such a person is certainly not disregarded in any undertaking.
Truly, in the midst of those who consume oblations, he possesses immense radiance—
Those practicing the five-fold austerity desire the heat, not the moonlight.
At the front of the battle, which had become impassable due to the upturned trunks of rutting elephants, horses, and foot soldiers,
the swords became clogged with the thick mud of the blood from the severed throats of enemies.
The sword-staff in the hand of the warrior is indeed stainless. ||52||
Possessing a radiant splendor and holding the quarters of the sky with the playful movement of his circle of rays,
he is like the sun during its stay in the day, devoid of any change.
The fortune of the king attends solely upon him alone. ||53||
A person who is crooked never becomes a vessel for fame, which possesses a radiance as white as a canopy of moonlight;
such a devious man becomes a mere staff for the banner of victory.
The bamboo stalk is not matted with the tips of fresh thorns. ||54||
Although it has reached the state of being a hollow comparison and has become utterly devoid of essence due to its dull nature,
the deer nevertheless placed its foot upon its lap.
Behold now the fruit of that heat of the moon! ||55||
That [moon],

being utterly devoid of shame and repeatedly humiliated by the sun, performs nothing at all that is worthy of the name "resplendent," which is merely a manifestation of the accumulation of its own dullness.
Even its shadow arises at night, yet it remains devoid of any remedy.
Since fortune is fickle from birth onwards, why would it not dwell by necessity in that cluster of lotuses,
wherein even its final decay remains unbroken?
The multitude of virtues residing in the treasury are present all at once in the army. ||57||

Peace shall not come for those who are afflicted by the dust of others' malice while this accumulation of vast suffering still persists in the world; [only] the sword-cloud can quench this intense heat.
As long as the streams of water do not fall without interruption. ||58||
When established even in a small or insignificant receptacle,
splendor manifests clearly within even a meager light;
for even a lamp emits its flame to dispel the darkness of the house.
How much more so, then, would a great hero act at the proper time for the sake of eradicating latent tendencies? ||59||
I believe that even though others exist who are naturally pure, only a few bear the burden of great men;
for among the waters of the ocean, there arose but one stainless conch.
The ocean is filled by the breath from the mouth of the Enemy of Madhu.
In this reflection, the light of those possessing fierce radiance exists as a manifestation of the entire world with all its measures limited;
yet for those who are truly luminous, their splendor is indeed infinite.
I think that unbearable [sorrow] dwells here within my heart.
By the slight contraction of her eyebrows, instantly displaying a harshness born of intense rage, and by the redness brought to her eyes,
that impatient woman of the curved brows manifested her acceptance of a profound sense of insult.
The heart burns even when the lower lip throbbed before her.
It is said that the three worlds, having attained vastness within the expansive heart of the Discus-wielder, reside there;
likewise, even the seven [oceans] abide fully unfolded within the steady heart.
"They stand clearly revealed"—this was my conjecture.
Since it was never performed even from birth,
that preeminent man [offered] his own prowess, which lacked commonality with others and possessed the quality of a fresh star.
He casts off his shadow, just as the moon sheds the night. ||64||
Some purpose may be served by even the most minute thing;
enough with the gross, which are useless to embodied beings. On the slopes of mountains, let grass, reeds, and the like suffice.
What is the use of masses of boulders resembling large cheeks? ||65||
This jewel, though small, is priceless; its mass of darkness is shattered by the crest of rays it emits, and it is better than [the vastness of the earth].
What indeed is the use of [the jewels] on the paths of the mountain ranges?
Indeed, [the mountain] is as if by boulders (gaṇḍaśaila) bereft of the splendor of their own flesh.
It is better that this silkworm here in the world becomes a thread,
for by ascending it, the insect climbs to the celestial realm;
whereas [the sun], though possessing the lofty height of the peak of the Western Mountain—
It was not the support for the sun as it fell from heaven.
At the time when the sun desires to reach the peak of the mountain whose summit has already set, its lofty nature becomes a useless support;
yet even that quality of the lotus stalk is praiseworthy for the demon [Rāhu].
Out of fear, the Lord of the Maruts approached Yama and took hold of him.
Let the glory of the waters of the ocean be consumed by the submarine fire until it has inundated the surface of the earth;
for that splendor is not capable of wiping away the physical form of one who brings about exaltation.
[She saw] even the streak of the spot on the moon that has arisen from its [own] nature.

With the tips of its branches reaching upward and exuding great loftiness, the tree that has its roots in a pit might perhaps boast of a downward course that is even praiseworthy for those who stumble.
I understand the matted locks to be the instrumental cause of their support. ||70||
Form a frown with your brows harsh with cruel anger; roll back the lids of your eyes and bite your lip.
Tear at your necklaces and clench your hands together.
Strike the surface of the earth with a pair of sharp heel-strikes.

Strike the mountain peak, which resembles a summit and whose status is resonant with the thundering roar of clouds; shatter his fortitude! Thus do you strive in vain for a fruitless and envious purpose—
With this [thought], the assembly of the Enemy of Smara does not now shine.
(A pair of verses) There is no knitting of the brows upon the face, nor a striking against the region of the shoulder, nor the application of biting the lip.
Without the manifestation of the power of wrath, the fire of destruction, with its unbearable flames, would reduce the worlds to ashes. ||73||

Where are you, whose arms are capable of overturning the world and easily casting down the circle of the great boundary mountains? And where is this fury, which contradicts the moon-like faces [of your enemies]?
Where is the splendor of your forms in the battles against the sons of Diti? (74)
This brief summary has been spoken by way of an exhortation through elaborate discourse;
for what need is there for such an urging of you, who possess such exalted splendor? [I shall now command] the engagement in a battle as terrifying as that between the lords of the Daityas.
O wise ones, do you understand the meaning of my statement here? //75//
May the fire of my roar of "Huṃ" in anger— its swelling intensity having shattered the formidable joints [of the mountain]— consume the lineage of the sons of Diti;
so that Indra may once again embrace his own lap, which has jewel-like peaks.
May he dwell as before, being praised by the hosts of gods. ||76||

Thus ends the eleventh canto, titled "The Description of the Arrogant Agnidamṣṭra," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the word "jewel" (*ratna*), composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—whose pen-name is Vāgīśvarāṅka and whose other name is Vidyādhipa—and who is a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
The Twelfth Canto:
When the Lord of the Gaṇas had ceased speaking these words, which expressed his firm resolve for hostility toward the enemy, [the following occurred...]
Then Aṭṭahāsa, his brilliance enhanced by a flash of a smile, laughed aloud with the desire to speak.
The pure string of pearls arising from the splitting of the frontal globes of the rutting elephants of his enemies,
clinging to his sword, bore the beauty of bubbles upon the spray of its clear stream.
Even though they were clothed in armor, possessed an inviolable form, and numbered in great multitudes,
his enemies were brought to destruction by him— who had himself reached the state of Time— as if they were the eons brought to an end by Śiva.

By him, having repeatedly conquered the forces of his enemies in battles, fame was spread abroad, which constantly bestows abundant and white prosperity that serves as a bolt against the encroachment of other quarters. 4.
Always possessing a thirst for drinking blood, having made an effort at rending many nights, his broad circle of teeth became like a demon of the sword for the destruction of his enemy. (5)
Bearing a splendor delightful with fragrance and a friendliness that was pleasing, and appearing as a warrior in battle amidst the shimmering ranks of arrows,
he swiftly scattered the army of the enemies of the gods like the autumn wind disperses the tufts of cotton-wool.
By him, his stainless fame—established in virtuous conduct and possessing the splendor of a polished mirror-surface—was rendered dark-hued by the breath-winds of the wives of his enemies. (7)
He who, having abandoned all sequential order through his speed, made the earth of the battlefield into a water-pot while remaining entirely without assistance,
churned the host of enemies into a thousand pieces, even though it was not stirred by a staff and lacked the essence of milk.

He maintained prosperity resting upon a fourfold foundation, crowded with numerous infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants; and while manifesting both peace and war toward his adversaries, he nevertheless ensured that the game of dice never lost its board. (9)
Even while possessing a form identical to his own, he distinguishes the moon from others by its qualities, maintaining a state of invincibility.
Adorned with the beauty of many eyelashes and possessing a magnificent, broad shoulder and radiant splendor,
he bore a pair of eyes with long, lovely pupils that seemed as if they were the two entrances to his fame.

By him, as he advanced, the row of kings was made to tremble—its stability destroyed in an instant by his skill at uprooting them, like a forest of trees whose roots have been severed by the wind of destruction.

Bearing a resplendent discus in his hand, he eclipsed even the pride of Indra; by his might, he made the battlefield like heaven, as the Supreme Person [Viṣṇu] did when he took away the *apārijāta* tree. (A Kulaka) His hand, shaken from its grip upon his head by the excessive fury manifested through the commencement of an attack, [fell]...
Lifting the ruby crown with his hand, according to its proper place, with the desire to set it in position.
His form was captivating, with a halo of shimmering light emanating from the emeralds sparkling upon his chest;
he bore the beauty of the celestial elephant Śiva, who is covered by moss clinging to him as he plunges into the waters of the triple-pathed river. 15.

With arms like massive pillars supporting the jeweled *sālabhañjikā* figures shimmering with the glory of victory, he playfully tossed up his brow—which was terrifying to those afraid of writhing serpents—and assumed a frowning expression born of deliberation. (16)
He placed the Goddess of Speech— whose spreading branches are the blossoming kalpa-tree of literature, radiant with clusters of jewels,
and whose filaments are the rays of light from his emerging teeth— as a pure ear-ornament for the lady of the assembly.
(Kalāpaka) She is a flock of swans brilliant with pure color, endowed with exceptional clarity and profundity.
Manoramā adorned his face, just as Sarasvatī adorns the surface of the earth. ||18||
Who would not hold in high esteem such a noble service as this you have proposed through these words?
For even the Goddess Lakṣmī makes that man her abode who spreads out lotus stalks, creepers, and flowers for her. 19.

What wonder is there that every word you have uttered here is pleasing to the mind? For it is precisely the nature of the speech of wise men endowed with discernment to be agreeable to all people. (20)

Therefore, although you, endowed with exceedingly powerful virtue, have spoken these words of universal excellence, I replied, "I have no leisure to speak"; nevertheless, I remained devoted to the weightiness of the task at hand.
The notion that "this dull-witted man—how indeed could wise speech arise from him? is not worthy of consideration.
Does gold of unimpaired quality not arise from a stone that is utterly dark in nature? (22)
How can your intellect, which is beset by the cataract of ignorance, be the cause for realizing the true nature of reality?
For the flame of a jewel-lamp, though appearing radiant, is never seen to be accompanied by soot. 23.
Constantly full of inner vitality and unwearied, those wise men who possess moral conduct and political wisdom maintain their integrity;
like trees with tufts of beard-like filaments, they produce fruits in the form of speech within the assembly. 24.

He who, having correctly examined the matter at hand on earth, waits for the proper place, strength, and other means, finds that his specific actions—being free from error—are beautiful and do not result in a tasteless outcome. (25)

For one who possesses unimpaired and exceedingly powerful excellence of valor and who seeks to swiftly repel enemies in battle, there exists no means of accomplishment equal to policy that is as effective as being well-established and free from the defect of negligence. 26.
Indeed, let the very state of those who are most venerable, burdened by the impressions of their past efforts, be awaited;
for a lamp does not maintain its existence without a wick that has been moistened with poured oil. (27)
For one whose conduct is stained and whose state is unrestrained, another's purity becomes defiled;
as he dwells incessantly in a house thick with darkness, the entire world falls into gloom. (28)
We conceal our prowess against the enemies of the gods, nor do we praise ourselves;
we examine only the path of policy, while the activities of the foe proceed according to their own desires. (29)

Indeed, the brush of policy, appearing in manifold forms, unfailingly reveals the entire work of the mandala—delightful with the lines of virtuous conduct and accompanied by the acquisition of territory—for all sovereigns. (30)
Just as wise physicians distinguish the five tastes and other qualities inherent in all substances,
so too do those seeking victory discern the constituent parts of policy when it is applied to counsel.

An undertaking that is beset by the fault of irrelevance, lacks proper sequence, is fraught with doubt, suffers from a deficiency in its connection, or contradicts place, time, and so forth, is not praised by the wise—just like a poem that fails to achieve its purpose. (32)

I perceive that Fortune, having arrived by the path of policy, does not remain unstable as she did when she rose from contact with the waves of the ocean; rather, O King, she firmly establishes her station once more. 33.

Who with a discerning mind would not find this other method of attaining Fortune—by which the ocean was spared the distress of being churned by Mount Mandara and the frantic confusion of the gods and asuras during the churning—most dear? Or rather, who would not prefer it? (34)

This counsel, though examined here by its authors through the seizing grasp of blazing and violent fallacies, does not abandon its fivefold stability, just as the Supreme Person does not abandon his fivefold state within the Upanishads of the treatises on political ethics (nītiśāstra). ||35||

When analyzed in many ways by those skilled in meaning and possessed of unhindered intellects, does policy—when extracted from the mixture of the dull-witted—not reveal its virtues, just as a lotus fiber reveals them when freed from its stalk? (36)
Just as trees on earth are devoid of means and their specific actions vary in their fruit,
so too those very same actions, when based on sound policy, surely bear fruit for kings with certainty, like the wish-fulfilling tree.

The wheel of activity, set in motion with its hub bound at the center of the mandala, possessing a collection of essences revealed through firm means and possessing spokes whose time is the unfolding sequence, never falls apart anywhere.

One who desires victory certainly requires the strength of arms, just as the wheel of the sun revolving over the mountain ridges of the earth requires its circle of horses, or as sound policy requires one who has already conquered the three worlds. (39)

The wise person who, desiring to ascend, has taken refuge in this succession of steps that serve as skillful means and follows them in due order, will surely before long be perceived as one who is established in the highest state. 40.

May this royal fortune, gradually adorned by various weighty expedients pleasing to a sovereign, and possessing clear discernment through the mirror of policy that reveals both virtues and faults, remain steadfast. (41)
Light itself, its vision obscured, passes in an instant like a flash of blindness;
a person whose intellect is impoverished by fate never possesses the capacity to foresee the future. 42.
For the wise who elucidate the various courses of action based on peace and war within the circle of states,
no errors in conduct occur through their constant reflection upon the proper sequence and its exceptions.

In a king whose roots are firmly established, who follows sound policy, and who has increased his treasury and army, prosperity attains a fullness of maturity like the pericarp of a fully developed lotus. 44.
Then, as the king’s powers— his own circle of allies, his virtues, and his means of policy— investigate their respective domains,
they fail to attain full growth because of the failure to determine the proper sequence of place, time, and action for one who is about to rise up.
Even the fish tear at the manes of the lion of fierce splendor as he plunges into the water— manes upon which swarms of bees rest, their cheeks moistened by the spray of rut.

In this matter, it is the manifestation of past time that prevails; for even an elephant, difficult to conquer during the month of *tapas*, becomes utterly contemptible when the summer season arrives, since his trunk with its mouth-like tip is then reduced to the state of a dog's snout.

Bearing here a long spear capable of piercing the mountains of the faction of the stars, the peacock-bannered god [Kārttikeya] bears his extensive policy through six qualities, as if with six mouths. 48.
The virtues resting upon the joints of his clearly perceived seat, radiant with the luster of the jewels in his ornaments, perform that miracle:
they adorn the splendor of those seeking victory even without their forms being polished. (49)
Having taken firm root among those of steady character— just as the earth rests upon the bodies of the world-elephants— and being as profound as the essence itself,
this policy, once firmly established by the mountains (the kings), does not waver from its course even when faced with the four strategic means.

If your mind proceeds with firm resolve toward the accomplishment of the goal, yet employs means that are not effective, then I consider the treatises on statecraft, which deal with the analysis of the sixfold policy, to have been rendered obsolete by you. (51)

Are you not like the various forms of the Self-born Brahmā, who, possessing the splendor of the sun at the end of an aeon, are able to perform the maintenance, creation, and destruction of the three worlds by himself alone, as if in sport? (52)
Even though you have abandoned the courses of action— peace and war— dependent upon the circle of states for those desiring victory,
nevertheless, being like walls of elephants, you are capable of crushing your enemies through the passion of martial fury.
I recognize that the Daityas are invincible in battle, and that your arms are as thick as the trunks of the elephants of the quarters;
therefore, in this crisis, policy alone is appropriate, like a bridge for those wishing to cross over a flood of water. (54)

Tell me, what is this lapse in speech on your part, when even though there are other means available, such a discussion regarding your enemies unfolds with a singular relish for fierce punishment? (55)
"This is merely a stratagem; this is our punishment, not one adopted by those advanced in statecraft.
Nevertheless, it is not appropriate for you to disregard such a grave matter as this. (56)

Do not the wise, who have well-stabilized their joints by making the entry of dullness slacken through the closing of the flow of the sensory apertures, rescue others here from the ocean of worldly activity—just as boats, when equipped with oars, carry others across? (57)
The suns consume the worlds during the dissolutions of the aeons, and the oceans overstep their bounds;
yet there is no such time when those like you, in their wrath, shatter the very foundations of existence. (58)
I truly understand that you are certainly not capable of subduing the enemy without your master’s command;
the waves are never able to overwhelm the ocean from its shore. (59)
Therefore, you ought to undertake this practice which proceeds in three distinct forms from the wielder of the trident—
just as the celestial river, established by the Ancient Foe for the welfare of the three worlds, flows in threefold divisions.

This Lord, manifesting as the unsurpassable power in deeds distinguished as divine and human, was called "Fate" (daiva) by wise men who contemplate the principles of policy, for He is inconceivable by them. (61)

The prideful playfulness of the tree-like arms of those desiring victory, and the intellects engaged in deliberating upon the sixfold policy, do not—though firm—ever attain the state of fruition through the application of expedients when he turns his face away. 62.

In whatever way this [destiny] conforms to the world, at that very time all specific actions of men are clearly set in motion for both the present and the future; indeed, even through its contrary, they become causes of accomplishment.

Whose wonder do his actions not produce—actions that, though clearly perceived by ordinary people as if they were contradictory in form, are far beyond the scope of the understanding of those whose delusion has been utterly destroyed? (64)

Right here, within the self of the moving and the unmoving, through the differentiation of the continuous flow of the movement of inhalation and exhalation, the entire sequence of the emergence and dissolution of the universe repeatedly assumes a state of being bound [to this breath]. 65.

From that enemy of Mura— who reclines upon the coils of the serpent Śeṣa, which rests within the belly of the ocean as its womb— there arose the Four-faced One (Brahmā), seated upon the pedestal of the pinnacle of the pericarp of the navel-lotus.
As that omnipresent Lord stands constantly pervading the worlds with His eightfold forms,
He swiftly shatters the fetters of men— the bondage arising from illusion (māyīya), that of the individual soul (āṇava), and likewise that of action (kārmaṇa)— through the power of remembrance.

When his own power, which shatters the long-lasting transformations of Māyā, unfolds for this self-born one, then the atoms abide within that very Self, abandoned by stability, following, and dissolution. 68.
Your intellect, which has discerned all the principles of that [Lord], ought now to determine the matter at hand;
being stainless and virtuous, why do you now act in vain, overwhelmed by heavy delusion? (69)
Having obtained from this sole teacher of the world—
the sun that shatters the bonds of the blinding darkness of ignorance—
permission for this task which is weighty with its essential meaning, let there be single-minded application.
You are fools, blinded by an inability to reach a firm decision regarding what ought to be done. ||70||

Why do you, being so impetuous, abandon the path of policy and—like elephants plunging playfully into rivers of profound fame—crush your own bodies with your trunks? [Or: Why do you, being so impetuous, abandon the path of policy and crush your own bodies with your hands, like elephants plunging playfully into rivers of profound fame? *Note:* The provided fragment appears to be the beginning of a verse. The final word "hāra" (necklace) suggests a possible pun or continuation involving the destruction of necklaces by the hand, contrasting with the metaphor of the elephant destroying its own body. A complete translation of the intended full verse would require more context, but based strictly on the given text: "Why, being so impetuous, do you abandon the path of policy and—like elephants plunging playfully into rivers of profound fame—[crush] your bodies with your hands [as if crushing] necklaces?"
Now you are defiling [it] with showers of dust. ||71||
The world is supremely negligent; though a means exists here, it rarely attains the accomplishment of its goal. It looks upon reality with eyes closed.
Nor does one see one's face upon the surface of a stainless mirror.
That reality of what is to be done, which is here introduced by words that dispel the mass of the darkness of delusion,
shall quickly shatter the wicked and perverse fools who are difficult for the intellect to approach.
He goes together with those whose fingers are crooked and deceptively beautiful. ||73||
In these discourses on kingship, you are thus capable of quickly determining the deliberations of counsel;
this cloud-demon does not devour you in such a manner.
Even now, the sun and the moon remain free from fear. ||74||
Having attained a superior purity based on the transformation of the form of the *vandhya* (the barren [nature]), it possesses unimpeded enjoyment of its own nature,
like the power of consciousness belonging to the mountain. Its deficiency—
Fortune remains perpetually empty and does not pass on to others. ||75||

Therefore, it is fitting for these venerable ones to act in battles, for they have discerned the relative strengths and weaknesses of others and possess the arising of powers and virtues necessary for the single course of action.
By which fire of remorse you are not overwhelmed. ||76||
Struck by the wind of mental conceptualization, why does this [mind]— devoid of stability and lacking any perceivable solidity—
behave like the tip of a blade of grass or a tuft of cotton, carried far away by the force of its own movement?
For indeed, you are merely wandering restlessly in empty space. ||77||
Those who know the proper means accomplish the harsh with the harsh and the mild with the mild, incessantly using that which is most effective;
as the sun constantly ignites the sun-crystal.
And the moon moistens the moonstone with its own radiance. ||78||

When the leader of the assembly had uttered these words consistent with right policy and ceased speaking, the hall became filled with the confused sounds of "well said! from those who had grasped the meaning of his speech.
Then, having heard that speech of the Lord of the Attendants, which was as deep in sound as a fresh rain-cloud, she became filled with fear;
yet there, she was immediately thrilled like a lavali creeper.
She became one whose emergence of fruit was esteemed as being of no small measure. ||80||
The hosts of gods praised those words of his with bees from their massive jeweled ear-ornaments, which flew up playfully as they shook their heads in wonder.
As if they had vomited forth the darkness of delusion through the cavities of their ears. ||81||

Thus ends the twelfth canto, titled "The Introduction of Aṭṭahāsa," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by gems, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
The Thirteenth Canto:
Then, from these words of Aṭṭahāsa, [he] yawning...
With a frown even more terrifying due to his agitation,
Caṇḍeśvara pressed his body against the joint of the jeweled pedestal, which was already worn down by the weight of his own form. ||1||

Like the frontal globe of a lordly elephant whose burden of battle has been fulfilled, his arm— with its forearm smeared by the mineral-like luster of the red gems in his armlet— bears a fierce wrath.
Striking his shoulder-blade with a harsh sound.
Rising from the opening of his cupped palms like a meteor from the fire of his immense wrath, she whose yellow-golden hue turned the quarters of the sky crimson,
[fell upon] the entire circle of the asuras.
The auspicious flame shone, foreboding the destruction of all things.
It was perceived by the circles of gods standing at its forefront— themselves agitated by the onset of intense fury—
as bearing a resemblance to a noose for dragging down adversaries.
The curved eyebrow of the Goddess of Fortune, in the assembly of the gods, [is like a bow]. ||4||
He bears a neck that is naturally harsh with the *kālakūṭa* poison, which possesses broad shoulder-bumps turned askance and from which streaks of smoke rise with the force of a playful crushing.
He whose crown is adorned with a digit of the moon has a complexion like that of a dark-blue peak.
With pearl earrings reddened by the radiance emerging from the circle of rubies in his armlets and the *makara* ornaments,
he of fair luster was like the Ocean of Milk with its coral.
The circle of foam was surpassed by the halo of light from the creeper. ||6||
Having cast off that portion of the tips of the young sprouts and shoots of his lip— resembling the tender foliage of a tree— which had been overstepped by the assembly of Dhūrjaṭi,
he whose ocean of fortitude was difficult to restrain and agitated by the fire of wrath...
A loud laugh, like the shimmering mass of a multitude of foam-sprays.
With his head trembling in agitation,
as if about to rise up suddenly like a mountain being shaken by an earthquake,
he who knew the inner truth of calculation spoke these words, unable to endure his pride. (Kalāpaka)
I bow to wisdom, which assumes manifold forms throughout the worlds, and to the primordial Speech, the cause of all worldly activity;
by virtue of relying upon them, even I possess the fortitude to speak.
O Leader of the Gaṇas, you too have uttered this [hymn] which contains the essence of political ethics.
With its flow unimpeded even upon the three paths, its hearing of pleasant sounds accompanied by purity, and possessing a graceful splendor,
it was like the daughter of Jahnu, whose ears were quickly joined as she flowed toward the jar.
Whose mind is not captivated by this stream [of words], or rather, whose mind is not captivated by the speech of the virtuous? (10)
When these [verses] are heard, even the conceptual fluctuations of the intellects of the wise burst open without restraint, like those of one awakened from sleep;
they distill an indescribable nectar of heart-warming form.
The words of mortals, with their deep and captivating compositions, captivate the ear. ||11||
An expert in policy, when proposing a well-determined task during deliberations, ensures it will be pleasant in its outcome;
thus Prajāpati sowed that precious seed in the waters.
From which this egg of the lotus-seated one (Brahmā) emerged. ||12||
O gentle one, by bearing a praiseworthy manifestation of blossoming— endowed with the beauty of the soft down of the radiance of your teeth—
you have attained a state worthy of praise.
He is surely like a tree with a cluster of jewel-flowers. ||13||
O Lord of the Gaṇas, it is no wonder that these words of yours, which have issued from your mouth, are so captivating to the ear;
for they are the cause of unsurpassed joy for the three worlds.
How indeed could nectar flow forth from the orb of the moon? ||14||
I think that Sarasvatī herself has assumed the form of a blooming, beautiful red lotus as a mere plaything here, unable to express [the truth] to the ignorant;
she who, by the force of her residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), has gathered the seven worlds into a single mass.
She bore a palm of the hand that was like the expanse of a tongue. ||15||
Since you too have spoken thus, containing within it the principles of established policy,
even though this world has fallen into such a state of being crowded with defective and false views,
I must indeed speak here with particular care.
There is nothing whatsoever that does not possess a gradation of dependence. 16.

It utterly complicates the thicket of affairs for those who have abandoned their zeal— its activity restrained by the impetuous pride of their staff-like arms— and for those who instead resort to policy.
It is a torrent of wind for men, thick with the clouds of skillful means. ||17||
Let even Brahmā chant the Sāman out of pride in his equality;
let the faces of the multitude of people be filled with dissension; and let you, O herds of rutting elephants, bestow gifts abundantly.
I have inflicted punishment upon the sons of Diti in battle, making them fools. ||18||
Those whose course is of feeble vigor remain clearly distinct,
their prowess sluggish like that of a lute or a drum;
whereas those who forcibly crush the circle of adversaries—
Having entered [the world], they are like the rhinoceros horn in this world. ||19||
Even compared to a hundred virtues, this single virtue is currently peerless; what need is there for six?
For by it, the parasol of his moon-like mass of fame—
This thick arm of yours shall become a staff. ||20||

There, this single cave, having come into the hands of Guha, shines forth— its interior marked by the thinness resulting from the friction of the coiled body of the serpent that was being mocked, and where Mount Mandara remained fixed in its uneven position.
And since power resides there [in the three], what need is there for any others? ||21||
His body was beautiful with a mass of quivering locks, and by his unfathomable depth, he bore the splendor of the pool of the daughter of Kalinda;
he was capable of crushing the one whose banner is a peacock in battle.
Like Kāliya brought under control by Acyuta, he remained there for the sake of subduing [the enemy]. ||22||
Seated firmly in the palace of the battlefield, they undoubtedly assume the splendor of their adversaries,
massaging the elephant-temple-sized surfaces of their feet.
They are capable of finding their place upon full and elevated breasts. ||23||
That noose for binding the string, which is placed upon the tip of the bow by the soldiers on the battlefield,
has been drawn with force and brought to a state of trembling.
The splendor of its opposite is bound more firmly. ||24||
Surely this much must be performed by one possessed of splendor: that,
regardless of place or time, even while dwelling in the forest by the power of divine destiny, he crushes the wicked-souled.
What is the use of speaking of the *śrīphala* fruit otherwise than by not eating it? ||25||

There is no place where his presence is not established; what need is there for time, which depends upon that [place], for the Lord who dispels it? What obstacle could there be to the destruction of the enemy produced by false conceptualization?
O slayers, why do you now address me with such apprehension? ||26||
Even when greatly diminished, a glorious person surely continues to uphold the burden of their duties in the world without obstruction;
for what need is there for the remainder of beauty that merely serves as a festival for the eyes?
Even the moon, though beautiful, does not produce night. ||27||
Beholding the ocean whose natural boundaries were transgressed at the time of universal dissolution,
and the sun rendered lusterless by its setting,
those of steadfast minds surely [felt] within their hearts—
Those whose nature is firm fortitude laugh aloud even in the face of calamity. ||28||
Surely, one who is by nature timid, having imagined fear even where there is no danger, falls into extreme despondency;
he reaches his end, even when thoroughly treated by physicians.
Having fainted due to the contact with the poison of fear. ||29||
He who made the vastness of the sky, the ocean, and the mountains appear cramped was clearly someone else entirely;
he by whom [the world] was fashioned so that it could not be contained within the hearts of the great.
This other creator exists as a final limit to his activity. ||30||
With faces overcome by yawning, succumbing to continuous gasping, their bodies trembling and eyes reddish and harsh,
the great warriors— whose minds were agitated by the fever of rage— [grasped] their swords.
O you, why do you not likewise desire the water of the [celestial] stream? ||31||
May the hearts of the fire of his wrath, his eyebrows with their frowns, his lips from the gnashing of the tips of his teeth,
and the shoulders of his soldiers struck mercilessly by his hands protect you.
They laugh simply because their own range of experience is under their own control. ||32||
The loud roar of the celestial warriors, who have effortlessly cast aside the wind and can endure the heavy blows of their masters,
brings forth instant coolness with its sharp intensity.
[May it be] like a putrid [smell] for you enemies who enjoy the heat exhaled from [their] mouths. 33.

In whom could there be unrestrained pride, with arms as bars [of a gate], amidst those who do not abandon their true nature even when the fierce winds unleashed at the end of the eon shatter the peaks of mountains?
Having crushed the Dānava warriors, you did not shine in battle. ||34||

The cause of your remorse torments your hearts, which were filled with longing for those who were bold in the markets of battle and whose splendors were as white as moonlight, in order to purchase fame.
Why is this shattering of pride not caused by someone else? ||35||
Even this wrath, fiercer than the fire at the time of universal dissolution, has become one whose fruit is utterly severed;
as if by the clusters of your rays, [the seeds] have been cut down.
The pearl necklaces laugh upon the surface of the jeweled floor.

The fame of his pair of arms— transparent, well-rounded, and full of passion— is even now clearly manifest as it was sportively grasped by the two Goddesses of Fortune; yet the winds of his breath do not soil it.
May it be for you a mirror for the graceful amorous gestures of the splendor of pride. ||37||
You have not been impoverished by the glory of your valor in battles,
and you have reached the further shore of the ocean of the path of policy through your wisdom;
what, then, has been severed for you by this false display of heroism?
Do you endure the state of being humiliated by enemies with such haughty pride? (38) [This is a yugma.
You who suddenly uproot mountains and effortlessly possess massive trunks when provoked by others—
For the path of battle, vast as the sky at the time of universal dissolution, is indeed the playground for you.
Who in this world does not recognize you as being swift,
with arms as thick as the trunk of the elephant of the quarters,
who effortlessly shattered the firm joints of the cosmic egg of Brahmā?
They are capable of reversing the two sections. ||40||
In the perils of battle where the realms of the gods were uprooted,
and during the dissolutions of the world when you raised up the mountains, it was impossible for your enemies to fathom your heart.
For the sky remains truly unshaken by the winds. ||41||
Having heard of the enemy's unbearable oppression, those who were concealed by the name "Fearless" (Abhaya) through their policy thus [acted],
making fissures in the earth with the blows of their hands.
Why do you not enter the surface immediately out of shame? ||42||
Why does the splendor of your cluster of pale white fame, which has long been rooted at the base of the world’s forest-circle,
now cause you no delusion?
The vine of fame for the predatory trees of poison that are rams. ||43||
This heat of the sun that is the prowess of the Daityas— having extracted the moon-like luster from the faces of the celestial damsels who were rescued from it—
why does it not cause your eyes to contract?
He whose lily-like fame is made white by the clusters of his rays of light. ||44||
The fire of the Asuras' prowess quickly diminishes your fame— which dwells within the hollow of the world-palace—
by means of its unrestrained, scorching heat.
Just as the gaze of a serpent [overcomes] the light of a lamp. ||45||
This resolve, indulgent in the desire for battle, has been fulfilled by Kālamusala’s words in an instant;
having abandoned the Mandākinī, whose virtues of merit are renowned.
Who else besides him is capable of filling the mine of jewels? ||46||
As I observe here the difference between living beings, it is my reflection that the one with expansive strength is superior;
for the lion brings down his prey with a mere fierce slap of the paw.
Moreover, he carries on his back the lion, the king of beasts, who is intent upon splitting the frontal globes of the multitude of elephants.
Indeed, there are many other distinct words by which the world is entirely pervaded without confusion;
yet even when heard, he causes the ichor-fluid of elephants to dry up.
That roar was something entirely different from that of the lord of deer. ||49||

[He saw] the expansive Gaṅgā of the Himalayas that is the lineage of noble warriors— a vast and lofty upper chamber for the playful abode of the manifest glory of heroism, which effortlessly conquered his enemies.
The crows of the heretics do not attain fame on the path of battle. ||50||
That state of mine, which lacked the quality of transformation that seizes what has not yet been attained, became tasteless even from birth;
does a spray of water ever become tasteless upon reaching the ocean?
The state of being a pearl occurs here within the cavities of oyster shells. ||51||
In the fervor of winning the battle, the warriors sportively struck the frontal lobes of the victorious elephants;
and the circles of enemies belonging to the denizens of heaven fell away.
Their bright pearl necklaces rest upon the slopes of the breasts of beautiful women.
In that abode of battle, strewn with a profusion of pearl-dust fallen from the frontal globes of elephants split open by sword-strokes—
there, O seeker of victory, dwells your beloved.
Fortune comes under control through sharp, arrow-like claws.
It dwells constantly upon its surface, which is as dark blue as a rain cloud and beautiful with the scattering rays of freshly set jewels—
just like the chest of Madhuripu, which is dark as a rain cloud and adorned by the sharp path of the jewel Kaustubha.
The goddess Śrī, free from the state of being tossed about, was honored by the silk cloth. ||54||
Surely this Lakṣmī, devoid of fickleness, is the very image of the body of the enemy of the gods (Śiva);
I suspect that upon this sword, which possesses the dark-blue luster of the autumnal sky, she resides.
With hearts full of passion for him, they established his image upon a silken cloth.
Having abandoned her bed of fresh lotus buds, which was celebrated by the songs of circles of bards moving on their six-footed feet,
she dwells constantly there out of an impetuous passion for the Hero.
I suspect that even in the Forest of Sword-leaves, Fortune dwells with ease.

For one who has conquered his enemies with the staff of his arms, there is never any attachment to worldly riches that may be obtained through mere circumstance; for the spirited man, the frontal globes of elephants are shattered by his very claws.
O noble lady, [your face] is like that of Hari amidst heaps of pearls on Mount Kūṭa. ||57||
Alas, this world is now overwhelmed by calamity and distressed;
for you, though possessed of mighty arms, have now thus abandoned the bonds of fortitude through misplaced agitation.
Devoured by the demonesses of crooked policy. ||58||
Arise! The glories of the Lord of Asuras, now slain in battle, have become as pale as a stalk of reed;
they are washed by the waters of his weapons, which are like smeared collyrium, drenching the feet of his city’s women.
And let their cheeks become soiled with dirt. ||59||
O Lord of Ashes, let the gods place me— who am eager to churn the ocean that is the king of the Daityas— for the sake of attaining the nectar of victory.
One should indeed offer it upon the back of a small tortoise, as if it were Mount Mandara.
Praiseworthy indeed is that very vessel among the worlds, from which [the Lord] arose with a greatness worthy of worship for the sake of the gods' mission,
overturning the ocean with a single mouthful.
Agastya drank the Vaikuṇṭha-kūrma-śaphara.
When a cause arises from some incomparable source, those things naturally weighty clearly undertake a most significant effect;
does not the Lord of the Ocean, having risen even from a jar, [produce]— ?
The venerable Agastya drank even the ocean, whose crest was its row of gentle waves.

The great warrior, having girded his loins for battle, turns the entire circle of the earth— extending with its mass of jewels and its rim of mountain ranges— into a wheel, drawing it back as far as the edge of his ear.
Surely it was as if with a bow made of the maurvī creeper. 63.
Now, let the celestial splendors, which have long been established within the belly of the mud-like multitude of the leaders of the Daityas, be drawn forth by their many virtues;
for they are scorched by the fire of humiliation.
The creeper of his white lotus-stalk of fame was nurtured by his desire for peace.
Like the ocean of dissolution upon the peak of the golden mountain, difficult to behold due to the shimmering rays of the sun,
[this weapon] is now for the destruction of the race of Dānavas.
I shall quickly fix the bowstring upon this bow.
The sun was distressed by the impact of the circular boulders from the temples that were splitting apart, becoming disordered, and rolling without restraint;
[the sun] who had been fashioned by the staff of his bow, O you of broad and beautiful fame—
For the sake of wealth and for the purpose of battle, I shall tear up the mountains from the earth.
Let the bowstring, as if its pain were intensified by the firm binding upon the broad curve at the tip of my bow,
roar like the submarine fire when struck into battle at the forefront of the fray.
It was as loud as the sound of the waves of the ocean struck by the force of a thunderbolt.
That very bowstring which the strong-armed one placed upon the tip of his bow on the field of battle is indeed the sole cause for the arrival of Fortune and the emergence of fame.
It bears the graceful manifestation of its clearly defined path. ||68||
In battle, I recognize the unbroken *oṃkāra* of the enemy host in the very *kreṃkāra* of my bow, which is drawn to the ear with its string firmly wound around it.
The root mantra for the firm and playful drawing forth of Lakṣmī.
While the Fame and Fortune of the warrior host were indeed running along the same path back and forth,
there surely occurred the mutual impact of their hard breasts.
They both create [the sky] entirely white with a broken necklace of stars. ||70||
Having attained a beautiful splendor through their physical forms by means of the excellence of their adversaries— which serve as a touchstone for the intense pride of intoxication—
they become fragrant, bathed as they are in the waters of their own fame.
Surely those rich in valor [are distinguished] by the fragrance of their fame. ||71||
By means of his heart-stealing luster, which rivals the radiance of Śiva’s throat and constantly imparts a weightier nature of supreme merit,
the great warrior quickly purifies himself in battle.
Having performed his ablution with the water from the blade of his sword. ||72||
O Lord, O Bull-bannered One, may this entire universe now be free of thorns; be gracious and grant me leave.
Let him, agitated by his own coils, swallow the sword— [of Śiva].
May the son of Siṃhī, whose fame is like the orb of the moon, bring you prosperity. ||73||
May the lords of the Pramathas, possessing a luster white as ashes, having fallen upon the quarters of the sky turbid with terrible darkness,
now shatter the army of the Danavas with their loud, boisterous laughter.
Like the severed [limbs] of the Enemy of Smara during the night of the time of universal dissolution. ||74||
O Lord of the World, let this battlefield now become like the abode of Vṛndāvana for the gods and demons—
a place where the clear yellow garments [of the warriors] are intensely embraced by those who have transcended all passion.
Possessing the splendor of a multitude of jackals, who are fond of them and accustomed to red-limbed women. ||75||
O Moon-crested Lord, may the path of battle be a dwelling place for the unhesitating crows and vultures amidst a multitude of skeletons—
a place where the *ṭāṃkāra* sound of bows serves as the very scaffolding for their flight.
May his armor, formidable with the narrowness of its engraved marks, protect you. ||76||

The lord of the Daityas in battle, his head cast upon the hard throne of his neck—its formidable bones severed by a sword—and with the orb of the sun falling from the cloud-scraping peaks of his crown; The king of the gods, having slain the enemy in combat, was honored by the gods who showered him with celestial flowers as he stood amidst the hosts of Maruts. The son of the Wind-god, having struck down the enemy’s charioteer with a mace, shattered his chariot with a blow and, laughing, seized the enemy himself. The son of the Fire-god, having cut off the enemy’s arm with a crescent-headed arrow, struck him with a spear; and the son of the Lord of Waters, having pierced his chest with a trident, drank his blood. The son of the Moon-god, having severed the enemy’s head with a sharp-edged discus, danced; and the son of the Sun-god, having split his breast with a spear, roared aloud. The son of the Lord of Wealth, having bound the enemy with a noose, dragged him along; and the son of the Earth-god, having crushed him with a mace, threw him down. Thus, the sons of the gods, having slain the enemy in battle, rejoiced together with their respective fathers and the hosts of immortals. The gods, having regained their sovereignty, ruled over the three worlds; and the demons, having been destroyed, entered the realm of Yama. Thus ends the [chapter] titled "The Victory of the Gods" in the [section on] the Great War. *Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a composite of several verses describing the slaughter of a demon (Daitya) by various gods (Devas). The translation reflects the narrative flow of these descriptions.*
Let the world of living beings behold it as if it were the peak of Mount Mandara. ||77||

O Lord of the Gods, one must never engage in deliberation regarding the descent into battle; alas, what need is there for reflection when the host of the enemies of the immortals is already devoid of joy?
This meditative absorption makes my smile not fruitless. ||78||
What else is there to contemplate? This world of weak-minded people offers this salutation with palms joined, filled with sweet and auspicious songs,
while their stout [lives] are being severed by the radiant and formidable sword of his hand.
The elevated circular regions of his ears served as fans for the *pīlu* fruits. ||79||
It was filled with swarms of bees descending upon the offerings of flowers released by the circle of sky-dwellers brimming with joy,
and it was perfumed by the dust of the earth crushed by the trampling of the army.
The entire expanse of the quarters was variegated by streaks of smoke. ||80||
Marked by the mud of the colored dust-clouds from the temples of elephants crushed by swinging maces,
[the field] was being dragged by the god of love manifested as the attacking warriors.
His fortitude was snatched away by the thunderbolt-like arrows discharged from his bow. ||81||
This dwelling-house of battle, with its couch of uplifted elephant tusks and its cheeks bristling with circles of horripilation,
[is filled] by the intense passion of embracing the Goddess of Victory— this...
Let the world of kings attend upon me this very day! (A group of verses:

Let there be today [the sight of] the joints of my necks bending under the weight raised by the bones of my exertion—exertion that dwarfs the earth with the surging flow of forces set in motion by the sport of an assault; let them remain thus.

The remainder [of the serpents] also possessed clusters of crest-jewels whose brilliance was made doubtful by the mass of sparks from the fire emitted by their broad, fully expanded, and clearly manifest hoods. ||83||

Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "The Presentation of Caṇḍeśvara’s Staff," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
The Fourteenth Canto:
When he had spoken thus, the Goddess of Speech (Sarasvatī), her cheeks adorned with a blossoming smile, [replied].
In the assembly, Puṣpahāsa began to speak in due order, his words harsh with political wisdom. ||1||

Bearing a power that was both unimpeded and possessed of natural excellence, and which was difficult to withstand when shattering mountains, he did not become arrogant even upon attaining lordship over the most venerable [lineage], for his intellect remained free from darkness. ||2||

Having attained a state of irresistible expansion, he became renowned throughout the worlds; like the submarine fire (Aurva-vahni), he utterly destroyed the lords of armies with his circle of weapons. 3.

The breasts of the beautiful women of the enemy's harem bore the hue of saffron-paste from the lotus-like eyes reddened by weeping, which were themselves the circle of the moon of his [the Buddha’s] face. ||4||
Although he established his rays even more extensively and swiftly than the sun across the quarters of the sky,
Rāhu’s sphere could not overcome his lofty orb, nor did it cause him any eclipse.
He never experienced humiliation, nor distress, nor the touch of suffering;
for he, whose conduct was pure and whose station was stainless, possessed a preeminent splendor like a gem in a mirror.

And his fame, possessing a luster as white as the rays of the moon and shining with a multitude of pearls in the form of its beautiful qualities, attained the highest state of ornamentation for the quarters like a string of pearls. (7)

And he, like the enemy of Kaiṭabha, attained a state of unimpeded height through his fame—glorious and far-reaching—which, spreading forth and remaining unswerving, swiftly rendered the three worlds impossible to transgress. (8)
By his vast abundance of flowers that were his glories—white as the rays of the moon—the entire vine-like Haris bowed down within the forest of the world when it was traversed by him. (9)
The jeweled statue of his fame, fashioned from exquisite carving, shone most brilliantly; it stood firmly constructed upon the wall-sections of the quarters that form the temple of the world. 10.
As he was speaking there at that time, a circle of rays from his teeth emerged;

like the Ganges, it attained oneness with the ocean of light from Śambhu’s face, which was as white as the moon. (Ten verses in a *kulaka*) His speech, which fell within the scope of the art of combat and was celebrated for its fierce blows like those of Kālamusala and others—
Who, having heard that which is both powerful and sweet, would not exert himself all the more to speak? (12)

In this forest of the assembly, which possesses the beauty of blossoming *kovidāra* trees and where blue-necked peacocks dwell on high, I, like a *droṇa*-crow, cry out something harsh and am ashamed. (13)
Even though I have heard these words spoken by the leader of the hosts, I speak this which I cannot endure:
Does not the owl, having the cry of a peacock enter its ear-cavities, shriek harshly? 14.
Nevertheless, out of sheer dull-wittedness, and fearing my enemy in battle, I have hastily uttered these defiled words; you ought to listen to them. 15.
This is not the time for anger; this is a state of profound darkness that has come upon men.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, look with another eye, for this task stands in extreme peril.

Or rather, with their stainless intellects— possessing unimpaired sharpness and the power to pierce through the divisions of enemies in battle— they accomplish their objectives, just as one whets the edge of a sword.
At the sudden utterance of his name, the gods—agitated by the onset of a fever of trepidation—assumed a state of dejection with their faces, their lips and palates parched dry. (18)

He, endowed with majesty and extreme intensity, eclipsed by his very shadow the circle of the king of the gods, just as the son of Siṃhikā eclipses the orb of the sun by depriving it of its luster. ||19||
Having crushed the enemy army that had arrived and scorched it, he gradually brought it into his own hands;
he rendered their circle of vassals capable of beholding his face, as if they were looking into a mirror of the self.

And he, who in battles—making the sky resonant with the lofty and virtuous shouts as white as the moon—placed his fame upon the palm of his hand like the conch-shell Kaiṭabha, whom he slew as his enemy. (21)

Even toward such a person as this, who clearly maintains a refusal to look upon the eyes of the enemy of the gods—tell me, what do you perceive in this: is it fortitude, or is it merely the manifestation of dullness? (A Kulaka of five verses) Indeed, the wise do not recommend a method of persuasion preceded by conciliation when dealing with those whose objectives must be achieved through force.
Bearing a face that possesses a steady freedom from anger and is first lit up by a blossoming smile—
know that this [state] accomplishes its purpose with skill, is devoid of the onset of any calamity,
remains established amidst the depths of differentiation, and is composed of five combined aspects. ||23-24||

For those ministers who investigate every faction of what ought to be done, victory is seen right before them when [the opponent] fails to cite the words regarding the constituent parts of the proof, just as it is for disputants in the case of a logical reversal. (25)

May this mantra of yours destroy the arrogance and delusion of your enemies—those whose state is clouded by infatuation and who are covered with a profusion of sweat-drops and bristling hairs—as mercury destroys the venom of serpents. 26.

Having demonstrated the five members of the syllogism in their proper order, those of refined intellect employ this statement to overcome the delusions of the followers of Kaṇāda, in order to conquer the formidable power of invincible adversaries. (27)

By those enemies of the gods, who have unimpededly expanded throughout the world in every direction— like the three types of logical reasons (trilakṣaṇa-hetu) that unfailingly establish what is desired— they have caused the celestial realms to tremble.
Bearing heads formidable with quivering jewels and possessing a vast, dark-blue luster, they were like serpents;
yet, for those enemies, there was neither the striking of staffs nor the infliction of injury [by him].
(A pair of verses) By him, whose soul was established in intense austerity while desiring to propitiate the bull-bannered Lord Śiva—
Just as a dense mass of smoke was formerly consumed by the cool-rayed moon, so too was darkness drunk up.
Even though he restored to life by means of his lore even the inhabitants of heaven whose lives had been snatched away in battles,

that son of Bhṛgu, who became a mere substitute for the dead, is indeed to be meditated upon by you. (A pair of verses) Now, as hearts have become expansive, the dullness of the intellect has arrived.
"Tell me, like lamps in the sky, what indeed appears to you, agitated by violent trembling? (32)
Indeed, the powers of counsel flash forth even more intensely for the wise in times of crisis;
when darkness has pervaded the horizons, do not the rays of the sun burst forth? (33)
"You are established in the foremost vow; yet even this power and vigor of yours must be considered—surely, in such a matter of action, let that be sought from which merit may arise. (34)

The circle of kings, which is the locus for accomplishing results that do not perish, is clearly revolved by six virtues alone— whose sequence has never been abandoned— just as the world is revolved by the six seasons.

Having fallen into a state of conduct that is fickle, devoid of flavor, and inconsistent with their own true disposition, and being carried away by the impetuosity of a deluded path, even goddesses clearly do not hold their husbands in high regard. (36)
Now, this desire of yours—possessing a vigorous form and swelling with the impetuosity for combat—distorts the path of policy that has been well-trodden on all sides by great men. (37)

Although in battles there was at times an excessive cause for your joy due to those of fearsome appearance, the creeper of your fame—dark as a water-laden cloud—was never abandoned by the serpents that were your swords. 38.
Although your fame, possessing a complexion as tender as the rays of the moon, has attained incomparable beauty, and although they urge you here with sword-blades as if for the sake of battle; (40)

The proclamations of the cry of "Victory! were drowned out by the lamentations of beautiful women whose breasts were struck [by grief], and the fragrant powders [of victory] were replaced by clouds of dust raised from the ground by the impact of combat. (41)
Pure pearl necklaces were scattered about like white chowries by vultures, driven by the force of fierce winds, as they tore at the throats of soldiers with their swords. 42.
The excellence of the color of betel leaves was surpassed by the blood from the faces of warriors slain and fainted;
the confusion of tight embraces from terrified women was eclipsed by the passionate embraces of Śiva in his state of rapture. 43.
With teardrops from wailing, miserable with grief, they produced showers of refreshing spray;
with the cries of the ghostly soldiers, they created the sounds of war-drums heralding victory in battle.
The shadows cast by the flocks of birds served as a mockery of the ceremonial holding of parasols,
while the circles of entrails from jackals hanging down became garlands for the auspicious victory.
With faces radiant as the petals of blue lotuses, they were the crest-jewels of Love’s dalliance;
with hands bearing heaps of pearls from the frontal globes of elephants pierced by their arrows, smiles blossomed upon them.

The drops of water from the sweat of battle-fatigue became sparse droplets of the *mohana* [intoxicating] liquor; the blood from the circles of warriors' bodies pierced by weapons became liquid paste of yellow sandalwood (*haricandana*). 47.

The spray from the bathing waters gathered there rose up as droplets for the consecration, while the sounds of deep, auspicious mṛdaṅga drums mingled with the syllables of wailing uttered in grief and dejection. (48)
The confusion of awakening at the break of dawn was caused by the long sleep following the onset of battle;
the tinkling anklets of the city women were drowned out by the rattling sounds of the fetters binding the enemy soldiers.
Even though their kinsmen were slaughtered in battles,

tell me, are those who possess the prowess of arms not still defiled when they swiftly attain the glory of victory? (A group of thirteen verses) You possess various weapons, and the arms of your warriors are stout.
But the lamp of wisdom, which dispels the darkness of delusion regarding one's duty, is difficult for men to obtain. ||51||

O King, the wise here make the royal fortune—which is by nature as fickle as a woman—firmly established and unrestrained, by binding its feet with the chains of policy whose quality is steadfastness. 52.

One who possesses discernment, having realized the distinction between the sattva and the Puruṣa and maintaining a self perfected through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, surely does not undergo even a trace of the affliction caused by the disturbances of transformation. ||53||

He who is deluded here regarding the matter at hand, though he possesses the light consisting of the daughter of Akṣa (Sītā), falls clearly into the hollow of a blind well like one holding a blazing lamp in his hand. 54.
A man of policy should not rashly attack an enemy of incomparable and great prowess;
for who, indeed, would cast his hand into the gaping mouth of a venomous serpent? ||55||

Who would be able to surpass this compendium of the science of polity, which is profound with the application of mantras, possesses the excellence of conciliation and sowing dissension as its means of proof, and is like the Vedic tradition? (56)
Let your fury here be appeased, for the gems in the joints of your bracelets have burst and shattered from being crushed in sport.
Let not the entire three worlds become fragile and perish prematurely through this conflict between the gods and the enemies of the gods.

May the hosts of gods and asuras rejoice together in the pathways of the Nandana grove, where the *yūthikā* jasmine flowers are made variegated by swarms of bees clinging to them, and which possess the beauty of plantain leaves.
Their thick necks were encircled by sprouts of lotus stalks. ||58||
And let the celestial nymphs, delighted by the cessation of hostilities between the gods and the asuras, joyfully release a rain of flower-showers,
with drops of nectar trickling from their *mandāra* garlands.
The bees, intoxicated with passion, hummed loudly at the clusters of blossoms. ||59||
May the circle of the sky's path be free from the dense, fierce flashes of lightning falling incessantly like fragments of the sun;
may the oceans not be agitated in every direction, portending the onset of war.
The banks were variegated by masses of scattered jewels strewn in abundance.

Thus ends the fourteenth canto, titled "The Introduction of Puṣpahāsa," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who bears the name Vāgīśvara and the alternative title Vidyādhipati, and who is a dependent of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
Fifteenth Canto:
While he was thus withdrawing from the onset of battle, as clouds in the sky withdraw from a gathering storm, in that assembly...
The assembly of peacocks raised a tumultuous clamor of "well done! with their loud, melodious cries.
As the host of warriors moved forward— their lotus-eyes blossoming with the joy of having reached the festival of battle,
their prowess esteemed, and their splendor as difficult to behold as the radiance of the fire of universal destruction— 2.
"How can this be?"—with his head bowed from the weight of contemplating such stratagems, he remained fixed in the view of emptiness;
while another stood there, embodying political wisdom, with a back clearly arched and a chest bent low.
While the dull-witted Maṇḍaviḍa held his head with his face turned away, his eyes closed and his cheeks blooming,
he stood like a mere puppet amidst the grand display of the itching pride that seeks to destroy the glory of the circle of his enemies.

Having fled to foreign lands out of fear of her, the world of her enemies—afflicted by calamity—now remembers the lotus-feet of that noble lady, which were once graced by the circle of her anklets. ||5||
Slowness was taken up excessively from his gait as if by women; extreme paleness from his bright cheeks as if by them;
and leanness from his waist as if by the bodies of his enemies' wives. (6)

The circle of his enemies, though once possessed of a voice like that of the golden-hued Garuda— eloquent with refined transitions and euphonic combinations— suddenly became as common as ordinary folk, utterly devoid of heat or passion.

In battle, by him who moved with playful grace, the frontal globes of the elephants—yielding streams of clear pearls—were made to coincide with the heavy breasts of the enemies' women by his arm, which had the sword as its sole companion. (8)

By constantly assuming a manifest wing and taking his stand at the forefront of battle, he swiftly caused his enemies to lose their wings, just as the wind at the time of universal destruction causes mountains to lose theirs. 9.
In that battle, where the sharp-edged sword was the evening twilight bringing the setting of his adversaries,
the sons of Diti— whose bodies were as firm as the essence of mountains— thirstily drank [the blood] to their hearts' content, for they were no longer poor in the wealth of their own arm-strength.
And his sword-blade attains glory, marked by a broad circle of white teeth, possessing the luster of a serpent grey with the mass of darkness emerging from its own body which is pale as the moon. 11.

Displaying, by means of the radiance of his clearly visible armlets, the arrangement of plantain leaves upon his trunk, as it were, for that elephant of irresistible prowess protected by his arms. (12)

Shaking his head with intense fury, he bore a mass of matted locks that were deep tawny in color, appearing like scattered crests of flame from the fire of universal dissolution for the purpose of burning the three worlds. (13)
Bearing a gaze whose eyelids were quivering with the agitation of deliberating upon his master’s task,
he slightly opened his eyes as if to refute the haughty speech of the Lord of the Pramathas.

With his ten rays, Nandisena— whose teeth displayed the beauty of the riverbanks through their purity and were lovely with the flawlessness of their polished surface— composed the *Sarasvatī*, having thus resolved [upon its form]. (A group of fifteen verses) His bright rays from the teeth are as if sprinkled with the dust of the mineral pigment of his quivering lips.
Then, emerging forth, they attained a splendor delightful like cascades from a pure mind. ||16||
As he spoke his words— weighty with profound meaning and uttered loudly in the assembly of Indra—
the moon, white as its own rays, seemed to clothe the quarters of the sky with the mass of light from its teeth.

That I, like one such as I am, should manifest such meager eloquence before persons like you, disregarding your presence—in this matter, she surely offends; for that is indeed the ignoble tendency of being subservient to one's purpose. 18.

That all people determine these matters to be otherwise than they truly are due to their lack of skill—that is entirely the merit of your eloquence; you, however, are always established in the true nature of things.
Let the world, its own power exhausted, resort to that which is called policy as its refuge from fear;
yet it is valor alone—this mirror of the pride of your tree-like arms—that leads to success for you.

When all the inhabitants of heaven had been forcibly deprived of their celestial abodes—those whose very names were derived from the meaning of their bodily parts—and were reduced to a state of existence where shame was their only refuge; ||21||
The clusters of celestial trees, whose stainless jeweled sprouts were playfully plucked away by the earrings of the Asura women,
had long since become objects of intense heat.

Within the vine-cottages of the celestial groves, the circle of eyes— like blossoming jewel-flowers— of the captive queens of the Lord of the Immortals, who had been abducted by the sons of Diti, became witnesses to their amorous dalliances.
With the celestial chariots withdrawn, the city— its center darkened by the smoke of fresh kālāguru incense issuing from the clearly defined lattice windows—
seemed to create a mandala for the moon as if it were being eclipsed.

In the lotus-pools of the creepers in the celestial gardens, which had been turned tawny by the saffron from the breasts of the wives of the gods' enemies who were submerged therein, and from which the jeweled lotuses had been plucked; ||25||

When the elephant born from the Ocean of Milk—white as the moon—was seized by the plow-wielder, his enemies’ armies fled with loud cries as they were mercilessly dragged away by his formidable plowshare, like a furrowed field. 26.

While the entire host of captive women belonging to the assembly of all the kings of the asuras—whose eyes were bloodshot and swollen from incessant weeping at the wood-like weight of their heavy suffering—were overwhelmed by a flood of calamity; ||27||

Now that the enemy of the king of the gods has forcibly brought his own state of servitude upon himself by extending the torrent of his splendor— his arms, which were once bursting with the weight of the itching pride of being the world's peerless warrior.
With his hope for victory stymied by the moon-crested Lord Śiva, he passes the days with great difficulty alongside the world-protectors in the realm of the gods,
out of a longing for the auspicious embrace of his beloved.

Why do you still remain idle, even now, though your resolve is firmly fixed on forcibly seizing the Goddess of Victory? Indeed, the hearts of warriors grow weary; why then these obstacles of contemplating other means? (Ten verses in a *kulaka*) For those who disregard the passing of time, whose mountain-rock-like shoulders rest upon staff-like arms—
The splendors of victory in battle dwell simultaneously upon the swords of the warriors who partake in the fray. ||31||
Indeed, the very thought of mantras has already been rendered useless for you as the battle unfolds,
since this wave of the eclipse, devoid of fear, approaches and swallows both the moon and the sun with its hundred-fold rays.
While the lord of the Daityas was displaying his prowess in battle, we remained with all our efforts frustrated;
this is the bitter and most terrible consequence of being deprived of the master’s command. (33)

"Shall we not, within the blink of an eye, grind the enemies of the gods to powder? O Moon-crested Lord, grant us your permission; for our fortune of victory has been destroyed by the lack of your exertion. (34)
Even though the time had thus unexpectedly passed, those who were proud of their valor perceived two kinds of time:
that which was designated as "the appointed hour" (samaya) having arrived for us in battle, and another, known by the name "the Destroyer" (samavarti), belonging to the enemy of the gods. ||35||
Surely that Andhaka has become impoverished by the royal fortune of the Daityas at the forefront of battle,
since by him the foreheads of you all, who were enraged, have been made to ripple with waves of knitted brows.
O Lord, those floods of water which fell from heaven upon the daughter of Jahnu were swiftly swallowed up by her;
yet that single matted lock of yours alone was released, for it was the cause of the destruction of the entire race of Asuras. 37.

O Lord of the Gods, when the multitude of warriors firmly embraces the Goddess of Victory at the forefront of battle, let the women of heaven be freed from anxious thought, rendered unconscious by the frustration of their amorous desires. (38)
