Having fastened their armor upon their broad shoulders, these Pramathas, with their terrible roars, shall traverse the sky with speed as they assume the appearance of a mass of clouds at the time of universal destruction, for the sake of battle. (39)
O Lord of the Gaṇas, out of eagerness to embrace you firmly, the Goddess of Victory surely bears your slender body upon the front line of battle,
made rough by the rising of horripilation.
There can be no reconciliation between him and his enemy— who possesses a mind fixed on enmity, who has attained sovereignty over the three worlds,
and whose nature is dark— just as there is none between the sun and the darkness of Śiva.
For he does not fall into the state of being one who must be subdued by conciliation, since he has attained sovereignty through the total eradication [of his enemies].
Even those within his circle who are bound in enmity toward the gods are certainly not to be divided [from him]. 42.
There is no jewel in the three worlds that he has not already made his own;
I consider it mere idle talk to say that your stability could be achieved by granting him such things. 43.
Thus, while this punishment remains here, let all our soldiers be present;
may these weapons, with their manifest skill in cleaving, serve us in encounters with the wives of our enemies, who are like celestial nymphs. (44)
Or rather, what need is there for these? Let the moon-crested Lord remain with his forehead split by a frown;
let the graceful charms of women who have strayed from the right path become a memory for even a single moment. (45)

In the liquid streams of molten gold flowing from the peaks of Mount Meru, melted by the heat of the fire-crested sun, the circles of the earth’s surface were submerged as they floated across the seven oceans whose boundaries had been overstepped. ||46||
While the seven worlds were shaken by winds spreading from the massed stars, and while the circles of clouds of the doomsday storm filled all the quarters of space with their deep thundering; (47)
During the dissolutions of the worlds, I have seen the many hosts of the Moon, the Sun, Fire,
and the Winds entering in various ways the broad-mouthed, deep-rooted palate of the Creator of the Universe,
whose eyes kindle the god of love and indicate that the fire has not yet been extinguished. (The Tilaka)
His fortune and his misfortune are like a literary composition in which the sentiments of the erotic (śṛṅgāra) are clearly manifested through various distinct variations. ||49||
If he had exerted himself for the destruction of his enemies—who bring calamity upon the world—this kind of humiliation would not have occurred;
therefore, this [state] belongs to you [the gods] forever as opposed to them. 50.
O Lord, what is the use of saying more? By this occasion of your neglect, the world of the Daityas will render all the gods nothing but a memory, so that they shall never sprout again.
The sun, fearing that he might be placed within the interior of a lotus fiber already consumed [by fire], keeps the cluster of lotuses awake, as if out of partiality for them. 52.

In the creepers of Namuci’s intoxication, which bore the beauty of the blossoming flowers of his smiles, those sprouts of delusion did not put forth new growth, as if struck by the flames of a thunderbolt. (53)

The foam from his mouth laughed, as it were, with its own delight at the thought: "I have instantly brought Namuci—who had disregarded the terrible fire of the thunderbolt—to the base of his cruel throat-pit, where he was cut asunder. (54)

Furthermore, having come to rest upon the stalks of the lotus fibers, Śakra— dejected with grief due to his extreme emaciation from the fear of the lord of the Dānavas— once again attains the state of being a locus for its blossoming. (Cakkalaka) When the peacock has been gradually brought to destruction by the enemy at the forefront of the battlefield, [the fate] of his wives...
He will clearly become another fire of separation for the purpose of burning her funeral rites. ||56||
Even the Wind-god, having been forcibly led to his destruction by the host of Dānavas,
now proceeds as the very substance of the heavy sighs of the women confined within the city of the Lord of the Gods.
Surely Pracetas, withered by the heat of the fire of the Daityas' weapons,
will regain his very self through the cascading torrents of tears flowing from the eyes of the women confined by the heavy burden of grief.

Having struck down Yama, the warriors of the Daityas— laughing with joy at forcibly dragging away the hosts of the dead— shatter the rows of door-panels on the gates of Naraka, as they did in ancient times.
Thus, let there be no such tumultuous roar as that of the trees on Mount Udaya crashing against the ears of the gods;
rather, let the warriors, whose staff-like arms are rafts for crossing the ocean of battle, advance to seize the fortune of their enemies.
(A group of five verses) May your army of chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry spread through the quarters of the world, filling the belly of the netherworld.
It filled the interior with smoke darkened by the fire of the hissing breaths of serpents, who were fainting from the heat of the ground being scorched by the weapons.

This has been stated here in brief: as long as the armies of the lords of the asuras do not arrive, shaking the circles of mountains with their overflowing waters out of pride in their difficult-to-restrain fortitude;
Therefore, it is appropriate for the moon-crested Lord [Śiva] to lead an expedition against him.
Let the army of the Enemy of Smara— whose surface of the earth is made to tremble by the tips of the hoods of the Lord of Serpents bent down under its tread—
be dispatched along the path of the Sun.
Like a succession of waves from the ocean at the end of an eon. ||63||
Just as the Lord set forth with thousands of armies for the festival of universal destruction against the host of arrogant Dānavas,
his mouth was opened wide, its lips gaping out of greed to devour them.
Having approached him, Death then runs right before him. ||64||
May the mass of the bodies of the enemies of the gods, whose necks were severed by the trident cast with ease,
now attain formlessness as they are raised up.
Imitating the offspring of a lioness, he tormented the moon and the sun. ||65||

Let the elephants, their bodies stained tawny by the dust of gold shaken loose by the forceful blows of their club-like tusks, and having struck down the ramparts, trample [the enemy]— their temples split open by the impact of the earthen embankments.
The slopes of Meru are made treacherous by the multitude of wish-fulfilling trees.
May the waters of the Mandākinī lake in the region beyond Meru, for the cooling baths of the moon who has taken up residence there,
serve as mirrors for the moon-like faces of the wives of your soldiers.
Its beauty surpassed the splendor of golden lotuses through its loveliness and radiance. ||67||

Surely these portents are indeed the massed rays of the sun, possessing the flickering brilliance of the tawny crests of the Kalpa-fire shaken by Death as he rushes forth in fury to devour all the sons of Diti;
they proclaim that the mountain caves along the shores are being swollen by the force of the waters of the overflowing ocean.
May [it] bring to you the assembly of the celestial damsels who rejoice at the discourse of battle through its roars. 68.

Thus ends the fifteenth canto, titled "The Description of Nandiṣeṇa’s March for War," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who is adorned by Vāgīśvara and who bears the secondary name Vidyādhipati, being a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
The sixteenth canto begins:
Having uttered those words in that place where the roar of the clouds had been surpassed—
When the battle between Śikhaṇḍin and the formidable, drawn-up army had ceased,
there arose a deep resonance from the echoing reflections of the thunderous, steady roar of clouds, which was closely embraced by the walls of the shimmering assembly hall.
His body was made beautiful by a cross-strap (vaikakṣyaka) and variegated jeweled garlands shimmering with rays of light, clear as the mass of moonbeams;
he bore the marks of the thunderbolt-weapon and the bow resting across his chest.
Bestowing a splendor resembling a mountain of frost.
In the assembly of the Moon-crested Lord, there is a serpent presiding over the sacred thread, its body reddened by the tips of the jewels on its swaying hoods;
it has turned the mountain of waterfalls tawny, as if washing away their mineral ores.
Displaying his playful grace, he spoke these words:
(The Tilaka) "It is no cause for wonder that the Lord of Knowledge, desiring to slay his sinless enemies, should utter such exceedingly powerful speech."
When he, wishing to burn up all the worlds with the fierce radiance of his rays at the end of the age, emits that [fire], what wonder could there be in that? ||4||
Nevertheless, you are worthy to grasp the essence of these words of mine now as I speak in this assembly—
words that are like drops of nectar from the pollen-dust of lotus-filaments.
Do not bees take [nectar] even from that which is not honey-colored? ||5||

This certain, wondrous, and stainless [form] of the Supreme Lord has a body composed of phonemes that serve as the locus for the countless manifestations of all speech, which reside within the belly of the three worlds contained therein.
Power stands facing the earth of those who possess wisdom. ||6||
By the power of whose grace this intellect of ours has discerned the true nature of our task and its faultless state;
[by that same grace] I shall speak these words, though they are by nature impure—
He causes the moon-crested Lord to speak clearly in the assembly.
O Moon-crested Lord, let this intellect— which has been soiled by the spreading mire of delusion and wanders here and there without restraint—
attain clarity and proceed upon the path of right conduct once it has been made manifest.
May this [work] be like a river bound by the season of autumn for you. ||8||
May all things in this world, even those that are soft, repeatedly be set in motion by the path of policy and attain a state of effective action;
for the flute, refined by the craftsmanship of a master musician, initiates [melody].
Even the sound of the lute brings about the destruction of virulent poison. ||9||
With my mind subdued by following the method of the means of accomplishment with due reverence, and awaiting the proper time,
there is no great impetuosity in my heart.
How could there be thick juice within an unripe mango fruit? ||10||

He alone, like the sun of dissolution, made Hari— who had manifested his body as a fish and a tortoise— into a treasury of jewels consisting of the waters of his pure fame, which had been rendered vast by his majesty.
His form was unrestrained, with the tip of his sword-mandala unbroken.
By him, whose arms were like the circle of a bow that served as a basin for the creeper of his fame dancing to the very tips of his ears,
those with bowed heads were released after being conquered in battle by one who was soft with compassion.
The immortals attained the true meaning of that renowned name. ||12||
He who, from the midst of the ocean of milk that was battle— terrible with swords appearing like streaks of manifest *kālakūṭa* poison—
raised up [the moon] with a luster as white as a night-lotus.
A bud upon the moon of his excellent fame, serving as an ear-ornament.
He who, at the onset of battle, clearly crushed [his foes] even with his arm, which acted as an assistant to the sword— that blade possessing the luster of a sixteen-bhāra cloud and a sharpened edge.
Possessing the exalted glory of the frontal globes of elephants crushed by those who are intent on murder. ||14||
That Andhaka too, whose footstool resounded with the clinking of the sun-like crowns of the entire circle of Dānavas as they rubbed against it,
had effortlessly cast down the unyielding lineage of his enemies.
Bāhudruma was on the side of those who were to be assailed by them. (A group of five verses.
Among those lords of the Dānavas who were crushed in battles by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, he was somehow different from the rest.
By which the other fire is extinguished by water, yet this very fire of Aurva reduces everything to ashes. ||16||
There is no cessation of capacity in any single thing; all entities possess degrees of efficacy that are never fully exhausted in their actions,
even by being consumed by the submarine fire for the duration of an eon.
Agastya swallowed the ocean with a single handful. ||17||
Having conquered those victorious guardians of the celestial world, he brought the Daityas under his absolute dominion;
and they too, having witnessed his prowess on the field of battle, each individually [acknowledged him].
They are unconquerable by the gods even through the exertion of a total assault. ||18||
Where, as the sky was stirred by the assault and the soldiers shook up clouds of dust from the earth upon seeing the host of gods,
he recalled the fire of the arrows of the one whose crest is the moon.
Of those possessing rows of smoke-crests from the kindled Triple City.
In battles, he held in his arm a sword-blade streaked by the mass of rays emanating from the fastenings of his golden armlets—
a blade trained in the skill of destroying the worlds.
Fortune is the touchstone for the excellence of one's valor. ||20||
Where the enemy host, having approached and fallen deeply prostrate at his feet, was bewildered by its own stubbornness and pride;
though it suffered excessive wounds, it did not move at all.
He discharged that supreme weapon, which flooded the surface of the earth with water. ||21||
Having reached the shorelines variegated with freshly polished pearls,
your fame— white as the crescent moon— is divided in many ways and spread far and wide by the waves.
He attained the splendor of the milk-ocean as it were, when recorded in writing. ||22||
Even when merely remembered, that Kālaketu causes the wives of his enemies to tremble with fear and agitation;
they bear rivers of tears resembling pure pearls.

[He was like] the coastal forests [clinging to] the creeper of his fame as it bore fruit. (A group of five verses) At the times of his military expeditions, [the elephants] were smeared with the dust rising from the surface of the earth, which had been torn apart by the trampling of his army.
The quarters of the sky turned dark, like funeral pyres enveloped in the smoke from the flames of his majesty, which had consumed the high-born lineages of his enemies. ||24||
While the wielder of the Śārṅga bow roared like a fresh rain-cloud, his lion-man form having its sprout-like claws broken against the rock,
[the enemy] fled as if by a newly risen shaft of precious gems.
Lakṣmī was made to dwell upon the region far from his chest. ||25||
On the floor of the forest of battle, from the multitude of enemy trees, his beautiful flowers of fame were gathered by the *avacikā*—
the clear sound produced by the striking of weapons and clubs.
Victory to the Goddess Śrī, whose tinkling sound is like that of ruby anklets! ||26||
Even the mountain kings, with their unrestrained elephant-armies, moved swiftly as if to follow him who had set out— the self-chosen husband of the Fortune of the enemy faction.
The surface of the earth trembled from the crushing of the army. ||27||
How indeed could that son of Hiraṇyakaśipu be conquered in battle, as he brandishes his triple-bent bow,
marked by the garlands of sandalwood paste and the luster of the jewels in his armlets?
With his staff-like arms serving as a lofty, thick, and elevated triumphal arch; (this is a *kulaka* consisting of five verses).
Upon him, when he flashes forth at the forefront of battle, the waves of Airāvaṇa’s ichor—once clinging to him with great force—now remain devoid of their flow.
I suspect that the swarms of arrows, under the guise of their whizzing sound, reproached his excessive valor because of their own excruciating pain. ||29||
As if from the intense heat of his unimpeded majesty, which was concentrated within the circle of the horizons, the wives of his powerful enemies were taken captive within the palaces.
It was suddenly turned dark by the orb-like faces of his [attendants]. ||30||
The body of that leader, when stretched out in battle against the enemy, experienced horripilation, a shivering numbness, trembling, excessive rolling about, and a lack of firmness.
Upon seeing him, her gaze became tremulous with agitation. ||31||
By him, whose sharp-pointed arrows were like fires with fierce radiance, those who acted as beloveds toward his enemies were scorched,
and thick smoke rose from the surfaces of the faces of those enemies as they were consumed.
The quarters of the sky appeared as if beautiful with the arrangement of braided hair. ||32||
Whom would that unrivaled warrior not bring peace, like a Vedic mantra, were he the demon Timira in the field of battle?
He whom even the dull-witted Śoka pities because of his soiled [garments].
[She was] like the moving glance of the wives of his enemies. (A *kulaka* of five verses:
When he was intent on the joy of military expeditions, by the masses of spray issuing from between the bars of his thick hands—
For his enemy hosts, as they flee, are wiping away the plaster of fame— white as nectar— that clings to the walls of the quarters of the sky.
For him who was endowed with the joy of truth, the blazing prosperity of those offering oblations in battles was swiftly consumed,
as if at the destruction of all the worlds by Śauri.
The firmness of his limbs was not perceived by those who were experts in the science of marks. ||35||
Thinking that no single earth was capable of bearing the flood of his white fame, the Creator fashioned for him in the sky,
under the guise of moonlight, the clearly visible coils of Śeṣa.
And under the pretext of its shadow, it was divided upon the surface of the earth. ||36||
The mass of pollen from the filaments of her ears,
though its movement was not yet fully reached from afar,
rose up from the divine flower ear-ornaments shaken by bees that had settled upon them.
There was no constant turbidity in the eyes of the Lord of the Gods. ||37||

How could he, whose fierce rows of flame-like rays are his majesty’s fire, be conquered in battles by the gods, even with the arrows discharged from the joints of their shattered bows? He who is known as Śatadundubhi.

I suspect that heaven and earth themselves have burst into flames outside [of me]. (A group of five verses) With a mind moistened by compassion, he protected the lives of those who had approached him with folded hands in salutation, even as his own thirst for the earth was waning.
By means of the waters from the edge of his sword, which had the sole purpose of pacifying affliction, he brought about the subduing of his enemies. ||39||
The royal swan, wandering upon the ground of the sacrificial arena— the dwelling place of multitudes of hundreds of lotuses—
playfully and for a long time destroyed those who bore white [garments], yet remained unbroken himself.
The wing [of the enemy] [destroys] the lotus-stalk creepers of his white fame. ||40||
The mountain peaks trembled, the waters of the ocean surged far along the path of the sky at every moment,
and the surface of the earth burst asunder under the circle of the army's force.
By whose march, it was as if the dance of Śiva were being performed by Mardana. ||41||
Fearing that his matted locks might fall away due to the tossing of the coils of the serpent whose dwelling is fixed in the opening of the netherworld,
he [the mountain] has the tips of its vine-like slopes jagged with the fruits of the sun and moon that have fallen from them.
The mass of its formidable cloud-leaves was being shattered to pieces.
By that single elephant of the asura Kāladamana, the splendor of whose radiant clusters of jewel-like star-flowers— the beauty of whose trampled ears, tusks, and tail-hairs— was surpassed;
The wish-fulfilling tree of the three worlds is not shaken. (43) (A pair of verses;
a *kulaka* consisting of five verses, containing a pair within it:
With arms as formidable as upraised swords of a hundred moons—
Leaping from the frontal globes of his rutting enemy elephant,
he seized Vaijayantī in battle— she who was as white as a beautifully washed silk garment— and who was like the personified glory of his foe.
At whose face they become agitated, seeking to conceal the extreme paleness born of the shame and distress caused by bowing at the feet of those who would harm them.
Their broad foreheads were covered by their palms joined in reverential salutation. ||45||
It was strewn with massive stones and bones that acted as protruding spears, shattered by the forceful application of heel-strokes;
even the elephant of the Lord of the Immortals bore the marks of rut upon it.
The region of her cheeks has its luster clouded by a smear of cosmetic paste. ||46||
The fire of whose majesty brought the expanding white fame of his enemies to a state of lusterlessness;
he who, having suddenly leaped over the shores of the ocean, [crossed] with a thousand...
Like the radiance of a ray from the orb of the cool-rayed moon. ||47||
Who now would be able to follow the noble one, who has spread his own net over the battlefields, like a lattice-window,
wherein the darkness of fear of the enemy found no footing?
[He dwells] in that which is enriched by the moonlight of his clearly white fame. (A group of five verses.
[He gazes upon] the lotus of Hari’s navel, from which Brahmā was born as he recited from his golden pedestal-like pericarp, and whose petals are beautifully curved.
He who, having uprooted [the enemy], desired to place him in the position of an ear-ornament for the Fortune of the King of the Asuras with his own hand. ||49||
Upon the desert wastes of the path of battle, where the sword-blades were shimmering with mirages formed by the clusters of rays from the sun’s fierce beams,
he encountered the shadow of his enemy, who was overcome by the heat of his own exceedingly stubborn and aged pride.
What wonder is there that he did not obtain the discus? ||50||
He who, as if performing the *utsṛṣṭikāṅka* dance, brought to an end that which had been violently expanding in battle, agitated by the crushing of the pride of his staff-like arms.
Alone, he [faced] the enemy with weapons raised for battle. ||51||

When Śeṣa raises his mass of hood-jewels, which possess a cluster of luster reddened by the dense, billowing clouds of smoke from the fire of his breath, they appear like a great, ripening fruit-cluster.
Deeply exhausted, he held the tender date fruit. ||52||
O Gaṇanātha, having abandoned that state of being composed of envy— which ought to be abandoned— meditate upon that [state] on the field of the forefront of battle;
for it has repeatedly brought about the sleeplessness of the flowers of the mind.
His valor manifested swiftly, like that of Madhu; (this concludes the group of five verses).
Having made his fame—established throughout the quarters—a ladder for his powerful enemy's army, he acted as if desiring to behold it.
Upon the lofty summit of his shoulders, which resembled a palace illuminated by the moon-like radiance of his fame, the goddess of the fortune of his arm-strength ascended. ||54||

The surface of the earth’s expanse, which had its moat formed by the overflowing ocean, was once bowed down by the weight of his [the enemy's] army, whose fetters were the expansive coils of the lord of serpents rendered slack.
by armies striking from all sides at the cardinal points. ||55||
Upon the temples of his enemy-elephants—
which were stained by the flow of discolored blood from the playful strikes of his palms and marked by the traces of that [blood] even though the ichor had ceased— [he left his mark].
And the bees, agitated by fear, disappeared for a long time.
And who would venture against him, who has effortlessly mocked Indra and whose fierce submarine fire of valor has scorched the ocean of his enemies— difficult to cross and fraught with calamity?
[He was] Prajaṅgha, who had surpassed the three worlds in victory— (a *kalāpaka*).
His sword shone incessantly as the cause for the falling of the teardrops from the eyes of his enemies' beloveds.
With his thick-set shoulders and formidable, towering staff-like arms, he appeared like the smoke from the fire of his own prowess issuing forth in battles. ||58||
The circle of the earth, bent low by the immense weight of the great strength and power of his leaping elephants, and whose stability was shaken among the lords of the world-quarters,
was somehow supported by Śeṣa.
He bore [the serpent] with its mass of hoods raised and contracted. ||59||
On the shores of the ocean, the soldiers beheld those whose waters were copper-red with waves streaked by the spray of crushed Cīna cloth, like the temples of elephants conquered by fire.
Like clouds that have internalized the submarine fire within them. ||60||
At the moments of his departure,
the sudden paleness born of the embarrassment and grief of those he has subdued is instantly concealed by the mass of light-rays from the nails of his feet.
By means of the paste of pure conch-shell upon the faces of the enemies. ||61||
When his fierce majesty was thus manifested, the sharp-rayed sun— with its orb-tip reddened by the scattered essence of blood—
was eclipsed by that tree of his shadow as it stood upon the path of battle.

"Form a battle array, energize the multitude of soldiers, draw your bow, and swiftly release your arrows— I perceive [the enemy] with particular intensity as they maintain a great height from afar. (A *kulaka* of five verses.)
"Shatter [them] in an instant! Crush the throngs of elephants and the horsemen!"—thus he crushed the host of enemies, as if [speaking] to a servant. ||63||
By him, whose body was rendered helpless by the illusion of worldly manifestation,
the entire assembly of gods and demons was struck with wonder even as they gazed upon that one who was white as the moon.
He quickly snatched away their fame, just as the enemy of the Daityas (Viṣṇu) seized the nectar of immortality.
In whose palaces the painted figures on the walls, their decorative materials left unfinished, become soiled;
their eyes devoid of the occasion for opening, [gaze upon] the blazing [fire].
They would perceive the Goddess Śrī as if she were unstable, day and night alike. ||65||
Whose face, even though he was in the prime of youth, was overspread by the rays from the nails of a single finger placed upon the surface of his cheek,
which was exceedingly tender at its base.
It bore, as it were, the whiteness of old age at the root of its ear. ||66||
How could that comet-like warrior,
firmly rooted in his position on the field of battle and adorned with the white banner of his exultant fame, be endured by other brave soldiers?
With his staff-like arms raised, blocking the entire expanse of the sky— (this is a *kulaka* consisting of five verses)—
he made the creeper of Lakṣmī blossom with flowers upon the Dānava Bali, making her heartening with its fruit.
Its roots were shattered by the unimpeded falling of the blade-edge of his sword, which was as clear as water from the act of bestowing gifts.
The fame of him, who for the sake of binding Bali, traversed the worlds together with his own self— his fame possessing a splendor as white as the moon—
is like the nectar of the honey from his lotus feet.
She wiped her shoulder as if it had been washed by the waters of the Mandākinī. ||69||
The sharp edge [of the sword], stained with the blood dripping from the severed and cruel throat of the Lord of Daityas,
was smeared as if by the application of a fresh whetstone.
Upon which his discus appears as if marked by a streak of mud. ||70||

The pair of his lotus-like hands, belonging to him whose form is the universe, shone brilliantly with their multitude of red petal-like fingers, which were like rows of eyelashes consisting of the rays of light from his trembling clusters of nails.
The seed-vessel [of the heart] has the orbs of the sun and moon suspended as its filaments. ||71||
For him who has assumed the form of the entire universe, his [rays] shine most intensely— long, straight, and having attained great abundance—
as they reach the thousands of women with full hips without exception.
As if their delight were in a firm embrace, [his] staff-like arms [stretched out]. ||72||
The splendor of whose effortless, unrestrained tossing upon his bed— the remainder of which had been dwarfed by the ocean that served as his pillow—
consisted of the mud of blood playfully crushed [by his movements].
The *madhu* and *kaṭabha* [demons] were like *ṭiṭṭibhas* submerged deep within [the ocean]. ||73||
The mass of flames from the fire of his breath,
which desired to consume the multitude of hoods of the serpent Kāliya,
was suddenly extinguished at the base of his crest by [the touch of]—
By means of the torrential streams of the flowing waters of the Yamunā; ||74||
Whose arm, possessing the dark luster of a fresh rain-cloud, was seen within the cavity of the face of the goddess with disheveled hair,
bearing a spreading flame from the mouth of the submarine fire.
It possesses the grace of the ocean waves tossed by the wind at the shore. ||75||
Terrified, that enemy of Kaiṭabha assumed a state like that of a forest region containing lions with gaping jaws;
from whom [the gods], with chowries in their hands, [looked up at] the King of the Immortals...
To those who possess the supreme Lakṣmī, whose eyes are intent upon their faces. ||76||

What is the use of praising here those many who have perfected themselves, or others? Indeed, I shall tell you this very essence; for the wise proclaim that this alone is the heart of political ethics (nīti).

That by which the strength and weakness of one's own and the opponent's positions are scrutinized. (A group of ten verses) Their lotus-hands remain perpetually in bloom, even though struck repeatedly by the rays of the nectar-moon of his face.
For wise men in this world, prosperity acquired through right conduct brings far greater joy to the disposition of their minds than mere wealth. (78)

Therefore, let some messenger, skilled in delivering messages and possessing knowledge of the true nature of affairs concerning the various constituent circles [of states], quickly approach that son of Diti.
For they say that for one who seeks enlightenment, even a vow is an enemy. ||79||
O noble ones, even if that lord of the asuras were to accept our sweet proposal regarding the affairs of the celestial realm,
he would remain exactly as he is in all his actions.
Then the punishment was duly administered according to the established legal code. ||80||
Thus has this, containing the essence of the qualities of policy, been proclaimed by me to you;
I have no fear here from the sons of Diti.
This Lord now stands upon the swing of action.
"What more could there be?"—thus we do not know the path that transcends reasoning. ||81||
Having thus spoken words following the path of policy with impetuosity— his cheeks being rubbed by the tips of his swaying jeweled earrings— he ceased;
and praising those words as "excellent," he appointed Kālamusala as an envoy to the enemy.
The wielder of the trident, amidst the shouts of "Victory! proclaimed by the bards, left the assembly hall. ||82||

Thus ends the sixteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Dispatching of the Messenger," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked with the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
The seventeenth canto begins:
Then, as the sound of the conch marking midday arose, his attendants, along with their graceful women, stood up.
With joyful hearts, they went forth from Mount Mandara to gather the flowers of the trees, followed by their retinues. ||1||
There, the mātuluṅga fruits were plundered by the hands of monkeys leaping about in their eagerness for the juice of various fruits;
and the clusters of gems upon its rocky slopes appeared like masses of jewels tossed about by the impact of the winds rising at the end of an aeon.
The sun was sprinkled with droplets from the trunks of elephants engaged in plunging into the long ponds of the celestial city;
meanwhile, the circles of yak-cows were agitated by the playful roar of lions within the forest thickets.
With its continuous rows of silver plantain groves on the tossing banks, it possessed the steady play of lightning amidst the clouds;
and the front walls of its cave-dwellings were dappled by the rays of gems from the ornaments scattered there by the celestial nymphs who had enjoyed them.
The fatigue and distress of the celestial nymphs were washed away by the clear waters of mountain torrents reflecting large boulders;
meanwhile, the mountain’s jeweled peaks and groves were clustered with masses of foam issuing from the mouths of the horses of the wandering sun-chariot.
They took delight upon seeing the clear waters of the mountain lakes and ponds, where bits of lotus stalks were being nibbled by cooing female *kādaṃbī* ducks,
and where vast quantities of fresh *aguru* wood were being consumed by forest fires. (A group of five verses) As they gazed upon the faces of the dark-complexioned women—
which seemed to eclipse the beauty of the autumnal moon— they appeared like the very countenances of the nights themselves.
That was a marvel of his state as a Sugata: that his feet, though possessed of it, appeared free from dense redness. ||7||

Assuming the form of massive headless trunks, conquering the entire world with the loud blare of their uplifted conchs, those young women bore freshly polished, gleaming swords and displayed the splendor of exquisite armlets. (8)
Bearing a beauty charming with the fatigue of incessant amorous play— beauty that surpassed even that of those [ladies] who had suffered the wounds of the arrows [of the God of Love]— those women,
following their leaders into the forest, moved forth like the armies of the Flower-Armed One (Kusumāyudha). (A pair of verses) As they went,
their feet, which surpassed blooming lotuses, joyfully traversed the groves of night-lilies.
Under the pretext of being drawn along by swans attracted by the tinkling of their anklets, they seemed to follow the young brides.
Just as the earth’s surface obstructed the beauty of the moon-like faces with the jar-like breasts of lovely women as they grew higher and higher,
so too did it expand its own breadth through those hips, as if to look upon that very beauty.

When her upper garment slipped away, the celestial nymph, seeing the nail-marks of her beloved upon the tips of her breasts, stumbled as she walked with an inattentive mind; oh, how strange! Love does not perceive danger anywhere at all.
Beholding the water with its clusters of shimmering lotuses marked by the circles of their lovers' kisses,
those women, languid from the weight of their hips, moved forward out of eagerness, their creeper-like arms cast around the necks of their beloveds.
Suddenly placing her footsteps upon his footprints, which were made dark by droplets of perspiration, she followed the path of her most beloved;
oh, how wonderful is love, so skilled in the manifold display of its various methods! 14.

As a certain woman was departing with graceful movements, her jeweled girdle, being loosened by her clinging creeper-like arm, cried out as if from the delusion of fearing an imminent fall of its precious hips. (15)
As if out of compassion so that no injury might occur to their tender feet on the rough path,
the women spread before them a carpet of fresh sprouts from their own shadows, using their ruby-studded anklets as the tools.
For a certain woman who was weary from traveling the road and was quickly being fanned by her friend, a fresh peacock-feather fan— white as the stalk of a young sprout—
became a crest-cluster upon her ear, its beauty reflected in her spotless cheek.

As another woman walked along the path, her hand grasping the hand of her beloved, the beauty of her face blossomed with the continuous thrill of horripilation caused by his touch, while her waist-knot became loosened as it slipped from the curve of her hips. 18.

In the thicket of trees, a certain creeper—seeming possessed by manifest curiosity—crept for a moment with its sprout-like hand, then embraced from afar, and finally coiled around the slender waist of a dark-complexioned woman. 19.

As they walked, the beautiful women, leaving behind footprints of their slender feet upon the sands of the ocean shore— sands that resembled the cities of the sea-nymphs— proclaimed through the deep indentations of their fresh nail-marks that those rugged riverbanks were their equals.

At the entrance, the women beheld the castor-oil plant, its form indistinguishable from a bird’s foot with its webbed toes and claws, its stalk and leaves exceedingly slender, yet standing upright like the terrifying, time-worn shanks of Death.

Bearing ears, eyes, breasts, hands, and feet that attained mutual comparison through their own beauty, they even made the rows of eyelashes—which abide upon the path of excellence—appear as if they had incurred reproach for being crooked. ||22||
Producing an exceeding delight through their most cooling and heart-pleasing touch, and possessing a steady radiance,
those women with lips like the *bimba* fruit shone like unprecedented flashes of lightning, their forms draped in shimmering, thick clouds.
Then, with their minds fixed upon their beloveds, that youthful assembly stood engaged in the clear manifestation of the flower-arrowed god [Kāma],
performing music with great splendor through the proper application of pitch, words, and rhythm.

Then the young women, possessing the splendor of flower-garlands and the luster of golden waistbands, assumed a fresh beauty upon their hair like a necklace of jewels formidable with radiant rays, as if they were the very cleverness of Kubera himself.

The world praised the height upon the jar-like breasts of the lordless women, the breadth across their broad hips, and the state of gradual emaciation in their waists; for the stability of a person’s condition within its own nature is worthy of praise.
Even those who have attained power possess helplessness through their lack of strength, yet those who have fallen do not cling to the state of being powerful.
Though their jar-like breasts were lofty, the beauty of those women rested upon their well-roundedness and their possession of four-cornered symmetry.

Then, with pearls possessing forms delightful through their qualities of extreme clarity and firmness, situated in excellent positions, and enriched by complete characteristics, the pearl necklaces did not lose their splendor—just as the graceful movements of beautiful women do not lose their beauty when performed by their full array of limbs. ||28||

Then Rambhā, whose thighs were like plantain stalks and whose beauty was marked by the four auspicious signs, displayed a fresh splendor like a newly composed *nāṭikā*—a performance characterized by graceful movements, charming and playful actions, and a hero who delights in the aesthetic sentiment of love (*śṛṅgāra*). ||29||

Bearing a fresh vine of lip-petals and sprouts that bore the lofty splendor of the flower-arrowed god of love, the deer-eyed woman captivated the person standing on the path; she was like the tide of the ocean of loveliness. ||30||

Touched by the sole of her foot, the aśoka tree—dense with hundreds of clinging clusters of blossoms and thick with spreading creepers—began to bloom most rapidly along the path. For who standing on the road is not a vessel for fortune? (31)
"Surely, having rested in this bower together with your husband, you may now dispel the fatigue of the journey"—
thus did a creeper, its tip caught in the hem of the young woman's fresh garment, seem from afar to offer a request.
The heavy hips of another woman, who was walking behind her, clearly bore an even greater weight;
for her lover waited for her for a long time with passion while she looked at a rival young woman.

The fragrant breeze from the grove began to waft along, followed by a swarm of bees, only so long as it did not reach the range of the women's perfumes; for who would abandon his current position upon finding something superior? (34)
While the drama of the fresh month of Madhu was being introduced behind the curtain of dense forest creepers, a warbling began from the actor that is the cuckoo;
it was a captivating prelude that stole away the ears of the assembly of women.
Bearing within it mango trees as if they were garments, delightful with the presence of fragrance and charming with *girikarṇikā* flowers,
that forest shone along the shore like the royal harem of the lord of the earth, adorned with magnificent pearl necklaces.

Beholding him— who stood as if in nirvāṇa, with his oil exhausted, neither reached by the high wind nor fanned by the gentle breeze— the women were consumed by a twofold heat of longing for love, like that of a lamp at dawn.

A lotus, appearing like the hand of the Sun with its shimmering petal-fingers raised up, was gazed upon by the dark-complexioned women; it seemed to bear a slender cup made of gold under the guise of its seed-vessel. (38)

While traveling on the road, the young men met in a grove and rested there; they engaged in unrestrained friendship with one another, for intimacy toward a friend is indeed the primary fruit of social interaction. (39)

The face, with its left eyebrow like a bakula tree in full bloom from being sprinkled by the fragrant wine of her mouth, is graced by the pollen of flower-clusters falling as their filaments are shaken by the feet of swarms of bees. 40.
Rising up, it was delightful with the fresh and exceedingly subtle fragrance of *avalava*, *līlā*, and *lavaṅga* flowers;
bees were clinging to the honey of the clusters of *mandāra* blossoms, which were in full bloom and whose pervasive scent spread throughout the circle of the quarters. ||41||

Having entered the dense forest, with his lotus-like hand clasped by the beloved’s hand resting upon his side, he was surrounded by bees who had fallen into a sleep induced by the excess of confidence and the pleasure of drinking the fresh nectar dripping from him. 42.
Then the young women observed that the weight of their heavy hips was increased by the swarms of bees;
for whom in this world does one who has attained her desired fruit, or one who is being relied upon, not become an object of honor?
(Cakvalaka) At that time, she was agitated by the approach of Rāma, while the *sāla* trees were shaken by the monkeys moving in succession.
Like Laṅkā itself, the forest ground shone forth, filled with clear-sighted śuka and sāraṇa birds, and interspersed with rākṣasas of dense and beautiful luster.

Drawing from the forests sprays of sweet nectar and filled with the astringent fragrance of *śephālī* flowers, the breeze brought joy to the slender-waisted women; for who, having attained superior excellence, would not be most blessed? (45)
Even a single arrow from that [god] is unbearable; how much more so he who possesses manifold forms and is beyond the scope of calculation?
Thus, when the heart of the proud woman was pierced, Kāma’s purpose was indeed accomplished, and his bow was no longer strung. (46)

The spring *kundavallī* creepers laden with blossoms and the summer *pāṭala* trees in full bloom on every mountain peak seemed, from afar, to mock each other’s boldness in breaking the pride of young women. 47.

At that time, the pride and fortitude of the women, which had previously surpassed even the fresh blossoms of newly blooming jasmine, reached its culmination at the onset [of the rainy season], just as the bud of the kunda flower reaches its end in the height of summer. 48.

Bearing the beauty of fresh sprouts, possessing rows of trees resounding with the cries of birds, and situated near the banks of rivers like the autumn season itself, the forest grove spread joy among the beautiful women in their intoxication. 49.
Even though they were blinded by thirst, the bees abandoned the tall mango branch in full bloom and wandered about;
for the wise, even when distressed, do not set foot upon something trivial, especially when a superior object—such as the fragrant breath from the face of a beloved—is at hand. 50.

As the vine-like woman danced under the influence of the wind, her leaf-like hand was seen by the slender-waisted women to resemble the sacrificial fire-altar (tretāgni), bearing the shape of the three upper coverings upon it. 51.

By the fingertips of the women, which possessed superior qualities, the breaking of the young shoots was forcibly accomplished; yet, because those very fingertips were stained with redness by their own fresh and brilliant luster, the breaking of the shoots was rendered redundant. ||52||

As she raised her arm—adorned with priyaṅgu flowers resting at its base—to pluck the blossoms on the tips of the tree branches, she caused her rival women to feel dejected; for even though it was but a wing, that of a timid bird, she desired it as if it were the fruit of immortality.
As a young woman, her mind impetuous with the desire to pluck the blossoms resting on the tips of the branches as she embraced them, the tree—
though it had not yet reached the emergence of its fruit-bearing season— attained a state of abundance, resplendent with a heavy burden of fruit.
A woman, bent by her full breasts, was unable to reach the flower situated at the tip of a tree branch that she desired to grasp;
there, having been plucked by her lover and handed to her, she appeared visibly as high as her rival. 55.
At that time,
the abundance of sprouts on the trees— which constantly bore the beauty of emerging passion and were scarred by the fingernails of celestial women— made their youthfulness truly fruitful.
The bees drank the honey from the flowers of creepers that were broken by the faults of countless calamities;
yet for those who are wavering and stained, compliance with their own interests never exceeds [their] fickleness. 57.

Another woman, eager for amorous play, did not clearly reveal her throbbing secret parts as she adjusted her garment—which had slipped down from her broad hips and was ill-fitting due to her lack of restraint—while her husband looked on. (58)

The beloved’s intention was suddenly perceived by her as his glance fell upon a thicket following the movement of his brows; knowing his gesture, she entered the path he took. Indeed, those who understand hints never delay in taking action when there is something to be done. (59)

Drawn by the breaths of the dark-complexioned maiden as she moved in agitation—breaths fragrant with incessant perfume—the bee wandered toward her face; yet, though driven away, it did not cease its audacity, for indeed, the impudence of the soiled one is never sufficient.
When the sprouts were forcibly seized by the lotus-hands of the beloveds of the enemy-slayers, what wonder was it that the trees, shaken by the breezes blowing from the groves, became dejected? 61.
The swarm of bees, appearing like a cloud of smoke, shone intensely nearby upon the Aśoka tree;
with its coppery hue, it seemed like a creeper that had suddenly leaped up, scorching the hearts of proud women.
The blue lotus, which had been brought by her husband to serve as the young woman’s ear-ornament while it was in full bloom,
seemed to gaze at its own reflection in the mirror of her spotless cheek, as if overwhelmed by the excellence of its own beauty.

Thinking, "There is no conflict between one who is superior and another of equal or greater splendor; rather, prostration is appropriate here," the woman with full thighs bent down her ear-ornament lotus far from her eye and, as it were, offered a hymn of praise through the humming of bees.
At that time, as he made his dwelling among the sturdy flowering trees— coppery, black, and white— the forest regions,
which were the very domain of the God of Love, came to possess a vast and long-lasting splendor through the thickets of blossoms.
The proud women did not wipe away from their eyes the tears that were reddened by trickling, which caused a charming pang in the heart;
like dust entering the eye, they did not touch them away as their lips quivered with indignation.

As she was picking flowers even upon an easily accessible branch, the youth himself, wishing to place his fingertips [upon her], suddenly obstructed the girl with thighs like plantain trees by means of various clever stratagems; oh, how love makes even that which is unfavorable favorable! 67.
The bride did not place such reliance on her ear-ornament, even though it was made of gold and set with a golden hammer-pattern, as she did on her rival’s earring,
which was beautiful with petals placed upon it by the hand of her beloved.
The swarm of bees, drawn by the fragrant breath from the mouth of another woman,
formed a broad halo around her moon-like face with clouds of pollen from the flower-earrings shaken by the wind of their wings.
Menakā’s beauty, her excellent bosom slightly bent by the playfulness of amorous gestures, received from her most beloved a flower brought nearby with its petals fully blossomed;
she took it from her rival, who was facing her, as she sat upon her lap.
When a certain woman was given a flower by her dearest lover as a token of affection, yet with the name [of another] uttered in reverse order,
she— her beauty marked by lips quivering in rage and eyes reddened— strangely enough, assumed a state of ill-will.
Another woman, her smile radiant as she rested upon the chest of her beloved, her soft forefeet awkwardly placed there,
her gaze wandering, took a stumbling step while her slender arms were entwined within his neck.
With her waist utterly exhausted from being raised up by her agitation, the lady of lovely form, having somehow regained her composure once more,
placed upon her head a floral ornament from which the bees had been drawn away by its fragrance— she whose brows were arched.
(A pair of verses) With a young tamāla sprout held at the tip of her ear by the lotus-hand of her beloved, a certain woman...
Her eye shed tears for her rival wife, as if incessantly struck by the smoke. ||74||
When her beloved was hidden by a dense thicket of creepers, the heart of the other woman became filled with apprehension;
for the God of Love, who possesses excessive jealousy, dwells within the hearts of women whose lovers are truly dear to them. (75)
Then, her beloved being far away from her crowded quarters, that fair-browed woman sang with a longing heart in the *pañcama* melody;
she wandered for a long time with the tips of her fingers like tongs, searching aimlessly for flowers.
With the beauty of her eyes and brows manifesting through various transformations, indicative of amorous form and unfavorable to her rivals,
a graceful gesture (hāva) blossomed upon the thighs of Rambhā as she gazed at her beloved— a gesture accompanied by incomparable, rhythmic contractions of her neck.

From the breasts of beautiful women, which were trembling due to the impetuous desire to pluck flowers blooming at the tips of tree branches, necklaces fell away; thus, there was no long-lasting union between those who possess virtues and those who are elevated. 78.

In the backstage, she of shapely thighs, established in a smooth and charming manner and bearing the quality of being infused with the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra), extended the joy of her beloved through the graceful play of noble dancing, like the Kaiśikī style of dramatic performance. ||79||

In the midst of the path, the hearts of the women were captivated by the amorous gestures of their beloveds, who were adorned with crests of various blossoming forest flowers and fearlessly drinking honey-wine, and who were filled with the intense passion of love. (80)

In the forest regions, the sweet warbling of peahens—possessing a beauty that delights the mind and providing a source of pleasure to the ear—attained the status of a melodic note and spread a luster as if performing a cleansing rite for the intoxicated women as they moved along. (81)

When the beautiful woman had attained union with her lover in a secluded and delightful place, the tears arising from the weight of her joy instantly washed away the decorative leaf-patterns on her cheeks;
for whom in this world would it not be a misfortune to be dull-witted? 82.
O fortunate one, this hundredfold power of yours is indeed unimpaired and truly marvelous; it was fashioned by the Creator with great care.
For while you wield the thunderbolt in your speech without hesitation as you shatter the mountains, it does not reside in your hand.

To her who was thus speaking from afar, the youth, bowing his head and wishing to appease her by calling her by the name of a co-wife, made that young woman—who had eyes flooded with tears and whose inner anguish was manifest—break into a smile. (84) [This is a pair of verses.
Having seen from afar in the forest a mango tree entwined with a creeper, which was like a leaping cluster of arrows with flowers for its shafts;
The young woman became free from pride and submissive to you; for who indeed would not feel longing upon seeing such beauty? (85)

The ear-ornament, its beauty of face raised upward from the desire to grasp the flowers of the tall trees, slipped from the base of the ears of the young women; that it fell after having climbed up is no cause for wonder. 86.
The pollen of flowers that had settled in the eyes of his beloved was blown away by her lover with the breath from his mouth;
by that very act, the eyes of her rival, who stood nearby, were brought far into a state of turbidity.
At that time, the beauty of the slender-limbed maiden’s ornament of real lotus petals was tossed upward by her desire to grasp a flower;
it withered due to the extreme delicacy of her creeper-like arms—for indeed, even those who are well-rounded may suffer distress.
Beholding upon his beloved’s body—a site for songs of clearly parched tones—such peerless beauty of face and hands, the lord of her life became a festival for his wide eyes. (89)

Another youth, his face turning pale from the onset of embarrassment as he tied a garland for a dark-complexioned girl— who was filled with extreme despondency because he had mistaken her identity— stood motionless, creating the suspicion that he was a mountain stream.
Toward her friend Sāgaska, she became trembling; her body was covered with a mass of horripilation drenched in perspiration.
This fair-limbed girl desired to maintain a pretense of indifference while attempting to seize him—oh, how love in young women is rendered perverse by the artifice of youthful innocence! 91.

Then, passing by the *karṇikāra* tree—which was nearby, possessed the beauty of brilliant colors, yet lacked fragrance—the young women approached the *lavaṅga* tree, desiring it for its scent; for even from outward appearance, one attains favor through excellence.

At that time, the festival of fresh creepers was not celebrated by the women, nor was it fully displayed by the young bees whose minds were delighted by their intense attachment to drinking the wine of the nectar of the flowers as they wandered about. (93)
Then, the cluster of lotuses was utterly defeated by their faces in terms of fragrance, dense luster, and tenderness;
consequently, it could not find a place anywhere among the swarms of bees. Indeed, those who are devoted to excellence are never deceived by others. 94.

Bearing naturally beautiful forms and skilled in the art of weaving garlands, they captivated their lords all the more; for a person of merit is drawn even further by an excellence in some other quality. (95)
Beholding those beautiful women, who possessed the grace of delicate and sparse ointments and whose lovely limbs were arranged in graceful poses—
resembling wonderful painted walls in a charming dance— the beloved person felt great satisfaction.
Sometimes, naturally beautiful things clearly come into union with an unreal quality over time;
even the fragrance of these women, which was worthy of being matched by *karṇikāra* flowers, has been surpassed by the succession of their sighs and breaths. (97)
Desiring to obtain the beauty of his beloved’s firm, rounded hips, the youth, his mind filled with longing, fashioned a girdle of flowers;
yet, having committed an offense through association with another young woman, he approached her with a heart full of regret.
Upon his arrival, she—her eyes crimson with anger at the memory of him and her lotus-face smiling—embraced him.

For generally, when fate is unfavorable, the object of men's meditation turns out quite otherwise than expected. (A pair of verses) At that time, in the forest region, she grew faint from the exertion of amorous play, her breasts shaking with her sighs.
The fair-browed woman shed a multitude of sweat-drops, like a shephali creeper releasing a rain of flowers when struck by the wind. ||100||

The gaze of another woman—whose eyes were like slightly drooping lotuses with curved petals, and which was beautiful with its pupils cast down—was captivated by her beloved as she grew weary from the playful wanderings in the forest. ||101||

As they gazed upon their most beloved in the forest on the mountain slope where the doe-eyed woman had wandered astray, the nail-marks situated upon the slopes of her high breasts shone, glistening with sweat and variegated by the drops clinging to her waist. 102.

As a certain woman approached with her sprout-like hand, a creeper—its leaf-design washed away by the perspiration of her fatigue—quickly drew a companion-like line upon her cheek with the pollen of its flowers that clung there. 103.

On that mountain, where the vines possessed a charming beauty woven from the splendors of all seasons and bore blossoms that never slept, they yielded their nectar most abundantly to the bees; for how can there be a final limit to the excellence of worldly things? 104.

Having pulled back the spotless garment of her new bridegroom, whose curiosity was made manifest by his gaze, the creeper-like woman clearly showed her moon-like face; for from whatever direction the virtuous turn their attention, there comes the accomplishment of their purpose.
Having become worthy recipients by performing in the drama of the flower-garden at the conclusion of the festival of the Love-god,
the lotus-eyed women then emerged from the forest grove through the clear entrance-path where they had stood as interludes.

Having subsequently enjoyed the groves on the jeweled slopes of Mount Mandara— which clearly displayed the paths of the *amṛgaḍima* dance, as well as the *saṭṭaka*, *vyāyoga*, and other dramatic forms— the beautiful women, their limbs overcome by exhaustion, departed for the forested banks of the ocean where the ten types of drama (*daśarūpaka*) were vividly manifested.

Displaying the sport of the *rāsa* dance in every direction, beautified by various trees following its expansive rhythm, that forest was left with great difficulty by those beautiful women; for what objects indeed can be easily abandoned when they are so delightful? (108)
Having plunged together with their beloveds into the forest floor, which was as beautiful as the slopes of Mount Kailāsa where the Goddess Pārvatī dwells as half of Śiva’s body,
the women did not perceive from afar the celestial river, lovely with its charming sandy banks.
Seeing before her a swarm of bees humming as they settled upon a blossoming *kovidāra* tree,
a certain clever woman, out of boldness, initiated a conversation with her beloved regarding the playfulness of those birds.
The flower-garland of the girdle-string, clasped by the hand of her beloved and hanging down upon the orb of her hips,
shone like the swarm of bees clinging out of greed for the abundant fragrance of the beautiful-browed woman.
It was adorned with tinkling bells that captivated the ear like a swarm of humming bees.
With their necks curved by breasts that served as the seat for ear-ornaments,
and with various blossoming flowers resting upon the region of their girdles, those lotus-eyed women shone like the very flowers of the flower-arrowed god of love.
They were like armories fashioned by Sugrīṣmaka. ||112||

Then, as if to wipe away the beauty of those women who were dripping with beads of perspiration born from the fatigue of wandering in the forest— a retinue of moons, planets, and stars— the bees, greedy for the fragrance of their breath, [flocked around].
They were being sportively fanned by the wings of swarms of bees.

Together with her lovers, she descends to bathe in the river that flows to the gods— a river whose golden lotuses sway and shimmer in the wind of its surging waves, whose sandy banks are strewn with the dust of powdered jewels,
and where the regions of her hips grow weary from the weight of her heaving breasts.
With graceful steps slow with playfulness, those women of curved limbs departed. (114) (A pair of verses).

Thus ends the seventeenth canto, titled "The Description of the Gathering of Flowers," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was honored by the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
The Eighteenth Canto.
While the sun’s radiance proceeded, causing exhaustion to his limbs, it was— as if out of resentment by the women who were walking along—
shattered into fragments by the falling glances of their eyes, which resembled blooming blue lotuses.

Even though the white umbrellas being held aloft by them were entirely eclipsed by the flood of moonlight consisting of their own pure, liquid beauty and luster that inundated all directions, they were nevertheless inferred to be present by means of their golden handles.
Another woman shone as she walked, holding a parasol white as the moonlight of the horizon;
its shimmering pearl fringe was like a cluster of stars, while the face of her moon-like countenance appeared like the radiant orb of the moon itself.

The faces of the women, delightful with their beautiful eyes, provided shade through their charming parasols—parasols that possessed lovely expanses, bore a whiteness, and attained the splendor of the full moon’s orb. ||4||
The earth was overspread by the circles of shade from the moving parasols of the celestial women,
which were as if the sons of Siṃhika descended out of greed to swallow the moon of her face, thereby increasing its vastness.
The dust raised by the road seemed to turn the natural, clear luster of the women’s beauty grey;
meanwhile, the creepers, shaken by the wind, appeared as if they were waving a multitude of yak-tail fans held by the women nearby.

Then she walked slowly, her hips—bound with girdles and possessing full, rounded forms—making the path narrow; it was as if she moved slowly because of the excessive weight of Kandarpa, who was manifesting within the lines of her limbs.
Even though it had not been rubbed off, the mass of lac-dye on the thighs of the women— set against the ruby stones inlaid upon their golden anklets and armlets—
was obscured by the reflection and thus failed to become visible.
"Because you were preoccupied with the desire to look at the forest, you did not see me as I went before you"—
saying this under a pretext, a certain woman struck her lover from behind with her two full breasts from close range.
As they walked, the rows of swans, drawn forward by the tinkling of their anklets, boldly followed ahead;
even the expansive temples of those women, with their radiant white luster, seemed to mock them with the nature of a smile.
A certain girdle, falling at her feet, obstructed a woman who was moving forward with fury toward her approaching lord, having cast off her clearly visible garment;
it did so because, through the intervention of her female friends, its binding had become loose.
As Sīmantinī was walking gracefully along the path, a necklace with its string snapped fell from the tips of her full, high breasts;
truly, such a fall is always appropriate for those devoid of virtue.
"O charming ones, from where does this radiant splendor of their feet come, which belongs to these lotuses?
Thus, as it were out of affection, the multitude of anklets spoke to the swans with its sweet tinkling. 13.

Even on the road, there was a blossoming of lotus-stalks that had taken root— those stalks which were the very support of Fortune, whose spaces between the quarters were variegated by the shadows of rows of bees in the form of their tremulous side-glances, and which never withered as beds of playful lotuses.
Then, having crossed the mountain paths where saffron flowers clung to the spreading vines of betel,
those moon-faced ones reached a flowing river whose waters were shaded by golden lotuses frequented by flocks of swans.
He approached a holy seat in this world that was perpetually filled with water for tranquility, yet bold with the breaking of waves;
it resembled the mass of clouds known as Puṣkarāvartaka, possessing the playful majesty of the time of the world's dissolution.
[She saw] a river whose golden lotuses were opened by the seal of sleep, whose pure waters were cool with the shade of lotuses,

where swans were scattered by waves rising from the water, and whose high banks were variegated by flocks of swans. (Tilaka) Having seen that the women on the bank had surpassed her own gait as she approached the embankment to bathe, [she proceeded].
Then the water, agitated by the surging waves, seemed to abandon the swans because they were situated among the pearls.

For the sake of honoring the beautiful women as they approached, the Mandākinī offered a vessel made of lotus petals, in which the multitude of pure water droplets appeared like a precious offering of clear pearls.
A certain woman, seated upon the lap of a pillar and desiring to bathe, her entire body radiant with the beauty of her own transparent loveliness,
was as if embraced by the water that rose up out of intense longing and affection.
Quickly cooling his limbs with their touch, delightful to the eyes with the sight of their clear reflections, those beautiful women fell upon him—
who was as dark as smooth lapis lazuli— as the rays of the cool-rayed moon fall upon the sky.
As the women were falling quickly from the high banks of the mountain stream, their heavy,
full hips sank into the water due to their weight.

With flower-garlands falling away, with locks of hair becoming disheveled, and with their strings of broad, tinkling pearl necklaces breaking asunder, the playful sport of the lotus-thighed women beginning their bath proceeded like the very goddess of amorous enjoyment being dragged away. 23.
The cackling of the female swans on the shore, as they approached, was surpassed by the girdles of those women;
as if seized by internal envy, the agitated waters rendered those girdles mute by overwhelming them.

Terrified by the water whose waves were tossed upward by the agitation of the jeweled steps, she clung to the hand of her beloved as she descended; and the heart of her co-wife was likewise gripped by intense pain.

Out of a desire for coolness, one woman, though unwilling to plunge into the water, entered the river at its edge out of compliance with her husband's wishes; what indeed will people not do out of love? (26)

A certain woman, her lotus-face radiant with passion, felt inward resentment as she saw the body-unguent from another woman’s limbs clinging to her lover; under the pretext of play, she rubbed it away with blows of water from a horn.
As the water was struck gently by lotus-hands performing rhythmic movements with the grace of drummers, the beloveds,
acting as dancing girls through the play of their arched brows, drew near to their lover with a charming, playful dance.

The row of foam, possessing the elegance of beautiful women wearing wreaths of *sinduvāra* flowers as a natural adornment, shone forth with the beauty of sloughed-off skins coiled and torn apart by darting, striped serpents. 29.
The water, its eyes— the fish— opening and closing as they were tossed about by the waves surging in every direction,
beheld the pervasive beauty of those women’s limbs as if out of curiosity for those submerged in it.
One woman, having been sprinkled from afar with water while her co-wives were called by name, fell into a state of burning anguish;
yet another, though not yet touched by the water, attained peace upon hearing her own name recited by her beloved.

Did the waves of the bees, resounding as they rose from the impact against the breasts of women, fail to grant the rows of filaments in the lotuses for them to drink? Or rather, let the mass of water mingle with the surging [waves]. || 32 ||

Having dived and emerged from within the water while his co-wife was looking on with eyes harsh with anger, he embraced a woman whose face was smiling; she considered that to be the fulfillment of her favor toward him.

"Those who imagine a resemblance between the faces of women and full-blown lotuses possess an incorrect understanding. As if reflecting this thought, the mass of waves, possessing the beauty of a smile of abundant foam, became the internal rival to their splendor. (34)
"May you attain from afar the splendor that is comparable to the face of a woman—let this much suffice.
Thus, as it were, did the lotuses address the bees with their humming sounds, for those bees had become a cause for shame for the lotuses as they drew near.

Seeing the full-blown blue lotus that had served as Sallīlāvatī’s ear-ornament fallen and scattered by the mass of water droplets in the Mandākinī, the lotus wept, as it were, out of brotherly affection.
The lotuses that once served as ear-ornaments for women were now submerged by the mass of water;
yet the lotus growing within the water remained just as it was—for who can uproot that which is firmly established in its watery depths?

"Having placed you upon its lap, this lotus surely holds you beneath it with the shade of its eyes"—thus the agitated water, as if out of affection for its offspring, drew the lotus away with its hands of waves. (38)
The water, having reached its highest point through contact with the lotuses worn on the ears of women,
was carried far away as if by the rising hands of waves in sport, and there it spread a foam-like laughter.
A certain newlywed bride, displaying horripilation, a trembling of her thighs under the pretext of cold, and hissing sounds,
clearly revealed before her friend the passion of love for her beloved.
A certain woman, experiencing joy, embraced her beloved who was agitated by the tossing of the waves;
for generally, even a disturbance that arises leads to the welfare of those who are tender-hearted. (41)
The sound of the women’s girdles clearly surpassed the beauty of the cries of swans on the bank;
as if thinking, "This [sound] has been interrupted by the floods of water," the river spread a smile upon its waves.

Like the white splendor of a flock of swans struck by surging waves, the shimmering mass of foam produced by the agitation of the tips of amorous women's breasts shone as it fell from their bodies, pale as the moon. 43.
With her long braid of hair, gathered by a mass of thighs and shining with the luster of the stalks of pale-red lotuses,
the woman attained the likeness of the coils of a serpent rising from the netherworld.

Bearing a thrill of horripilation as if from the touch of cool water, the fair-browed woman, her love revealed by her embrace, laughed aloud as she was surpassed by the splashing of another who had approached from afar with her beloved.

One girl, taking a lotus-stalk fiber from the tips of the stalks scattered before her during a game of water-sports, desired to fashion a necklace out of the clusters of pearls; for who, possessed of such innocence, has the power of discernment? 46.
The pure, unblemished tip of the jeweled neck-ornament of the fair-browed woman, shattered by the pressure of play,
shone as it fell beneath the ocean like a crescent moon slipping from the path of the stars.

Then, the arrows of glances released by them— whose shafts were the playful, trembling outer corners of their eyes, made beautiful by the petals of their rows of eyelashes— rendered the forest land devoid of deer.

The waves, breaking against the flocks of swans on the riverbank as they were being submerged by the women together with their lovers—who were tossing about due to the agitation—possessed power even when rendered ineffective; oh, the potency of the dull-witted! 49.
Having drunk deeply of the nectar of their beauty with masses of waves due to its abundance,
it surged upward again under the guise of foam appearing from their agitation, as if reeling.
Upon the cheek of the playful woman, a full-blown blue lotus was reflected in her clear shadow;
it appeared as if it were stationed nearby, seeking service, in order to draw back the very essence of her eye's beauty.
Having gained entry into the circle of her navel and playfully striking the breasts of women,
the flood of waves surged within himself like a mass of billows and, overflowing with an onset of joy, broke against the banks.
Even when the collyrium from their eyes was washed away by the breaking waves, there was no loss of their natural splendor;
for that which has not been commenced does not perish therein, and from the absence of such [an effort], an over-extension [of the argument] would arise. (53)
As the breaking of the waves drew near, a certain form appeared boldly for a moment like a carved statue,
its shape clearly manifest as it shimmered against the wall of lofty crystal pillars.
Sītā, possessing beautiful eyebrows and bearing lines across her waist, was another field for the cultivation of love;
her form was refreshed by sprays of water cast from the lotus-hands of her beloved. (55)

With the redness of their feet and faces fixed by contact with the waves of the liquid lac trickling from their feet, those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra appeared like royal swans moving amidst the lines of red lotuses before them. 56.
At that time, the water— its foam indistinguishable from it— was rendered white by the sandalwood juice trickling from her limbs as they were struck by the surge of waves,
as if it had been turned into the nectar of beauty itself.

The mass of hair on a passionate woman’s head—its ends disheveled with curiosity as it grasps the tips of flowers—was led to a state of expansion by the network of ripples, like the lotuses of a mountain stream. (58)
In the mutual splashing of water, one newlywed bride, drenched from head to foot by her lover with water not even requested, did not strike him back;
for among those whose wealth is modesty, shame overcomes boldness.

With heavy breaths, playing her lute of teeth loudly with intense trembling and great force, the lady with arched brows and limbs covered in horripilation shone as if afflicted by cold or as if seized by the fever of passion. 60.
With their eyes, charming with the beauty of clearly trembling eyelashes and scattering radiance in all directions,
the women seemed to mock the river by vying with its blooming blue lotuses.
When the lotus, being defeated by the face of a young woman through its pale luster,
ceased its rivalry, the river then concealed it with masses of foam that seemed to break forth out of shame.

Driven by her husband at the start of the dramatic performance of the ceremonial bath, the mass of foam— its remaining water trickling away due to the intensity of her trembling— shone upon her head like a handful of white flowers offered at the parting of the hair.

As the bright strings of pearl necklaces were broken apart, the goddess Śrī restored them upon the breasts of the city’s women with the rising, clear sprays of water; for whose prosperity would such a union not be conducive? 64.
"Let not others see me fallen from the lap of Karna into the water like a coward's lotus"—
as if thinking thus in its shame, the ear-ornament lotus departed somewhere, fleeing from the agitation of the waves.
Even during the day, bearing a shadow yet possessing unimpaired beauty, a form accessible to slender women,
and not causing alarm or sleepiness in the lotuses, his moon-like face shone forth as something unprecedented.

The eyes of the women, surpassing the beauty of the lotus by the luster of his face, made the waters wash away their collyrium as if out of anger; for even a slight offense against an enemy leads to pleasure [for one's own side].

Due to their fullness, the mass of breasts of beautiful women—thick and lofty—seemed to pour forth a rain of nectar-like loveliness under the guise of the moonlight emanating from the flood of pearls dangling from their necklaces. 68.

The line of foam, concealing the tips of the slender-waisted woman's breasts— which bore the marks of fresh nail-scratches made visible by the body-unguents washed away by the glances of another’s wife— manifested its own envy.

A certain woman with tremulous eyes, warding off with her fingertips the swarms of bees attracted by the fragrance of her breath, seemed as if she were about to begin the practice of tossing a ball, being herself so fond of play.
Seeing another woman standing nearby being struck by her lover with lotus stalks,
another woman— though herself unstruck— was pained to see her face bearing a coppery hue from suppressed anger.
He took a garland of golden lotuses which he was to bestow upon a passionate woman;
yet, flashing before the eyes of another woman, it acted as a flame of the fire of her humiliation.
"Is this a lotus with a bee resting upon it, or is it the hand of a woman marked by a sapphire ring?
Thus did another man reflect as he gazed from afar at his beloved's hand after she had plunged it into the water and drawn it out.

The mass of spray, rising from afar and mounted upon the breaking waves, kisses the tips of the woman's breasts and her expansive cheeks; for who would not say that attaining a high position is for the sake of excellence? 74.

As if thinking, "Is not the true state of things indeed more excellent? What purpose is served by these [ornaments]?"—so it were—the water from their lips washed away the collyrium from their eyes, and the water carried away the sandalwood paste from the tips of their breasts.
Seeing the full-blown blue lotus that had been used as an ear-ornament by Sallīlāvatī fallen to the ground,
the Lotus-born Brahmā trembled on the earth out of joy, as if beginning a dance, at the wonder that it did not cause her any offense.
As if to drink the nectar of beauty from the moon-like face of the lady with the parted hair, his gaze, having burst forth,
opened wide toward the tip of her face from afar with waves of longing.

At that time, she halted before her a swarm of bees that were wandering about as if agitated by the sounds of the swans—which, like the resonance of the anusvāra, were causing a disturbance in the beds of lotuses blooming upon the Mandākinī. ||78||
