Struck by the mass of waves, the earring of the beautiful woman—delightful with the sound produced by its clear impact against her ear-lobe—slipped from its place;
for who, being well-rounded, is not cast down by the floods of water? (79)
As that very sandalwood water, having fallen like a torrent of frost upon the flowing tears of the women in their distress,
clung to their eyes nearby, it took on a pale-red hue through its resemblance to the luster of red lotuses.

Then, having fallen from his ear-ornament, he—his splendor now turbid with the waters of the ocean—was no longer placed upon it by women; for the restoration of those who have suffered a fall is difficult to attain.
The golden pollen from the lashes of her play-lotus did not fail to kindle the god of love,
like the flickering flame of fire rising from the third eye of the one who has the moon as his crest-ornament.
Emerging for a moment from the agitation of the waves,
the multitude of youths beheld from afar the clear circle of bubbles on the lips of the women, which bore the reflection of the circle of stars following their moon-like faces.

Adorned with necklaces that possessed the luster of clearly visible garlands of *guñjā* berries and were tawny with saffron water, those women, wearing the leaf-patterns of a lotus pond, bore the graceful charm of the wives of the Śabara tribes. 84.

Even though they had then surpassed the multitude of lotuses with their own shadows as they stood there, the deluded world did not perceive them to be lotus-eyed; alas, how difficult it is for a firmly established notion to be overturned! 85.

Clearly being overcome by the luster of their eyes, the blue lotuses of the beautiful women seemed to shrink from the path of their gaze out of a sense of shame; struck by the ripples of the Mandākinī, they ceased to quiver. (86)
A mass of foam, raised by the agitation of the waves, spread out in all directions and enveloped her broad hips;
for a moment, it lent beauty to the white silken garment being placed upon the woman. (87)

Then, the garments slipped away and, clinging nearby to the breasts of the women with masses of foam arising from the spray of breaking waves, they attained the splendor of being placed by command in their proper positions. 88.

The expanse of the grass-blades trembled from the blows of the multitude of her lotus-feet, which were exerted in tossing and lifting them, while her long braid—having attained its fame by being freed from all slackness—maintained its great length. (89)
With their broad, darkened hips submerged within the water, and their breasts exceedingly high, they—

whose slender trunk-like arms were weary from the difficulty of the task— leaped up and embraced their beloveds nearby. (A pair of verses) Then, the graceful charms of those women with lips like the *bimba* fruit vanished as their lotus-hands quickly became interlocked with one another.
As they emerged from the banks of the Ganges, they were like dancers performing their final poses.
Like some lovely woman desiring to see the aesthetic flavors (rasas) and so forth,
she shone with her four eyes revealed upon her moon-like face,
her cheeks being bright due to the removal of painted leaf-designs.
She bears an upturned lotus that is a reflection from the two walls. ||92||
The water of the women, turned tawny by the dense pollen stirred by the rows of lashes that were golden lotuses trembling from the tossing of great waves,
was urged forward by the hands of their lovers.
The counsel delighted the heart, even though it had already been resolved. ||93||
In that place, scattered with cool droplets from the spray of water-waves shattered by the friction against their breasts,
the lotus-leaves were barely discernible to the touch.
Within the womb, it is like a row of strings of fresh pearls that have been shattered. ||94||
Their heavy curls, rolling upon the slopes of their foreheads and moist with the essence of fresh bathing,
seemed as if they were about to inhale the fragrance of a lotus from the surface of their spotless cheeks.
He desired a blossoming, tender-petaled lotus reflected in a mirror. ||95||
Having entered within, desirous of drinking the nectar-essence from the breasts of women— which possess the fresh luster of gold— he, with the tread of his feet,
made the hearts of those whose golden lotuses were prone to sleep suspect him of being a bee.
Clinging repeatedly, the bee scratched her face. ||96||
The hand of the noble lady, marked by rows of wounds from her own lovely nails, appeared as if submerged in the water of her own loveliness and grace,
like a handful of seeds for sowing the sprouts of her body’s charming amorous gestures.
Like a plow pulled by the farmer that is Desire. ||97||
With their hair-tufts rendered beautiful by the mass of water squeezed out from both hands pressed against the ocean,
and with their clear [eyes] distressed by the flood of water that washed away the collyrium;
By the radiance of her cheeks, which were pale with the glow of beauty and loveliness. ||98||
With breasts covered by trickling sprays of water that mimic the mass of rays from their swaying nails,
and drenched by droplets of water clinging to their bodies as they heaved deep sighs;
by those who had undertaken the laborious task of lifting up their slender bodies, which were draped in fine silken garments; ||99||
By those [women] who were distressed by stumbling upon the steps of the jeweled platforms— slippery with the mass of spray from the waves—
and who, in their sudden agitation at that moment, had Manojñadatta hidden [from view]:
She was helped down by women with broad hips who offered them a supporting hand.
(Tilaka) Gradually, she reached the sandy banks of the river of the gods, where the ground was strewn with jewel-dust, as its waves were stirred by the impact of their broad hips.
Having emerged from the water, the women put on white garments; they were like the clear splendors of autumn days, resembling masses of clouds. ||101||

Thus ends the eighteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Water-Sport," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
The nineteenth canto begins:
The solar orb, with its clearly throbbing rays as its filaments—

Then the day-lotus, with its broad pericarp, closed up; it was a lotus whose petals were the eight directions, which had dispelled the darkness at the rising of the moon, and upon which swarms of bees—the approaching night—had settled. ||1||
The orb of the sun, possessing the luster of yellow pigment (gorocanā) and radiating beams of light, shone for a long time until it reached the setting mountain;
its reflection was like a lotus struck by the winds at day’s end.
As if being leaped over by the dust from her upturned eyelashes. ||2||
In the ocean, the sun beheld its own orb reflected, copper-red like a cluster of safflower blossoms, with a straight and brilliant luster,
reaching even to the peaks of Mount Asta.
He suspected that the golden wheels of his chariot had been shattered by the impact.

When the friend of the lotus reached the peak of the western mountain, he bound the vastness of the quarters— now turned crimson and tossed about by his rays— into a state of exhaustion, as they were gathered together in succession.
Then, the splendor of the day [took] a crest of bandhūka flowers. ||4||
By virtue of the sun’s orb hanging down in the evening and the full moon emerging from the crest of the eastern mountain,
it was as if the bronze cymbals had been seized by Śiva while he danced at twilight.
The splendor of heaven appeared as if it were merely two palm trees. ||5||
Then, like the deep union of the daughter of the mountain king— who wears a crown of crescent moons fashioned from fresh passion—
and [Śiva], the body of day and night was joined by the twilight.
Fortune blossomed forth, its movement unimpeded across both parts.
With the regions of the sky and the directions turned tawny by the mass of dust from the thick minerals reddened with the blood flowing at twilight,
she fell like a range of mountains plunging into the ocean.
The splendor of the day, distressed by the falling thunderbolt, was overwhelmed. ||7||
The tips of the forest creepers in the quarters were agitated by the clamor of flocks of birds eager to build their swaying nests;
[the mountain] was visible from afar due to its form being brightened by the rays of the sun.
The path of shadow became the tree that subdued Niśumbha.
When the sun, having reached its station upon the peak of the western mountain,
had set, the lotus-beds, possessing a straightforwardness that follows the ways of the world,
seemed to pay homage with haste to the evening twilight.
Their hands were joined in the gesture of the *mātāmraka* bud, forming a lattice-like network of palms. ||9||
For a moment, the western mountain appeared like a cloud clinging to its side, reddened by the glow of twilight,
with one portion of its orb resembling a drop of blood flowing from a wound inflicted by a thunderbolt.
He appeared like a bird whose wings were severed and hanging loose. ||10||
As the day-lotus in the lake of the sky reached its transformation at evening according to the course of time,
the seed-vessel of the solar orb, with its rays as falling eyelashes, began to fade.
The wheel bore a thick, greyish hue from being thoroughly soiled.
The lotus-born ones (Brahmās) stood with their necks upraised as if out of eagerness to behold the remainder of the sunlight,
which had taken its position in the lofty space.
The white lotuses were made terrifying by buds that were bent down as they fell.
It was as if being dragged by the long-tusked iron bar of the elephant stationed in the western quarter,
from the lake of the sky’s surface, which was made terrifying by the bubbles of shimmering stars.
A red lotus, [as large as] the orb of the sun, [was suspended] from the stars. ||13||

The orb of the thousand-rayed sun, its surface reddened by the dense glow of twilight, has fallen upon the ridge of the setting mountain like a spark from the fire flashing forth when Śiva was provoked to anger by Kandarpa.
The distinction [between them] was concealed by the upward-moving pupils of the eyes. ||14||
The sun shone, its pale-red rays grey with the twilight mingled with emerging darkness,
like a flame of smoke scattered by its own sighs.
A face that mocks the splendor of the jewels upon the broad hoods of serpents. ||15||
With his garments stripped away, his splendor soiled as it was plundered by the thief of darkness,

his injuries laid bare, and his brilliant red beauty suddenly devoid of its day— like a man naked, robbed of his wealth by a thief in the dark, with his wounds exposed and his radiant complexion vanished.
The sun's rays entered the forest of the western mountain.
In the streaks of vermilion, amidst the dense and shimmering variety of other colors, it shone upon the painted walls of the palace,
indistinguishable from the redness of the beaks of aged parrots that had been surpassed [in brilliance].
The orb of the sun, its surface overflowing with passion, [is like] a circle of hands. ||17||
The surface of the sky, reflecting the waters of the ocean which possess a hue reddened by the glow of the day’s end,
imitates the ocean as it was once shaken by the trunks of the elephants of Madhu and Kaiṭabha during their assault.
Tawny like the pollen from the interior of the lotus-navel of Vaikuṇṭha.
The twilight glow brings a variegated hue to the neck of the moon, which has recently inhabited that staff-like tree whose topmost part was bent down by its own weight.
The circle of moonbeams was shimmering and vibrating.
With the orb of the hot-rayed sun appearing like the back of an overturned tortoise,
and with the clear cries of birds, the twilight descended slowly from the peak of the western mountain like a river.
The beauty of the day in the ocean has mud for its dawn-red glow and the sun for its water. ||20||
The splendor of the dawn, greyed by the thickening darkness descending like night,
assumed a pallor like that of fragments of coral-stems struck by streaks of smoke.
The mass of its rays bore a resemblance to the multitude of the sun's rays.
May his established status come to an end as he descends from the peak of the mountain of setting— having abandoned his lofty nature and resembling the middle of a valley—
as he falls from the expanse of the sky, supported by the masses of its rays.
He who did not fall into the ocean together with the thousand-rayed sun. ||22||
The beauty of the day fell upon the sun in the ocean, as it had reached the decline of its supreme brilliance and was being overwhelmed by the darkness of evening.
For those who establish the nature of being distinct, this alone is logical. ||23||
The sun, its orb hanging low over the ocean as it gradually descends from the sky, has attained a softness like that of the moon;
it is now reflected upon the breaking waves of the lofty waters that have been stirred up.
His splendor bore, as it were, a dullness born from contact [with the water]. ||24||
The solar disc, from which a thousand tawny rays were falling away and from which a thick stream of blood was gushing forth,
fell with speed into the ocean as it was severed by Kāla.
With his sword, he [severed] the head as if it were the radiance of the day. ||25||
Like Gaurī, whose beauty surpassed the dark luster of her body as it rested upon the neck and crest of Śiva,
she turned dark in the ocean, like a streak of gold being rubbed on a touchstone.
Then the twilight, mingled with the dimness of a tawny hue, arrived. ||26||
Like a row of chariot-horses of the sun wishing to enter within, the line of horses— beheld by the gazelle of the shimmering water—
suddenly caused [the lake] to waste away with their breath-winds.
The water of the ocean, with its circles of waves shaken into foam. ||27||
As the sun descended toward the ocean,
its splendor was obscured by its downward-facing aspect;
yet, as if out of a desire for service, it was uplifted by the wind from the waves.
The mass of manes scattered about the ears of the monkeys. ||28||
Desiring to behold their beloved, who had passed from the range of sight like the sun, they sought him through forms fashioned by internal conceptualization, and gazed upon him with unswerving love.
The lotus-beds closed their eyes, as it were, through the contraction of their stalks. ||29||
At that time, the darkness— its brilliance overpowered by the descent of Śyāmā who had assumed a soiled form—
was like [the light of] a loha-kānta gem.
He violently dragged the black iron [weapon] forward. ||30||

Meanwhile, by degrees, the surface of the earth was [covered] by the rays of the beloved sun, which were like the hands of the women of the quarters distressed by the feverish heat born of separation from him,
shedding tears of falling collyrium.
It was filled with fragments of darkness, as if with heaps of dust particles. ||31||
Then, exhausted by the assault of the sun’s fierce rays,
the shade took refuge in the young trees, while the darkness resorted to those whose half-closed eyes were resting in playful slumber.
The circle of deer, their gait slow with the act of rumination, [wandered about]. ||32||
When the sun had fallen, the surface of the earth was turned dark by the paths of shadow— vast, wide, and long— which followed in the wake of the spreading of darkness.
From Mount Kalinda...
[They were] like masses of water divided by the swirling currents of a maiden's garment.
When the day had ended, swarms of bees emerged, clinging to the honey of the red lotuses whose filaments were rippled by the touch of a gentle breeze.
His mind was overcome by the army of the darkness of the approaching night. ||34||
When the sun had reached the side of the eight-peaked mountain,
people wondered whether the moon had risen or not;
then, like spies dispatched by the darkness of night—
And for a long time, the female bees hovered over the grounds where his feet had trodden. ||35||
When the sun had reached the peak of the western mountain,
the forest edges became shrouded in dense, clinging darkness,
even as the ichor was being taken up by the swarms of wandering bees.
The elephants, with the darkness [caused by] the heavy scent from their cheeks as they were rinsing their mouths; ||36||
As long as the lamp of the day, possessing a radiant glow and situated within the house of the world, continued to burn until the falling of the sun,
so long did a certain affliction of the eyes arise from somewhere unknown.
The clever, soot-stained darkness. ||37||

When the sky, shining as the adversary of frost, was occupied at night by darknesses as swift and dark as iron nets— darknesses bold enough to engage in unequal combat with heroes— then [the moon appeared].
At night, they spread in every direction with continuous, steady lines.
For the lotus, which was traveling to another region under the influence of the sun’s heat and driven by the persistence of its anxiety,
there arose a state where the rows of its eyelashes were bent down by the weight of its closing.
My lotus-eye, with its pupils like bees, was closed. ||39||
By the dense web of nocturnal darkness, thick with clinging drops of water and possessing the luster of collyrium,
the pleasure of beholding forms was forcibly snatched away from the eyes of people.
Or what auspiciousness could there be for one who is impure at heart and possesses power? ||40||
Then, blinded by the grey mass of darkness— the vast expanse of Tārāvatī’s gloom— unrestrainedly yawning as it overpowered the stars,
they were unable to discern the true form of the world.
The eyes of all people seemed as if they were closed. ||41||
Gradually bringing all the shadows of the forests to a state of uniformity, variegated by the remaining rays of the sun,
with clouds dark as the dissolution, and possessing extreme density—
Having reached them, the quarters of the sky were soon made clear by the darkness.
Now that the directions are obscured by manifest darkness,
let us go comfortably and unnoticed to the house of our beloved,
along with the women going to meet their lovers, who are beautiful with their hair tied in elaborate braids.
As if out of love, they bore him for a long time upon their heads. ||43||
Turbid with the mud of the marshes clinging to the broad tips of their fangs, which were formidable like tusks, they rose up from the water,
clutching fragments of half-moons within the thick darkness.
Then, like mountain peaks, the leaders of the forest boar herds [appeared]. ||44||
"How has the sun departed now, leaving me after I have entreated him with my hands joined like a closed lotus bud?"—
as if by these words, the humming of bees held within [the buds] spoke thus.
The lotus-pond, having found sleep at night, was as if dreaming. ||45||
With its seed-pods revealed by the falling filaments, its roots loosened, and its pale leaves sparse and thin in their intervals;
with buds formed only with difficulty, O you of straight and long thighs—
The lotus, though mature, did not become formidable. ||46||
The mass of pollen from the filaments was made muddy by the trickling drops of dew that formed as they clung to the tips of the closing petals;
it was being gathered step by step into the deep cavity of the interior.
He fell asleep upon a bed of fragrant lotus groves. ||47||
At the onset of night, the night-lotus was not yet fully opened by the moonbeams, nor had its petals been slightly spread apart by the bees;
thus, it neither immediately blossomed nor closed.
The surrounding circle of the lily grove was thrown into utter confusion. ||48||
With its circle of fresh buds clearly visible in the intervals between petals that were closed and withdrawn,
it was as if it had felt aversion at the touch of the moon’s rays.
Lakṣmī slowly abandoned her seat upon the lap of the lotus-pond.
Its back was variegated by rows of swaying, formidable, and pale leaves that formed a continuous line;
it shone as it drank in the light through the openings of its visible bud-like faces.
Like a lotus that serves as the path for the emergence of moonlight. ||50||
With difficulty it attained closure, its fringe of eyelashes slackened by the mass of withered, decaying petals;
its seed-vessel possessing a spreading, pale yellow luster.
The wheel is an ancient lotus upon the lap of the source of lotuses.
Having experienced the joy of their union at dawn,
the cakravāka birds hurriedly passed the night within their hearts;
yet, trembling with the fear of separation, they traversed the day with great difficulty.
Happiness arises from suffering; it is right that there should be no suffering when there is happiness. ||52||
With the continuous humming of bees obstructed within the bellies of the large, opening buds of white lotuses,
it was as if the moonbeams were emitting a sound faltering from within their mouths.
The lotus-beds lay down, their heat, fatigue, and exhaustion dispelled.
Meanwhile, the circle of houses, its courtyard-gates wide open, had the expanse of the sky stained by the rising forms of those pure-souled beings;
it was like the interior of the shell of the ocean, which serves as a lid for the orbs of the sun and moon.
It resembles scattered fragments of fresh jewels fallen from their settings.
With a cluster of flowers from the forest of the radiant midnight,
with a mass of bubbles upon the ocean of the sky,
and with a circle of pearls within the shell of the cosmic egg.
She surpassed all ornaments with the multitude of stars in the night sky. ||55||
The mass of dense nocturnal darkness was pierced by the collection of rays from the moon, white as mist,
and the circle of shimmering stars became visible.
The sky was turned into a stage, its vast expanse filled with manifold illusions.

The night gave birth to luminous bodies that bestow fortune, whose thick masses of rays— rendering the quarters of the sky variegated— forcefully shatter the darkness, and whose splendor is intense with delight for the night.
The jewels were shimmering like rows of wish-fulfilling trees.
The arrangement of the tips of his fangs was rounded from being ground against crushed rocks and rubbed against the primordial mountain;
it variegated the clouds with the luster of droplets from the spray of the Ocean of Milk.
Then the circle of planets shone brightly in the sky. ||58||
Having abandoned the rooftops of their mansions,
flocks of domestic peacocks, with their feet perched upon the tips of the poles supporting the eaves,
spread out their tails like uplifted moon-patterned canopies.
Under the guise of its shadow, it rained down thick darkness. ||59||
On the slopes of their breasts, where various leaf-patterns were fashioned from scattered black aloe-wood, and nestled within their braided tresses—
[there appeared] the emergence of the lotus-eyed women, variegated with white gems.
As if creating darkness upon the very places intended for ornamentation of the moon. ||60||
The nocturnal darkness fell with great intensity into the vast cavities of the earth-born mountains,
and it clearly spread through the mud of the ponds.
Just as herds of bewildered buffalo plunge [into it]. ||61||
With their filaments spread wide by the wind and turned tawny by the spreading glow of the twilight sun,
the lotuses situated in the midst of the forest have awakened from sleep as the day has faded away.
It blossomed forth with other lines with impetuosity, while it slept with yet others. ||62||
As they drank the rut-fluid from their temples— which were being parted by the mass of shimmering rays from their broad, bar-like tusks—
their joy was increased by the obstruction of their vision.
The temples of the wild elephants were boldly struck by swarms of arrows.

The evening was illuminated by the fragments of peacock crests, as dark and jagged as smoldering collyrium, which had taken up residence upon the rooftops of the houses, following their flocks like a retinue.
With lamps whose flames were reddened like the hands of children at twilight.
With windows that, like eyes, have lines drawn by the paths through which tufts of cotton emerge, scattered with particles of the collyrium-dust [of smoke],
and which bear streaks of smoke born from the incense of aguru—
The houses shone with their peaks smeared with [the pigment] niryāṇa. ||65||
Even as the darkness was being pierced by rows of lamp-light shining through the lattice windows,
it became thickened within the interior of the house as it was being consumed by fire.
By means of rows of dense columns of smoke arising from black aloe-wood incense.
Then, like a circle of sunbeams resembling the bow of the enemy of Smara (Śiva) when its tip is fixed with fire-arrows and set upon a city,
the hearts of those named Cakra, distressed by separation, were consumed as if they were the host of Asuras.
First, he cut away the roots entirely from the earth;
then, following that, he severed the connection of passion manifested upon the peaks of the mountains; and finally, having leaped into the path of the clouds, he desired to cast down heaps of jewels.
The spreading shade, possessing diminished splendor, withdrew its heat. ||68||

Thus ends the nineteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Close of Day," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked with the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—whose pen-name is Vāgīśvara and whose other name is Vidyādhipati—and who was a dependent of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
The Twentieth Canto: [He] bore the Goddess of Fortune, like the moon hidden behind the mountain of sunrise...
Then, with the clusters of her arms being the tips of her exceedingly long rays,
she who possesses the luster of lightning began to cast off Indra’s blue-hued garment of darkness in successive directions.
The sky seemed about to rise up, as if it were a lake in the ocean whose dark mossy tendrils of darkness had been swallowed and now gasping for breath,
under the guise of hundreds of pearl-oyster shells scattered upon its shore.
Like a female swan following its mate, the form of the Moon followed by its jars.
By him, who was aided in pacifying the continuous fainting fit caused by the burning pain of the uneven fire of the poison within his womb,
[there arose] at that time a moon with waves as high as a palm tree.
The ocean, as if longing for him, seemed to have moved far away.
Bearing a visible reflection that seemed marked by streaks of mud clinging to the bottom of the ocean, like the orb of the moon,
it was bright with the clear bubbles from the waters of the dark Yamunā.
He desired to ascend the sky, which was clustered with clusters of stars.
Having eclipsed the splendor of my husband, the moon,
as he rose by casting aside his orb with the mass of his rays,
look! I see that sun fallen into the ocean upon the mountain—
It seemed as if [the moon] had ascended the peaks with its fresh moonlight. ||5||
Meanwhile, the moon, situated at the beginning of the night when the stars are motionless and the luster of the lotus clusters has been eclipsed,
clearly kissed the peak of the mountain with its distinctly rosy glow.
The twilight, raining down a shower of nectar, licked the orb.
The moon, its splendor gradually concealed by the mountain of sunrise with the radiance of the surrounding groves of blooming lotuses,
oppresses the circle of nocturnal darkness—
Do not cause the world to gasp for breath with your upward-pointing rays, as if it were the day. ||7||
She shone, fair as saffron paste, resting upon the peaks of the mountains that were her curved eyelashes;
she was like the dawn when the wheel of Madana’s chariot-pole has been shattered by its violent descent.
The crescent moon has the form of a fragment of a ruby. ||8||

Then, having shattered the darkness, the curved digit of the moon— red-hued like the throat of Namuci as it winds around it— abandoned its attachment to the beauty of the peak of the mountain of sunrise.
Bearing the graceful play of a circle of shimmering spray.
The Lord of medicinal herbs, whose central portion was variegated by clearly defined markings, assumed the state of being a half-moon;
he was like a cloud dappled by droplets of flowing ichor.
It appeared with the shape of the tip of an elephant's ear. ||10||
While the mass of darkness— motionless, bearing the grace of celestial nymphs, and thick with manifest mire— enveloped the quarters of the sky,
there arose [a light] as pale as a blooming saffron bud.
The lunar orb was not perceived, appearing like a shaft of gold.
The orb of the moon, its center turbid with a visible halo and its redness intensified as it rose upon the mountain of sunrise, shone forth like the face of Brahmā,
whose middle is split by the emerging Viṣṇu, his body stained by the blood of the demon Madhu.
The seed-vessel arisen from the lotus at the navel of Vaikuṇṭha.
The orb of the sun has risen upon the crest of the eastern mountain, its natural whiteness abandoned as it is embraced by passion;
it is being overtaken by the pollen of its filaments which has been shaken loose.
White as the petals of a night-lotus awakened from sleep by the moon. ||13||
Gazed upon at the onset of night by the night-lilies with smiles of teeth and throbbing filaments that captivate the heart,
the clusters of day-lotuses shone as if out of fear of being tormented.
They were like the rays of the newly risen moon, as if resting upon their own radiance. ||14||
The orb of the moon, its nectar slowly ebbing away as if shattered by its collision with the jagged peaks of the eastern mountain’s summit,
was clearly marked by the fading glow of the fresh twilight.
The streak of red in the sky turned into whiteness. ||15||
As the orb of the cold-rayed moon, pale as a fresh *tinduka* fruit and free from sleep, began to pour forth its stream toward the celestial river,
its shadow bore the splendor of the deer-marked one.
The beauty of the flowing stream of the Yamunā’s waters has now departed. ||16||
The moon bore a bimba fruit whose luster was darkened at its center by a fresh mark, as white as a fresh kunda petal;
it resembled the chest of Balarāma, marked by the deep impression of the rear half of his firm plowshare.
Marked by the scars scratched by the tips of his prancing hooves.
The lake, with its shimmering water, bore the beauty of the moon’s reflection— its center mottled by thick masses of mud appearing in the guise of its spots—
as it was being filled by charming jars.
The form was like a wheel of Time whirling in a lake. ||18||
In its central portion, the lunar orb bore a pale whiteness marred by a fragment of the hare’s spot,
like a fallen tip of a dark elephant hide.
She possesses the grace of shoulders white with pure ashes and adorned with the moon as an ornament.
The full-orbed moon shone with the luster of its dark spot, resembling the hue of the Kālakūṭa poison situated at its center,
like the Milky Ocean with the base of Mount Mandara.
The moon is made circular by its playful revolution. ||20||
The mountain of sunrise, with its clearly visible marks, appeared like a painted panel on a wall for the goddess of love;
it was as if she had applied a wick of soot-stained paste to create the illusion of his form.
It was like the orb of the moon marked with the figures of a lotus leaf and a sea-monster. ||21||
The orb of the moon shone forth, having momentarily found its place upon the peaks of clouds turned tawny by the twilight glow tossed by the wind,
as it was being carried away by the serpent-eater.
It was beautiful with nectar-jars radiant with rubies. ||22||
When the forest-thicket of the day-cranes was suddenly torn open by the arrow of Rāma— the descent of night— with its newly formed feathers,
the covering of the petals of the lotuses was clearly shattered.
A row of swans, which were the rays of the moon, was departing.
Is this the moon, marked with its spot, risen from the belly of the ocean with its central portion melted by contact with the weapon-fire of Aurva;
or is it a tuft of rays as beautiful as the luster of camphor powder?
Its rays were harsher than the sun that illuminates the quarters of the sky after they have been washed clean.
At the edge of the forest that is the earthly realm, the circle of planets, white as blossoming *kunda* flowers,
shone like a dark *śyāmā* creeper under the guise of the deer-mark on the moon.
As if emerging from the circular basin surrounding a lotus bud. ||25||
Will his face not come into correspondence with that of the village women, whose cheeks are variegated by decorative streaks made from my unguent-paste?
Is this bimba fruit not likewise mottled by him?
The moon, as it were, bore [the spot] because he had wrongly imagined it to be a mark. ||26||
Relying upon the entire moon,
which had arisen from the eye of the Great Sage as a commonality of birth,
[the world] was rendered slow by the excessive weight of its burden of bliss.
As if out of an impetuous partiality toward that [object], it was as though for the eyes themselves. ||27||
Suddenly uttering his own mantra with a tinkling sound at nightfall, the practitioner,
exerting himself, [approaches] the opening petal-mechanism.
Like an impassioned lover, the bee, having entered the inner chamber of the night-lily, began to enjoy its essence with intense passion. ||28||
The moon, with its broad orb overspread by a mass of rays that were not pale,
appeared like a lotus clinging to the water of the river of the sky after it had been uprooted.
It possessed the grace of a celestial elephant with its trunk spread out. ||29||
The moon shone with rays as white as the waves of the milk-ocean, which, assuming their own reflection, traversed the path of the clouds,
as if seeking protection from the fear of the lotuses closing.
With hundreds of tender, split lotus stalks belonging to Khaṇḍa. ||30||
Upon the young Madhūka flowers,
pale as the moon, which had not yet attained the artful painting of petals, there appeared the reflections of playful women whose dark spots were wiped away by the radiance of their loveliness.
Upon the regions of her cheeks, the reflection of the moon shone even more intensely.
Like the nectar-rayed moon in the season of frost, when the circle of the quarters and the sky are shrouded by a mass of moonlight and dew,
he bestowed firm embraces upon his beloveds.
Not causing distress to the beauty of the fragments of the white lotuses.
Having swiftly shattered with his rays the mass of nocturnal darkness— the cause of obstruction to vision— like the application of collyrium, he, with his blameless forms,
[opened] those whose petals were closed by his rays.
The minds of the lotus-ponds were not diminished [by the heat]. ||33||

Then, casting off the darkness that was as blue as a cluster of *sairēyaka* flowers and indistinguishable from a garment soiled by bodily excretions, the quarters of the sky quickly clothed themselves in a radiance as white as silver.
A silken garment from the wish-fulfilling vine of the chapter on the radiance of the mind. ||34||
When the moon had risen, its shimmering rays— white as the shell of a conch—
studded the sky and the quarters of space; yet the darkness, as black as a *tāpiccha* flower, persisted in following the crevices.
The darkness of the twilight, as if its deceit were dissolving away. ||35||
Due to the absence of the sun, having quickly attained union with the darkness and with the night-lotuses,
they [the bees] were situated within the bellies of the water-lilies at the rising of the moon.
The bees, enemies of the womb, have emitted their sweet sound. ||36||
By those desiring to take refuge, wandering slowly in the sky amidst the buds of the night-lotuses whose petals were slightly unfolding,
the remaining traces of the clouds— shattered by the moonbeams— were [observed].
It was darkened by bees resembling the darkness of night.
The moon alone, with its mass of rays, dispelled those very darknesses which had risen up in succession when the sun had taken refuge in another world and had enveloped the universe in gloom.
For the power of the great is indeed devoid of commonality. ||38||
Gradually casting off her dark garment like a skin of deep shadow, Gaurī became radiant, holding a crystal rosary and a leaf-patterned mark of fragrant aloe-wood paste.
The surface of his cheeks was like the lunar orb, marked with a beautiful shadow. ||39||
As the beautiful women, like the goddesses of love, created a festival of touch with their limbs— anointed with intense passion—
the Jāhnavī and other rivers deeply embraced the groves of night-lotuses.
They were embraced by circles of moonbeams. ||40||
When the darkness had been dispelled at night by the clusters of rays from the sun and the beams of the moon,
the beautiful forms of the celestial nymphs became clearly visible.
The masses of hair seemed to have reached the state of being its objects. ||41||
And the cool-rayed moon rose up, dispelling the darkness with clusters of rays that carried forth floods of nectar;
he also removed the sorrow of the closing of the night-lilies.
The virtuous are never thwarted by obstacles when engaged in accomplishing the welfare of others. ||42||
Then the clusters of night-lotuses and day-lotuses were embraced by the moon’s rays, which were as white as crushed conch shells;
these rays settled within the hollows of the buds formed by the petals of the blossoming flowers.
The swarms of distressed bees became scattered all around. ||43||
In the mansions, the dense mass of darkness was dispersed by the pale rays of the moon that reflected from all sides; [there,
the women] possessed arms as thick as the trunks of elephants.
Slowly, the world was again joined with sight from afar. ||44||

Having taken up the thick mass of smoke from the burning agallochum incense upon the cheek-slabs of the celestial nymphs— as if wishing to paint decorative leaf-patterns with fingers moistened by the essence— ...
Their hands fell upon the openings of the windows made of leather. ||45||
The rays of the cool-rayed moon, streaked with the dark smoke of aguru incense issuing from the lattice windows, bestowed beauty upon the palace,
like the waters of the Milk Ocean churned by the overturned Mount Mandara.
Like sparks from a fire, they were as if leaping with deadly black poison. ||46||
The beloved moon, with its rays as pure as fragments of lotus stalks, embraces the Lady Night, who has cast off her garment of darkness, while his friends,
the quarters of the sky, are drenched with the outpouring of nectar.
As if their faces were adorned with flashes of laughter, they cast aside their weapons. ||47||
The quarters of the sky, their spaces brightened by the moonlight as soft as washed silk from the petals of lotus buds closed and bent in sleep,
shone with a clear radiance throughout the night.
Like kasha grass at the onset of autumn, their darkness has been quelled. ||48||
Then, in due course, together with the night-lotuses, the quarters of the sky—
whose presence had become clear through the recovery of their breath and were visible from afar— attained full bloom and shone brightly under the lunar rays.
The darkness of night was dispelled by their clusters of rays. ||49||

The white moonlight washed away the splendor of the sky, which was as if streaked with the hue of the petals of a cluster of night-lotuses fainting under the weight of being drunk by his playful rays; it was like the throat of a cuckoo.
The quarters of the sky were turbid with the darkness of night, while a flood of rays [shone forth]. ||50||
The quarters of the sky, their continuity of dense darkness shattered, were strewn with [the rays] possessing a vast whiteness, as if with the beauty, charm,
and luster of freshly plucked clusters of white water-lilies.
The moon illuminated [the world] with its rays, which were like lamps.
Strings of pearls heavy upon the breasts of the beautiful women of the quarters, with gems and corals as sharp as the flow of nectar,
slowly pierce through the darkness that is as black as a mass of collyrium.
The moonbeams are gentle toward the world, for they are the very essence of its life.
Having abandoned the eastern quarter, its wealth of beauty now vanished in an instant, the sun now desires the western direction;
it propitiates other quarters, having conquered the white lotuses— [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be incomplete.]
He gracefully caused the quarters of the sky to bow down with the falling of his beautiful head. ||53||

Having spoken thus, as if by striking with the palms of her hands, she [awakened] the night through the humming of swarms of bees upon the blossoming night-lotuses, which were being struck together by the impact of the nocturnal breeze.
For a long time, the night-wanderers [the bees] were delighted by the night-lotuses. (A pair of verses.
The winds blew, bristling with droplets from the water of the blue lotuses, scattering fallen petals, and brushing against the tips of the buds of split lotuses.
The midnight breezes were cool, bearing the abundant fragrance of *śephālikā* flowers whose bees were silenced.

The forest shone, bearing the shadows of the trees which had vanished as the sun set, yet remained variegated by the cool rays of the moon that had found entry through the gaps in the leaves shaken by the wind.
The earth was like a cloth covered with a variegated deer skin. ||56||
The cool rays of the moon, white with fresh foam, flowed across the sky, leaping over the clusters of stars—
a circular expanse of grains of sand made of the jewels of its rising rays.
Resembling a mass of waves upon the waters of the Mandākinī. ||57||
The sky was overspread by the rays of the moon, pale at its base like the petals of a swaying, full-blown hundred-petaled lotus;
it resembled the gaping maw of the Time-Demon (Kālakola) at the end of the world, agitated as it upholds the universe.
Her fangs became like the splendor of the earth, white with radiance. ||58||
The sky shone, white with the spreading moonlight mingled with the circle of stars,
bearing the long, curved, and aged coils of the serpent-like twilight.
[She possesses] the grace of a wide silk bodice shimmering with pearls. ||59||
The sky, variegated by a multitude of pupils whose youthful skin was washed clean,
bore the appearance of a lake whose waters had been entirely dried up and whose mud had been sucked out.
The beauty of the lake, with its lotus stalks and roots crushed by the visible [elephants], has been destroyed. ||60||
With her lotus-like eyes dimmed, her posture unsteady due to trembling caused by continuous sighing,
and bearing a pallid hue as if seized by old age, she underwent a contraction.
The entire circle of the lotus grove by means of its soft radiance. ||61||
At night, the female ruddy goose, bearing a lotus that was closed by moonlight, its stalk rising above the water and containing a serpent,
appeared as if her eyelashes and body hair were bristling with joy.
[She felt] the suspicion that her lover, standing at her feet with his face turned upward, was far away.
Then the circle of night-lotuses, submerged in the flood of fresh moonlight-water that inundated the surface of the earth,
appeared as if clinging to the shore due to the gentle onset of the breeze.
With its palāśa-leaf arms set in motion, it shone brilliantly. ||63||

The night, dark as the moon with its multitude of hands— hands that are formidable to the longing night-lotuses and yet blunt in piercing the white lotuses of Vaikuṇṭha’s conch— has clearly departed, empty of purpose.
Its splendor, pale from the destruction of darkness, attained a state of resemblance [to the moon]. ||64||
Her beautiful hands, with their clusters of petal-like fingers, were like night-lotuses bursting under the full weight of yawns;
her line of body hair was resonant with a swarm of bees that had been raised up.
Upon suddenly beholding Rindu, the night-lily then became full-blown. ||65||
Struck by the rays of the moon— which possess the delicate softness of abundant flowers— like the arrows of the Mind-born God,
[the women] bore upon their faces the night-blooming lilies from which the nocturnal fragrance was exhaled.
The night-lotuses bloomed with droplets of perspiration. ||66||
Moistened by the spray from the cascades of nectar flowing down,
and rubbed by the mass of moonbeams, the lotus-pools, whose formidable buds had been opened, suddenly closed at midnight.
Their bodies covered by garments of leaves, they were as if afflicted by the cold. ||67||
The breeze, cooled by droplets of tears of joy flowing from women moistened by the happiness of union with their beloveds,
[carries] a gradation of thinness acquired through its successive binding.
There was an abundance of dense fragrance arising from the *saugandhika* lotuses. ||68||
"Lest the evening breeze steal away even the slightest trace of the fragrance of my anger," as if out of fear,
the lotus thus held its scent close.
The state of being contracted, constricted, expansive, and bud-like. ||69||
Those lotus ponds, which during the day were not touched by the rays of the sun and did not wither even when touched by the fire-filled [rays],
now withered all the more even by the moonbeams moistened with nectar.
Alas, those lotus-eyed ones have indeed abandoned their virtuous conduct! ||70||
To drink the honey from the lotus, the bee, its passion for the water-lily intensified, rose up with wings fluttering,
its feet pressed within the closing embrace of the lotus petals.
As if under the sway of jealousy, the lotus-plant bound [her]. ||71||
There is nothing in this world that cannot be accomplished by one who possesses skill; for the moon, with its rays serving as ear-ornaments for all the quarters of the sky,
has led away the masses of water from the ocean on every side.
That even the moonstones attained a state of moisture at that time. ||72||
Because the moon oppressed the cluster of lotuses at its front with its rays, making them pale and shriveled,
they now appear like a row of teeth amidst its throbbing, formidable filaments.
As if out of joy, the night-lily laughed with its exceedingly bright white.
Stirred by the god of love whose arrows are unerring, the night-lily, having attained sleep while being caressed by the moon's rays,
awoke as if uttering a "hum" from within its heart.
By means of the continuous warbling of swarms of humming bees. ||74||
Even the moon, when it was placed playfully upon the lotus-eyed lily, became like a fresh lotus petal for her who had fainted from the continuous anguish of separation from the beloved sun.
The stalks of lotus-fibers, so tender, lead only to exhaustion. ||75||

Drawing back the surface of her breasts, which were full with great waves, and the region of her waist, marked by the folds of the ripples, the moon placed the tips of his rays within her navel-like whirlpool.
She has red lotuses and her lotus-eyes are closed. ||76||
Its interior cavities were filled with golden arrows and discs from which straight filaments were emerging,
and its slightly opened bud-like faces were illuminated by the splendors of the moon.
It assumed the playful grace of the quiver of the bodiless Love-god, like a white water-lily. ||77||
When the water consisting of moonlight, possessing the luster of nectar and released from the clouds, fell into the shell-like cups of the night-lily petals,
it became a mass of large droplets of nocturnal water clinging to them.
Through this artifice, it attained the state of being a pearl drop. ||78||
At nightfall, the night-lily is delighted, its surface agitated by a continuous succession of horripilation as it bears a weight of bursting thorns;
it is shaken by the thrusting rays of the moon, which dispel the luster of the lotus.
With her beautiful breasts like blooming white lotuses, she shone like a wheel.

Agastya rendered the waters free from poison at night with his hands, which were moist with nectar and capable of making them completely pure— waters that even the moon, though possessed of cool rays, was unable to bring to such a state.
In a particular task, only a specific person possesses the requisite power. ||80||
Ascend to the distant heights; delight the sluggish;
gladden those with moon-like faces who are tormented by love;
scatter the cruel darkness with your rays; and cause the tips of the flower buds to—
And the destruction of the clusters of night-lotuses by those rays of terrifying beauty. ||81||
He caused the bees to alight upon the kunda flowers— those with filaments curled by the kissing of the tips of beaks, and those with petals bent by the movement of the bees;
flowers possessing long stalks and petals as white as jasmine.
While the night-lotuses were blooming far and wide with joy. ||82||
Close your mass of petals, O sharp white lotus; adorn the directions with the splendor of your manifest circle.
Agitate [the waters] with the playful swaying of your longing to burst forth!
And the water of the ocean, turbid with masses of surging waves. ||83||
Kindle the God of Love, who brandishes his bow with a concentration made beautiful by the drawing of a continuous stream of unerring arrows;
shake off the steadfastness of women as it increases—
Arrogant with pride, he was hostile toward those who were separated from their kinsmen. ||84||
"O Pārī, please the guests with your drinks;
with your splendors, you are like masses of camphor dust. Acting thus, he of beautiful luster shone like the moon.

The circle of eyes of the people who were intent on the single contemplation [of him] performed worship. (A *kulaka* of five verses) He possessed a dense luster reaching to the depths of the netherworld, like the radiance of the coils of Śeṣa;
he had a deep blue hue around his neck, like the loud laughter of Paśupati.
Having scattered a circle of darkness nearby in the sky, the moon, possessing stainless splendor, shone forth, bestowing brilliance upon the heap of jewels. ||86||

Thus ends the twentieth canto, titled "The Description of the Moonrise," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked with the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
The Twenty-first Canto:
Then the Lord stood upon the floor of the moon-chamber atop his lofty palace, upon a costly couch that had been prepared.
Thus he spoke to his beloved, who was seated upon his lap, having beheld the enchanting splendor of the moon.
O slender-limbed one, behold now the moon, its characteristic mark revealed, as it has risen from the eye of the Three-eyed God;
its orb shines with its interior path licked by the luster of his stars. 2.
As if wishing to play a sport by striking with handfuls of its own saffron-colored luster,
the lotus plant causes the lotus-eyed one to close his eyes, which are as thick-lashed as a deer's.
Clearly, for one who is averse to the supreme consecration, stable and stainless prosperity arises;
for thus, O lady of curved limbs, this world of darkness, pervading all, has been entirely consumed by the moon.
That moon causes the rows of lily-bosoms of the night-lilies to swell;
they are adorned with the pearl-strings of his own radiance and patterned with the leaf-designs of the black aloe-wood of the bees. ||5||

Is this the moon, its waters deepened by the guise of reflections, that has been turned newly red by the hollowed hands of night-lotuses and water-lilies raining down showers of honey-drops and spray? (6)
These lotus-pools, their eyes closed like lotuses and momentarily made startling by droplets of dew,
possess a beauty as if they were beloved lotus-ponds with perspiration rising from the thought of their lover, the sun.
Having received from the moon’s face a gift of ruddy luster, this night-lily, her lotus-face upturned and unveiled,
drinks it with longing for a long time, O lady of arched brows.
Tearing apart the mountain ranges of nocturnal darkness with the tender luster of his sprout-like fangs by means of his own streak,
this moon always bears the grace of the Primeval Boar through his constant carrying of Lakṣmī.
O slender-waisted one, what pride can you take in this face of yours with its full cheeks?
It bears a beauty exactly like the orb of the moon that rises every month. (10)
As the moon touches her with its rays, the lotus-plant seems to turn away her lotus-face in anger;
she bears upon her back a braid of bees that has assumed the beauty of a dark line across her lotus-breast.
At the onset of night, the moonlight clearly falling into the ocean was drunk up by oyster shells;
for otherwise, how could the production of pale white pearls from those waters released by the clouds have occurred? (12)
With its rays at the tips reddened by the saffron-like pollen of the filaments,
the moon stands as if desiring to paint a decorative mark upon the beauty of the night-lotus grove, which has the swarms of bees hovering about for its loosened eyebrows.
The night-lily pond attains a beauty like that of Lakṣmī, bearing in her hand the white water-lily whose petals are its throbbing fingers,
while the swarm of bees resting at its side creates the illusion of a conch shell encircled by a smile.
As the God of Love hurls his arrows, which mock the minds of longing women, cool breezes gradually begin to blow, as if gathered from the very wings of those arrows. (15)

These women, veiled as they go to the houses of their lovers seeking to win favor, are like female messengers (abhisārikās) who, having arrived above, form a circle with bees drawn by the fragrance of their crest-ornaments; those bees, hovering there, seem as if they themselves desire to bring about that same splendor.
"Why was this sweet lotus created by the moon, who is so intent on causing contraction?
Thus, as it were, the bee censures him with its humming; for a person always feels affection for that which is favorable to them. (17)

O lady of beautiful hips, this orb of the moon, reflected in the water of the night-lotus ponds and caught within the noose of its wavering ripples, bears the likeness of a conch-shell with shimmering whorls. 18.
Upon the circular feet of the lotuses, a row of jeweled anklets consisting of swarms of bees is fastened by the lovely tips of their petals, which act as closely pressed fingers of reddish hue. 19.
With its interior filled with water reddened by the saffron-like spray of nectar from the night-lotuses,
the mass of white lily buds seems to cast itself away with graceful motion, as if to strike down the moon.

The moonlight attains the splendor of the moon; it is a mass of foam from the belly of the ocean of the sky, anointing itself with the ashes of the lords of mountains and serpents, and a trailing garment of silk for the night-blooming kalpa-creeper.
Thus, when the moon-crested Lord had revealed himself at that opportune moment which was like his own reflection, kindling the god of love,
he spoke respectfully to the daughter of the Himālaya mountain and became intent upon performing the evening rites.
Then, his heart filled with joy, he worshipped the body of the Lotus-born [Brahmā] at twilight,
which appeared reddish as if from being sprinkled by the pollen scattered from the lotus-throne within the navel-lake of Murāri.
During his recitation, Śiva shone with the circles of light from his teeth, which found their exit through the opening between his parted lips;
he appeared as if drenched by the waters of the celestial river entering through the path of the aperture in his crown.
As his lofty nose and downcast eyes drew together the rows of his tawny eyelashes,
he made his forehead— marked by a streak of gorocanā— appear as if it possessed a third eye.

The mass of his rays, emitted from the clearly reddish, upward-turned soles of his lotus-feet fixed in the *padmāsana* posture, was dispelling the darkness of the luster of the slender circle of his throat. ||26||
With his two lotus-like hands raised upward, their radiance shimmering from the contact with the navel he had attained,
and his broad shoulders rendered firm, the moon-crested Lord meditated for a long time upon some object within the sphere of his samādhi.
(A pair of verses) [He beheld that which was fashioned from the seeds of the lotuses resting upon the countless Brahmās of the past.]
Chanting with his own mudrā upon his own rosary, he turned the lotus-hued [discus] with his other hand.

And as the Daughter of the Mountain King gazed upon him whose eyes were narrowed in meditation, she fixed her gaze—reddened by the rising glow of anger—as if it were crimson with the dust of the twilight sun. ||29||
Then, with her lower lip reddish-grey and distressed by the heat of the sighing breaths of the common folk,
she emulated the beauty of spring, whose lovely sprouts are marked by swarms of bees.
Even the Lord, having completed his evening rites, beheld her standing with her back turned toward him;
then, with a smile and words of consolation from whose core he was moistened with passion, he won her over after a long time.

Then, with a smile, he who was skilled in the conventions of love had Jayā, the moon-crested one, drink from him in turn that nectar brought by Madhu, which arose from the blossoms of the blossoming Kalpa-tree.
With her cheeks possessing a perpetually glowing luster, she captivated the heart of the Moon-crested Lord;
bearing the beauty of a creeper with red lower-lip sprouts and fruit turned tawny by ripeness. 33.

The moon-crested Lord beheld her standing on a portion of his own body, as she gazed upon a female ruddy goose separated from her mate who had gone to a lotus pond in the palace, fearing separation due to her extreme timidity.
Fearing separation from her, he too settled her at the very edge of his own body;
for there is nothing desired by a lover that is not accomplished through the excellence of the quality of affection. (35)
How indeed will my hand, dejected by jealousy, be employed in joining the *añjali* during the twilight prayers?
For even the spray of water from the Gaṅgā upon my head, though cool as ice, shall not fail to burn me. (36)
Thus, as her beloved remained joined with half of her body, she became for a moment troubled in mind by doubt;
yet, fearing separation from him, she did not again take account of any flaws in their love.
(A pair of verses) As he was released from her side, [she looked at him] as if terrified by the hissing of the jewels flashing on the serpent-crests.
He stands with the circles of rays from his crown-moon gathered within his tawny mass of matted hair. ||38||
Resembling the orb of a newly risen sun shimmering after being eclipsed by Rahu, tawny like fire,
with its upper portion rising up while its melted lower part is intermingled, it shines forth as he fixes his gaze upon the half-star.

When the eye is fixed within the inner boundary of the closed lashes—lashes that are curved and formidable—the festival of beholding the lotus-face of the beloved is produced at that very moment through meditative visualization alone. (40)

By raising her brow high upon the path between her eyes, forming a deep furrow on her forehead, she reveals the state of her agitated upward glance—a movement of the eye that has ascended the chariot of her longing to behold Śiva. ||41||

The pupil of the eye, having moved swiftly to the outer corner by force of habit, remains there with some difficulty due to longing, though slowed by the distress of not seeing the beloved’s face. 42.

Bearing a splendor made grey by the stain of betel-juice adhering to it, the straight line in the middle of her lower lip clearly establishes a delicate boundary for the division between her two forms. 43.

From the body part descending upon her breast, which is covered with a mass of horripilation, it is inferred that there is a festival arising from the joy of delightful touch, wherein her eyes have their lashes closed in a tight embrace. (44)

As if her eyebrows were slightly arched in a frown directed toward the state of emaciation— which she resented as a confusion caused by his occupying half of her forbidden body— the region of her waist remained fixed solely by the pretext of the folds of skin (balis).

Upon her hips—which have attained an exceeding abundance of expansive beauty through the bliss of being settled within that enchanting interior—the jeweled girdle falls downward, its string of gems broken by the weight. 46.

Thus, by the daughter of the Mountain King, who had taken her place upon the body of her beloved, all women in the worlds were surpassed in their excellence of beauty and other virtues. (47) [Ten verses in a *kulaka*:
On one side, a serpent-bodied [form], dark as a water-laden cloud—
The girdle, resting upon the slope of her hips,
assumed the graceful charm of a stream flowing from the reservoir of the Kālakūṭa poison located in the hollow of her turned neck.
Upon her hips, a jeweled girdle— sweetly tinkling and causing the rays of darkness to fade—
bore a splendor that resembled a sandbank upon the lake of the beauty of her loveliness.
A row of swans upon the expansive, lotus-like surface of her hips. ||49||
The spotted deer skin being fastened upon his thighs attained a variegated luster like that of the moon-ornament;
he bore it while maintaining a passion fixed by the sight of the moon upon his crown.
She possessed the beauty of the curved eyelashes of the dark fortnight held by Tārā.

His garment, fine as a delicate skin and shimmering with the rays of jewels from his variegated girdle-string, appeared exceedingly beautiful as it clung elsewhere, as if bearing the five colors of a rainbow and rippling with waves. ||51||
"May the union of these two bodily parts, blossoming with mutual love, endure for a long time.
Thus, as it were, did Gaurī’s foot bestow this blessing under the guise of the tinkling of her anklets. (52)

Do not indeed crush me— my head with its jewels ground by the surface of the earth as it bows under the weight of dancing circumambulations— thinking me to be white with ashes like the serpent Śeṣa at the foot of the Moon-crested Lord.
The serpent, coiled and with its head resting at the tip of his foot, shone brilliantly. ||53||
The moon-crested Lord bore upon his chest, which was elevated by half the orb of the nectar-rayed moon come to serve him,
a reflection whose circular form was visible as it entered within.
It was enveloped in purity, like the breast of Gaurī. ||54||
His face, with its wide-open eyes, is perpetually beautiful with a girdle of bells that expand like a festival at twilight;
it is graced by the splendor of supreme majesty, marked by the digit of the moon.
He fashioned the two bodies of Śiva and Śivā as one and indivisible. ||55||
At that time, as their eyes remained motionless and closed due to the continuous experience of the pleasure of mutual passion,
no physical movements arose from those two whose minds were inseparable.
Their speech is bound by the limits of the continuum. ||56||

Thus, having composed this drama— which possesses a structure never abandoned by the cultivation of aesthetic flavor (rasa), which relies upon the poetic excellences (guṇas), which bears the auspicious marks of celebrated limbs, and which embodies a nature inclined toward unprecedented creation—
the Moon-crested Lord, like a poet, has brought it to completion with its joints properly joined.
When half of Śikharisutā’s body had been offered, his mind became filled with longing for the woman. ||57||
Thus, when he remained united with the jewel-like body of his beloved, their clear bond of love serving as the cause for severing the affliction of the spreading fever of separation,
showers of arrows fell upon the body of the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva) at that time, focused on a single target out of the excess of his joy.
The glances of the attendants, with their pupils rolling in wonder and their lids wide open, [beheld him]. ||58||

Thus ends the twenty-first canto, titled "The Description of the Half-Body of Gaurī’s Lord," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—whose pen-name is Vāgīśvara and whose other name is Vidyādhipati—and who was a dependent of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
Canto Twenty-two: ...thus established in a state formed by half a body, his head—
Then the Lord of Rivers, having approached Gaurī— who was intent on showing contempt for the Gaṅgā—
became agitated as if with anger, his splendor intensified by the moon. ||1||
Leaping far away, he followed [the deer] as it plunged into the path of the clouds from the lap of the moon;
while he remained in his own place, turning about for a moment—
He remained like the ocean, with its waters stilled and tranquil.
The ocean, having assumed such a state of stillness, with its pearl-oyster shells— the very eyes of the moon— now opened and imitating them,
[received] the touch of the moonbeams, moist and cool with trickling nectar.
He rose up like one who had been unconscious from the effects of a severe poison that had now subsided. ||3||
As if desiring to sportively join the moon’s orb with its head in order to instantly ascend the path of the stars,
the moon was reflected upon the surface of the dancing waves.
The Lord of Waters swiftly released half of his waters. ||4||
The ocean, filled with rising fish, sea-monsters, crocodiles, and various types of crests, and crowded with waves, banners, elephants, and horses,
went forth with great force, its fire exceeding that of Aurva.
It was as if the body of water were fleeing in haste from the onset of the gift-giving. ||5||
Scorched by the flames of the submarine fire within them, the lordly serpents in the form of waves— resplendent with jewels yet dark-hued—
shone in the ocean as they embraced the cool spray.
They possess clusters of sandalwood trees that cast a luster like the rays of the moon.
Rising up with impetuous arms like surging waves, he covered the surface of the sky; then, upon the seat of the earth's surface,
he obtained from the ocean, that treasury of jewels, the weapon.
The joy of embracing the Indus was like that of one who, though pure, feels sorrow from afar. ||7||
The circle of whirlpools in the ocean, possessing the luster of autumnal clouds, shone forth as it was pierced by the shadows cast by the emerging, massive coral stalks throbbing within,
like a lotus flower released from its sleep.
Like the navel-wheel of the Enemy of Madhu, it is a red lotus. ||8||
With its lofty jeweled pediments and cornices flashing with the reflections of the lunar discs upon all the statues seated within,
it was constructed above the ocean by the water-deities.
The line of waves shone most brilliantly like a streak of lightning. ||9||
With the hosts of stars, white as mist, seated like reflections within the waters of the ocean,
it was embraced firmly by the staff-like arms of its waves.
Possessing the beauty of moonlight, summer heat, water droplets, and spray. ||10||

The moon’s disc, complete and newly risen as it entered the shadow [of the mountain], clearly formed a circle; it fell upon the agitated ocean like a pearl necklace with a deep blue luster, its garment of sky having been cast off.
The mass of its waves was like the multitude of arms of the lord of the Daityas.
The ocean, with its waves that were like the breasts of the celestial river Gaṅgā— pure as white necklaces and resting upon the surface of his back—
[embraced] him whose enemies were the hissing of the serpent’s hoods, with its hands of ripples.
With new, heavy leafy creepers darkened by streaks of smoke. ||12||
Her arms were like waves turning in circular whirlpools, resembling precious conch shells with their bodies tossed upward and swirling;
she was a shore-dwelling woman whose dark, collyrium-like hair was disheveled like a black serpent.
The river Sindhu seemed to make her braid-like creepers dance for a long time. ||13||
Manifesting for a moment the entrance to the netherworld (rasātala),
which is the cause of a festival for the night-lotuses of all eyes,
she seemed as if out of curiosity to behold the world of the Nagas.
Lakṣmī has cast off her upper garment of the waters of the ocean.
The ocean, shattered by the impact of the coastal winds,
violently [scatters] its fresh clusters of jewel-like flowers,
while its small forest groves tremble with the surging waves.
The fire of destruction at the mouth of the submarine mare reduced it to ashes.
With its trembling coral bracelets red as the thousands of flames of fire from the arrows lodged and clinging to the moon-crested Lord’s head,
it was like the three cities of the ocean shimmering with sapphire.
The water from the sky fell down, its waves obstructed by pillars.

Seeing the waves tossing about the women of the celestial chariot-dwellers as they moved along, the men in the water gazed at them with passion; yet, due to their failure to attain them, those waves manifested like the submarine fire (Aurva-vahni) burning within them.
Like sorrows, they quickly cast themselves into the ocean. ||17||
Thus cast upward by the restless breaking waves of the ocean,
the rafts moved along with the throngs of celestial chariots,
as the women of the gods gazed upon them with longing desire.
The voyagers considered it to be a fall from the abode of the gods. ||18||

The open mouths of the submarine fire, with their circular tongues of flame resembling coral-red water, shone forth as if to drink the waters of the ocean, which were filled with the glow of quivering corals.
The unbearable heat of the Aurva fire—
Like the water of moonlight, [it flows] as if under the power of craving. ||19||

The ocean bore the reflections of the cool-rayed moon amidst the breaking of its waves— reflections as clear as clouds scraping the sky, and possessing beautiful jewels that served as the dwelling place for dark-complexioned women.
It possesses the grace of palatial mansions constructed with dark stones and provided with windows.
When the ocean reached its fullness,

the women of the shore swiftly snatched away the vessels filled with the white silk robes of the serpent-king, which were as bright as the luster of the Ganges and possessed the distinct laughter of foam.
[It was] pulled by the tips of fingers that were like clusters of curved young shoots. ||21||
The splendor of their flushed faces was made resonant by the arms of those who, agitated by the itching of mutual blows delivered while gazing at one another,
were like the breaking waves of a conch-shell hilt firmly grasped.
In the bellies of the swords, the waters of the ocean were drunk by men.
The ocean shone as if filled with deep pits where jars of abundant jewels had been extracted,
due to hundreds of circles of whirlpools violently cast about.
With floods of iron chains consisting of serpents coiled around their extremities.
That which was seen by the world at the onset of night— the splendor of the pollen of Kashmiri saffron belonging to the cool-rayed moon—
appeared as if it were being churned from the surging depths of the ocean.
The orb became pale white from the spray of the waves.

The clusters of blossoming night-lotuses on the body of the moon— washed by the breaking waves of the ocean tossed by the clouds— are being incessantly drenched by the drops of the dark spot falling from it.
They became variegated, as if by swarms of bees forming circles. ||25||
The circle of waves of the ocean, colored by the streaks of mineral pigments washed down from the ridges of the coastal mountains,
shone like the morning sunlight emerging from the hands of Anūru.
Like a mass of peaks scraping the sky, belonging to the abode of stone. ||26||
With waves for hands and the shells revealed upon the chest-like slopes of the mountain daityas torn apart with ease,
the ocean, like Nṛsiṃha, acts with a loud roar.
The crest of flames from the submarine fire was suppressed. ||27||
It shone, embraced by a mass of rays emerging from the millions of golden peaks of the mountain of the womb—
the navel-lotus of Madhusūdana, who dwells in illusion.
It was like the water of the ocean with its thousands of filaments scattered about. ||28||
At that time, the waves on the shores of the ocean shone forth, streaked by the rays of the ruby-like crest-jewels of the foremost serpents,
as if they were the flames of the submarine fire clinging to the banks.
The waves have, as it were, attained a state of intent flight. ||29||
When the moon, the cold-rayed one, has risen from the ocean, the rivers— having attained an increase as if through the trickling waters of moonstones—
strike against the surfaces of the rocks on their banks.
The waves, shimmering with the luster of sparkling jewels, swelled forth. ||30||

At that time, the submarine fire of the ocean reduced to ashes the body of the one whose banner bears the devourer of serpents (Garuda), which was then visibly seated upon the coils of the lord of serpents.
No one here is capable of protecting another in times of calamity.
It shone with the light arising from the moon-like reflection, which was as bright as a swarm of bees mistaken for a *lakṣma* mark;
its surface was like a mass of petals formed by waves curling at the edges.
The beauty of the ocean [is reflected] in the lotus-stamen of her palate. ||32||
She shed a continuous stream of teardrop-like pearls, as if pained by the impact of thick smoke from the submarine fire in the mouth of the Vadava, which was wreathed in flaming tresses.
With the eyes of pearl-oyster shells spread wide across the ocean. ||33||
The sandy banks flowed with streams of wine-like foam from the circular radiance of freshly polished rubies,
while fragments of young *kesara* branches from the forest on the shore...
Like the lines of waves upon the ocean for the sake of the ritual of initiation.
Conch shells, smeared with the smoke of the flickering submarine fire and clinging to the tips of the sprouts on coral branches,
appeared like copper-colored stalks upon the waves of the hand-like waters.
It possesses the beauty of a blue lotus bud, like the splendor of a cloud. ||35||
Stationed in the sky above the domed roof of the tortoise,
they appeared variegated by the colored rays from the jewels on the hoods of serpents,
creating the illusion of a mass of clouds streaked with lightning.
The breaking waves [reach] the shore where the flocks of swans have fled. ||36||
Spread by the force of the wind, the clouds— made into arrows by the red glow of masses of thick sparks—
bore the splendor of the submarine fire's smoke as they emerged from the ocean.
Their long braids were like the lines of rivers marked by those very signs.
With their tossing waves, which resembled the spray from jeweled goads marked by gaping fangs and possessed the luster of the throats of black crows,
they seemed to lick the heavens.
The lords of serpents [were shaken] by the waves of the agitated ocean. ||38||
With its far-spreading waves, variegated by masses of mineral pigments from the luster of shimmering jewel-rays,
the ocean swiftly crossed the sky as it surged upward.
Having attained a towering height with its peaks, it was like the Vindhya mountain. ||39||
The god of love attained a splendor through the rays of pearls scattered by oyster shells tossed about by the collision of waves,
as if they were the paths for the movement of his newly arisen [chariot].
Of the cool-rayed moon, which dwells upon the crown of the Lord of the Pramathas. ||40||
As if struck by the sharp peaks of mountain-crags fallen from the ridges of Mount Mandara as it was being whirled about,
[the ocean] bore a coppery hue from the flow of blood visible through its surging breaths.
From being cut off, the crocodiles in the ocean held their necks [aloft]. ||41||
The ocean shone as it was surrounded on all sides by the river-maidens, whose bursting foam displayed the beauty of a smile,
as if they had approached from behind with the intent of playing a joke.
His body is covered by the hands of the great waves, while his eyes are like oyster shells.
By the force of excessive drinking of water, the fire residing within the belly of the ocean— its intensity having been dulled by the hands of its broad waves—
seems to seek stimulation from the interior of the forests on its shores.
The ocean drew forth a mass of powdered tālīsa.
With frequent tremors fully manifesting and accompanied by a continuous succession of violent surges,
they were struck by the blows of the arrows of the leaping god of love.
The riverbanks, having been embraced [by the waters], fell into a state of extreme agitation.
The very moment of his rise attained a particularly profound splendor through hundreds of forms resembling the lofty peaks of the mountain ranges;
as if to wipe away the stain from the orb of the moon, [the sun rose].
The ocean swiftly plunged into the path created by the uprooting of the plantain trees. ||45||
The ocean shone in every direction with rows of clearly visible foam, white as the moon,
expanding like the long coils of the lord of serpents amidst its tossing waves.
They possess the beauty of a mass of feathers from which the sheath has been cast off. ||46||
Causing agitation, with its high waves acting as a bow and its unimpeded currents standing for arrows like those of the submarine fire,
it was like the eye of the Lord of Gaurī situated upon his forehead.
She rendered the fire of the fish-bannered god (Kāma) intensely radiant. ||47||
As if for the purpose of quelling the continuous heat from the thousands of flames of the fierce submarine fire,
the rivers, with their wave-hands, brought [the water] to the one whose banner is the fish.
Anointed with a paste of sandalwood as beautiful as a spray of foam. ||48||
Because of contact with the wine remaining in their bellies after being drunk by the host of gods who had rushed forward impetuously,
the mass of waves fell down, having shed their garments.
Like the ocean whose majesty is characterized by surging intoxication and delusion. ||49||
Beholding him alone— the cause of a festival for the eyes of the entire world— filled with intense joy like the ocean at the sight of the moon,
[the ocean] shed tears in the form of drops of pearls.
His eyes were like pure oyster shells, the essence of a gathered abundance. ||50||
At that time, the excellent jewels of the ocean, dappled by the spreading diffusion of their rays, shone most intensely,
as if they had taken up blazing torches to dispel the darkness of the netherworld.
Like lamps in every direction, with broad waves for their hands. ||51||

The row of ocean waves, shaken by the force of the wind from the fourfold flight [of the chariot], rose up toward the path of the stars (the sky) in such a way that those situated in its midst were, for a moment, [as if]—
The fortune of Māra’s hosts is as transient as a cluster of shimmering bubbles. ||52||
Then, streaked with masses of smoke from the fire spat by the serpents due to the rows of surging waves,
the orb of the moon fell from the sky, bearing [the marks of] its flight.
As if by the impurities clinging to it, like those of the ocean. ||53||
Disregarding the burning heat of the Aurva fire,
the ocean swiftly caused the rivers flowing toward the cardinal directions to enter its mouth with speed, as they were possessed by the flow of its waters.
Even toward one who is affectionate, a fool never feels any regard. ||54||
