Did the oceans swell, washing the quarters of the sky, their jewel-lustre flowing as if by the force of the breath-winds rising from the hissing of the circle of hoods of the serpent Śeṣa dwelling within? Or was it the moon?
The waves, produced by the forceful impact upon the abode, [arise] with speed. ||55||
The orb of the Tālūra mountain bore the rim of the potter’s wheel for the ocean, which had reached a state of agitation and whose waves were spreading out, breaking, and gradually becoming vast.
Possessing the grace of a series of arrows being fashioned and transformed.

The waves of the ocean stood still for a moment like the flames of the submarine fire (Aurva), their crests bearing massive tongues of flame, as they clung to the path of the sky variegated by the planetary jewels coated in the light of a moonlight as clear as large pearls falling from the mass of sand scattered upon the shore.
As if out of a thirst for the touch of the cool moon to pacify the burning heat of his penance, he ascended upwards. ||57||
Spreading their splendor through the constant formation of caves, with the slopes of their banks made beautiful by the shimmering luster of radiant gems and groves of forest creepers,
the waves shone like mountains that serve as dwellings for serpents.
Rising up after having left behind the ocean whose mass of waters was agitated. ||58||
The tiger skin of Śiva, its seams loosened by the rapid movements of his twilight dance and its middle portion freed from knots, shone as it slipped upon the ground like the earth itself—
its golden tablelands gleaming on the mountain peaks where the interior is agitated by fear of the thunderbolt.
The water of the ocean possesses a variegated luster from the intermingling of its spray with the stalks of the lotuses.

The clear garlands of stars quickly settled upon the heads of the elephants emerging from the waters of the ocean, whose broad faces were dusted with the spray of particles from the masses of minerals on the slopes of the mountain ridges.
They spread forth splendor with rows of jewels cast from their undulating limbs.
Having cast upon the shores those heaps of priceless gems that had dimmed the luster of the moon, and having uprooted that circle of trees laden with succulent fruit which stood in their favor,
the surges of the ocean’s waters, having surged far, instantly fell into the submarine fire.
Or who, having fallen into calamity, do not undergo transformation due to the cause of dullness? ||61||
Then, taking up conch-powder swallowed by the submarine fire, they dragged from the forest lands on the shore heaps of *nāgabalī* leaves; meanwhile,
the breaking waves shattered the joints of many broken areca-nut trees and *khadira* logs.
In this manner, they maintained the unbroken continuity of the betel-leaf, just as the moon maintains its presence in the ocean.
He has attained an indescribable splendor, such that by the waves as high as the peaks of the Kulagiri mountains— waves whose swelling begins at the very moment of his rising,
and which are formidable with their massing waters— he is unable to wipe away the stain of the moon that rises in the night sky.
In that place, the ocean bore the flames of the submarine fire like a heart emitting smoke.

The ocean, with its mass of water acting like a staff of waves, bore away the wives of the gods— those women whose moon-like faces were smiling with the impetuosity of the intense pleasure of amorous play— and who, their minds turned away from remembering any offense against their lovers, had set upon them; thus the ocean carried away the very banner of Kandarpa, complete with its fish-emblem and its staff of ripples.
He cast aside that which was delightful with the resounding roar of victory drums clearly manifesting through various kinds of agitation.
In every direction, the rays of the moon— fitted with windows like lattice-work, bestowing the beauty of blooming night-lotuses,
clearly devoid of monkeys, and grasping the peaks of vast trees and mountains—
resemble hosts of monkeys once again leaping across the bridge by the force of their speed.
The entire ocean was agitated, its sandy banks strewn with various scattered jewels.

Thus ends the twenty-second canto, titled "The Description of the Ocean’s Exultation," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who bore the name Vāgīśvara and the secondary title Vidyādhipati—and who was a servant to the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
The Twenty-third Canto:
Thus, in the ocean, having obtained joy at the rising of the moon...

In that city, where the beauty of the dance was provided by the arms of the waves of the Mulla river, the womenfolk, anticipating the arrival of their beloveds, applied themselves with focused attention to the task of adornment.
Then the feet of the noble ladies bore the splendor of the moonbeams, as they swayed and brushed against their toenails—
feet that were now bent low before their beloveds who had committed offenses against them.
They bore [it] as if it were a concentrated, embodied grace.
Possessing a most solid orb of hips acquired through a wealth of passion overflowing with manifest excellence,
he was truly worthy of being borne by the women of the gods who long for love.
The tattered garment possesses a beauty captivating through its patterned arrangement of horripilation. ||3||
The row of toes on one foot shone with a dense, crimson luster from the applied lac-dye,
while the other foot was adorned with a wreath fashioned from the blossoms of the Ashoka tree by a timid woman.
The splendor of the five arrows of the god of love, whose shafts are bees.
Upon her broad hips, which resembled a surface of stone, a golden girdle was fastened tightly by the young woman,
while a delicate and charming line of hair had begun to sprout there.
It attained the splendor of a circular basin made of jewels. ||5||
O Lady, let it be that you are indeed bound by your rounded hips; for one who delights in them, liberation has already occurred.
It is as if [the hips] say, "Do not be so vainly noisy with your cries."
He spoke to Kāñcī, the anklet tinkling at his feet.

Standing in the middle, she bore a beauty like that of a golden embankment fashioned with care, her lotus-feet resting upon the ground with loosened girths, and her waist adorned by a girdle as formidable as molten gold.
For a moment, it was like some city of the god of love. ||7||
The beauty fashioned by girdles upon their hips and the established presence of jeweled necklaces upon the slopes of their breasts—
as if thinking, "We have not been adorned," the women with shapely hips [seemed to reproach them].
Their waists bore an unrestrained leanness. ||8||
The womenfolk of the city bore a splendor like lotus-pools in the forest of the Flower-Arrowed God, with their creeper-like limbs being mossy tendrils in the waters of loveliness and grace.
With the spreading rays from the crests of their emerald necklaces. ||9||
The strand of pearls, resting between her two breasts that were not bent down, shone intensely like the luster of a row of stars;
it was as if a pair of fresh lotus buds were opening up.
The face of Vilāsavatī was split asunder like a lotus stalk. ||10||
The moonstone situated in the center of her necklace silenced the string of her girdle by means of the floods of water trickling from it as it was touched by the rays of the moon.
Even when maintaining neutrality, the tarala (a gem or a fickle person) does not lead to prosperity. ||11||
Her pair of breasts captivated the mind, their tips surpassed by the rays of emeralds shimmering from the center of her jeweled necklace,
as she playfully held a fresh sprig of water-moss.
Her thighs were graced by the playful charm of a pair of ruddy geese at the tips of their beaks.
When his beloved had passed away, he could not fasten the garment even when it was pulled by a hand other than the lotus-hand whose fingers were tightly interlaced with difficulty; rather,
it slipped down there out of grief.
In that empty space, in an instant, was the braid of her with the curved locks. ||13||
With the tips of their nails— each beautifully curved like the feathered shafts of arrows fixed individually—
he surpassed the quiver-staffs of the God of Love.
By the fingers of the hands of young women playfully extended. ||14||
A woman, her slender body gracefully adorned with ornaments upon arrival,
playfully applied red lac to the bud-like sprouts of her own lower lip.
A certain woman placed [him] in her heart, the lord of her heart.
At that moment, having experienced the pleasure of a kiss from one whose noble self had inflicted wounds with the tips of his fangs,
the passion of the lotus-eyed women [was transferred] to their lower lips.
What wonder is there that it was carried by the petal of a lotus? ||16||
The line upon the middle of the lower lip, beautiful with the hue of betel, stole the heart of the deer-eyed woman;
it was like the line drawn by the string on the back of the most excellent bow, the fish-bannered god’s sword-blade, or his staff.
The splendor of whose wounds and sores was produced by the falling of the *dhāraṇī*. ||17||
There shone a certain splendor, surpassing the beauty of the reflected orb [of the sun], a mass of radiance bursting forth from her lips,
as if the flower-arrowed god [Kāma] had entered within and was there nourished by the fullness of that weight.
As if vomiting forth the nectar from within a steel arrow. ||18||
Fearing that her stainless beauty might become sullied here, she did not draw a leaf-design (pattralekhā) on the wall as a companion; instead,
she caused no distress to this [wall] by drawing the moon reflected therein.
The radiance of the bimba fruit is surpassed by the cheek of the young woman. ||19||
The cheek bore the beauty of a *lakucha* bud, pale and radiant, charming with the vine-like tendril of a swelling mole,
and marked by the deer of its reflection resting in its shade.
Like a forest of bow-staves, the elevated [breast] of the woman. ||20||
Upon the surface of the cheek of that other moon-like woman, whose pale orb was concealed by her dark complexion,
a musk-paste leaf-design was clearly visible in its distinct form.
A row of leaves was made beautiful by Lakṣmaṇa himself. ||21||
They bear cheeks variegated by the application of leaf-designs smeared with dark aloe-paste that shines like royal lac,
and [cheeks] illuminated by the lamps of gems red as the tips of their earrings.
Her curved eyebrows were as if smeared with spittle and soot. ||22||
The left-browed woman shone, her cheek— pale as a withered saffron flower— adorned with a streak of aguru paste,
like a dark figure painted upon a silver wall.
Bearing qualities unequaled in the graceful play of a creeper.

With her beautiful brows, she shone as her long, dangling ear-ornament cast a dense radiance, thickened by the mass of light from the nails and fingers of its branch-like hands, which were as formidable as the rays of the moon turned sideways.
Placing on her ear a ruby earring that radiated brilliant rays.
As if longing for the nectar of the spreading radiance of her beauty and loveliness, the moon, though already filled with a mass of ambrosia,
descended upon the bride’s cheek under the guise of her reflection.
Who among those possessing virtues is truly virtuous? Only he who is contented with his own virtues. ||25||
The deer, as if out of longing for the woman’s well-trained, playful, and amorous gestures— those flickering movements of a moment—
seems to have entered the moon under the guise of its reflection.
She made her dwelling upon the smooth surface of her cheek. ||26||
Washed by the flowing stream of the water of loveliness and grace, the mark on her cheek rested like a reflection upon the surface of her face;
it shone there as if released from the moon in its pristine state.
As if out of fear for the noose of her ears, the crescent moon rests upon the breast of the slender-bodied one. ||27||

As the rays of the moon fell upon her, turning her dark complexion ashen with a mass of fresh *lodhra* pollen— intended, as it were, to wipe away the pride of the God of Love— the women of the city gazed at them as if they were mirrors of Kandarpa.
They fell upon her cheeks, which stole the luster of the lotus.
Beholding her, whose single golden ear-ornament rested upon the surface of her high,
swelling breast, and who was marked by the four clearly visible wheels ready for action—
He possesses the splendor of one who carries a bundle of flowers for the mobile god of love. ||29||
Another young woman shone, wearing a single conch-shell earring whose broad, pure radiance was like the expansive orb of the moon, unobscured by clouds. She was perched upon a balcony—
The ear-lobes at the tips of her ears were marked with earrings.
The beautiful woman bore a splendor like that of a cluster of bees, her ear-ornament consisting of pearls strung together with a central section jagged with large sapphires.
Of the tender Kalpavallī creeper, its clusters of blossoms were variegated. ||31||
Disregarding its own excellence of luster, this [river] dares to seize the true essence of the other at their confluence;
thus, as if with indignation, she obstructed her own course.
The earth was the ground for the sight of him whose eyes were like blue lotuses.
In the oblong pond, whose splendor was intensified by blue lotuses resembling the shimmering circles of wandering stars,
the bees were clearly marked by a spray of soot-like pollen.
They met his glance like a row of bees upon the eye of a long-lashed woman.
The curved brow of her whose eyes have lashes like those of a doe shone with a luster exceeding that of collyrium applied with a slender stick,
as she drank the nectar dripping from the blue lotus resting upon her ear.
Or by a row of honey-drinkers who have approached out of greed and other such motives. ||34||
The drop of musk-tilaka upon the forehead of the moon-faced women produced an intense splendor,
like the wheel of the feet of the wandering elephant of the flower-arrowed god.
Like the impression of a seal, its beauty is grey with mud. ||35||
Bearing a forehead-plate that possesses the charming beauty of a jewel, with its trembling and flickering tilaka mark swaying like a swing,
she bears the splendor of the moon and the celestial bow merged into one.
The lady with arched brows imitated the sky marked by fragments [of clouds]. ||36||
If light were to dwell together in one place with a mass of nocturnal darkness, it would be a virtuous thing;
yet the gazelle-eyed women have taken up their residence along with the crescent moon.
The ground of hair and hands would bestow a state of equality upon slaves and others. ||37||
With beautiful flowers clustered in their blossoming curls, moistened by drops of nectar from the rising dust,
and casting off the long arrangement [of their braids] within their thick tresses;
The bonds were loosened by the matrons; the remaining [bonds] were beautiful. ||38||
Then, as those women with thighs like the trunks of young elephants rushed impetuously toward their beloveds, the mass of smoke from the perfumes used for grooming their hair shone forth,
shattered by the rays of the moon.
As if producing the darkness of night. ||39||
A supreme cosmetic ointment was prepared by them in the form of a garland, intended to eclipse their own beauty and charm.
Stability soon returned to his body, which had been previously emaciated by the religious observances arising from the constant contemplation of his beloved’s arrival.
His body, marked with the mud of fresh saffron and made the target of the God of Love,
bore a splendor like that of a mountain peak thick with the pollen of the filaments of flowers recently shed.
It was as if the very essence of the woman's passion were concentrated and intensified within it.
Having donned hundreds of ornaments in vain, this luster of the body of the lotus-eyed one has been defiled; for the reflection of the beautiful-browed girl’s face upon the clear wall of her cheek—
In that region, the moon laughed exceedingly with its rays. ||42||
The swarm of bees, agitated by their turning away due to their longing for the thick fragrance of her manifest body-unguents,
[seemed to form a cage] of iron out of fear of the falling arrows of irresistible Māra.
Another shone as if fashioned from the space between two coats of mail. ||43||
The bamboos, with their straight, lofty, and beautiful nodes, captivated the hearts of the people;
the young women bore mṛdaṅga drums in the form of their breasts,
while their swaying jeweled earrings served as bronze cymbals.
They were like the concert halls of the playful god of love. ||44||
Adorned with a girdle of bright, polished steel, her hands beautiful with bracelets, and wearing a string of pearls, she shone like the elephantine form of Kāma, full of passion and pride.
Her excellent thighs were like the slopes of a jar-like breast adorned with a garland of stars. ||45||
By the turbidification of their beauty and splendor through her faultless body-staff, which was the cause of their own delight,
the very name "lotus-eyed" became literally false for them.
Even of ornaments whose brilliant luster was cast aside. ||46||
With her mind elsewhere due to the thought of returning to the house of her lover, she held the reflection of the moon in her house within the clear water,
while her friend distinguished between the appropriate and inappropriate arrangement of her various ornaments.
One who was indeed empty gazed at his face. ||47||
Beholding her face, made beautiful by the application of variegated cosmetics, in the surface of a mirror, she sighed repeatedly;
perceiving his intention toward the abode of her beloved, she fixed [her gaze].
By means of which a clever messenger, though not yet dispatched, has already caused passion to arise.
"She has already gone," [he thought], yet an obstacle was created for the long-lashed-eyed woman by the weight of her thick-set hips;
as she was departing toward her beloved, she seemed to look back with a sidelong glance.
With a light state of mind, he went forward to speak. ||49||
Having fashioned a sound pleasing to the ear, the woman approached the beloved cloud that had arrived with its course moistened by rain,
just as a beautiful woman approaches a distant region.
Fortune [is present] with a jeweled pin of bristling horripilation. ||50||
Then, as her pupil rushed along the path of her outer corner from afar to behold her beloved,
her thick [eyelashes] appeared like drops of tears of joy.
They fell together like droplets from a spray of perspiration.
A certain woman, through drops of the essence of Dharma flowing from the joy of the firm embrace of the Lord of Mind— whose form was fashioned by conceptual thought—
bears upon her the marks of immersion in the waters of beauty and splendor.
He bore a body like that of Vṛndā, with its hair standing on end.
Terrified, the bride was unable to look her husband in the face because she had been married so recently; then,
she could only see the face of him who stood behind her, except for his sighs.
Seeing it indistinctly in the mirror of the self, she was pained.
One woman, whose beloved was lingering long, bore a lip-stone that had lost its luster and become a seat of sorrow,
as it was darkened by the continuous succession of her sighing breaths.
It was as if split apart by the turbidity of the darkness of his wrath. ||54||
Having arrived, the lover, trembling with inner guilt, beheld the decorative leaf-patterns made of black aloe-paste belonging to the women of the city,
which were marked by a continuous quivering.
Like a streak of ichor on a temple elephant, turbid with the smoke from the fire of pride. ||55||

O lovely-faced one, even though he is ashamed, you must not say anything unpleasant to him for the sake of his remorse; for when his offense is manifest, tears do not arise from a beautiful-eyed beloved.
The pillar seemed, as it were, to have resolved to speak harshly. ||56||

When her lover, who had committed an offense, bowed down before her, a swarm of wandering bees— fragrant from the scent of the flower that served as his crest-ornament— shone upon the lotus-foot of the young woman.
For a moment at his side, she possessed the beauty of dark-blue stone anklets. ||57||
With his hands smeared with clinging collyrium, as he forcibly wiped away the flood of tears from her eyes— tears that were flushed with passion—
the lover became like an elephant to the slender-bodied woman.
Like the darkness of pride, it is an obstacle to the enjoyment of pleasure. ||58||
Her hand, marked by the three-fold crease, touches her face as her vine-like braid kisses her dark, long, and curved sides and hips;
now she tilts her brow and closes her eyes.
One woman yawned before her lover out of the passion of love. ||59||
Another, moreover, has her staff-like arms raised upward with impetuosity, their hands positioned in the *uttānakarkaṭaka* gesture,
while her eyebrows are upturned at the roots, curved, and knitted together.
Her broad forehead was furrowed with lines of frowns.
The beauty of her full breasts is raised by the dark, thick braid that kisses the slopes of her swaying hips; meanwhile,
the extreme slenderness of her elongated waist causes her sides to disappear.
Her limbs produced a whirling and turning of her body. (A pair of verses.
In the graceful play of their glances, the blue-blackness of their pupils was distinct from the path of their outer corners.
They bore the beauty of masses of soot emerging from eyes reddened by rolling tears, like streaks of rising dust.
Having arrived at the time of dusk, they were gazed upon with playful, sidelong glances by women whose pupils were as beautiful and dark as the luster of shimmering sapphires.
Young men [are the suns] for the lotus-eyes of women blinded by pride. ||63||
Their glances, which mottled the regions of their cheeks with rays from the clusters of lashes and tremulous pupils,
tossed the hearts of their lovers like fish in a net.
They are the playful, enchanting, and delusive movements of her amorous sport. ||64||
Then, as another woman rose impetuously from her seat upon beholding her beloved,
a jeweled mirror fell gracefully from the tip of her hand at the base of his foot.
By the radiance of his face, he surpassed the splendor of the moon. ||65||

Thus ends the twenty-third canto, titled "The Description of Adornment," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel [of its author], composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who bore the name Vāgīśvara and was also known by the alias Vidyādhipati, and who was a dependent of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
The Twenty-fourth Canto:
Thus, at the onset of night, as the gazes of the cakora birds met with their beloveds...
Others, due to separation from their beloveds, fell into a state of extreme distress. ||1||
The curved digit of the moon bore the grace of the staff of Cupid’s bow;
and the rays emanating from it, like arrows impelled by that [digit], caused pain to the slender maiden.
At that time, there was no darkness anywhere, nor was there any visible distinction from the moon's domain;
yet it produced a long-lasting blindness for her due to the expansion of her separation from her son.

The wind, born from the feathers of the arrows of the flower-bowed god, fanning the fire of the anguish of separation, quickly consumed the hearts of the fair-browed women, which had lost their steadfastness.

Who here does not become adverse when beset by calamity, even if he is faultless? For even the moonbeams, which are streams of nectar and possess beautiful forms, act like fire during separation from a beloved. 5.
Then the other woman was pained by the dense darkness of her heavy swoon as she beheld the form of her beloved reflected [in the mirror];
moreover, even though her mind was clouded by her sighs, she was like a mirror [reflecting the image].
Like a delicate flower violently struck from its stalk by the southern breeze,
the heart of the girl with curved eyebrows fell away from its own dwelling.
Desiring to fashion for himself another string for the bow of Love,
the wind shook the lotus-fiber stalk resting upon the body of the left-eyed maiden.

O beloved, her heart—oppressed by the heavy burden of profound anxiety, as if exhausted by the intensity of its agitation at the prospect of a meeting with the one she had set out to find—breathed heavily. 9.
Abandon your grief before this fever of separation departs;
take heart for a moment, for it is by fortitude that one is able to dispel such calamity. (10)
Circling with sweet sounds out of longing for the blue lotuses that have long adorned [her ears],
a bee approaches the vicinity of her ear as if to console her in this way.
(A pair of verses) Here, due to separation from their beloveds, anxieties enter [their hearts] without hesitation.
Smara, having pierced her with his arrows, seemed as if he had found her mind to be an open gateway. ||12||
With the expansive reflections of his beloved’s love, which remained intact through an unbroken lineage, he,
free from anxiety as if having reached a sacred ford, took birth within her mind.
Bound by a garland of mental constructs consisting of unceasingly turbulent thoughts of love,
the beautiful-browed woman’s meditation followed her beloved as if it were exceedingly long.

And the pitiless Madana did not desist from stringing his bow, though it was bent by her emaciated state, nor from placing upon it the bowstring, while she possessed a body as delicate as a flower. ||15||
Those who were suffering from the heat instantly reduced another woman, who had been anointed with sandalwood paste,
to a state of heavy emaciation through desiccation, just as the days of the fierce summer heat wither a lotus pond.
The bees, drawn by the abundance of her manifest fragrance, drank in the breaths from her body;
though overwhelmed by its heat, they found it to be nothing but pleasure, even though it was the cause of their greater suffering.
For her whose brows were graced by moonlight, the sharp arrows of his bodyless shafts instantly inflicted a wound upon her heart,
causing the harsh dust of the saline soil to appear like a shower of moonbeams.
As if in pain from the distress of being overwhelmed by the heat of the fire of separation, her heart was about to flee;
yet Aparā did not restrain it with her hand, which remained fixed in deep anxiety.
Thus, with his arrows, the God of Love pierced the eager heart of Sudṛś, which was like a target;
yet he could not string his bow again, for it was deprived of its undivided parts.
At night, she shone like another riverbank, with the Makara-bannered god (Kāma) having attained growth, as the pearls of teardrops fell from the shells of her eyes. 21.
The circle of cheeks of the fair-eyed woman was seen, pale as a sleepless madhūka flower;
through its being overspread with thinness, it appeared as if it had reached extreme concavity by means of the floating droplets of her tears.
The bees, intoxicated by the honey and drawn by the fragrant breeze of her sighs, brought another woman— who had already fainted—
to a state of extreme agitation, like serpents attacking a sprout of sandalwood.
On the bed in the lofty moon-chamber of the palace, she who did not find sleep for even a moment at night— fearing long separation— having first rested her head upon the neck of her beloved.
Another, having fixed her longing upon her beloved after receiving a vision of him in a dream, alas, even he disregarded her greatly—
oh, how wondrous is the diversity of the course of destiny! (A pair of verses) Thus,
in separation, a certain woman, having become weak, became exceedingly anxious.
How she released her tears, pressed by her closed eyelashes, with great difficulty. ||26||

Like a female friend for one afflicted by a fever, the stone statue of Śālabhañjikā— made of moonstone— experienced an internal moisture within herself in order to alleviate the intense heat of that fair-browed woman.
As the moon rose from the ocean, its rays— whose tips were embraced by that very fire of poison within its depths—
rendered the night thick with fainting, as if overwhelmed by distress.
A mass of camphor was applied by her affectionate friends to her body;
it appeared like her own complexion, which had slipped from the surface of her cheeks out of fear of the distress caused by weeping.
It is a marvel that, despite the intensity of the fever of love, the bewilderments of the fair-eyed woman did not wither away,
for they possessed a splendor radiant with the ornament of her flower-like smiles, like the blossoms upon the sprouts of a tree.
During the throes of passion, the young woman placed her hand upon her face as if in a playful gesture of concealment;
it appeared grey with trickling collyrium, as if scorched by the heat of her sighs.
With her lotus-eyes closed and her skin bristling with horripilation, a certain longing woman quickly withered like a lotus plant under the rays of the moon. 32.
The sound of bees dwelling upon the blossoming lotuses used as a bed was heard like the clinking of ornaments on her body from the fire of separation. 33.
Even upon the arrival of his beloved, he observed her future state and, through the horripilation and other signs produced by his mental constructs,
performed [the gestures] upon his body as if practicing them once more for the sake of the lady with arched brows.
The fire of passion, further intensified by the breezes that had long since brushed against her body as they were deflected by the lotus petals used as fans,
burned all the more intensely in that deer-eyed woman.
With her creeper-like locks disheveled and resting upon the palm of her hand,
she revealed through the moon of her face the state of suffering from the heat of love, even though she did not speak to her companion.
For the lotus-eyed women, strings of moonstone necklaces did not bring relief;
rather, they were like drops of water trickling from their skin, which was parched by the fever of love and then moistened as it broke out in perspiration.
In their separation, when the dissolution at the end of the age had unfolded for those whose eyes were like those of young fawns,
their bodies— tender as fresh lotuses— became discolored by the falling of frost.

As her beloved tarries, the women—successively leaping toward the lunar orb in the sky, violently agitated by longing, and repeatedly fainting as their desires are frustrated—become utterly bewildered. (39)
Surely, the heat arising from the repetition of entering the center of the sun's orb, which is now free of frost,
has been seized by the burning bodies of young women separated from their lovers.
Touching with the rows of rays from the tips of his hands, he [the moon] acted [as a mirror]. ||40||
This is an incomparable marvel: that even those things consisting of blossoms, which rain down a multitude of drops of nectar,
[cause distress] to the fair-browed women whose minds are overwhelmed by separation.
Alas, his body is being withered away by the falling arrows! ||41||
As if smeared by the streaks of *hālāhala* poison surging forth under the guise of the mark produced during the churning of the ocean,
the rays of the moon brought about a swoon with their nectar-water.
Even the tears flowing from beautiful women afflicted by the pain of separation. ||42||
When the moon is thick with clouds and bestows great joy upon the elephants, the broad earth scatters a fresh,
sap-filled shower [of rain], appearing like a string of pearls formed from large drops of tears.
May he emerge from the interior of the oyster-shell of his long-stretched eyes. ||43||
Truly, the state of being of a person whose mental faculties are deranged becomes quite different from what it was before;
for the rays of the moon, though moist with nectar, consumed young women who were distressed by separation from their beloveds. 44.
With their creeper-like arms tossed and swaying, they seemed to offer a share of the lotus-bed through the honey-drops of light radiating from the petal-like red fingers of their lotus-hands.
They made the drops of nectar dry up with the heat. ||45||
It shone as if by the pretext of the tawny pollen-particles from his lotus-throne, struck down by the wind of his sighs—
pollen that seemed like the very fire of separation fleeing in fear.
It was like some collection of atoms of a fair-complexioned body. ||46||
Slipping from her lotus-like arm upon the jeweled floor, the streaks of light from her nails— clinging to the red lotuses of her face—
are being pulled away by young swans who have raised their necks and are greedily tugging at them.
Her body appeared like a young sprout of a lotus stalk. ||47||
The crescent moon, reflected upon the smooth surface of the slender maiden’s cheek,
assumed the beauty of the barb from the sharp arrow of Love plunged into her heart.
It appeared like the beak of a heron drawn out from its hidden place. ||48||
A certain woman held her fish-like cheek against her lotus-hand, which she had made into a pillow,
as it was heated by the hundreds of flames of the fire of love kindled within her.
As if out of anger, it sought to block even the space occupied by the reflection of the moon. ||49||
Thus, at that evening when the ocean of jewels surged with the rising of the moon, the fair-eyed women fell into a state of disarray; as their lovers’ first passion blossomed, they became agitated.
The pangs of separation caused by pride and exile, and the distress of being parted from one's dwelling. ||50||

Thus ends the twenty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of Separation," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
Canto Twenty-Five:
In this manner, [the lament] of the celestial beauties, swelling forth upon beholding the rays of the moon...
Some female messengers, approaching her in that state with great agitation, spoke to her on behalf of their friends. ||1||
Her hand, possessing the delicate softness of a lotus petal,
and her cheek, which bore an extreme paleness upon its surface, both remained as did her slender body, while she lay upon a bed of flowers.
Drawn by the fragrance of the breath of her sighs, and deeply distressed by the heat of that very breath, the wandering bees desire to drink; thus, the streams of tears from her eyes fall down. (3)
By the god of love, manifesting at the onset of the moonrise,
the state of being distinct pearls of tears was clearly produced for her from the oyster-shell of her eyes, just as it is produced for the shoreland by the sea.
The lotus stalk, placed by her friends upon her slender body— its tenderness surpassed only by the sprouts of her arms—
causes a burning sensation all the more intense, as if out of envy for that very frame.
The forehead-slab of the slender woman, bearing a streak of sandalwood paste,
attains a beauty like a line of waves from the milk-ocean when a crescent moon first appears— pale as it is from the torment of separation.
At this moment, she bears two breasts whose interiors reflect the bees drawn by her sighs;
they seem to have attained a paleness as if scorched by the spreading spray of her intensely hot tears.
Now, as if with anger firmly fixed even toward the Mind-born God (Kāma), she releases a rain of arrows;
her long eyes, like lotus petals, are reddened by sleeplessness.

For her, who endures a state deeply intensified by manifold thoughts and doubts during separation from you, you alone are the sole cause of both her happiness and her sorrow, whether in dream or in the activities of her waking life. (9)
At the very moment my distressed friend was separated from you, helpless and sorrowful, that moon— beautiful as the god of love, yet like a singed orb— arose, desiring to consume her.

While you were depriving that fair-limbed woman of her opportunity with arrows that reduce the body to emaciation, the bodiless god of love pierced her with his keen shafts; this wound, however, is deeply heavy upon my heart.

Like moths rushing toward the flame of a lamp, the arrows of Smara— possessing the beauty of gathered eyelashes— caused her, whose lovely luster was blazing, to tremble as they struck her who had already reached the end of her life.
As if tormented by the heat of the fire of separation burning within, and having become thirsty, the nectar of the lovely-eyed one’s lower lip is now being drunk by continuous streams of sighs. 13.
At night, with a stalk of lotus fiber— the staff of her rays— placed upon the slender rod of her body,
she appears as if her very essence of beauty were being drunk up even by the moonlight.
Bearing a bracelet of lotus stalks, she—pierced by the thorn of longing—did not shine, though she was like a jeweled bangle for the fortune of beauty and a halo for the moon of her form. (15)
As if out of curiosity, the slender maiden wears her heart encircled by lotus-stalk fibers placed there by her friend’s hands, as if to find a space between her two breasts.

I perceive that very mark of the fish, its beautiful splendor revealed, resting upon the sole of her foot—she who, rich in auspicious marks, carried away the mental state of young men as she walked. ||17||
In separation from him, her heart possesses neither hardness nor tenderness;
for though pierced by the arrows of Love, it neither attains firmness nor does it shatter. (18)
At the onset of night, my friend is attended by the enemy of the cool-rayed moon, which has entered the shadows of the jeweled walls of the palace and, through its moisture,
seems desirous of inquiring after her well-being.

With their passion intensified, leading her lover—who has suppressed his weariness—to the path of sight, the slender-limbed woman’s mental projections assume the likeness of her circle of friends, as if they have captured their very hearts. (20)

Now, the delicate woman’s lotus-hand placed upon her cheek does not shine, as if she fears it might wipe away the continuous flow of thick streams of tears; thus, the dark aloe-leaf ornament clinging to it loses its luster.
She is tormented by the falling new flower-clusters, speckled with bees,
which appear as if they have been gazed upon by the arrows of Love— arrows that resemble the flames from the eye of Śiva, consumed by fire.
As if to fan the fierce fire of her separation,
the girl with arched brows carries upon her body a straight lotus-stalk tube placed there, like a pipe for blowing into a furnace.
Upon the surface of her jar-like breasts, where the lotus petals have withered, scorched by the fire of separation from you, drops of tears fall incessantly with a soft *cham* sound. (24)
Her slender body was consumed by the moon during the nights as it bore the goddess Lakṣmī upon its lap, as if out of passion for the dolphin at the tip of the banner of the God of Love.

She bears upon her forehead a crescent-moon mark, like a streak of foam from the ocean of the jewels of loveliness—a tilaka smeared with sandalwood paste, a plantain tree for the dalliance of Kandarpa. (A pair of verses.
Sandalwood-smeared hands were repeatedly placed by her friends upon her heart to soothe it.
Their fingers were like channels for streams of water from the rays of their clear, outpouring nails. ||27||
In the nights, the reflection of the moon was visible on the surface of her emaciated cheek;
it bore the likeness of Lakṣmī, appearing as a dark callus upon the finger of her hand that served as a pillow.
Scorched by the fire of separation, her body—beautiful as a crescent moon—seems to melt away under the guise of perspiration, spreading distress among her friends. (29)
The fair-browed woman was perceived as if by a string of pearl necklaces intended to extinguish the fire of separation;
her slender body was drenched by the showers of sandalwood water from her own radiance, as if by a friend.
Adorned with circles of lotus-stalk vines and full-blown blue and white lotuses, she,
drenched by her tears, bears the state of being like a garden pond belonging to the God of Love.
His mind, agitated by the web of conceptual constructions, wanders aimlessly,
as if being driven by the gusts of wind from the feathers of the multitude of arrows discharged by the God of Love.
Her lip-bud has already been scorched by the gusts of her breath, which carry the heat she holds within;
before her entire body is consumed, go to her at once, casting aside your pride. (33)

Her face, with its lotus-like hand, does not shine, for her gaze is vacant due to anxiety; it lacks the reflection of the moon that was once fixed upon it as she kissed a previously unseen, fully blossomed lotus. 34.

With a forehead marked by sandalwood paste like a lotus-pond, her face adorned with *ketaka* flowers, possessing the clear waters of serene beauty and pale breasts, she was like the Goddess Śrī herself in autumn. (35)

With the trembling of their breasts caused by the breaths that—driving the flow of tears to a state of exhaustion—seemed as if they were shrinking back in fear from the pain of being eclipsed by the beauty of the luster of her bimba-like lips; (36)

Reproached by the bees, who had increased their distress by the flow of honey from flower-beds they themselves had withered, she was as if scorched from afar by the heat of a fire resulting from separation from her body. ||37||

At night, under the influence of manifold amorous imaginings, the girl with the arched brows bears her cheek— now bristling with horripilation— as if it were pained by the cold touch of the moon’s orb reflected upon it. (A *cakralaka* [set of four verses]) Fainting,
persistent sighing, delirious speech, wakefulness, trembling, and yawning;
She has indeed obtained the fruits of her purpose by offering herself even to you for the sake of happiness. ||39||
Vain is the necklace; fie on the bed strewn with lotus stalks; or rather, cast the camphor far away along with these chips of snowy stone—why all this?
Do not indulge in such false distress; she suffers from some most grievous fever of love.
Thus, O fortunate one, her friends then spoke to one another, their eyes overflowing with floods of tears. ||40||
"Come then, before my friend falls into an irreparable state due to separation from you"—thus encouraged by the words of the messenger, someone arrived in haste. 41.
There, amidst his friends who were busily engaged in providing cooling remedies,
he beheld his beloved seated within the interior of a plantain bower inside the palace.
She was holding her fingertips— darkened by the collyrium from streams of tears— as they rested upon the surface of her cheek,
appearing as if scorched by the very breaths she exhaled when covering her mouth with a yawn.
With her two breasts, which were exceedingly high, she bore a necklace of pure pearls drenched in their luster,
appearing as if it were melting away from the intense heat of the fire of separation within her.

"By these arrows made of flowers, he who is born of no other source pierces the hearts of women separated from their lovers"—as if saying this, she withers the flowers upon the ground of her service with the hot breaths of her sighs. (45)

She was staining [the ground] with the hot breaths of her sighs, as if desiring to create a sacrificial altar for the God of Love, while the falling teardrops— like washed collyrium— displayed the beauty of lines of syllables.

She bore the state of the god of love, which had attained an increase through the rising of the moon, which was like a heap of scattered pearls and whose new coral sprouts were the waves of the shore. ||47||
She was repeatedly emitting long columns of sighs, which seemed to grow stronger as they fell within her, stirred by the wind from the wings of Cupid’s flower-arrows,
causing the tips of her lofty breasts to tremble.

Bearing her bimba-like lower lip, which trembled as if out of fear of being scorched by the spreading spray of excessively hot vapors, and which was rendered utterly restless by the continuous flow of sighs; (49)
She bore her bimba-red lower lip, trembling as if in fear of being scorched by the spreading spray of excessively hot vapors, and exceedingly agitated by the continuous succession of her sighs. (50)

She had her face like a moon playfully upturned, as if she had attained the state of being a pearl through the falling of tears from her own ear-shells; she was seated upon a bed of white lotus garlands.
She seemed to extinguish the swarm of bees clinging to her with the essence of her fragrant breath— even as they hovered before her despite the heat of that breath—
by means of the spray-like water from the rays of her teeth flashing forth.
She was shaking her friends in that place with sighs of breath that were tawny with dust shaken from beds of creepers and clusters of lotuses,
as if those sighs were smeared with the intense passion residing within her heart.
Along with her garland of breast-ornaments she has reached a state of withering; along with the floods of tears falling from her eyes;
and along with the mental states of her circle of friends, she is consumed by the continuous succession of the torments of separation. ||54||
She bore a splendor that was delightful with the creeper-like eyebrows as its swarm of bees and the petals of her lips;
by means of the lotus-like radiance resting upon her face, she surpassed the orb of the moon at every glance.

Her face was distressed by the rising and falling of her long, intensely hot sighs, which were smeared with sandalwood powder that swelled playfully upon the tips of her breasts as they beat against one another. (56)
"Lest my life-breaths, tormented by the pain of separation, depart along with this sigh"—as if thinking thus, she quickly checked her throat with a suppression of tears. (57)

She was carrying away the drops of tears from her eyes—drops that had entered the path of her nostrils whose openings were wide with agitation—and which moved with a slow, rolling motion over her deeply sunken cheeks due to her emaciation. (58)
She bears a face marked by a gaze of vivid emptiness bound up with anxiety, its hollow cheeks resting upon her hands, and its forehead embraced by the lines of her knitted brows. (59)
She was drinking, as it were, the flow of tears that had reached her nostrils— cool with the fine dust of pearls from her necklace—
driven by the thirst born of the internal heat of the fire of separation.
Neglected by the swarms of bees that were her wandering glances, with her lotus-stalk-like arms cast aside,

she was like the lotus-pond of the elephant of Love, broken by the exceedingly sharp iron arrows that served as his tusks. (A Kulaka) Having started in alarm, the vine of her body bristling with horripilation, she gracefully—
Then, while her beloved’s arrival was being announced,
she somehow closed both her eyes— the lashes of which were made heavy by the droplets of tears of joy.
To cool, as it were, her lower lip— which was soiled by the heat of the breath and wind and heavy with a burning sensation—
she repeatedly shed cool teardrops that clung to it.
He caused them to fall, as they were clinging to the tips of his curved eyelashes.
Then, as if to wipe away the paleness caused by the application of the paste of beautiful sandalwood water,
her joy rose up as she immersed herself in the water of perspiration.
Her slender body, bristling with horripilation, sank [into the water]. ||64||
"What is to be done by you here, now that your beloved has arrived, while your slender body— its essence dried up by grief—
is smeared with thick sandalwood paste? Thus [the moon] seems to say.
It was manifested by rows of horripilation that had emerged. ||65||
When her beloved had departed, she, longing for his happiness, hurriedly wiped away the tears from her eyes;
yet it was clearly as if they were smeared with a fresh layer of collyrium.
He told her of the limit of their weeping.

Then, as her beloved approached— his body smeared with sandalwood paste broken by horripilation, fragments of lotus stalks falling away, wet with trickling water, and his necklace slipping loose— she [was overcome].
Together with her, she released ten beds made of lotus petals. ||67||
Then, as her lover closely embraced her, the pure pearl necklace released its pearls— pearls that had been dried by the heat of the fire of separation while they were being severed from the thread.
And the clusters of teardrops from her slender body were thin. ||68||
Alas, let it not happen that, due to the height [of our breasts], we fail to obtain the touch of our beloveds because our waists are made thin;
for they have been, as it were, bent into circles by the force of embracing them.
The breasts of the slender maiden instantly assumed a smallness.
Then, as the two youths— whose bodies were gradually becoming thick with horripilation—
attained a state of trepidation through their embrace after a long period of separation...
The construction of her entire body became thoroughly heated and very firm. ||70||
Thus, for the youths who had arrived upon hearing the sweet words of the messenger,
there occurred an unprecedented and praiseworthy moment, adorned with a profusion of horripilation,
as their beloveds were exhausted by the affliction of long-standing separation.
The necklace, marked with gems and pearls, its weight loosened by his firm embrace, was slipping down. ||71||

Thus ends the twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Resolve of the Messenger," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—whose pen-name is Vāgīśvara and whose other name is Vidyādhipati—and who was a dependent of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
The Twenty-eighth Canto:
Then, out of fear of the sun, upon the western mountain—the mirror for the orb of the moon—the lady Night...
When dawn had fallen, she departed elsewhere, bound by the jeweled chains of the crescent moons of her new bridegrooms' rows.
When the woman, distressed by the fever of impending separation from her beloved, made herself frantic with loud wails, the drum,
struck at the end of the night, produced a sound that was a fitting counterpart to the emptiness of her heart.
With her body reclining in the blissful sport of resting upon the pillow of her most beloved’s arms,
she who was naturally charming remained with her eyes closed for a moment, as if the night had indeed not yet passed.

Suddenly, with her moon-like face deprived of its luster and her gait faltering, the night— whose starry beauty was obscured by thin darkness— became like a spent day for those filled with longing, no longer conducive to love-making.
"O fair-limbed one, by the constant bending of your slender body, your waist is becoming thin.
Thus did the row of conch shells seem to speak in a low, warbling tone to her as she yawned.

Then, with the grace of a very firm embrace, a certain woman with arched brows caused her lover’s heart—its fortitude wounded by the impending separation—to meet with her own heart as if with great speed. (6)

In the morning, the cheeks of those with slender eyes shone in such a way— adorned with tilaka marks and leaf-patterns, marked by the gaze of their rivals' harsh eyes, yet bearing the signs of their beloveds— that they had never shone so before.

On the slope of the eastern mountain, the rays of the moon—whose darkness has ceased and who causes the lotuses to bloom—quickly shone upward as if clearly able to measure the entire orb of the sun that had vanished there. (8)

Vibrating across the surface of realization and turning the quarters of the sky tawny like owls, the twilight shone like a row of flame-tips from the fire of the breaths of serpents exhausted by pulling the chariot of the sun. 9.

At that time, at the end of the night, the sun ascended the peak of the mountain of sunrise; his rays, which dispel great distress, swiftly pervaded the quarters, and his long reins likewise spread out instantly. (10)

At dawn, the rays of the sun, radiant as the fire of universal destruction, assumed a fleshy thickness that was soiled by the stains of black aloe-wood incense; yet they cast forth the densest darkness, whose luster was darkened by the smearing of musk. 11.
In every direction, clusters of stars, possessing the hue of the saffron-colored twilight, descend;
they create the illusion of a multitude of drops of honey-dew falling from the calyx of the world-lotus. 12.

The twilight, like a mass of dust made formidable by a cloud of Chinese powder, attained the splendor of the trunk of the lordly elephant of the day, which was held aloft by a lotus stalk as white as a crescent moon. 13.
At dawn, the rising sun made the sky appear with rays that seemed like eyes blinking in various shades; and young men were seen by their beloveds as they turned their necks toward the lake. 14.
Then, in every direction, heaps of stars—whose light pierces the dense darkness—vanished, as if suddenly pierced by the emerging rays of the sun, like poorly cut gems. (15)
At dawn, when the sky— acting as a cooking vessel— contained the fire of the abundant, shimmering glow of twilight with the smoke-crests of darkness,
the clusters of stars momentarily assumed the beauty of parched grain being roasted in sparse quantities.

"I was not cast aside by the young woman, whose modesty had melted away with intoxication and who had her lover's garment taken from her"—thus, at dawn, the lamp, tossed by the wind, seemed to dance as if under the influence of passion. 17.

At the hour of dawn, throbbing with stainless radiance and spreading a yawn of awakening in every direction, she assumed a spotless splendor like a bed of lotuses, delightful with its far-reaching and vast fragrance. 18.
In every direction, bees hovering rapidly above out of greed to drink the nectar settled upon the night-lotuses, as if to ward off on all sides the touch of the sun’s rays. 19.
Even while intending to settle upon it, the swarm of bees approached the lotus from afar and remained there,
so that the young sun’s rays might not find an opportunity to quickly pierce through it.
The breeze, delightful with the exquisite fragrance of blossoming lotus buds, blew toward the water and stirred the heart of the lotus pond as if it were agitated by longing. (21)

Then the lotus-pond shone forth, possessing bees clever in their charming movements, with the wings of swans as its ornaments, and the beauty of clusters of hands joined by the most excellent men, like lotuses with shimmering, pure, and radiant stalks. 22.
As the skin of darkness was torn asunder from the sky by the impact of the staff-like rays of the sun,
something resembling blood appeared, seemingly bound together under the guise of the shimmering glow of the dawn’s reddish rays.
At dawn, the winds blew, turning the atmosphere tawny with the pollen from clusters of blooming white lotuses,
and bringing relief through their incessant crushing of the nail-marks upon the breasts of the beloveds of Death.
Then, struck by the assault of the sun’s rays and drenched with the tears of the night-water, the night-lily’s eye quickly closed, as if pained by a violent ailment. 25.
The sun rises with its orb of special decorative dots reddened at the edge of the eastern quarter,
while the surrounding darkness of night remains exceedingly dense, as black as a thicket of tamāla trees.
At that time, the mountain range of the Northern Mountain (Udaya), its peaks rendered clearly visible as the darkness of night was gradually dispelled,
appeared in every direction as if it were swiftly rising up from the midst of the ocean.
At dawn, the lotus-navel of the Enemy of Mura— seated in the bliss of reclining upon a bed that imitated the coils of the Lord of Serpents—
attained the splendor of a lake whose proud, blossoming white lotuses were trembling with swarms of bees.

Bearing a circle of sprout-like creepers formed by the rays of the sun, and possessing a beauty derived from the moon that had already set, the jewel of the day spread forth from the ocean of time upon the shore of the world with radiant splendor. 29.
At dawn, the bee— sighing as he withdrew from the closing water-lily, and rejoicing with a delighted heart at the opening lotus—
trembling before both, licked the flower which was overflowing with the dripping of sweet honey.

The orb of the sun, anointed with fresh saffron-paste, shone like the face of the Fortune of Day as she leaned out from the lattice-window on the peak of the Eastern Mountain, captivated by the curiosity to behold the world. 31.

Then at dawn, the lotus grove assumed the beauty of a forest of night-lilies, with bees released from their confinement as the petals were parted by the clear rays of the moon, whose joints had opened wide.

The bees, rendered helpless by the intoxication of honey, clung to the tips of the lotus petals— petals that were muddy with nectar trickling down from the weight of their eyelashes-like rows of filaments, which had been shaken by a gentle breeze.

At dawn, when the petals of the lotuses had fully opened and the circles of bees were humming, the sun did not merely break open the cups of the lotuses; he became the beautiful abode of Fortune’s splendor for the duration of the day.
At dawn, when the moon’s smoky orb was about to sink, the night-lilies—already clearly seized by agitation—trembled violently as they were gently stirred by the soft breeze. (35)
Beholding the white lotus in full bloom, the swarms of bees, drawn by their sweet thirst for honey, fell upon it with joy; and as they settled, they caused the rows of petals to tremble.
As long as their eyes were veiled by the pollen falling from the tips of their manes, which were trembling violently in the wind, they could not even see you standing right there;
yet that very sight slackens the attainment of the desired goal for those who are timid.
(37) [Yugma] [And so it was] within the interiors of the buds of lotuses, where the filaments were shaken by the bees whose anger was thwarted.
In every direction, the humming of bees, like lions, broke forth as they awoke from their sleep.
A swarm of bees abandoned the temple of the elephant's cheek, which was soiled by mud from his resting on the surface of the earth;
for nothing that is associated with the wicked is worthy of being served.
Then, scratching the surface of the earth with the tips of their hooves out of weariness from not finding even a blade of grass,
they quickly devoured the coarse fodder brought by the groom.
Descending very swiftly from the flagpole,
the peacocks with their tails reflected in the mirrors made the jeweled floors of the king’s palace appear as if they were suddenly composed of various kinds of gems.
The cock, its feet curled as it uttered a most distinct cry that was charming with continuous nasal resonance,
crowed incessantly, its neck and throat-tip quivering, bending, and rising.

The bees, confined within the narrow interior of that lotus which had fallen asleep upon being touched by the rays of the sun, caused its petals to burst open as they were shaken by their own bodies moving under the weight [of the flower]. (43)
Just as the night-lotus, awakening for a moment, suddenly became favorable for its upward leap;
indeed, what is there that is difficult to overcome for those who are united when they have fallen into the misery of despair?
(A pair of verses) May this Sun quickly liberate you, casting off the confinement within the interior of his mass of petals.
Thus, as he moved above the lotuses, the bee spoke to the honey-drinkers with sounds like the humming of bees. ||45||

The sun, dispelling the all-encompassing nocturnal darkness of the *dalitas* (the downtrodden) and bestowing upon the lotus-pond the excellence of its reflected beauty, quickly caused the lotus to turn upward with its full glory through the radiance of its blossoming petals. 46.

In every direction, birds whose bodies were being consumed on all sides by the spreading fire, and at that time the young wives, agitated by the desire to depart at dawn, both perished in the state of separation from their beloveds. 47.

Having dispelled the darkness that was as black as the throat of a young *khañjarīka* bird speckled with distinct spots, the thousand-rayed sun bore a beauty even more intense, appearing like the orb of a white lotus for the circle of the three worlds. 48.
The balconies of the palace, adorned with statues of women carved from moonstones,
instantly withered as if out of grief when the moon fell, struck by the rays of the sun.

In the sky, the disc of the moon had lost its luster; on the water, the reflection was indistinguishable from it—both failing to cause the night-lotuses to bloom, both having dispelled the darkness nearby, and both causing the day-lotuses to close. (50)

The lotus pond, with its mass of spray from the wine-like rays of the shimmering, reddish sun reflected within the interiors of shells of blossoming gems, trembled as if overcome by intoxication due to the onset of the morning breeze. (51)
Moving swiftly over the lotus pond, the swarm of bees shone forth from the bed of night-lotuses, like the night itself fleeing in fear of the sun, grey with the spreading gloom of darkness. ||52||

Having mounted his chariot-boat, which was bound with chains of formidable serpents, he approached the sky-ocean as if he were a ship-merchant clearly desiring to seize the multitude of planetary jewels. ||53||
The forest floor was occupied by birds that bore the heat of being scorched by the clearly manifest fire of passion;
it offered a state of existence through the longings of the minds of the celestial women as they proceeded toward their gratification.
Having quickly driven away the night that had arrived elsewhere,
the sky long bore the moon-like face of the sun as it bent low at dawn, as if in anger, unable to endure its gaze.
Beholding the sun delighted, the moon— fearing the touch of the tips of its shimmering rays—
seemed to hasten toward the sunset mountain, as if holding the night in his lap under the guise of the clearly visible deer-mark.
In the forest of the three worlds, the cluster of blossoms that was the moon— its form already severed by the falling axe-strokes of the harsh rays of the sun—
gradually withered away like a honey-scented bee clinging to a night-creeper.
"O Sun, do not overwhelm my moon by casting aside this most beloved light of yours!
Thus did the Night-lily, her beauty manifesting in the form of folded hands like buds, entreat him as if with great sorrow. (58)
At dawn, the swarm of bees, blinded by their longing for honey as they hovered above the lotuses, fashioned, as it were, a garland of blue water-lilies for her beloved Sun nearby. (59)

At the end of the night, the grove of night-lotuses, as if having attained happiness through the sounds of lutes accompanied by clear and sweet melodies and the humming of swarms of bees, entered into sleep.
The dark row of bees, occupying the central space of the region beside the lotus bud, bore the manifest splendor of a dark line on a vessel made of green gems. (61)

The darkness, having filled the spaces of the quarters of the sky with a tawny hue at nightfall, did not fill those same spaces with the rays of the sun; alas, for the power of that which is impure is indeed greater.
"O you who have come from another land at night, you who have displayed passion elsewhere, are you not ashamed that you touch me with your rays now?
Abandon me! To whom do you belong?"—thus she spoke, remembering the rebuke she had received at the end of the day.
Having fashioned a lotus with trembling bees as its petals and lovely sprouts as its hands, the lotus-plant, as if full of jealousy and anger, spoke thus to the sun through the humming of the bees:
"Like the autumn season, she possesses the grace of the day's arrival and is endowed with beauty through her total radiance. (Yugalaka) 64.1–2.
Having washed away the impurity of darkness, she quickly led the quarters of the sky to a state of radiant clarity, like rivers reaching the sea. ||65||
As if unable to endure the touch of the sun immediately due to its innate purity,
the night-lotuses in every direction have closed up and now touch him with their reddened petals from afar.

At that time, the serpent-like night—whose venom was the mass of darkness being crushed by the staff of the sun’s first rays, and which was adorned with the jewels of the host of planets—had shed its slough of moonbeams. (67)
Reflected in the water, the sun— angry at the lotus plant for the offense of breaking its day-long vow—
fell at the base of her lotus-feet, whose toes were reddened petals, as if out of a desire to appease her.
"The moon’s orb has fallen! Alas, why is the host of stars no longer seen in the sky?
Thus did the night lament, as it were, with the humming of bees trapped within its buds in the lily groves. (69)
At dawn, the garlanded one with rays, possessing the beautiful and lofty red crests of his flames,
shone intensely in the city of the Lord of the Gods as if with a splendor consisting of pure light, having caused the lotuses to bloom.

Then, in every direction, the darknesses—acting like wild buffaloes in the lake of the sky—were scattered by the rays of the sun’s cresting red beams, which were as lovely as streaks of molten gold; thus, the darkness stumbled away.
Desiring at once to cross the ocean of the sky, variegated with the jewels of the planets,
the summer-rayed sun stretched out his arms of rays far in every direction, as if out of a passion for swimming.

Then, struck by the rays of the sun, the lotus-face of the river Kuśeśayinī assumed a coppery luster; though devoid of the intoxication of honey and lacking the smile of its rows of teeth, it shone with a radiant glow.
At dawn, the sun-god, with the tips of his rays, instantly made the mirror of the three worlds—cleansed of the mire of dense darkness—fit for observation. 74.

When the moon attained its state of fullness, the bed of night-lotuses was separated from its beauty, the owl, overcome by excessive distress, abandoned its joy, and the multitude of stars suddenly met their destruction. 75.

Bearing a palate of throbbing, reddish *palāśa* petals and having attained the fragrance of fresh clouds, the lovely lotus-face of the lotus-pond yawned, its teeth of filaments becoming clearly visible as it awakened from sleep. (76)
At that time, the lotus pond, its beauty enhanced by the heavy rhythmic beat of the swaying kalahaṃsa birds, became agitated by swarms of bees as they yearned for the abundant nectar;
it was as if the pond were overwhelmed by the weight of a great dance performed in every direction.
When the sun was clinging to the tips of the blossoming copper-hued petals out of greed for drinking the nectar,
the lotus-eyed bee bore away the splendor of the lotus, as if it were a sidelong glance cast by her.
Then, at dawn, the orb of the moon—its beauty fading and its spots clearly manifest—became like the center of the great ocean agitated by the onset of the winds of the time of destruction. 79.
Upon the altar-like peak of the mountain of sunrise, the solar disc, possessing a luster as red as fresh blood, lay upon a vast bed of the womb that brought forth the beauty of the day’s arrival. 80.
The splendor of the day bore a face whose forehead-mark was anointed with a fresh application of Chinese-silk paste, which eclipsed the luster of the moon; its lotus-eyes were shimmering. (81)

At dawn, the distant path through the clouds was variegated by the floating mud of dispelled darkness, as was the row of honey-drinking bees in the lotus grove, whose humming was intensified by their contact with the morning heat.

Washed by the canopy of shimmering rays from the sun, whose brilliance was intensified within by the dense flames of fire, the day gradually attained a state of extreme purity on all sides, like a garment cleansed by fire.

In every direction, as if desiring to offer with her essence the lotus-stalks that served as the footstool for the Lord of Day, she shone forth, extending her cupped hands of lotuses, ruddy with fresh sprouts. (84)
When the sun had risen, the lordly elephant of the western mountain spread its splendor with the rays of the moon, which were as white as clusters of night-lotuses,
as if it were smeared with a profusion of radiant ashes.
At dawn, as if startled by the grief of separation from his preceptor, the moon wiped away with his rays the teardrops of dew from the lotus-lake,
using the spaces between his own large-petaled eyes.

At dawn, the sun bore a splendor like that of an elephant with its temples split by rut-fluid; its vast beauty was slightly curved as it was broken by the impact of the quivering rays of the dawn-red sun.

As they muttered prayers in every direction, their mouths—with rows of teeth as pale-red as the radiance of the rising sun—attained a beauty that seemed like a passion for betel leaves, though such was entirely unseemly even for their ascetic vow. (88)

When the thousand-rayed sun had ascended the eastern mountain, the fresh, tawny splendor of day’s arrival imitated a drinking party, with its lovely cups being the shimmering, fresh lotus stalks. (89)

In every direction, rows of mansions were seen, marked by intoxicated elephants belonging to rival lords and illuminated by the circles of manifest thunderbolt-like weapons, imitating the ground of a battlefield. (90)
The ten directions, having become stained by the defect of contact with the dust raised by those who had not yet been tamed,
were driven far away by the sun, which, with its throbbing ruddy luster, seemed as if in anger.
Then, having risen over the mountain of sunrise, the sun, desiring to dispel the darkness of night,
made all directions obstructed as if by forest fires with his rays throbbing with crimson glow.
The darkness, struck by the rays of the sun which had completely consumed the host of planets,
departed from the path of the sky like a cluster of blue lotuses driven away by a mountain torrent.
Like the daughter of the mountain (Pārvatī), her hopes fulfilled by the sounds of beaten, unrestrained drums, the grace of the twilight bore the joy of the arrival of the new day. 94.

At the end of the night, the sky became manifest as it revealed the quarters of space by dispelling the mass of darkness; simultaneously, the clusters of lotuses began to open their petals, and the rays of the sun, the dispeller of cold, suddenly fell upon them. 95.
In every direction, during the night, the sun shattered the unrestrained darkness gathered by the tips of his rays;
for one who possesses great luster cannot endure even for a moment the bold presence of an adversary before him.

In every direction, the lotus-pools took on the splendor of villages inhabited by the Śabara hunters that are the bees; these pools were houses of lotuses whose clearly visible palāśa-panels were secured by the bolts of their dense, throbbing filaments. 97.
Gazing with intense anger at his body marked by fresh nail-scratches from their lovers, their eyes became bloodshot; surely the fire of the God of Love’s prowess dwells there within them. 98.

With the beautiful interior of her chest made white by the rays of her pupils falling as she trembles with emotion, another woman seems to hasten like a circle of eyes, desiring to instill a state of moisture with passion. 99.

As if unable to contain the expansion of the flow of nectar entering her heart through the intensity of its blossoming, the row of her eyelashes, though slowed by being weighed down by the excessive burden of that rasa, draws back even further. 100.
Even as Tāraka proceeds with some difficulty along his long, sidelong path, her radiance suddenly surges before him; it seems he is unable to endure it for even a moment.
Thus, as her soul expanded through the throbbing longing to behold her beloved,

the beauty of the young woman’s pair of eyes— tremulous from the arrows of Love and shimmering with passion— blossomed forth. (Cakkalakam) When the sound of loud trumpets reached the path of her ears, the fickle-eyed girl displayed the splendor of her blossoming [beauty].
Her pair of eyes attained the beauty of the Yadu clan, being delightful through their novelty, darkness, and whiteness.

From the cheek of the lotus-eyed woman, which was heavy with the weight of intoxication, the decorative patterns of aguru paste fell away, broken by the incessant flow of thick tears; indeed, how can there be long-lasting stability for that which is already soiled? 104.

Having attained at dawn a splendor that was not previously possessed and yet did not abandon its former beauty, the cakravāka birds indeed rejoiced exceedingly, as if having found a true friendship. 105.
The ruddy goose consumed the juice of the white lotus stalks, drawn up with its wide-open beak,
as if they were somehow the digits of the moon fallen from the vault of heaven due to his anger at being separated from her.

Approaching with impetuous motion the lotus bud caught on the tip of the wide-open beak of a female ruddy goose in the lake, the male ruddy goose pulled it away like a probe of the pain of separation from his heart. (107)
The ruddy goose (koka) pulled out the web of fibers from the half-eaten lotus stalk of his beloved of the night, which had been severed at the tip by his beak,
fearing the great moon that was hidden within it.
Like the wheel of a potter's hand within the hollows of the kiln, so it was for the enraged Moon. ||108||

The tips of their prominent pericarps were jagged and raised, with their edges bitten by the points of filaments whose petals and sheaths had fallen away; their green luster was shattered by the rays of the sun.
The stalks of the lotus buds expanded their petals like nets.
The swan, whose copper-colored feet find their resting place upon the surrounding lotus-beds of the quarters, bestows his radiance upon the blossoming lilies;
he is like the stalk of a lotus-root for the full orb of the moon.
He slowly pulled out the network of cords from his hand from the fragment.
With its body half-bent down and half-raised out of fear at the sudden impact, shaking off its rows of feathers through its steady,
measured steps, it descended from its perch while uttering loud cries.
The fire from the fortress, distressing the women who were already afflicted by separation, [spread abroad]. ||111||
Rising quickly from her bed, desiring to depart, she pressed against her garment as she panted, her hips visible;
while her husband looked on, his eyes half-closed.
It is said that out of shame, the eye of the cakora bird fell upon the leper.
On the slope of her hips, where the intense pain caused by the marks of her fingernails was present, the beautiful-eyed woman did not fasten a girdle;
rather, the row of her own footprints became her supreme ornament.
But on that mountain, rugged with golden rocks, there was then—113.
Drawing back her earlobe with one lotus-like hand— her eye fixed upon her beloved—
and failing to find a joint with the other, the woman stood still.
She was tossing her ruby earrings to and fro.

Standing at the door, her form half-concealed by the single wooden panel of the door-swing, the young bride possessed the beauty of the Daughter of the Mountain; with one pupil motionless, she gazed upon her beloved.
Another woman gazed at him as he went, with her eyes whose lashes were bent down.
Whirling far around the region of the breasts,
stumbling slightly at the slender waist,
and obstructed by the expansive curve of the hips, the breezes blew upon the young women.
The morning breezes dispel the exhaustion born of the passion of lovemaking.
By the bees that had been confined within the hollows of the dense bud-cottages of the fragrant *saugandhika* lotuses—
their petal-seals having burst open—
and which now resembled evening clouds at the time of sunrise;
The orb of the hot-rayed sun, youthful and possessing the luster of a ruby.

[The mountain] is rendered tawny by the splashing of the shimmering, golden light of the sun; it is charming with the illusion of sweet honey-dripping caused by clusters of thick, dripping drops of night-mist;
and its mouths are resonant with the tumultuous clamor begun in excitement as [bees] enter through the openings of the leaves.
The clusters of lotuses shone, filled with swarms of bees that had attained joy. ||118||
As if undergoing a state of thinness like that of water due to the calamity of the moon’s fall, gradually manifesting the quarters of the sky and displaying the smiles of blooming lotuses,
the rays of the sun spread across the firmament, which was once densely packed with masses of most intense darkness.
The rays of the sun, possessing a luster as beautiful as freshly squeezed lac-dye, streamed forth, spreading far and wide.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth canto, titled "The Description of Dawn," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
The Twenty-ninth Canto:
While the sun had risen clearly, its rays as rosy as shimmering young sprouts, [the attendants] performed their morning rites upon waking.
With voices of great sweetness, their articulation flawless and elegant, they approached the Lord, the Guru of the great ones.
Let the sun release his bed;
with rays as red as coral crushed by his hands, he makes the mountain of sunrise appear clearly as if it were made of rubies, shimmering in succession.
In your palaces, these statues carved from sapphire, struck by the brilliant light of the sun,
seem to be giving birth to young sons of the Sun-god under the guise of the mass of sparks of fire flashing forth from their wide-open eyes— sparks that dispel the darkness.

This lotus, its stalk quivering with the breezes from the mountain slopes, seemed like the eye of the Goddess of the Lotus, opening to announce: "In this very moment, you shall have a reunion with your most beloved, the Sun."
The rays of Vivasvat, which dispel the darkness of night and possess a brilliance as pale-red as a blooming hibiscus flower,
shine in the sky like streaks of golden ochre upon a floor of black gemstone slabs.
When the sun had risen and dispelled the mass of darkness, people, overcome with excitement, offered their sight to him;
yet when the moon sought to leave its path in the sky, it did not fall from its station, for it does not become an object of veneration merely by its descent.
Then, when the sun, the stone of the mountain of sunrise, touched that [world] with its mass of rays,
the surface of the sky appeared turned tawny by the twilight, which possessed the luster of fire arising from it.

The face of the Fortune of Day, streaked with the deep crimson glow of dense, thick rows of clouds, shines resplendent as if bearing a cluster of blossoms fashioned from the brilliance of freshly applied saffron. (8)
Unable to sustain its splendor, like the light of the moon when its brilliance is struck down by frost, the night now enters the mountain caves with its vast stars closed away. 9.
When the night finally arrived, how it was passed by him, distraught at the unfolding of separation from her!
