Yet, when his most beloved is thus beheld, she brings such joy that she does not cause distress even to the bird separated from its mate during the night. ||10||
Just as the moon, about to fall behind the western mountain with its moonlight shattered by the rays of the new sun,

clearly brings about the arising of even greater happiness from the calamity that has befallen its enemy— its own wealth— so too [does this happen]. (A pair of verses) At the onset of night, the fresh nail-marks upon the breasts of the deer-eyed women, afflicted by love, were newly applied.
The fresh sunlight, falling upon the circle of her cheeks, does not surpass the exceedingly lovely glow of her natural complexion.

As if with the intent of quickly seizing the honey flowing from the wombs of the quarters in every direction, the lotuses, by means of the guise of their massed petals, mutually extend their circles of coral-bead oyster shells. 13.
This ground, bitten by the tips of fresh kuśa grass and drenched by a spray of nocturnal dew-drops,
creates the illusion of blossoming pale-white flowers as it trembles under the weight of those who are reeling from the elixir of immortality.

These peacocks, drenched by the waters of the night, illuminate the quarters with their circles of tail-feathers offered as oblations—circles that shine like hundreds of manifest celestial weapons under the guise of the moonbeams streaming forth from the clouds. 15.

These lamps of your palace, possessing a brilliance so pale as if scorched by the fire of the gazelle-eyed women’s sighs, bear a resemblance clearly manifested upon the surface of their white-washed cheeks. 16.
The one whose eyes are covered with lotus pollen does not behold his beloved who has approached;
alas, for the wretched man of fate, even happiness that has arrived after a long time undoubtedly goes far away. 17.
Hearing the pained sound of the drum signaling the end of the night,
lovers who had slept for a moment longer now close their eyes, which remain reddened from staying awake during the passion of love-making.
Not considering the distress born of separation at dawn, the young woman accepted his conciliation;
she did not fail her friend who was eager to depart, nor was she pained—for how could there be happiness for those who do not foresee the consequences? (19)
"The night is not yet over; let us linger. Do not delay again when he arrives.
Thus, with tears flowing from her eyes, the lover's words cause the heart of the longing woman to falter as she thinks of her departed beloved. 20.
Though she was suddenly awakened by the sounds of drums signaling the end of the night,
the longing woman, even as she desired to reach the embrace of her beloved, did not loosen the cage of her arms.
Now, at dawn, the houses are being barred to prevent those who cannot endure the grief born of separation from departing;
yet, with the loud creaking of their open and exposed door-panels, they seem to be urging the departure of the lady with arched brows.

There, descending from the sky, the multitude of planets shines upon the mountain of the setting sun, having momentarily formed a cluster within the forest-trees of the rugged slopes of the western horizon,
possessing the beauty of a clearly visible circle of bird-eggs.

These rays of the sun, risen with the dawn, shine forth: they are like new golden girdles upon the maiden of the quarters; they possess the brilliance of the submarine fire in the ocean of the sky; and their sharp points are like thunderbolts that cleave the mountain of dense darkness. 24.
With the playful charm of a firm embrace upon her broad orb-like chest,
this cool-rayed moon bears, under the guise of the hare, a cluster of fresh leaves and sprigs of dark aloe-wood from her lofty breasts.
Furthermore, the moon, rising clearly once more, will dispel that previous affliction of bondage for you;
therefore, let it wait until then, and do not feel even the slightest grief that destroys your great splendor.

When the moon has lost its luster and fled into the abyss of the setting mountain, this [moon] seems to console the night-lily as if it were a woman, using the guise of the humming bees as its dark spot. (A pair of verses) The night-lily, with bees settled within it due to the clear loss of honey, is like a heart whose bees have hidden away because of the manifest loss of wealth. He bears [the earth], grey from the burning of hundreds of crests of flames blazing with the fever of separation from the sun.

Now these women of the quarters, devoid of moonlight and the application of sandalwood paste, their jeweled girdles lacking the host of stars, possess a beauty like that of women whose hair is disheveled by the moonless night. (29)
As if desiring to quickly protect the moonlight dwelling within her belly from the assault of the sun’s rays,
this night-lily here closes its petals, forming a tightly sealed enclosure.

O bearer of the moon, for him who drank copiously of honey with his beloved every night and slept upon beds of lotus petals, the binding together with the night-lily is now truly fitting, as their life-sustaining essence has been consumed. 31.

Thus, the bee, rendered unconscious by intoxication from drinking your sweet nectar within the hollow of a lotus bud, will now clearly awaken, having gradually become unaware of the pain of its confinement. (32)
Having emerged from a grove of night-lotuses, he bore a body disfigured by the pollen of blooming ketakī flowers;
he was pale white, as if bathed by hundreds of flashes of moonlight shimmering within his belly, like a swarm of bees.
This radiant splendor, shattered in every direction by the striking of the chisel-like rays of the rising sun,
falls away like the distinct form of King [Rāvaṇa], whose body was cast down upon the mountain of sunset by the illusion of the sun.

O Lord of the Gods, when the darkness of the moon, overwhelmed with fear by the impact of the rising rays of the sun, flees under the guise of the hare-mark, it seems as if it remains together with its adversary; for how can there be mutual hostility between two who are in a state of calamity? ||35||
Now that the sky has become like a gaming board, its surface variegated by the clearly visible and slightly curved stars,
the moon and the sun— seated respectively upon the seats of the eastern and western mountains— seem to engage in a game of dice.
Just as the circle of sunbeams, fierce in piercing the petals of the lotus, begins to shine forth, so too the sky appears as if it were rising up, casting aside the mass of accumulated darkness. 37.

Having perceived the delusion that "my body has fallen below" as it was being reflected in the water at the edge of the mountain by the Moon— who himself bore that very same delusion— the Moon then descends from heaven as if desiring to seize that reflection.

Now, O Bhava, this lotus of your abode bears a splendor that is both beautiful and mingled with impurity, like the goddess of the ocean’s waters reeling from the violent impact of a mountain-like blow. (39)
O Lord, having gone from the quarter of Indra, you now desire to proceed in due course to this region of Varuṇa;
the lotus-pond proclaims your arrival, O Master, as if with the humming of swarms of bees in a great assembly. 40.
The bee, having been held for a moment like a half-fallen chain by his foot— which was as delicate as a lotus petal—
now glides away swiftly with its bond released, yet still clinging to him from contact with the honey.
As if from the long process of beholding her lord without blinking, this lotus-plant bears its blossomed lotus-eye, dripping with thick streams of tears, drenched by the waters of the night. 42.

These arrows, at dawn, now perfume the quarters of the sky with sprays of nectar from the clusters of full-blown kunda flowers clinging to their bodies, as they spread the wind from their fluttering feathers. 43.

Now, from the lotus—the very glory of the lake, adorned with shimmering minnows and accompanied by swarms of hovering bees—the sun, with his mass of rays, draws away the moonstone pillar that mimicked its dark luster. (44)

O Lord, now the Maker of Light delights the lotus-lady, who possesses charming smiles and laughter, whose lotus-eyes are clearly manifest with trickling tears, and who has now assumed a state of amorous agitation (kilakiñcita). 45.
Eager for love-play, the intoxicatingly beautiful woman, her thick breasts pressed against his chest, stretches out her vine-like arms which she wraps firmly around the neck of her most beloved. 46.
"How could your girdle possibly reach your hips, which are so swollen with the particular intoxication of the festival of love?
Thus speaking loudly at dawn, the parrot causes the fair-browed woman to laugh. (47)
Nowhere have I seen such lightness in the playful grace and movement of her body’s glances;
it is as if the girdle, fastened to the circle of her hips, speaks sweetly through its tinkling sounds.
Having passed the night together with her lover, she who stumbles repeatedly as dawn approaches sets out;
anxious for him and her fortitude gone, the young woman gazes at every moment with her neck turned back. 49.
Rising from his bed, his broad flanks struck by the spray of the dust of the earth,
Lakṣmaṇa’s elder brother bore a splendor like that of another elephant, intoxicated by the rut of the Dānavas.
The sunbeams, rising from the interior of the dwelling of the clouds, make the day fragrant;
these particles of dust, struck by the rays of the sun, fall in every direction throughout the day like swarms of planets.
Sarojinī bore within her heart, as it were, the sun reflected upon her waters and resting upon her banks;
yet she was not satisfied by that stream of nectar arising from the blossomed lotuses. ||52||
This row of bees, drawn by the flowers on the upper terraces of the mansions scattered across the broad streets,
approaches like a circle of kinsmen drawn by the darkness of night.
He laments for the monkeys whose lives have been destroyed with piercing cries. ||53||
His form is seated upon a golden throne with a lotus pericarp, while a swarm of bees, drawn by their attachment to drinking the nectar of his own lotus filaments,
hovers incessantly above him.
O Lord, Lakṣmī seems to be teaching [the world] the nature of instability. ||54||
The swarm of bees shines, clinging to the drinking of the nectar of the red lotuses from which sleep and languor have been abandoned,
as if by the Lord of a Hundred Sacrifices who had dwelt there upon a stalk of lotus fiber.
The embryo was like a thousand eyes cast away. ||55||
The sunset mountain bears upon its head the wives of the stars, who are the harem-ladies of the moon as he desires to depart for another world, distressed by the fierce heat of the sun.
For those of lofty spirit, this alone is certainly accumulated. ||56||
Surely the conch shell, though its resonance culminates in a piercing sound, pains the hearts of the virtuous when it cries out in distress at separation;
for it clearly manifests its own external purity even as it proclaims it.
Alas, from whose heart, so exceedingly crooked, can there be peace? ||57||
Now, for those lotus-eyed women dwelling near the outskirts who are distressed by the fierce fever of separation from their beloveds,
the cry of the crane is like a stroke of lightning to the ear.
Cutting into the vital organs with a piercing *karakara* sound as it fell upon her. ||58||
As her beloved embraced her without her having first asked for it,
her full-bodied eyes were veiled by a flood of tears; then, the two hands of that woman, whose body was trembling with passion, were turned into cymbals for the lute of Love’s dance.
O Lord, the breasts of the deer-eyed woman momentarily assume the grace of the *līlā* lotus. ||59||
Playfully touching their bimba-like lips with the tips of their fingers, which are as tender as lotuses, they produce sweet hissing sounds caused by the swelling produced by the fresh bites.
Now these beloved women depart from the presence of their lovers.

Do the throngs of celestial women sing of you, O Moon, as you perform your manifold amorous play with your eyebrows, while the lutes with their unimpeded resonance are struck? Or do they sing of the Lord of Men?
At the time of dawn on Mount Maule, your [song] was in the *bhinna-ṣaḍja* mode.
The bees, their wings fluttering in flight, drank with unquenchable longing from the very sky— the direction of joy—
as it rose from the large, orb-like lotuses formed by the blossoming mass of petals.
The wind scatters the pollen of nectar high aloft.

Having heard these words, he whose crest was the incomplete moon bore upon the surface of his neck a distinct mark— the imprint of the jeweled necklace formed by the interlocking embrace of his beloved’s arms.
He abandoned the golden couch, which was marked by fragrant perfumes. ||63||

Thus ends the twenty-ninth canto, titled "The Awakening of the Blessed One," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked with jewels, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
The Thirtieth Canto:
In this manner, the playful enjoyment of the impassioned moon—
The jeweled bells of the necklace, severed from the night,
were being made to resemble the clusters of stars gathered along the path of the peak of the western mountain.
In the lotus ponds that were slowly blooming, where the filaments were beautiful with the feet of swarms of bees clinging out of greed for the trickling droplets of honey, during the summer heat—
The joints and connections of the circle of its petals were split open by the rays of light.
In the reservoirs of water where the tips of the filaments of white lotuses were struck by the morning breeze,
[the swans] cast off their limbs as they stirred from sleep.
In that mass of dust, which possessed the splendor of the fragrance of the bride Lakṣmī.
Like Śailāli, Kālamusala, having worshipped the feet of Mṛgāṅka, reveals the beauty of the face’s color during the day through the process of manifesting all its distinct qualities.
The crest-jewel ascended to the path of Dhruva’s abode. (A circular verse) By him,
as he was flying up toward the sky, there was seen the broad orb of the moon, its markings clearly visible, situated at the zenith.
He appeared as if being seated in the midst of a mass of pavilions white as the petals of a blooming kunda flower by the serpent Kāliya. ||5||
He beheld a fragment of cloud, not very large, lingering in the sky with a continuous flash of lightning;
its neck possessed a luster reddened by blood visible through its sighs.
Like a great fish cutting through the water, he severed that which was mired in the mud.
The masses of banner-cloths at the tips of their crests were torn asunder by the friction of leafy ends tossed and entangled with one another;
and the half-moons [ornaments] slipped from their peaks as they were being uprooted.
The tops of their golden archways were inlaid with the luster of jewels.
Struck by his arrow, which possessed the speed of the wind, the hosts of gods and *siddhas* in their celestial chariots quickly fled in all directions;
the triple city appeared as if set ablaze by the fire of that arrow.
Bearing a multitude of various shifting forms, (this pair of verses:
those who had taken up residence in his hair for a moment, possessing a luster as dark as collyrium, appeared like assassins of Kaṃsa.
The clouds became encircled by flashes of lightning that were doubled in brilliance by the rays of light from the jewel on his crown. ||9||
As he suddenly rose at the boundary of the path through the forest,
his ear-tip assumed an unsteady splendor,
like a heart split by a turban as it clings to a thundercloud.
[It was] possessed of a cluster of gold as formidable as lightning.
In the sky, his orb of a face was followed by a thousand crests of fire from his tawny, upward-gazing eyes;
[he was] with a mass of water, due to the turning of the wind arising from his movement.
With a fragment of a cloud, like a flash of lightning at its tip. ||11||
For a moment, the sky was filled with the river as it moved against him, its waters tossed by the wind of his motion;
it dimmed the brilliance of the sun’s orb and rendered its upward radiance pale.
As if out of fear of being dried up by the heat of the fire from his eye, the Gaṅgā [remained afar]. ||12||
At that time, he made the garment of the sky— the Ganges, white as the falling moon— slip from its waistband of stars;
he loosened the broad sash of the firmament, which was like a cloudless moon.
His thirst was fixed upon kissing various lotus-like faces. ||13||

The year passed for him as it was carried away by the deep, high-pitched, and sweet resonances of the circles of bamboo thickets on the slopes of the Himalayan mountains, whose hollows were filled by gentle breezes.
The rows of horses, with their ears pricked up, resembled the poles of a boat.
He beheld again and again Mount Kailāsa, the sole refuge of the three worlds, its circular rim of eyelashes spread wide like a blossoming golden kalpavallī creeper.
It was the white lotus of Lakṣmī’s graceful play, ever-present. ||15||
[He beheld] the Bhagirathi, whose seven horses were steady and swift, adorned by a circle of chowries as white as a mass of foam,
like the pole of the chariot of the Sun.
Having beheld him on Mount Ekapiṅgala, he joyfully paid him homage. ||16||
By that [sound], the sky was made resonant with the stumbling, clattering, and jingling of thousands of formidable, massive trunks resembling the peaks of Mount Kailāsa,
as they moved toward the lotus feet of Viṣṇu, who had descended to slay Kaiṭabha.
The daughter of Jahnu appeared like the celestial Gaṅgā, shimmering with the brilliance of her moving nails.
He beheld that path along the shore, delightful with the laughter of the ear-ornaments falling from the maidens of Kubera as they bathed,
resembling the breaking waves upon the waters of the expansive Lake Mānasa.
Its waters, with golden sands, have their spray scattered abroad. ||18||
He beheld the Acchoda lake, its waters turned tawny by the pollen of golden lotuses shaken by the wind and tossed upon the waves— waters that had been trodden by the feet of the celestial damsels.
The surface of its rocky slopes was marked with lines of red lac.
As if with the intent of adorning the necks of the Daityas of the Kaśyapa lineage who were intent on propitiating her,
the goddess Caṇḍī was being offered [gems] from the peaks of the jeweled caves that serve as his temples.
The bells hanging from the wide-spread archways resound.
Then, the radiance of his massive sapphire peaks,
which illuminated the entire expanse of the quarters,
suddenly intensified as if desiring to ascend further along the path of the sun.
He beheld [the river] like the loosened locks of hair from Mount Mekala.
(A pair of verses) Its thousands of clusters of waves were shattered by the agitation caused against the surface of the jar-like breasts of the Śabara women immersed in its playful sport.
Having beheld the Revā river, whose banks were adorned with groves of *sarala*, *vañjula*, and *jambū* trees, he took his delight. ||22||
Then, as he embraced her neck with affection, he beheld her who was like the beauty of the Vindhya mountains, girdled by the radiant jewels of Maṇiśikha,
and possessing the broad, full, rounded hips of the river Revā.
It was like a garment that had slipped off and remained clinging to his broad feet. ||23||

He beheld the beloved of Varuṇa’s abode, possessing the beauty of dark blue water-garments agitated by the restless wind, with clusters of *tāla* trees grown upon its banks and surrounded by groves of *tamāla*.
Like the daughter of Kalinda [the Yamunā], as if with the intent of a playful rendezvous.

He beheld Mahendra, who, as if through skill in service, was creating a multitude of clusters of smoke-pennants from the abundant incense of black aguru burnt by forest fires— smoke that was no small amount.
The fragrant silken garments of the wish-fulfilling trees belonging to the gods.
He beheld the river Lāṅgūlinī, its banks lined with floating masses of water where the waves were sparse and broken, and which was white with clearly visible foam.
Like a cow that has come within the range of his feet. ||26||
Beholding the rows of trees in the forests of the Sahya mountains, adorned with garlands of blooming clove flowers,
he took great delight in them as they were rubbed by the temples of the celestial elephants.
The clusters of *sarala* and *tāla* trees were broken down by their playful movements. ||27||
He beheld her wearing as ear-ornaments the abundance of her own flowers, which were being woven by her friends— the creepers of the clusters of trees on the blossoming banks—
and which possessed the dark luster of bees. She bore those waves...
Thereafter, she beheld the Bhīmarathī river, which was like a creeping vine of dark reeds. ||28||
The Godāvarī river, whose foam-like laughter is the radiance doubled by the luster of the pearl necklaces resting upon the jar-like breasts of brides with wet locks,
and which is frequented by flocks of cakora birds eager for its water— [may that river protect you].
She saw the water, shimmering and agitated, kissed by the tips of the beaks. ||29||
The Veṇā river, whose middle reaches are crowded with a multitude of nāga families surging like waves upon their thousand hoods formidable with glistening spray,
and whose palate is exceedingly deep with shimmering darkness—
He beheld its base, which resembled the surface of the netherworld.
The waters of the Pāriyātra mountain ranges followed his tracks along the paths of the ridges, their depths cooled by clusters of coconut fruits from the groves on the riverbanks that he had enjoyed.
They constructed dwellings on the mountain for the sake of the pleasure of enjoyment.
And by him, the water of the Kāverī was observed, formidable with the cries of kurarī cranes tossing about in the waves of water struck by the impetuous leaps of schools of fish;
and it bore that [water].
Its banks and marshes were crowded with flocks of fearless cranes.

The group of women from the city, traveling with his army, moved gracefully along the path on the sandy banks of the Carmaṇvatī, their cheeks made charming by smiles that were gradually becoming visible. His captivating...
He had his ears filled with the warbling from the throat of a myna bird. ||33||

For him who has taken up residence on its banks, the breezes from the ripples of the Siprā— capable of setting in motion the rhythmic dance of the broad leaves upon the trunks of the groves of palmyra trees— are like the attendants of the women of his retinue.
They abandoned the pain from the wounds on their full breasts during acts of love. ||34||
He took delight in this mountain, Mṛkṣavat, which possessed the splendor of a dwelling on the surface of the earth and was even more magnificent than Himavat;
for he had bound his feet to the ground for only a few days.
Remaining there, his vision was as if stolen by darkness, like that of one at night. ||35||
He proceeded toward the vast camp on Mount Suvela,
which was strewn with fragments of golden stone and [echoed with] the breaking waves of the ocean tossing upon the shore.
He beheld it from afar like the submarine fire overturned. ||36||
By him was beheld [her face], rich with clearly ripened *bhallātaka* fruits appearing like swellings upon the surface of her cheeks,
and fragrant with fresh sandalwood pieces that perfumed the nostrils.
The beauty of the forests on the Malaya mountains is pure and delights the heart. ||37||
The foot of the Malaya mountain— the abode of Lakṣmī, possessing a universal height bold enough to traverse the three worlds,
and a source of merit like the base of the feet of Viṣṇu— is [like] the ocean of clouds.
He rejoiced in that Tāmraparṇī river which had arisen from her portion.
Having established his military encampment on the shorelines bristling with sprouts of scattered jeweled rays,
he gazed upon the ocean with its surging waves.
The path of the moon was obstructed by thousands of masses of waves.
Its banks and marshy shores were crowded with blue lotuses, *nalas*,
*vañjulās*, coconut palms, and encircling betel vines;
it was a treasury of wonders, ever serene.
Even water that is naturally turbid attains beauty when it is purified. ||40||
With its pure girdle of water slipping away,
it seemed to embrace him excessively with the hands of its waves,
while its bright golden waist-bands were formed by the jewels of its bracelets.
The thick, rounded buttocks of the dark-limbed women were like sandbanks. ||41||
As if in a flurry of playful offering, he seems to place the river-bride— who dallies with the embrace of his lap—
into the cups of his whirlpools, using his waves as hands.
They had plucked away the clusters of flowers from the trees on the banks to serve as their ear-ornaments.
With arms that are the waves of the immeasurable ocean, its surface covered by clouds of pure conch-shells and mother-of-pearl fragments tossing about,
and with hair as formidable as the tawny crests of the submarine fire;
Having leaped up repeatedly, as if toward Bhairava, he cried out with a loud roar. ||43||
As if arising from the grief caused by the abduction of Lakṣmī, Surā, the stainless Kaustubha gem, Pārijāta, Candra, and Amṛta,
[the fire]— with flames as formidable as the peaks of Mount Hemādri— [acted] without regard [for anything else].
Do not cast yourself into the fire of Aurva. ||44||
As if for the purpose of quelling the burning of the remaining fires of the Kālakūṭa poison lodged deep within her womb,
she pours forth the nectar of moonlight at night through the rows of her formidable pearl-like teeth.
[He was] drinking [nectar] from mouths like opened shells, possessing beautiful lips. ||45||
Carrying water that is streaked by the rays of swaying coral shoots and made deep by the revolving circles of whirlpools,
[the ocean] is scattered over by the tips of the rays of the Kaustubha gem which correspond [to its own luster].
The chest of the enemy of Mura, made terrible by the wounds inflicted by the weapons of the Daityas. ||46||
Though shattered into fragments by the impact of a mountain, it remained unbroken; though its jewels were extracted, it attained the status of a treasure-trove;
and though its condition was scorched by the intoxication of prosperity, it was not consumed by the fire of the peerless bow.
[He was] one who, though she had long since departed, did not abandon her as he was distressed by the burning [of grief]. ||47||
Resplendent like hundreds of great sapphire mountains submerged in waters terrified by the fear of a thunderbolt strike,
it was like the darkness within the womb of Śeṣa’s thousand hoods.
Emitting [light] that was being seized by the rays of rubies. ||48||
Having approached that [city], which filled the sky with masses of banners whose crests were veiled by hundreds of shimmering, fierce rays from jewels,
and which possessed abundant horses, elephants, and wealth;
He was swiftly grasping all the quarters of space, like one desiring victory. ||49||
The shore, with its beautiful women on all sides, whose silk garments of foam were tossed by the wind from the swaying stalks of the trembling waves,
repeatedly offered them [garlands] as they were driven by the force of the water.
Dense with strings of jewels, they were as white as the shimmering moon. ||50||
Having risen up repeatedly to a great distance, [he protected] those who had sought refuge from the impact of the thunderbolts hurled by the Lord of the Gods;
and though they were constantly [besieged], the mountains remained entirely free from fear.
He appeared as if looking in all directions for a cause of fear.
From all directions, the impassioned rivers arrived with impetuosity, following one after another in an unbroken succession of surging waves,
while the white water of their milk-like foam expanded clearly.
Embracing from nearby that state which captivates the heart. ||52||
For us, who were eager to immediately distinguish the moonlight from the sunlight situated amidst thousands of masses of formidable waves— mistaking it for milk—
the royal swans on the shore [were the first to perceive].
It was being attended by a herd of spotted-necked deer. ||53||
Beholding the water on all sides like a flickering life-span being swallowed by the fire of the Kalpa-ending conflagration,
it gradually reaches a state of tastelessness and quickly perishes.
The ground of the forest on its banks was thick with the filaments of excellent *kūrca* flowers.
Though it possessed hundreds of Aurva-fires as its weapons, it was not subject to the heat of fire;
though it was turned upward, it was followed by extreme depth; and though it contained elephants, it did not possess the crumbling peaks of mountains.
Though abandoned by the light of the moon, it was rich with the brilliance of clear moonlight.
Even when there was a flooding of the waters of the delightful Nirjharavati river, which had rushed in with impetuosity from the circle of the horizons,
its beauty was rendered tasteless by the water, as if by the nature of the submarine fire (aurva).
[He is] proclaiming, with the sounds of fire and thunder, that [it] is not easily abandoned. ||56||
There, resting upon the waters— deep and glowing with the saffron hue of jewels— and upon that bed formed by the coils of the infinite lord of serpents, he dwells,
his body supported by the vast expanse of the hollow of his formidable belly.
He alone, Hari, is the supreme essence, whom they carry as their preeminent support. ||57||
With his hand— the coiled body of a serpent with five upraised hoods— he was swallowing the water that reached the clouds,
while the sounds of the waves, shattered by the impact of the coastal winds, [resounded].
It was as if it were constantly threatening with the fire of Aurva.
Upon the slopes of her hips, thick with waves and beautiful with the whorls of eddies and hollows,
her eyes are the scattered shells, and from them flows a clear and captivating stream.
Upon the jewel-luminous garments of the river-brides. ||59||
The forest expanse, filled with real snakes mixed with harmless ones, crowded with sprouts and seals, having reached a state of being unassailable,
and containing monkeys eager for the beautiful *śrīphala* fruits— this [forest]... [is like the ocean].
Carrying pearls, aloeswood, and the essence of camphor. ||60||
With its surging, formidable breaking waves that reflect the image of the crescent moon of the eighth day of the lunar fortnight in every direction,
it makes one imagine [the ocean] to be fashioned from molten gold.
Like a row of illusory horses in the water. ||61||
By gradually consuming the waves— which possess the beauty of fish and shells not destroyed by the mass of clinging droplets, and which are adorned with rows of shark-teeth—
the physician-like [fire] constantly...
It was surrounded on all sides by the fire of the submarine mare, which had been released by the Daśvānas.
He beheld the rivers rushing toward him, their foam appearing like a bright white smile, their currents deep and overflowing with flavor,
as if out of a sense of reverence they were looking upon him without distinction.
With eyes like whirling wheels, turning sweetly; ||63||
The creepers, shimmering with waves scattered by the rays of the sun-gem and tossed by breezes carrying droplets from the breaking of the ripples,
seem as if they have taken up [the form] of women intoxicated and moving toward the trees.
The tremors were shaking the groves on its formidable banks as it flowed along. ||64||
With its surface reddened by the rays of emerging jewels,
it possesses the coils of serpents as its hands, their hoods flickering like fingers;
as if out of anger at being obstructed from their full expansion, they coil themselves around.
Scratching the river upon the planks of its longing waves.
With thousands of billowing masses of waves, variegated by the rays of rubies whose intense luster flashes in every direction,
expanding across the entire circle of the world-mandala of the Lord of the Universe.
It was as if it were constructing a wall made of beryl.
With shimmering jewels whose entire expanse of directions was variegated by the lovely, pale-red hue of blooming *japā* flowers,
[the mountain] stood like a mass of fire whose hundreds of flickering flames were tossed about by the wind from the shore.
Like massive clusters of sparks from the submarine fire. ||67||
It bore a whirling wheel, with its rim consisting of the rays of various jewels revolving as far as the navel— the cavity at the base of the belly—
possessing the beauty of a curved conch like the Imperishable One (Viṣṇu).
With a face dark as a rain cloud, with breasts that are elevated, and with a heat [of passion] that has spread.
[He saw] the fire, whose flames were tossed by the wind at the shore, bearing upon its belly the marks— as if signaled— by the falling streaks of wicks from the lamps on the gables.
[The mountains] whose foothills serve as the foundation for firmly established settlements; (this group of thirty-one verses forms a *kulaka*).
Within the midst of whose stainless waters, the clouds—blue as the pigment *abhraka*—appear like reflections in a mirror.
It displays the grace of a mass of mud that has entered the cavity of the netherworld through the breaths of the tortoise who has entered her womb. ||70||
In which [ocean], the multitude of shadows had their wings tossed about by the mass of waves shattered by the playful surges of the tide,
and were thus perceived by people as the mountains within its belly;
As he wandered upon the ground by the shore, creating the illusion of a mountain peak.
The ocean, as if freed from the elaborate displays of its constant pursuit of the shore, approaches with its exceedingly restless hands of waves,
which possess the luster of coral gems and reach toward his teeth.
With rows of distinct dots resembling the manner of cutting [the hair]. ||72||

Like the path of the lord of horses [Uccaiḥśravas], which arose from the waters tossed about in sport by the base of Mount Mandara when it was being whirled by the gods and asuras, [he followed] with delight.
There, he shines forth, beholding the submarine fire known as Vaḍavāmukha.
Praiseworthy is the lord of cows (the moon), who stands as an object of worship for the destruction of darkness,
hanging from the surface of the path of the clouds; like the cool-rayed one, he [the king] possesses a true radiance, his own reflection— just as the moon's reflection is in the water.
He alone bears the earth, which is inhabited by deer. ||74||

That abundance of water which, by means of its long-established and beautiful arrangement made with thick rings of clinging stones, attains the splendor of Lakṣmī adorned with bracelets and a serpent.
Just as the moon-crested Lord [Śiva] is with the daughter of the king of mountains.

He who bore hands in the form of waves spread out and extended in play—the mass of which was fashioned from the reflection of the moon, lord of the stars, fallen into his shadow—and which possessed the copper-red glow of shimmering coral;
He who bore [hands] with the copper-red hue of quivering coral;... [the verse continues].
He bore the likeness of the lord of elephants with its trunk resting firmly in his palate. ||76||
Because it was constantly marked during the nights by the waves of intense red light from a canopy of fresh coral,
his mental state followed the elevated path of Lakṣmaṇa.
The shore of the ocean shines, illuminated by the rays of the moon.
Piercing the darkness within the house of the world’s dwelling, the sun— whose fierce rays are concentrated in a single spot—
presides over it like a vessel filled with pure water and oil that has been spread out.
He made his belly full, like a lamp fed by the fire of Aurva. ||78||
He alone, whose majesty is of unsurpassed splendor, having been sought by Lakṣmī who assumed the form of a crab, attained a state of greatness—
just as a king, supported by his warriors, attains a firm standing through his own vigor.
And by various kinds of beings dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla). ||79||
He alone, the lord of reservoirs, maintains his station amidst the waters,
which possess the excellence of full-blown lotuses;
and by the beauty of his shore, graced by his presence, he is further adorned.
And with Hari, he danced for a long time amidst a succession of waves. (This concludes the group of eleven verses.
Having crossed hundreds of mountain ranges and rivers of various kinds, he was filled with joy by the sight of them from all sides.
From afar, he beheld that [palace], which surpassed the Himalayas and cast a shadow over Mount Meru like that of the sun at its zenith. ||81||
He who stands established upon the earth, which is circular with its boundaries licked by the encircling moat of the ocean,
and rests upon the broad shell of a tortoise’s back—
It possessed the splendor of Mount Mandara, shimmering with the rays of gold.
He bears a circle of rays upon his hand, which has arisen from the region of the hips of the expansive, lotus-stalk-colored stone-slab,
and which clings to his shoulder like the Great Boar (Mahāvarāha) when he was rubbed there.
It possessed the beauty of a mass of manes with parted locks of hair. ||83||
By him, the high Ilāvṛta mountain shines forth, its golden peaks variegated by the radiance of jewels;
and by him, with his lotus-seat, the circle of petals has been awakened.
It is like a lotus born from mud that has not abandoned the mark of its central seed-vessel. ||84||

In which [pillar], the ground of a broad lotus stalk accompanied by a creeper of moonbeams shines forth like a golden pillar within the darkness of the night; and from which, in the presence of the Lord, the world of moving and unmoving beings appears as if it were a mere reflection.
A dark-blue luster like that of a bee was fixed upon her, as if by a maker of shadows. ||85||
With silken garments from the wish-fulfilling creeper— pure with the brilliance of fire cleansed by the flames emerging from the sprouts of expanded sun-gems—
and with moonstones dripping thick drops of water;
With the root-sections that create a gloomy darkness by crushing the creepers. ||86||
With its branches resting upon verandas of red stone, where the orb of the sun— whose fierce heat was inferred by the fire concealed within the hollows of the roots—
had established its seat.
By those who displayed the twilight hues at the onset of the night of destruction. ||87||
With clusters of blossoms as beautiful as strings of pearls released from the bow-circles of Indra, which were struck by the sprouts of the vajra;
with *khañjana* and *khañjarīka* birds turned tawny by the rays of jewels.
With groves of *mañjīra* trees, more beautiful than the most lovely [others], and possessing the quality of resounding jingling. ||88||
With the golden [trees] standing upon their cloud-piercing treetops, which—
due to the mass of light emanating from the middle of their basins woven with large sapphire fragments— give rise to the suspicion that they are a flood of watering water.
With the locations of their treasures inferred from the kumbhīphala fruits. ||89||

At every moment, he beheld that vast expanse crowded with celestial wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*), whose clusters of jewel-studded sprouts were swaying like creepers with tips trembling in the breeze beloved by bees.
With the resolve, the means, and the fruit [of his journey], he [approached] Maṇimekhalā. (A group of nine verses follows:
Then, as he proceeded, the host of stars was made to tremble by his mounting the swing of the dangling jeweled necklace.
The mass of manes on the horses at the front of the chariot-pole appeared as if they were the rays of the rising sun, shimmering like the tips of emerald light.

The sky was marked by clusters of stars embraced [by clouds], while the bells of the celestial chariots of the gods and *siddhas* resounded with a continuous, delightful jingling as they struck against the pillars.
[He] bore a shimmering crescent moon, like a fragment of the moon when it is half-concealed by doubt.
He beheld that gateway, its arches adorned with gems and cloth, fanned by hundreds of yak-tail whisks whose tips were shaken clear,
and where drops of nectar trickled down, delighting the bees.
He arrived, his forehead adorned with a garland of *mandāra* flowers used as a mark of salutation.

(Tilaka) His gaze was fixed upon the slopes of the mountain ridges, where the heat of the sun had been swallowed by the shadows cast by his dark body, which resembled the sky when the sun is eclipsed; he rested there amidst the jeweled plateaus.

As the three watches of the night drew near, the young women— whose minds were now set on their immediate task, yet who were being drenched by the intense passion of love— quickly completed the arrangement of their ornaments.

Thus ends the thirtieth canto, titled "The Description of the Division of the Path," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.

From the path of the stars, he [Śiva], whose most weighty task rested within his heart...
Having established its foundation upon the back of the mountain that shatters cities,

Its waves were broken by the trumpeting of the celestial elephant submerged in clouds variegated by sprays of nectar dripping coolly;
it was beautiful as its broad, thick trunk struck them down.
[She] whose waters were mixed with the nectar of golden lotuses. ||2||
The foam-masses of its pure water droplets caused doubt as to whether they were the swans that serve as the vehicle for the lotus-seated Brahmā immersed in his divine play;

[She is] one whose waves and breezes are intensely drunk by the lord of serpents.
She bore expansive regions that resembled sovereigns who have attained success through the diligent practice of the mantra of the Lord of Blazing Gold,
and which were not at all inferior to the caves of every mountain.
Possessing a profound beauty that delights the hearts of women.
The water, bearing the story of the burden that was consistent with reality—
containing fish, turtles, and the aged king of the Matsyas—
was rendered even more captivating by its swaying, which surpassed the dancing of Śiva.
She was like the Ganges with its mass of waves at the time of the dissolution of the world, clad in pure white garments.
[She was] like a mass of bubbles and droplets of moonlight, mistaken for the circle of white planets descended for her bath,

It was tawny with the rays from the emerging golden bands, with its lotus-stalks of jewels uprooted, and its swarms of intoxicated swans [the gems] fleeing.

He beheld himself bound upon a massive *kalpavṛkṣa* tree, whose golden creepers and jewel-blossoms were cast down by the force of the singing of the *tāla* rhythm from his swaying ears.
[He saw] Dairāvaṇa, the crest-jewel of the entire race of Nāgas. ||8||
Upon her cheeks, which possess an exquisite beauty due to fresh ichor flowing from the temples like the crushing of demons in a great battle,
bees have taken up their station upon her broad ears and flapping fans.
bearing a mass [of flowers] shaken by the breeze from the swing. ||9||
Adorned with beautiful chowries upon his ears, possessing a fair complexion like the orb of the cool-rayed moon whose impurities have been long dispelled,

Bearing a surface of the face as if it were a cluster of blossoms. ||10||
Raising his excellent, thick trunk upwards to smell the scent of the ichor from another herd of elephants,
he appeared as if split by the luster of a forest of coral trees.
Possessing a broad palate with the luster of a ripe mango.
He bore a manifest splendor that surpassed even the moonlight, which was concealed by the similarity of his body’s radiance;
he was struck by the rhythmic tapping of his slow-moving ears.
The pure conch-shell at the ear, trembling with the movement of the swing.
With his conch resting playfully upon the peak of his ear,
he bears his elevated cheek as if it were the moon risen from the depths of the ocean of milk.
And being kissed with intense passion by his brother. ||13||

A trunk as white as moonbeams, acting as a bolt upon the door of his hand, which held aloft in the sky a fragment of cloud sluggish from sipping water out of disdain, and possessed of straight, noble branches.

With bees wandering incessantly, drawn by the greed for the abundant drink of ichor flowing from the temples of his cheeks,

As if being embraced by continuous masses of thick darkness. ||17||

he was graced on all sides by the pure Nārada, who added to his splendor.
It was as lofty as the summit of Mount Sumeru, the abode of the celestial rishis.
The young moon, spreading a beauty more enchanting than that of the path of stars at night— which is marred by the onset of eclipses— bears a resemblance to the time of dawn.
His body’s luster was set upon by the twilight, and he possessed the beauty of a blossoming lotus.
And his body, adorned with Lakṣmī who— possessing a girdle of jewels— is never forsaken by him,
shines as if with the very grounds of the battlefield, owing to her casting side-long glances from afar.
The forms [of the lotuses] were occupied by bees standing motionless, as if holding morsels of food. ||22||
As he turns his head, the water from his hand— which imitates all noble conduct and clearly subdues the virtuous—
rests upon the surface of his cheek as if it were a demoness.
Whose nature is delightful due to his unceasing bestowal of boons. ||23||
He whose body was adorned with the marks of an elephant, whose form followed the [royal] camp, who had acquired glory through a splendor that surpassed the greatness [of others],
and whose stability was established upon a noble lineage of ancestors— [he] obstructed [the enemy].
It bears its back as beautifully as a mountain of frost. ||24||
By the elephant-fighter, who was graceful in his arrangement of the girth-straps, possessed of a majestic body, and who had been trained [in the arts],
he was employed upon the battlefields with his trunk extended.
Out of pride, by which he struck down the elephants of his enemies. ||25||
By the mass of fresh mineral dust rising from his temples,
heavy with the weight of it shaken by the rhythmic flapping of his ears and having swallowed the waves of the ocean of rut,
the height of the Vindhya mountains was surpassed.
And he who bore Fortune [Lakṣmī] just as the sage Agastya bore [the river] Śoṇa. ||26||
He whose body is sought by the enemies of the gods in battles,
who bears an excess of heroism, and whose glory of arm-strength is unsurpassed, maintains his position upon the elephant-like shoulders of others, like a crow perched upon an elephant's temple.
Like a woman of turbid luster, so was the swarm of bees drinking honey.

Like the king of mountains, he whose temples were like crags from which flowed streams of trickling rut-fluid, and who— like a mountain— had the tusks of elephants following him shattered by the crushing of various forces, [shone forth].
The beautiful one bears a splendor that surpasses even the appearance of a mass of clouds. ||28||
He whose splendor is enhanced by the peacock-like grace of his desire to embrace the ever-present Lakṣmī, who dwells upon the dust raised by the feet of those worthy of love,
and who proceeds auspiciously at the onset of battles with the sounding of drums— [he is the Lord].
The son of Siṃhikā (Rāhu) is situated upon the lower lip, which is the playful manifestation of Kālī. ||29||
The lord of serpents also maintains an unswerving disposition toward his entire retinue of coils, being capable of bearing the heavy burden he has taken up;
and he constantly displays the splendor of blossoming night-lotuses.
In battle, Supratīka shines like Airāvata. ||30||
He whose body’s luster and the brilliance of his garments pervade the worlds, who shines in battle with the tail-like movement of his banner,
and who is exceedingly dear to the inhabitants of heaven— his...
The state of those whose drum-beats are clearly resonant attains prosperity. ||31||
By him, whose body was sufficient in its giving, sport was attained even while resorting to the conduct of a Danava;
by him, whose sacrificial rites were unimpaired, it was attained as if through the path of the Vedas.
The fortune of the elephants was increased by the weighty conduct of their master.
With a lofty body, his girth bound by the defeat of the entire host of elephants, he possesses the manifest splendor of a clear proof like an extreme nihilist (atīnāstika);
he bears a mass of [elephants] like a vast wheel.

He [beheld] that river of heaven, whose waters were turned tawny by the mud of silver and in which lotuses with gems nestled within them shone, formidable with many rising water-jars. (A *kulaka* of twenty-six verses.
In that stream of the celestial river, where the waters were made brownish-yellow by the mire of silver...
As he moved along, he beheld the swans of the lord of waters, whose beaks were occupied with lotus-stalks as delicate as jewels.
Then he beheld a wild buffalo belonging to Samavartin, its broad and thick neck adorned with bells that had fallen from the quiver of his son, who was frequently broken in battle.
marked by the golden mud of the pools of the Mandākinī river; ||35||
In those [waters] whose inner reaches were agitated by the clamor of the sporting flocks of swans moving in harmony with him,
and where the cranes were filled with excessive alarm at his playful charm;
His gaze moved toward the lakes filled with the essence of jewels.
Beholding that riverbank, whose sands were delightful with gems laughing amidst the fallen ear-ornaments of the young wives of the Lord of the Gods as they bathed,
he attained an incomparable bliss.
Like daughters of the Mandākinī, they were pools filled with jewels. ||37||
He rested upon the path along the bank of the lotus pond, where flocks of swans were struck by spray scattered by the waves;
having reached it, he found it covered with the dust of pulverized pearls.
He [made] it cool by means of thick, closely packed sand. ||38||
On a tree on the bank of the Mandākinī, he saw a fresh cloth fluttering from the gentle impact of the breeze,
serving as a bandage for the wounds inflicted by Airāvata’s tusks.
She was like a wish-fulfilling creeper that seemed to bestow what was not even desired. ||39||
He beheld with distinct clarity those women who were beautiful with swaying jeweled earrings, lovely girdles of fine gems, and foot-ornaments; they resembled the Kalpa-tree.
He [beheld] creepers and celestial women, fair as gold. ||40||
Beholding the divine couples rejoicing within expansive golden vine-cottages,
their enjoyment enhanced by the fresh sprouts plucked from their hands by the wives of the *siddhas*, he was filled with joy.
Then he [beheld] the Mandāra tree and the Nandana grove.
Beholding those sandbanks whose shores were strewn with jewels and fine sands, marked by the beautiful footprints of pairs of migrating swans,
he [beheld] the golden... situated near them.
He gazed for a long time upon the ponds filled with blossoming lotuses.
He beheld a herd of deer agitating the sky before the stage of the grove of the gods,
their fine bodies and feathers inlaid with the luster of jewels.
bestowing the grace of an entourage upon the starry deer. ||43||
There he beheld the Pārijāta tree, whose canopy of shade had been snatched away by the cresting rays of the rubies on the sprouts; yet even so,
it remained possessed of its splendor before the celestial damsel.
[He] has plucked tender jewel-flowers from his lotus-like hands. ||44||
Under the guise of the mass of clear rays emerging from the tips of the gem-studded sprouts shimmering upon the wide floor,
[he appeared] like a golden [lotus] situated within the circle of a jeweled basin.
It was as if water were being vomited forth from him, burdened by an exceedingly great weight. ||45||
Nor was it [the case] with those [flowers] being plucked by hands whose fingers were like a circle of red lotus petals,
which were themselves made doubtful to be fresh sprouts;
for even as they blossomed, at that very same moment—
"Bearing Lakṣmī, [adorned] with various other jewel-flowers" (the *tilaka*). Thus,
the moon-crested messenger reached a state of wonder at the sight of ever-increasing excellences.
For a moment, he remained at the top of the golden archway inlaid with jewel-lustre in the city of Indra. ||47||
In which [city] he dwells within a palace of jewels, situated amidst courtyards of sāl trees and rows of sapphire and ruby halls,
[a city] as expansive as the staff-like arm of Madhusūdana.
She possesses the grace of Mount Mandara situated in the midst of the Mandāra grove. ||48||
In which [city], the rays of the moon, mingled with the mass of light from the walls of palaces shimmering with emeralds and rubies,
flow through the tubular stalks of the *kurabaka* tree blossoms.
Having attained a greenish-pale hue, they have lost their splendor. ||49||
Wherein the doors, though closed, possess a splendor that appears as if their faces were opened wide from afar by the rays of lapis lazuli set in their panels during the nights.
In every direction, there was a row of jeweled palaces scraping the clouds. ||50||

In that city, the splendor of the abundant fragrance of aguru incense, issuing forth through the lattice windows, perfumes the silken garments of the celestial wish-fulfilling creepers of the nearby groves effortlessly from afar in every direction. (51)

In which city, during the night, the moon-like faces of the women— smeared with pearl ornaments brightened by the rays of the moon and shimmering with drops falling from moonstones— shine like the lunar orb covered by a cluster of dewdrops.
The water shone like a cascade of nectar, cool as it flowed forth. ||52||
Wherein the moon, rendered grey by the mass of rays emerging from the crevices of sapphire eaves,
bears a body that is exceedingly emaciated like Rāhu.
The moon [possesses] a luster as if it were soiled by having been squeezed out. ||53||
There, celestial maidens assume a splendor born from their association with radiant sapphire palaces,
possessing the beautiful grace of lightning flashing amidst a mass of clouds heavy with water.
Where the waves of the celestial river flowing nearby, having entered the path of the windows of the ruby palaces, dispel the exhaustion born at the end of lovemaking.
The breezes, cooled by following the waves, [refreshed] the women. ||55||
In that city,
the circle of Sāla trees, coated with silver,
was gazed upon by hosts of sky-dwellers stationed in distant regions as a fire whose flames were like whirling circles of firebrands.
It possessed a magnificent splendor, formidable with its broad wheels fixed in place by inscriptions.

In which [city] the multitude of houses, never abandoned by prosperity and filled with lords of serpents as delightful as the luster of the blue-throated one (Śiva), bears the beauty of door-sills, just as Śambhu, whose nature is lofty, bears the beauty of the daughter of the mountain (Pārvatī) when not forsaken by his fortune and accompanied by the lords of serpents. 57.
She bears [her beauty] as if lengthened through the pair of her eyes, as if concentrated upon her cheeks and the region of her breasts,
and as if spread wide across the slope of her hips.
And in that [city], there was a multitude of women possessing the splendor of loveliness. ||58||
In that city, the circles of trees in the children’s groves had their roots drenched by cascades of water trickling from the conduits of moonstones in the palaces at the rising of the moon.
The splendor of all the seasons is embraced from every direction. ||59||
And there, at night, the mountain peak— delightful to Rāma and appearing like a mass of distant palaces by its radiance—
shines forth, having destroyed the advancing force of the radiant Mārīca, whose emblem was the form of a deer.
That [glory] which, under the guise of the Vaijayantī banners upon standards white with masses of moonlight, has surpassed the splendor arising from various other cities,
and which is as pale as the rays of the moon, spreads through the quarters of the sky.
She is perceived as if scattering her fame without interruption. ||61||
Where, even though tightly bound by his thighs, the report of the cries of the flocks of peacocks perched upon the jeweled palace terraces reached the ears of one traveling along the path,
causing him to turn his circle of hoods.
The row of serpents loosens the bonds of the chariot of the Sun. (62) (A group of sixteen verses).

Thus ends the thirty-first canto, titled "Description of the Splendor of Heaven," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked with the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, whose pen-name was Vāgīśvara, and who was also known by the name Vidyādhipati.
Canto Thirty-three.
Then the lord of the Daityas, having heard the elaborate speech uttered by him,
with his heart filled with indignation yet possessing the beauty of a white smile,
[addressed] the descendant of Bhṛgu who was seated nearby on the occasion.
He gave the command to speak by means of his brow alone, which was raised with sweetness.
Bearing a bodily luster streaked by masses of rays from a circle of golden chains shimmering forth,
like the dark daughter of Kalinda [the Yamunā].
[He was] pierced by the glow of the jewels on the hoods of the black serpents that had been raised up. (A pair of verses.
Urged by him, he [Śiva], as if smearing the enemies of the gods with the luster of his teeth like the moon with its moonlight, [proceeded].
Having reflected thus upon the message of the messenger of the one adorned with the crescent moon, Uśanas spoke slowly.
His fair body was seen streaked with the luster of the bodies of the lords of the *danuja*s standing nearby;
its belly was clearly marked by the yellow of his vows, made manifest by his pure nature.
[He was seen] by those standing on the floor of the assembly hall as if he were a column of incense smoke situated within its sections. ||4||
She, the Goddess Śrī, who rests at his feet, gazes upon the face of him who has made the world a tribute to his irresistible prowess; indeed,
[she does so] because the guardians of the world, bowing down with humility, are difficult for him to conquer.
Upon the circular mirrors of the jewels in the crowns of the guardians. ||5||

The tree of his valor shines upon the frontier of the forest of the world, its radiant beauty like a cluster of blossoms formed by his stainless fame— the moonlight of which whitens the tips of all the creeper-like quarters as they bow down— while his enemies...
It has its firm root bound by the matted locks of women with parted hair.
And the creeper-like sword held in his lotus-hand, with its mass of flickering and formidable rays,
was entwined by the lotus-hands of the daughter of the Nanda king, who had firmly established her position upon it.
It appeared like a row of bees falling due to greed. ||7||
Though the pride of those who hate the Daityas was heavy, it vanished from the surfaces of their foreheads as they bowed down in agitation, as if by the friction of their jeweled footstools.
Furthermore, the creeper of his frown sprouted from that seed. ||8||
Day by day, the circle of enemies darkens before him who, with sharpened sword in hand,
has caused the vast array of his soldiers to overrun the entire circumference of the quarters.
His fame was like the dust of the earth shaken off and struck away. ||9||
By whom, in battle, the flames of the thunderbolt’s fire— cast aside with ease like a mere plaything by the enemy of Vṛtra— were seen clinging to the trees of his arms,
where they were held fast by beautiful armlets and rubies.
In battles, there was the confusion caused by the delusion of the radiance of jewels.
O rogue of a jackal, you have no reason to fear speaking here before Hara, who was easily conquered by her;
for thus [is the power] of the monkeys among the Pramathas, who are more restless than the wind.
What speech could be more eloquent than this? (A group of seven verses):
First displaying the terror of the destruction of the asuras, and later characterized by an excellence filled with sweetness;
By your variegated words of message, our minds here have been rendered utterly bewildered as to how to respond.
When he, having suddenly fallen helpless like a pillar in battle-forests thick with impenetrable essence,
underwent defeat as he turned and rolled about;
The wielder of the Śārṅga bow found his heart's desire shattered.
This is another [manifestation of him], by whom the entire circle of the mountain ranges of his enemies was crushed by the firm blows of his thunderbolt-like arms; yet,
though soft with compassion, he remained utterly humble when abandoned in battle.
The immortals attained the true meaning of their renowned name. ||14||

If this lord of light had existed in the world, he would have filled even a tiny fraction, a mere trace of a portion, of the shadow of that majesty which is capable of consuming the lineage of his enemies.
Nor was its power diminished by being struck by the blows of Tvaṣṭṛ’s chisel. ||15||
Just as his face bears a countenance with cheeks blossoming with a smile, yet he says nothing clearly,
I think that the circle of the gods will likewise come to pass.
The forest fire, with its thousands of quivering flame-tips, [blazes]. ||16||
Let alone the sovereignty of the Lord of the Gods;
even among his great followers, Hari did not obtain it. Even the existence of a tree is dependent upon its leaves.
Does the sun's heat ever cause the earth to wither? ||17||
Bearing this city occupied by the haughty Asuras,
which possesses a renowned state of pride and possession,
these bold warriors of Danu’s sons do not feel ashamed.
How much more so, then, even the rays of the sun as they pass over? ||18||
That the moon, rendered turbid by the fragmentation of its shadow, is daily tormented by the hot-rayed sun without any remedy;
and that the ocean is consumed by the submarine fire— [all this is for the sake of others].
I consider that contemptible [behavior] of those two to be the manifestation of their own dullness. 19.
Granted that there may be hundreds of noble lineages in this world,
how could they possibly possess equal majesty and power? For the glory arising from qualities exceeding those [of others] is what is embraced [as supreme].
Even that word which is the object of expression belongs to the dull-witted. ||20||
Does the mass of roots feel any resentment toward the cluster of creepers that, having attained growth from a single seed and sprout through the course of time, have suddenly reached upward?
For the trees, whose growth was established within the space at the summit. ||21||
What purpose could there possibly be here in the depths of the netherworld (pātāla) with all those other countless serpent heads?
Even that single [head] of Śeṣa’s thousand hoods is praiseworthy.
For he bears the Mūrvī plant, which is as heavy as all the lords of mountains without exception.
Indeed, there are thousands of mountains whose quarters are washed by the cascades of their shimmering cool-rayed [moon-like] torrents;
yet how few among them truly possess the strength to support the surface of the earth!
They are capable of being designated as belonging to the family that abides unimpededly. ||23||
The lord of the Daityas, with a smiling face, released those whom he had spared out of extreme compassion while they were still alive in battle; tell me,
O you who have ascended to the three worlds, how did they dwell in the depths of the netherworld?
Are they the immortals, or perhaps the lords of the asuras? ||24||
Having spoken thus to the enemy of the gods, who was filled with indignation toward the preceptor of the thirty deities, the messenger of the Foe of Tripura shook his head,
making a sound like the roar of a waterfall from the mountain of his lofty pride.
Having filled the assembly hall with his speech, he spoke thus. ||25||
What can be said? Here, destiny is all-powerful;
this assembly hall of the lord of the Danujas is to be pitied, for you—who have drunk deeply for a thousand years—[are now gone].
With your mind darkened by smoke, you have resorted to heaviness. ||26||
"Let not this entire world become unstable through the crushing conflict of the mutually antagonistic hosts of gods and asuras;
for I have spoken that which does not abandon the essential nature of duty."
That has been grasped otherwise by you, who are foolish. ||27||
For one whose vision is impaired by delusion, every object everywhere undoubtedly becomes a false appearance;
[just as] the water of the Mandākinī appears white like moonbeams—
It is constantly imagined by the Piśācas to be blood. ||28||
Though possessing a white brilliance and bearing the splendor of cool-rayed moonlight, the enemy of the gods, having joined the opposing side,
was exceedingly crooked-hearted and displayed only a passion for battle.
By praising [him], you shine forth; you do not appear like a conch shell in this manner. ||29||
Even when praising those who are censurable, and even when disparaging those whose nature is devoid of the power of virtue, such is the behavior of the deluded;
for embodied beings under a wicked master fall into extreme wretchedness.
Fie upon this life of subservience, which finds its delight in following the whims of others! ||30||
Now these rays of yours, their brilliance eclipsed, do not gladden the minds of wise men;
even now, they are like smoke swallowed while residing within the hollow of a belly.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, the syllables in her speech seem as if they have been turned dark. ||31||
Even while concealing its own impurity, one of crooked conduct reveals his virtues abundantly on the outside;
for even the venom contained within the belly [of a cobra] reaches the very top of its head.
Like one who has lost his way in the brilliance of jewels, he is utterly bewildered. ||32||
It is evident that here, by the power of its substratum,
this person, though devoid of that nature, partakes in its very essence;
the breath of air attains straightness within a bamboo flute.
Furthermore, its curvature within the interior of a conch shell is proven. ||33||
He whose roar split the hearts of his adversaries— its hollows made resonant by the breath of his sighs,
which had taken its place within the cavernous interior of their bellies— [is he].
Like a conch shell emitting a sound most terrible due to its resonance, it quickly [blew].||34||
The clouds at the horizons, struck by the wind generated by the force of the whirling tips of his trembling fingers,
were rent asunder by the rays of his discus.
They fell, their splendor broken into fragments by the falling showers. ||35||
The playful power of Hari manifested as the flame of the fire of his harsh "huṃ" roar, which issued from his mouth,
fanning the heart with its breath and shaking the secret navel.
[She possesses] the playful grace of the pollen of the tawny filaments blooming from the lotus. ||36||
He whose chest,

struck by the hands of the women of the city as they wept at the parting of their hair, is even today followed by the echoes of their cries, [resounding] like the blossoming and swelling of the Pāñcajanya conch.
Like the sounds of conch shells from within the dwellings of great asuras. ||37||

There you shall behold the solar orb, rendered skillful in producing a vivid smile by the lotus-faces of the celestial damsels upon the hands of the Lord of that city— the throat of the enemy of Kaiṭabha, the sovereign of the Asuras.

Upon the seats, the wheel quickly revolves— (this group of five verses). That wheel, which receives no space within its heart for the mass of darkness from the fainting caused by the blows of the weapons of the Dānavas in battle;
It was as if being eclipsed by the rays of the rubies resting upon the hoods of the thousand serpents he had swallowed. ||39||
By him, the cool orb of the moon was shaken from the sky by the force of the wind from his fluttering golden wings,
so that it was cast down as if it were a mere fragment of an egg clinging to his body.
which caused the three worlds to tremble as it whirled in battles. ||40||
Even now, the wind from its wings blows here,
which formerly moved with such speed along the path to the netherworld that it caused thousands of serpent-wives, distressed by widowhood, to cry out.
Because of the indication of heavy sighs accompanied by tears. ||41||
Moistened by sprays of nectar-essence forcibly extracted by swarms of bees agitated by the weight of their fresh fragrance,
they bear rows of wings as bright as polished gold.
Like a fire with smoky crests, it was as if a series of straight flames. ||42||
Tārkṣya, whose flashing and unfailing thunderbolt-strike was honored by the release of birds whose wings were lopped off by his own talons in battle—
[he who] steals the hue of dark clouds and is skilled in deceitful maneuvers...
In a single moment, he will crush you, O serpents! (This is a *kulaka* consisting of five verses.
These hosts of Gaṇas, whose taste is even more harsh than that of Śiva—the enemy of Dakṣa—and who are skilled in the sport of transforming the entire world without exception—
The Asuras, shattered like mountains by a succession of winds of universal destruction, shall fall into some indescribable state. ||44||
In these rivers of consecration, whose waters have their heat darkened by the mud of the ichor from the elephants of the gods,
the intoxicated great fish that are the great Asuras— whose wings have been destroyed and whose throats are clearly visible— [are seen].
They do not survive for long, gasping for breath as they are severed. ||45||
Let alone, for now, the lords of the Pramathas who possess the skill to traverse all seven worlds;
[consider rather] him whose jeweled peaks are turned by the machinery of his staff-like arms.
I myself shall create the netherworld; what need have you? ||46||
While the lord of the Gaṇas was thus speaking words harsh with inner intent for the sake of inciting the fury of the lords of the sons of Diti,
that assembly hall— its rows of jeweled pillars struck by palms— [shook].
It was like the slopes of Mount Vāmana, where the Kalpa trees have been shaken down. ||47||

Thus ends the thirty-third canto, titled "The Rebuke of Bhārgava," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
The thirty-fourth canto:
Then Krodha, his vision dimmed by a flood of darkness, trembling violently and intensified by the practice of transgression, [approached her].
With his head-shaking firmly bound [by his resolve], and his petal-like lower lip quivering with a continuous flow of sighs, he slowly looked around.
A mass of smoke from the *huṃkāra* of Uśanas, the sovereign of the asuras, was seen approaching in front;
it embraced his entire body like one who has consumed the essence of his religious observances.
Like the sun obscured by smoke, as it were, due to the power of excessive familiarity. ||2||
The enraged Agnidamstra, whose body was variegated by streaks of smoke produced by rubbing against the surface of her chest,
[climbed] onto the seat of her full, beloved wife’s jar-like breasts.
He bore [her] like a creeper of leaf-patterns from a heap of black aloe-wood. ||3||
The broad chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu’s son shone, split open by the intensity of his longing for battle,
with fragments shattered by the falling of thick chains of bone.
With masses of wounds whose blood was turbid with the spray of falling torrents. ||4||
The frown formed by him out of anger, with drops of perspiration reddened by the rays of the rubies in his crown,
shone like the twilight of the night of universal destruction.
The beauty of whose circle of pupils was reddened by a flash of passion. ||5||
With the surface of her cheeks reddened by the agitation caused by the beauty of the full-blown blue lotuses serving as her ear-ornaments,
she resembled the night of the full moon when the moon is eclipsed by Rāhu.
Bimba struck Śatadundubhi loudly with his hand.

Vikumbha, whose chest-wound caves were strewn with a profusion of droplets from the spray of perspiration, bore upon his arm— like the trunk of a lion that had torn open the frontal globes of an elephant— the sword of Śiva, which was as dark as a fresh raincloud and marked by the splendor of the crescent moon.
It possesses the grace of mountains whose caves are houses with pearls scattered within.
From the wounds torn open by the intense passion of battle on the broad breast-slopes of Anala-tāraka, whose mind was possessed by pride and envy, there poured forth [the blood].
They were like fragments of the tusks of the lordly elephants of the gods that had been shattered.
With his face, which was radiant with fury and possessed the brilliance of a clear laugh, he— whose neck was tawny like that of a lion—
[appeared] like the ash-dust of the ocean of burnt waters being vomited forth.
It assumed the likeness of the mouth of the submarine fire within the ocean of the stream of existence. ||9||
The crest-jewel of the serpent, shimmering amidst the spray of the pure water of the Dharma scattered by the rays of his slightly copper-hued gaze,
is like a reflection within the mass of waters of the Yamunā.
The formidable form of Kṛṣṇa became the very frown of the Kali age. ||10||
The face of Rāhu was not clearly visible, its palate-root blackened by the smoke from the crushing of his firm dental mechanism;
it resembled the mud-stain of the moon’s digit being swallowed by the lords of the Daityas.
It was spreading forth as if soiled by contact with worldly associations. ||11||
The smoke-streaks arising from the friction of his jeweled headbands— streaks as long as the coils of the lord of serpents— emitted by the son of Siṃhī,
[seemed to be the] stain of the moon who was being swallowed whole.
Like lines rising up, they filled the intervening space of the sky. ||12||
As if vomited forth by the interior of his mouth, which was overflowing with a heavy burden due to the stream of nectar he had swallowed,
[there arose] from that man of extreme cruelty a hideous, loud laugh—
The assembly hall and the palace shone, illuminated by that radiance. ||13||
With her body whitened by the spray of dust from the pearl necklaces that had been crushed and turned to mud by the sweat of the enemy's army,
she shone like one anointed with sandalwood paste. The moon-bannered god [Kāma] appeared as if he were the very embodiment of the enemy’s pride.
Of one whose mind was eager for union with Lakṣmī. ||14||
The face of Vajrabāhu shone with a coppery hue, made difficult to behold by yawning, trembling, and heavy envy;
it was like an ominous portent with its middle obstructed by a gaping fissure.
Like the clearly manifest circle of rays from the hot-rayed sun. ||15||
Then, for the destruction of the entire host of his enemies, a mass of smoke from the Malaya mountain rose toward the forehead of Kālāntaka,
like drops of nectar trickling from a flower-ornament.
Desiring a drink, she fell down like a row of bees seeking honey. ||16||
He attained the splendor of a mountain peak inhabited by black serpents, which were being overwhelmed by the rays of his eyes, red with rage. ||17||
With his two arms locked together, Subāhu held aloft a mass of flickering flame-tips;
Tvaṣṭṛ [fashioned it] from the sparks arising from the striking of the chisel upon the ornamental architrave.

He will surely release his arrows at the celestial beings before long.
Abandon the discourse of clear-cut lethargy; you are on the path of valor whose prowess is unhesitating. Indeed, fortitude and heroism are not easily attained by those who are indolent.
Fortune, whose heart is captivated by heroic pride, dwells only in rare instances. ||59||
Surely, when the rival women have become like the quarters of the sky with their circles of clouds soiled by darkness,
the crest-jewel [of the hero] is obtained by the conqueror of Madhu, as if by Viṭaṅka.
Even I have fallen asleep, my body constrained by the lotus posture.
As my dull grey sword— clinging to the wretched cries [of my enemies] and bearing the splendor of night— falls upon them, he,
his mind distressed by separation, will quickly abandon my side.
Like a female cakravāka bird [separated] from her mate, she was like the daughter of the Himālaya mountain.
While Andhaka was thus speaking, his swelling pride manifest, Kāñcanākṣa— perceiving the other’s bound fury and his own lower lip quivering with the desire to speak from within—
was agitated by the spray-like droplets from the cascades of light-rays emanating from the tips of the curls on his garland of jewel-hangers.
Bearing [the fire] that was being extinguished, it seemed as if his chest were intensely scorched by the flames of a small thunderbolt.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth canto, titled "The Dialogue of the Asura Andhaka," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked with the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
The thirty-sixth canto:
Bearing the daughter of Kalinda as if out of envy for the celestial river sportively borne by the Moon-crested Lord.
With his head, the crest of whose crown darkened the circle of the sun's rays with the tips of the shimmering emerald beams from its peak. ||1||
His ear-ornament was rendered tawny by the mass of jewel-rays clinging to the tips of his swaying gem-studded earrings;
striking against his broad shoulder-slopes with an uneven impact, it—
He spoke thus to the Asura Vyaṃsa who was standing nearby:
(this pair of verses) "O Lord of Daityas, why do you speak with such shattered fortitude, displaying this agitation that arises from a non-entity?"
Even while the warriors of charity stood ready, eager to receive the command for battle, and were shattering the mountain-like hosts of their enemies. ||3||

Upon those very arms of the lord of the Daityas— which were like the temples of world-elephants standing nearby, with sprouts formed by the trickling ichor of rut— and which were like the Night of Destruction at the end of the enemy's existence;
Your hand grasps the blade of your sword like a creeper.
Why do you look to the side with a frown, your hand trembling in anger as if wishing to seize the thunderbolt?
Your own arm alone performs that task for you.
He who effortlessly shattered the entire circle of mountains representing his enemies. ||5||
Even a single one among them, though small, fights the enemy more fiercely than a multitude of your elite warriors;
she alone suffices for the fire kindled by fuel.
Even a tiny spark, when applied, is capable of burning [it].
O Medhāsita, is this Mekalā mountain not indeed your arm? It bears this formidable crest as its bracelet; and here, upon the edge of its rocky peak, lies this sword-blade.
