The intensely potent Hālāhala creeper brings about delusion. ||7||
It is true that you alone are capable of shattering the entire circle of the hosts of gods in battle in a single moment;
let him reduce it to ashes without the submarine fire.
Who indeed [could drink] the water of the ocean, thick with surging waves? ||8||
The brilliance of your unimpeded, blazing majesty has been pared down by you with the blows of the chisels of your sharp arrows,
like that of a firebrand fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ for an archer prepared for the turmoil of battle.
And he fashioned a wheel that was most brilliantly radiant for the world. ||9||
Truly, having heard your words, I bear my own form filled to the brim with a flood of horripilation;
such is the indescribable power of the cloud's sound by which this occurs.
The distant ground reaches the emergence of the sprouts of jewels. ||10||
Let one of eloquent speech speak these words, if there were someone there capable of discerning between the real and the unreal like you;
for from stone one may obtain gold.
Nowhere does he find a touchstone for that [gold]. ||11||
Although my wisdom possesses little power, it does not entirely dispel even this slight application of discernment here;
just as the moonlight, though diminished by the dark fortnight, does not entirely dispel the heat of the sun.
The digit of the nectar-rayed moon does not abandon that which is worthy of itself. ||12||
Though it possesses an innate lack of flavor and repeatedly attains a state of insentience, this speech— of immeasurable conduct and heavy with essence— is, after being examined by the teachers...
Wisdom is the source [of all], just as gold is produced from ore. ||13||
"O lords of the Daityas, like bees toward the pollen of a flower, you who are dark as clouds deserve to grasp this very reality now residing in our speech within this assembly."
A drop of nectar that has undergone transformation within the womb.
The blood spurting from his heart as it was being pierced by the five claws of the one who had assumed the form of Nṛsiṃha— his hand having been cast aside—
is, as it were, reflected out of anger in the mirrors of his own nails.
The blood of the lord of the Daityas was also drunk by his mouths. ||15||
It was obstructed by the fear of a double fall into the netherworld caused by the earth-goddess, who was seized by his fangs with great agitation;
while the seven worlds within were whirling and thrown into disorder.
And his breath was the month-long duration of the Boar-incarnation. ||16||

Having previously reflected that "this Rāhu is a devourer of the living," he will speak with such generosity as to sever the painful bonds of the joints that revolve at the edge of the wheel of death for the givers of gifts.
By whom [the demon] was reduced until only his facial orb remained. ||17||
At the head of the battle, that conch Pāñcajanya was not clearly blown by him with effort; yet,
by the mere movement of his breath from the seat of his heart, it filled the seven worlds.
The passage to his cavernous mouth was blocked by his distorted shape. ||18||
How could that wielder of the Śārṅga bow— who in battle has his feet playfully wiped by the lotuses of Lakṣmī’s trembling hands—
not come within the range of thought for the path of the Daityas?
May he, whose beautiful form is like the orb of the sun at the time of universal dissolution, protect you! (Five verses in *kulaka* meter) May he,
who in the field of battle makes the expanse of the sky tawny with the sparks of the fierce flames of fire spat forth [from his mouth], protect you!
How indeed could the Kaumodakī mace—forged as a meteor for the destruction of the hosts of enemies by his staff-like arms—have slipped from the path of my memory? (20)
Who could endure even Nandaka on the path of battle, that sword which, as if from the weight of the joy of severing the throats of the asuras,
was stained by the fierce rays of the sun's rays?
Under the guise of a mere line, he creates the production of another sword.
In battles, as he moves about, the rays from the tips of the sprout-like fingers of Murāri’s hand,
which part the darkness far away, [shine forth].
The quarters trembled, as if out of fear that their continuity would be broken by the downpour.
The body of Janārdana, which was like a golden mirror for the deities of the quarters and emitted sparks of fire, grew even more expansive;
yet the stream of fire from the throat of the enemy of the gods, though thinning, did not satisfy him.
By means of the streams of blood flowing unimpeded from the arteries. ||23||

Who indeed could obstruct his wheel in battle— that wheel which casts a darkness over the quarters of the sky with its swirling, grey dust, while his moon-like fame, as tender as the petals of a blossoming jasmine, shines forth?
[This is] the thousand-rayed orb of the sun that nourishes the writing.
(Tilaka) May this joint of the skull-binding between heaven and earth not be split asunder by the wind of the leaf!
Having meditated thus, he who had arisen in an instant from the shell of the egg became, in the sky, one whose flight was exceedingly fierce and magnificent.
By whom the body of the younger brother of Indra, which has surpassed the three worlds with its playfulness and is bound by serpents,
is carried far through the sky upon a multitude of horses; ||| 10 ||
Stealing away the light, it was like a chariot with a single, throbbing wheel. ||26||
He who, as if with the desire to devour a thousand massed serpents,
caused the circle of mountains to shatter while making the earth’s surface appear like a path through the clouds by the wind of his wings.
The seven great oceans, being agitated, became one.
He who, though dwelling within the interior of the cosmic egg, perceived that he had not at all emerged from his own tiny egg;
whose eyelashes were narrowed by the confinement of the walls of the quarters of space—
The mental state is sluggish, tending toward flight, and ill-situated. ||28||
He who, even in his childhood, descended into the great ocean—
the very essence of which was captured in sport by the forms of an elephant and a tortoise—
was gazed upon by the tremulous eyes of the terrified wives of the *alagardas*.
The Tortoise became the support for the people who were terrified by the trembling of the earth. ||29||
Having reflected thus, Tārkṣya extracted the essence of nectar from the ocean of milk— though it was guarded by the gods— from within its depths,
seizing with the tip of his beak the broad lotus-stalks held by Śeṣa.

The royal swan on the banks of the lotus-lake within the depths of Pātāla. (A Kulaka of six verses) How [could he be seen] by one who somehow emits the rays of the jewels upon his fingers— the tips of his copper-red, jagged hoods— acting as claws?
The earth, entering the cavity of the netherworld with speed, was propped up by his arm of formidable coils.
Being shattered by the hard tips of the hooves planted by the Great Boar as he lifted up the circle of the earth,
[the mountains] were covered with masses of reddish-brown dust like fresh vermilion powder.
Even his jewels possess the beauty and sweetness of the piṣṭātaka flower.
The Enemy of Mura made that very ocean, which has the end of a kalpa as its limit, his sole abode for his bed;
[he who witnessed] the wondrous movements of the three worlds having entered within his belly— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.]
His sleep of meditative absorption was interrupted by the confusion of speech. ||33||
He is the Residue, from whose dancing strides— sufficient for the cosmic dissolution and causing the world to bow down—
the earth somehow slips from the shoulder-peaks of the elephants of the quarters.
Holding onto a blade of durva grass, he gasps deeply, overcome with exhaustion.
Who indeed could bear to look upon the wrath of that moon-crested Lord in battles— a wrath terrifying with the knitting of his brows—
nor upon his trident, which instills fear with its three prongs?
And with glances that possessed a form neither bewildering nor fierce— (this is a *kulaka* of five verses)—
she who, seeing the host of Dānavas intent on flight in battle, was laughing;
The brilliant white splendor, flashing from the jewels in his teeth, shone as if it were the pale beauty of the slopes of the Himalayan peaks at dawn. ||36||
Who could withstand her on the field of battle— she who makes the three worlds tremble, who covers the expanse of the sky with her staff-like arms,
and whose passion for unrestrained dancing at the destruction of the world [is so intense]?
One might endure the fierce power of the enemy of Smara as if it were his mere play.
(A pair of verses) On whose temples the roots of trees are ruthlessly uprooted by the force of the wind from the swinging, powerful flapping of his ears;
Even the mountains, having fallen, bear the beauty of swarms of bees clinging to them out of greed for the flowing ichor.
Even the mountain of the gods could not, by any means, be uprooted by the collisions of the peaks of his lofty shoulders; yet,
as he rubs against the surface of his cheek, the river of ichor flows forth.
Like a Mālanapādapa tree, he attains glory. ||39||
From whose single tusk-staff, white as a digit of the moon, there issued forth a mass of foam-like necklaces rolling upon his chest—
a stream that mottled the walls of the sky’s path with the brilliance of moonlight.
Like the Mandākinī river flowing forth from the Himavat mountain.
In whose stainless sky-lake the orb of the moon bears the beauty of a red lotus,
with its straight rays as filaments and its formidable base as the stalk of a lotus-root.
[He] whose hand-staff was momentarily grasped [by her] as she playfully cast it aside. ||41||
At the assembly of Gāṅgāyani, by the fall of his horn like a thunderbolt, the mountain range of the Dānava clans was shattered,
strewn with the fragments of its formidable skeletal rocks.
In an instant, he will lighten the burden of this earth. (A Kulaka of five verses:
With his thick, long neck raised up, as if out of passion he wished to kiss the row of clouds;
He who is gazed upon with impetuous longing by the peacock,
whose plumage, shimmering with grace, covers the expanse of the sky above.
He who, in his childhood, during the periods of universal dissolution, sportively struck with his lotus-like hand the jewel-ball that was the orb of the sun and tossed it about upon the earth.
She gazes with love upon the one who has the bewildering moon as his crest-ornament.
To that Skanda, who is the Mandara mountain for uprooting the Goddess of Fortune from the milk-ocean churned by the lord of the Daityas,
and whose sharp tip was blunted by the merciless crushing of Mount Krauñca;
No one here among the asuras is capable of enduring her power. (The Tilaka mark.
Her body is beautified by a mass of swaying peacock feathers, and she possesses the splendor of the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā) due to her unfathomable depth.
Capable of crushing the one whose banner is a peacock in battle, he possesses the splendor of Acyuta, like [Kṛṣṇa] who swiftly struck Kāliya. ||46||
At the time of being granted an audience by the moon-crested Lord who daily occupies the threshold of the gate,
they hold him in high esteem by virtue of that very sight.
Even those in the lotus posture and others [are unable to stop] the falling glances. ||47||

Who indeed would dare to withstand, in battle, the trident of the son of Śilāda— a trident that has swallowed the ocean with its mass of sparks from the fire of the sun’s orb at the dissolution of the world?
He might be able to endure the son of Śilādatta in battle,
but he could not endure the continuous whirling caused by the passion for combat at the onset of the fray, with his head being violently shaken during the assault.
(A pair of verses) At the front of the battle, [he would be] one whose head is tossed about in the midst of the attack...
Death cannot endure even the tumultuous *ṭāṃkāra* sound of Caṇḍeśvara’s fierce frown, which crushes the fragments of the skull of Mauleya as it strikes against it. 49.
Even Krodheśvara,
providing satisfaction for the elephant of Yama by means of the trunks of his sword— heads that had rolled in battle after their necks were severed— performs his ordinance.
Like heaps of earth on the battlefield, it was impossible even to look at. ||50||

Even Indra became terrified of him, whose splendor lay in eyes that possessed the beauty of a transformation as lovely as a circle of full-orbed moons. He was like a peacock to the one who had destroyed the sacrifice.
How is it that he, Vīrabhadra, is not even considered by you? ||51||
I have no fear of those other delusions— the revolutions of the world and the play of its whims, which manifest as the confusion of days of dissolution; nor do I have any concern for their course.
I have no fear regarding the inner meaning; surely there is no partiality in my speaking words that contain the essence of policy toward them. ||52||
Therefore, having abandoned all talk of dispute, exert yourselves to grasp the nectar-like essence of the ocean of activity churned by the mountain of wisdom’s discernment.
O Asura warriors, will you not surely meet death by encountering him? ||53||
Someone who is afflicted by even a slight transgression at critical junctures will inevitably meet with a calamitous consequence;
indeed, one who has a carbuncle [is harmed] by even a blade of kusha grass, a sprout, a thorn, or the like.
He is pierced incessantly during the risings of the Kulikas. ||54||
For the manliness of one desiring to conquer the enemy force— which is unrestrained by the itching sensation of constant combat and which possesses a radiant splendor—
is indeed a state devoid of the complexities of political strategy.
It does not shine, like a lotus from which the seed-vessel has been extracted. ||55||
O Daityas, do not despise the host of gods, who possess a vast and invincible prowess in battles;
for the noble-minded call them "ungraspable" by their enemies.
In this world, where valor is unrestrained, dullness is not met with fortitude. ||56||

They do not desire that the dense thicket of effects— which must be accomplished through the specific application of the excellence of wisdom— be abandoned by delusion; for it is to be pierced by the mass of flames from a blazing lamp.
When was form ever pierced by blinding darkness? (57)
Some are distinguished by the quality of valor, some by policy, and others likewise by both;
yet others possess a conduct that is entirely independent of those two.
By the power of divine influence, they attain prosperity. ||58||
Every undertaking born of the efforts of those of perverse intellect inevitably results in something else entirely and with a different fruit;
for the *śarabha* [attacking] the elephant's back merely serves to scratch its itch.
He constantly brings about destruction by means of that [which] leads him to ruin. ||59||
O Lord of the Daityas, restrain your wrath toward others; let this impetuous, martial prowess be set aside for now. Let him first be honored in the assembly through the mouth of an envoy.
These are the words of him who wears the crescent of the moon as his ornament.
Thus, having uttered this jewel of a speech, the ocean-like son of Diti ceased,
his cheeks being kissed by the intense luster of the pearl-ornaments released from his ears, as if out of satisfaction with their manifest qualities of logic.
Possessing unfathomable fortitude, he stood firm upon that ground as if with a pure intellect. ||61||

Thus ends the thirty-sixth canto, titled "The Introduction of Kanakākṣa," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel [of its title], composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
The Thirty-seventh Canto.
Having thus addressed these words to the enemy of the gods there...

While [the assembly] remained silent, Vajrabāhu, letting out a loud laugh with upturned face and filled with indignation, began to speak thus in the assembly: "Then he commenced to speak, his chest expanding with a yawn. (1)
O Kāñcanākṣa, if even Uśanas were able to speak such words as these, which you have uttered with the essence of political wisdom,
then even my preceptor would find it difficult to hear this, let alone to speak it.
What indeed could one of naturally dull intellect say? ||2||
Relying merely on its outward form, let the flower of the *vibhītaka* indeed mock the beauty of the *madhuka*;
yet it cannot rival the moist spray of droplets from its trickling, lovely nectar.
Whence, moreover, could its state of being a filament arise?
Nevertheless, some degree of intolerance on the part of the world of enemies compels me to express this unfavorable view;
for herein lies the establishment of my own position.
But those sons of Diti who see [this], let them go forth here.
You are worthy to grasp even this subtle word of mine,
for you are free from the conceptual constructions of non-discrimination;
for is not even a tiny drop of nectar and pollen gathered by bees?
For sweetness is indeed derived from honey, not from the Madhūka flower.
Or perhaps, because I am intoxicated, my speech does not rise up to touch the hearts of you who possess cultivated intellects;
for how could sprays of nectar moisten the salt ocean?
The source of the digit of the moon, white with dense radiance.

Those who, with their hands, uprooted even Mount Mandara— whose central portion had been thinned by the playful rubbing of the coils of Vāsuki— and who did so without encountering any resistance or blow;
In their ease, they shone, having accomplished the tasks for which their powers were intended. ||7||
These too, who were arrogant in unrestrained combat, having shattered [their foes] with the staff-like arms of their shoulders whose hair stood on end in pride; [and who,
by their mere] roar, caused the trembling King of the Gods—
Who could withstand them in battle when they have their hands joined in the *abhaya* mudrā?
(A pair of verses) How could those with tremulous eyes ever prevail in the presence of the son of Siṃhī as he suddenly rises up in combat?
Alas, tell me, O messenger, if your Pramathas and monkeys, being naturally fickle, remain there without fear! 9.
In whose battles his form, harsh with sparks of fire, scorched the three worlds like a blazing sun of fierce majesty;
and as if exhausted by the weight of that very heat, his sword—
The goddess of his enemies' fortune dwelt for a long time in the shower-house.
By the hosts of serpent-wives who had been taken captive, unable to endure his majesty as it were,
a state of looseness was manifested due to their weakness born of despondency.
With the circles of their white silken garments and bodices slipping down.
In whose battles, amidst the perils of fear, he grew great by the succession of the breath-winds of his enemies—
[breaths] consumed by the specific heat and intensity of Bhīṣma’s fierce radiance.
His majesty is more intense than a hundred fierce lineages of enmity. ||12||
The swords of his enemies, which had split trees mercilessly, were raised on high in agitation;
yet by the clusters of flower-buds that were their own drawn-out fame, those very swords brought him no distress.
The quarters [of the sky] were filled with spreading winds from the falling of creepers. ||13||

The Fortune of Sovereignty, taking refuge at his feet, bestowed her radiant hand upon him whose arms were the sacrificial posts for the altar of battle against invincible enemies, while the world-protectors, inclined toward bowing before him, [offered their tribute].
Her playful lotus-face was clouded by her sighs.
Why would Subāhu— who bears the fragrance of battle— turn his back on the snowy mountain of white fame?
Having crossed over [the enemy], he has reached the shores of the ocean, just as the sun reaches the shores of the sea after traversing the sky.
His prowess became even more intense, pervading all directions. (A Kulaka of six verses:
With eyes crimson with fury, he whose smile was as white as an autumn cloud sent forth small clouds whirled by his sighs.
He trembled as if deeply pierced by her glances, which were filled with agitation produced by the play of her thick, tawny eyebrows and her knitted brows. ||16||
The frown upon his face, manifesting spreading darkness, throbs playfully with a gathered form;
it is a marvel that the faces of the wives of his enemies [are eclipsed] by it.
He brought his long locks of hair to a state of complete graying. ||17||
The interior [of this hall] is turned tawny by the mass of shimmering rays from fragments of red jewels set in the hanging pillars;
it is a banquet for drinking the blood of the host of assassins.
The blade of his sword acted as if it were a suitable [partner] for her. 18.
During the tumultuous storms of battle, may the splendor of the crescent moon find peace and ease through the dark clouds of my sword or through the water from its blade.
O Lord of the Daityas, why is he being led away? Is it not Nīlakaṇṭha? ||19||
Even for me, on the forefront of battle, the discus of Murāri was seen springing forth from my chest,
like the sun rising over the slope of the eastern mountain.
The solar disc was as crimson as blood, like a portion [of the sky] stained by gore. ||20||
The fame of my world-enemy, once as white as a jasmine bud, has suddenly turned dark;
now there flow tears stained with the soot-like impurity of collyrium.
Afterwards, there were the tears from the eyes of the women with shapely hips. ||21||

The Discus (Cakra) suddenly performed an embrace with him, whose sprouts of thick horripilation had burst forth and who was moistened by the nectar of affection— a state unattainable even by hundreds of the edges of other weapons.
The body of the moon, exceeding its usual flow [of light], was like the beloved of Rāhu. ||22||
While the immortals gazed on, [the weapon] became terrifying with thousands of streams of sparks from the harsh fire-breath of his spittle;
then, snatching that jeweled earring from his palm—
"I shall now swiftly set the wheel of injustice in motion. (A pair of verses.
Having previously encountered the edge of the sword—the cause of total delusion—in battles, like the wielder of the plow [Balarāma] encountering wine;
Surely, in the past, your slender bodies must have fallen, with your beauty of eyes reddened by swirling blood. 24.
Whether he be armed with a discus in battle, or armed with a mace, or armed with a trident, or armed with a thunderbolt—
I shall slay those very weapons with this very arm of mine.
In my emptiness, I shall reduce the complexion of your face to a pale ashen hue. ||25||

It is quite clear that those of exalted intellect, having set out upon the path of policy, have performed their duty with such instability as if mounted on a swing; yet it is my conviction that this task was already accomplished. 26.
O Lord of the Gods, what is the use of much praise? For now,
I shall make myself resemble a lake dried up by the heat of summer— once as lovely as the laughter of the swans and the essence of the lotuses that had descended there.
I shall strike down that army of your enemies, mixed with crows.
Even Tārkṣya, at the onset of battle, will surely fall with his head shattered by the blow of my fist,
after having swallowed thousands of serpents whose venom has been rendered ineffective.
With eyes closed as if from the onset of the darkness of a swoon. ||28||

By whose arrow, which ascended far upward, the three ancient cities were reduced to ashes by a fire whose mass of matted locks was formed by the flames leaping from the orb of the sun, its heat now dulled.
And with his eyes, he whose body was like that of the god of love shone forth with force. ||29||
When her followers had been slain by me in battle, Jyotsnāvatī remained with the burning pain of her grief unrestrained,
like a banner-top whose tuft of hair has turned white with age.
[They are] encircled by white chowries with handles like staffs. (A pair of verses.
When your fame, shining with stainless luster, dispels the darkness across the circle of the quarters like the moon upon your crest, [the world is illuminated].
O Lord of Asuras, the shadow of the Enemy of Smara (Śiva) clearly shines forth above with exceeding intensity; this is surely his dwarf-form.
O you who shake the three worlds, be gracious; let this frown of yours on your broad forehead dispel the dense darkness that has been bound upon you, O you who are difficult to withstand in battle.
And now the army, with its circle of enemies trembling, [advances].
In this battle, where the interior of the mountain-caves of the gods resounds with the twang of the slender bow whose string vibrates, and which contains within it the son of Danu—
how much fortitude can be maintained by one who is not entirely restrained?
Śambhu [was embraced] by the daughter of the Himālayas with her body and by [the Lord] with his heart. ||33||
I shall forcibly tear away from his body that which has been applied as a powder made from the essence of a mass of pale, clustered fame, using it to shatter the betel-nut fruits of his enemies.
As if out of a passion for the red dye of betel, the betel vines [clung to them]. ||24||
The river with its pure waters mottled by the long-accumulated streaks of smoke from the fire of the blazing eye on Hara’s forehead—
smoke that issued forth from the orb of the cool-rayed moon.
She bore a complexion that seemed as if followed by the hue of the mark on his forehead. ||35||
Let the Mandākinī flow upon his head, its splendor filling the sky with the loud, resonant humming from the thickets of his matted locks,
like the rays of the sun rising with impetuous force at the end of an aeon.
By the force of the falling of fierce fire, spears,
and arrows, even Mahiṣadhvaja will bring about the withering [of his enemies] in battle now that Caṇḍī has found some opening as she quivers [with power]. (A pair of verses)
Or perhaps it was out of remorse for having slain the elephant that was itching with pride in its mastery of battle, crushed by the impact of his feet. ||37||
The form of Heramba, with his tusk uprooted like a pestle, his temples drenched in the thick blood flowing from frontal globes split by arrows,
and his trunk-tips smeared with the mud of uprooted lotus stalks; the elephant turned—
I shall make her leaf-like, as a lordly elephant does a lotus pond. ||38||
With the tips of my lofty arms covering the sky, standing firm like a girdle of mighty serpents and unshakable,
may you not break my wings as you did the lordly Krauñca mountain.
Having encountered him, neither Guha nor Śakti could release their arrows before striking him down. ||39||
Now, having taken up his bow-staff— which has a string as terrifying as the lord of serpents, Śeṣa— made of gold,
he who has effortlessly conquered Śiva with an arrow by force...
I shall now, this very moment, pierce even the seven worlds from afar.
Beheld by the circles of gods and asuras filled with wonder, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow suddenly severed the head of Caṇḍeśvara,
as if out of weariness arising from his repeated traversing of the worlds.
The joints of its vast skull were shattered by the blow of his playful sport. ||41||
On this day of battle, I, whose complexion is tawny like the flickering flames of a blazing fire,
cast my shadow over the son of Śilāda.
He was like the sun at midday, possessing incomparable majesty. ||42||
Where will Krodheśvara go, he who encircles his own neck with a wreath of smoke from the fire of his *huṃ* utterance,
and who is bold enough to swallow even Time itself in a single mouthful?
As if its circumference were obstructed by his noose at the front of the battle. ||43||
With its peak like a jar of thick bones, marked by the lines of gifts bestowed with the sword, and possessing the beauty of a splendid trunk,
my arm is capable in an instant of [crushing] every rival king.
Displaying his sport in order to overcome Vīrabhadra in battle. ||44||
By those sons of Diti, even Samavartin was broken in battle along with his majesty and his rod of punishment;
they would be worthy recipients of great honor in the performance of the seven-threaded sacrifice.
Who indeed would praise the chest of these [heroes], other than Vīrabhadra? ||45||
When I roar with a loud cry upon the battlefield,
the host of enemies abandons its pride;
for that sound belongs only to a lion, who is terrifying.
By hearing which, the entire host of Māras becomes dispirited. ||46||
I believe that very speech [was uttered] by him whose mind was inflamed with rage at the enemy's malice during battles,
in which the exceedingly fierce and impartial wheel of the King of Justice (Dharmarāja) was shattered.
The bh.kuṭī of Dhānibhaṭa, for the purpose of repair. ||47||

Beholding the faces of his enemies as they died, the powerful warrior, whose arms were resplendent on the battlefield and who possessed a continuous flash of luster, instantly crushed his foes. As he looked upon those dead, he saw only the supreme state of the departed.
I am truly unable to achieve equality with my Lord. ||48||
The enemy host, with its formidable *pīlu* trees in the form of upraised arms and its beauty composed of ranks of soldiers,
does not long remain upon the battlefield-forest of that great warrior’s bow.
Like a doe startled by the sound of a *ṭāṃkāra* cry, Lakṣmī [vanished]. ||49||
In the battles between the gods and the Daityas, may [the weapons] strike with drops of spray that cause a hissing sound as they are released by their hands,
following the path of the hollows of the trunks slipping from the interiors of the frontal globes.
Like intoxicated elephants with clusters of pearls dropped from their trunks.
In battle, they drew their bows, making the quarters of the sky appear as circles,
while the twanging of those bows was as deep as the roar of the ocean when its waters are agitated by a tempest.
Afflicted by the agitation produced upon hearing the roar of the bowstring. ||51||
Let him sportively devour the lord of the day, bearing an ear-loop marked by a circle of golden earrings,
out of a lingering desire for the severed bracelets on his neck.
Today Rāhu, as it were, has swallowed the clear golden disc of the sun hanging down. ||52||

With the appearance of a mass of droplets from the spray of her tears, she seems to scatter forth intensely the rays of the lunar seed-syllable (*candrabīja*); surely, when the moon has been swallowed by this [fire],— [The eyes] of the one whose eyes have become like the petals of a blue lotus... (the rest of the verse follows).
Because of the mother’s extreme grief, which was the cause of his birth from her. ||53||
When the internal vital airs were reeling from the profound exhaustion caused by sleeplessness due to continuous grief,
and even though he was of a suitable lineage, he became emaciated through the oppression of the asuras.
Let the breeze now attain fullness.
[The army] was being surged by waves of horses that were swift and unattached, like moving mountains consisting of tall, auspicious elephants;
[the army] whose limbs were turned to glowing coals by the sparks from the weapons of the asuras.
The hero-warriors were stationed in the courtyard of the sky, which was joined to their laps.
The circular array of the army’s warriors, adorned with wonderful maneuvers and skilled in the four types of combat— truth, falsehood, wheel-weapons, and the four modes of death—
was fashioned from gold and decorated with iron arrows.
May there soon be a fierce battle with the moon as its crest-ornament! (A pair of verses.
On the path of the clash, even the aged warriors, their complexions white with age, appear like clusters of playful chowries.
O Lord of the Daityas, these [serpents], having mounted with impetuosity,
are capable of propelling even the wind before you.
As the lords of the asuras repeatedly turned toward the clash of his fierce majesty with their upraised clusters of leaf-like arms,
they were like lotus groves before the moonlight of the night-maker.
Even the stainless fame of the Moon-crested Lord falters. ||58||
The drops of perspiration on his brow were like droplets of water from the exertion of scattering pearls released when he split the frontal globes of elephants shedding ichor;
they resembled the furrows of the knitted brows of the enraged God of Death.
"May this small sword of mine be formidable in battle. (59)
Let Śukra arrange the composition of the battle arrays;
however, O Lord, your power is irresistible in combat.
Let there be a formation that brings about beauty, while the remainder—
For the pupil of the eye, being free from turbidity, does not look [at its own reflection]. ||60||
Out of anger, this [weapon] is capable of annihilating even the three worlds, including the entire circle of gods and asuras, in an instant;
let it be raised at the front of the battle like the Night of Doom.
Perception has a fierce and crooked brow in the form of a curved knife.
Their shoulders were formed by the broad manes shimmering upon the hard throat-pits of Narasiṃha, which had been playfully torn away;
their pearl necklaces were melted by the heat of their valor, like moonstones.
These [elephants] have chests made formidable by the spray of water droplets.
The warriors of the Daityas, filled with the longing for their mothers and the desire for battle, flash forth intensely in your assembly for the sake of destroying the gods;
for among those possessed of splendor, there is a certainty in the destruction of darkness.
Is there indeed any natural distinction anywhere even in the three worlds? (A pair of verses) In this world, which is to be enjoyed by heroic men alone,
what is this desire of yours for the conceptualization of divisions?
Indeed, the lions, having easily subdued the deer, dwell at their pleasure throughout the entire circle of the forest.
By whom even Time was made to have his reddish eyes drenched by a spray of tears following upon the bursting of his heart due to the intensity of excessive torment,
as he clung to his neck with hands pressed tightly against it—
In battles, his noose was forcibly dragged away by him. ||65||
What comparison can there be between the gods and the race of the asura kings?
For lions do not become one with deer.
[The lion] shatters the frontal globes of the scent-blind elephants of darkness by the division of his rut-fluid.
With the tips of his quivering claws ever raised, he may sometimes be a lion, or perhaps the lord of beasts;
yet I consider neither of these two to be a fit object of praise. (A pair of verses)
By him, the moving mountain of elephants was playfully felled with a mere stroke from the tip of his throbbing thunderbolt-like hand.
Thus, as if applying a smear of sandalwood paste to his cheeks under the guise of the radiance of pearl earrings, the hero [Vīra],
whose head was beautiful with a nod made formidable by a crest-jewel, spoke these words to the warriors:
Having spoken thus to the assembly of Andhaka while beginning his composition of praise, he became silent.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh canto, titled "The Manifestation of Vajrabāhu," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by jewels, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
Now begins the thirty-eighth canto:
Then, while that enemy of the gods stood there, having uttered words filled with burgeoning fury, [the following occurred].
The messenger, whose firmness was unshakable due to his vigor, spoke these words once again.

Victorious is that singular Intellect alone, which dispels the darkness obscured by the lamp of scripture, which carries an unimpaired wealth of intuition, and which, as the cause of worldly activity, effects the definitive determination of reality. 2.
The tongue of embodied beings incessantly distinguishes the entire collection of their sensory organs;
therein Sarasvatī, whose intellect is perfected through inference arising from that which has not yet emerged, establishes her foundation.
When a servant who seeks his own welfare speaks at the three times of day to his Lord— whose mind is solely imbued with devotion and who is auspicious throughout the three periods of time—
those of noble conduct will surely not disregard him quickly.
Some perceive even from this [world] the transformation into misfortune. ||4||

And by the jewels of words from this ocean of Daityas, which entered deep within the cavities of their ears, the dense darkness of these [demons] was dispelled, as if from the caves of the mountains on the shore. (5)

Having attained the form of a golden vessel, the speech of the virtuous— carrying an inexhaustible sweetness— acts as the cause for the birth of auspicious seeds, because it has grasped the state of being perfectly round through its exceedingly well-rounded heart.
And what lotus-stamen here would not take away the beauty of the lotus? ||6||
O Lord of the Daityas, the intense longing for battle among these warriors flashes forth before us like a thundering rain-cloud filling the quarters of the sky with its deep resonance.
They shine forth like the crescent moons of fire-crested peacocks. ||7||
Do not think that these words are excellent simply because they are being dissected by people with diverse minds;
for those who possess discernment are rare in this world, while fools are indeed beyond counting. 8.
Generally, a person of deluded mind, attributing to himself a high estimation based on qualities that are in fact meager,
maintains a mind that is full of disdain even toward those who possess great merit.
The world itself, through its frivolous conduct, becomes an object of ridicule. ||9||
Those of base intellect, having cast far away the excellence of their own conduct, boast of themselves with thousands of tongues;
yet for those of praiseworthy soul, there is surely [no such need] in the grasping of the multitude of their own virtues.
They become like elephants with their tongues lolling out. ||10||
A virtuous person, even if small in stature, surely shines by virtue of their excellence, like a bow-staff that has been set within a fine circle;
whereas a base person, in contrast to that upright and noble conduct, [is like the string].
He is considered unfit for grasping, like a person with withered arms. ||11||
I declare both him who is a virtuous person in this world and he who subsists solely on wickedness to be speakers of falsehood;
for the one [the wicked man] praises the very non-existent virtues of another.
The other, it is said, speaks of concealing even those things that truly exist. ||12||
Let the virtuous man, having attributed even to the non-existent distant virtues, speak well; let the wicked man, however, remain one whose conduct consists in denying them.
But as for him whose mind finds solace in excellence—
Even among those on the periphery, there was not even one such as he.
For the disposition of the mind is indeed won over at the very right moment by the words of a virtuous person through their extreme courtesy,
just as the fresh mango-stalk is bent when spring has arrived without ceasing.
It is rolled about by the tossing of the Malaya breeze. ||14||
Like a fresh sindhuvāra flower, the pure beauty of the lavalī creeper spreads the splendor of the face for the virtuous;
yet, like a poisonous cluster of blossoms, it causes a piercing pain in the head.
But the words of a wicked person, when repeatedly whispered into the ear, [take root]. ||15||
O beautiful one, indeed, those who bear partiality for the arts, who have conquered the wayward god of love, and who ride upon the bull—
though their speech be stained with impurity, they yet cause it to issue from their throats.
He possesses the splendor of the three-pronged weapon of Śiva, yet it is like poison to those who are virtuous.
The hearts of the great possess a profound depth, their steadfastness being unfathomable like the waters of the entire ocean emulated;
they have attained a state that serves as a refuge for those whose innate courage is slight.
But I think they bear fruit equal to that of the udumbara. ||17||
Even by means of common virtues, a man of light disposition attains great esteem; yet another, however, does not possess such esteem even through those same virtues when they are transcendent.
With a wavering mind, he exhibits the state of having a stiff neck. ||18||
May even that quality exist in this world for the contented man, in whom the radiance of all other virtues shines forth, while the multitude of stars fades away as if before the moon.
He too has pride in his mind; fie upon his lack of shame! (19)
A man attains the reputation of being a "man" only when he is adorned with a multitude of virtues as bright as the cool-rayed moon; otherwise,
even if his lineage is renowned, he remains nothing more than a mere stone, though it be a gem-mine.
Whose hands, having shattered the darkness, do not throb? ||20||
For even when the process of blooming has been undertaken,
those whose fragrance of intellect is shattered by the wind of pride and vanity possess no splendor;
they are like flowers whose only remaining part is their stalk.
Men who are devoid of virtue and of good form bring about [only] months [of hardship]. ||21||
Indeed, there are no words in this world that touch the reality of things which arise from the capricious speech of the wicked;
they consist only of self-praise and the denial of the noble conduct of virtuous people.
And how could that fool not commit sin by means of it? ||22||
"I alone am worthy; as for those qualities which do not exist in me, how could an evil person disparage them?
For one who has attained a state of being soiled by public scandal—"
Indeed, those who possess virtues are constantly pained by them.
Salutations to those who, though themselves devoid of merit, possess firm affection for the virtues of others— those who are the crowns of all virtuous people;
but as for those who, despite possessing virtues themselves, are full of envy...
My heart feels contempt for those who find fault with the excellence of another's virtues. ||24||
For that man whose very self is empty of worldly existence, who is here constantly engaged in the pursuit of grasping the virtues of others,
there is indeed a firm standing in the assembly and in the perils of battle.
Neither his tongue nor his palm bears the mark of calluses. ||25||
Oh, how wondrous is the heart of the great!
Oh, how vast is the heart of the great!
Oh, how expansive is the path to heaven for those born of the lineage of Tālavana!
For even with their slender forms, they are bound by all the pure qualities of others, serving as unrequited slaves day and night. ||26||
They do not feel envy toward the virtues of others, thinking, "These do not equal all my own virtues";
rather, they attain either equality with or even superiority over them.
And though he was born noble and virtuous, his mind became deluded by envy. ||27||
Let others be possessed by minds utterly deluded by excessive envy, or let them remain with the beauty of their complexions and faces marred;
I, however, shall become adorned with the ornaments of bristling, swelling thrills of joy.
Truly, by virtue of praising the virtues of others, I alone [am purified]. ||28||
He who cannot be satisfied by countless virtues of established excellence, even when they possess great weight within himself,
is instead easily gratified by very few qualities belonging to others.
"Oh, how marvelous is this deed of the Great One!"—thus he was struck with wonder.
It is evident that even the wicked conceal their own nature,
yet the virtuous, free from envy, constantly exalt the qualities of the righteous, even when those qualities are submerged in the thick mud of the depths of the underworld.
Like great jewels from the ocean, they emerged like the breaking of waves. ||30||
One whose mental state is seized by the malignant planet of self-conceit never finds delight in the virtues of another;
yet another person rejoices even in those virtues, however slight, as they are inevitably present.
They shine like pearls of auspiciousness in this world for those who offer the guest-water (arghya). ||31||
Let those whose minds are utterly deluded by extreme envy indeed harbor malice toward the virtues of others; however,
as for those in this world whose hearts [are otherwise]— constantly...
Those virtues do not attract others at all by means of those very qualities. ||32||
The moonbeams, cool as the ripples of the waves of nectar, have reached the pinnacle of excellence for those who are intensely envious;
indeed, for them, the virtues of others are merely instruments of pleasure.
Fie on those who harm themselves, who lack self-control, and whose births are in vain! 33.
Having given praise for the virtues of others even while remaining outside, yet burning within from the fire of the poison of envy,
the fool’s heart finds no relief through the craftsmanship of its own conceptualizations.
Having imputed some imagined fault to them... (34)
Praiseworthy indeed is that wish-fulfilling tree in the grove of Mount Sumeru, his own lineage,
by whose excellence of virtuous conduct even virtues that do not exist anywhere in the three worlds become worthy of veneration.
Like the Ganges rivers of fame flowing forth from the feet of Śauri. ||35||
It is better that the intellect be poor in brilliance; what is the use of vital energy for one devoid of wisdom?
Does the śarabha meet its destruction by leaping into the roaring ocean? No, it does not. (36)
On account of their being overwhelmed by fear, they [seemed] to be performing the graceful waving of a circle of fly-whisks as white as moonlight,
as if it were the irresistible seizing of the hair of the three worlds.
Her beauty shines forth like old age itself in flight. ||37||
"May Caṇḍikā not slay even my buffalo at the front of the battle out of her zeal for the side of the gods"—
as if bearing such fear from Yama himself, those who had conquered death cast off all apprehension.
Even those inhabitants of the third heaven were conquered by you, despite having previously been won over by the power of Yama; thus,
time has here in these three worlds become unrestrained.
"Aha! He plays with the sport of victory and defeat.
(The *tilaka*) "Not even the entire circle of gods and demons can escape the firm, long-reaching noose of the cruel elephant of Time."
He attains mastery over the playful acts of devouring and scattering the entire world, which is but a single mass of diverse forms. 40.

Even today, the womenfolk tremble at the sight of him, who was once the lord of the Daityas, by virtue of his having been filled with the mass of foam-circles swirling from the throats of the sons of Diti.
From the rows of pearl necklaces strung with pearls at their tips. ||41||
Even he, by whom hundreds of thousands of mountain peaks were reduced to fuel for the fire of the thunderbolt, was defeated in battles;
what more can be said— who indeed possesses certain victory?

Indeed, the entire world has been embraced by impermanence. (Tilaka) The oceans, distressed by the grief caused by the destruction of the earth, fill the horizons with the sounds of their clashing waves as if with cries of lamentation; they mingle with one another. (43)
The remainder [of his body] bears a broad and hollow throat, thick with a canopy of knotted and formidable veins,
and slow sighs escaping from slackened shoulders.
His thousand hoods were light in movement due to the burden having been cast off.

The lords of the elephants of the quarters do not experience the pain arising from the striking and tearing caused by the goad-like claws of the serpent Śeṣa, whose body is relaxed and contracted as he has cast off his excessive burden. 45.
Having reached the surface of the netherworld’s palate, he who made his abode upon the shell of the cosmic tortoise— dark as the creepers at the edge of the forest—
dragged [the mountain] far away with the plowshare of his staff-like arms.
as Sīrapāṇi [Balarāma] did with the Mūrvī creeper, like the daughter of Kalinda [the Yamunā]. ||46||

Where is that great lord of asuras, Hiraṇyākṣa, in the form of a boar, whom Śauri slew and suddenly raised up the earth—submerged in the netherworld—along with the splendor of the lord of the gods? (A group of five verses).
When the surface of the earth was suddenly propped up, broken...

The masses of rays from the sun, together with the luster of the jewels on the head of Śeṣa, enter the deep darkness situated in the crevice of the netherworld and encounter the throngs of serpents scorched by the sun's heat.
With a mind filled with wonder, as if desiring to sportively behold the earth agitated by the movement of the primordial pillar at the beginning of the kalpa,
[he saw] the ear-shell-like temples, their roots loosened and their bodies slackened;
The lord of tortoises stands with his neck outstretched and his feet firmly planted. ||49||
As he moves sportively through the depths of the ocean, where sea-monsters are crushed by the snapping of his fangs,
the earth appears as a mere target within the cavity of his long ear.
Because its water had been drunk up, it was visible in front [of him]. ||50||
Struck by the wind from his nostrils and falling back into the depths of the netherworld,
the earth quickly assumes once more the pale-white luster of moonbeams grasped firmly by his claws.
The earth, its circle of mountains shattered by the blows of his snout and its surface of the netherworld upturned by the expanse of his body,
shines as if it were the site where the broad hood of Śeṣa has been cast off.
With white fangs that firmly grasp the moon.
Shaking his massive body and striking his snout with a deep, gurgling, and terrible roar,
he scatters the masses of thick clouds— those unbroken formations— with the blows of wind from his mane.
Their graceful gait, which had been hindered by the clouds covering the path of the sky over the region of the Potra mountain,
now falters as they contemplate entering the interior of another world.
The breezes take refuge in the hollows of the ears that have been pierced. ||54||
The earth is honored by the hosts of stars falling swiftly toward it, struck by the wind from his shaking mane,
as if offered by the palms of the goddesses of the quarters.
It was as if a mass of the finest pearls were clinging to the ship's prow.
As he assumed a body that pervaded the entire universe, shining with the dark luster of a polished, stainless sword-blade,
the sky seemed to lose its capacity for space, as if the whole firmament were hidden within him under the guise of his own reflection.
Enveloped by the darkness of the subterranean abyss as if by a new cloud-blue veil,
it was surrounded by an obscurity so profound that it was difficult to discern, while the nocturnal gloom was thickened by the sun being blocked by the broad surface of the plowshare.
His fangs reveal his form as it rises up into the sky. ||57||
Thus I behold the earth, uprooted from its surface by Hari in his boar-form, appearing like the city of that [boar] and as dark as a cloud;
it is as white as a kunda-creeper and resembles the bulbous root of a lotus.
Hanging from the tips of his fangs like the teeth of a saw— (this is a group of eleven verses)—

in the circle of his hand-timer, his five-facedness finally attains its true meaning in that terrible mouth where the clear reflection of his own face, appearing as he prepares to tear it apart, clearly arises. (58–59)
And her tongue, emerging from the cave of her mouth which has opened wide in a yawn, bears the hue of a flame of fire;
it quivers with the wind of her breath over her deep-set navel.
With the playful grace of pale-red lotus petals, gently swaying as they breathe.
As if out of an impetuous desire for instruction and advice through its deep, exceedingly loud, gurgling, and terrible roar,
a mass of clouds at the time of cosmic dissolution rises up into the path of the sky.
By the collisions with the wind from their manes shaken by their fury. ||61||
A fire, with its circle of thick sparks, falls from the cave-like mouths and bellies of the hideous [demons],
like the mountain of the gods (Meru) when its heaps of jewels are scattered by the unrestrained winds of the cosmic dissolution.
Resembling a mass of lightning reflected in a shadow,
she shines as she falls upon the chest of the son of Diti, red with rage;
she is like the lotus-navel of Viṣṇu dwelling within, concealed inside.
Her vision was as if clouded by the flow of the fetus and the honeyed mace. ||63||
The moon’s orb falls from the midst of the sky before him, its mane and tail whisked away by the wind,
as if in a frantic struggle against his sharp-pointed claws that rend it.
As if to seize his very form, which had been instantly made its target. ||64||

Terrified by the roar of the "huṃ" syllable uttered in fury, which resembles the whirling tongues of fierce, blazing fire, the quarters of the sky become filled with clouds streaked by flashes of red lightning like scattered rays of light. (65)
Hearing that piercing sound, more terrible than the thundering of clouds at the time of universal dissolution that has surpassed the roar of the ocean's depths,
they shrank within their own limbs under the weight of fear.
They desire to enter as if from afar, like elephants of the quarters.

As if transformed by the edge of a discus held in their hands, the tips of their fingernails, being whirled around with sharpness, pierce through the broad bones of the collarbones and the chest. (67)
Where has that Daitya gone, who had overrun the entire world, whose destruction the poet Murāri thus brought about in his lap, as if it were a fine drama with a noble hero?
Your protector Hiraṇyakaśipu, along with his kinsmen—(a group of ten verses).

With his toe-tips reddened by the luster of the jewels on the crowns of the hosts of gods and demons, he first withdrew his own form in a dwarfed state; thereafter, the fortune of the Dānava lineage was destroyed.
With their limbs and joints pressed together, moving with some difficulty as they turn slightly toward the rivers,
they proceed upstream through the exceedingly narrow openings of the belly.
Having established their foothold, they were being shattered by the waves of the ocean.
From the water-pot in the hand of the Lord of Obstacles, who was offering oblations,
a white lotus fell along with the long stalk;
and from his lotus-seat and water-vessel, a staff—
In his foot, which shattered the fragments of the shell-like lids of the cosmic eggs.

The faces of the quarters quickly turn dark at the foot of Him who has risen to traverse the entire world, whose splendor is like the playful luster of the Yamunā, while the faces of the wives of the Daityas flash with the brilliance of that very foot.

Upon his lotus-feet, which shone with a luster that filled the space obstructed by the shell of the cosmic egg— the abode of the worlds— and which were honored by the other feet of the serpent Śeṣa at the very edge of the netherworld;
The earth, as it enters [the underworld], somehow manages to support itself.
As he rises to leap across the worlds, the host of the Seven Sages, arranged in a clockwise circle reaching down to his ankles,
shines with the grace of jeweled armlets upon his foot.
With the radiance of the orbs of the moon and sun held for a moment by his outstretched arms, and with the sky shrouded by that light,
he bears a splendor as if another beautiful conch had been fashioned.
Her form, leaping with great speed, was like a wheel. ||75||
By the shimmering of the golden bowl rising up from the impact of his unimpeded staff-like foot, which leaps across the three worlds,
the sovereignty of Maghavan over the thirty gods is being uplifted.
Like a playful parasol for the lineage of the gods. ||76||
Thus, by the conquest of the entire world, where indeed has the fortune of the Dānava Bali gone before the feet of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
together with those feet that have been washed by Viriñca?
With showers of water from the vessels held in their lotus-like hands— (this group of nine verses)—
even the navel-lotus of the Enemy of Mura, who reclines upon the coils of Śeṣa pressed down by the weight of his playful sport, [is sprinkled].
By which [hand], together with the heart of the daughter of the ocean, it was made to tremble through the striking of the tips of its palm. ||78||
The lotus from the navel of Hari, struck by the waves, masses of clouds, and winds in the ocean,
is made to blossom even now by the friction of his palms.
Trembling as if from the agitation of the memory of slaughter. ||79||

Where indeed has that Madhu gone, who, together with Kaiṭabha, vanished when the waters were pervaded by the blood from the crushing of his limbs by the hand of the Primeval Person— blood from which the crimson throats of the peacocks with blossoming plumage were clearly distinguished?
The great crocodiles, with their gaping mouths, moved about amidst the hissing breaths. (Tilaka) What is the use of praising here these many lords of great serpents,
who were slain on the battlefields by the younger brother of Indra?
In brief, O Lord of the Daityas, this expedition of the Moon-crested God against me is merely an obstacle to other news. 81.
Now, the army of the Eight-formed Lord (Śiva), clearly manifesting its punishment and having visibly loosened the bonds of its military resolve,
approaches you, white with ashes, and brings [this] about.
Trembling, like the onset of old age manifesting itself. ||82||
Its crest was variegated by the tips of its feathers, which were tawny and fierce like fire streaked with fragments of white lotus stalks;
its dense downy filaments were mottled with masses of foam.
Like a great ocean of milk with a grove of creepers. ||83||

With the slow, rolling motion of their dangling skull-cup interiors within the hollows of their crests— crests whose movement is suppressed by contact with the tips of the fresh, cool rays of the moon upon his crown;
and which, white as powdered conch-shell, are rendered noisy by the clattering "khalakhalā" sounds of stumbling— ;
The mass of water from the Mandākinī loosened the knot of the tresses of the Daughter of the Mountain. ||84||

It bore the crescent moon like a lotus stalk uprooted from the celestial river, which was being sprinkled by waves of pure water and moss floating in the bower of Kapila’s matted locks, while swan-like skulls rested upon its sandy banks. 85.
Having encountered the moon-crested Lord at the front of the battle,
their bonds of difficult-to-sustain fortitude are utterly shattered by his majesty; thus,
their pride abandoned, they become insignificant and flee in all directions.

Together with his glory, the Daityas will not remain for long. (Cakkalaka) [The city] where masses of foam, pale from being crushed by the celestial elephants whose itching temples are scratched by playing amidst the pollen within the dense, opening petals of clusters of tall lotuses;

O lords of the earth, before you, the divine river once again becomes like the beauty of intoxicated kārṇḍava birds, with its sudden waves shimmering against the tips of the breasts of the lovely wives of the gods.

The interior of their eyes, dripping profusely, was being swallowed by hovering tawny bees that resembled their throbbing eyebrows; these eyes were like the soft sprouts and buds of the *kalpa* creeper, their beauty barely visible as their lids grew slack and drooped in the pleasure of yawning, while playful maidens used them as ear-ornaments.
In the Nandana grove, the celestial women, with impetuosity, quickly efface [the marks] with their hands out of love. ||88||
Those chowries, white as moonlight, continue to shimmer in your assembly, their handles grasped by the fingertips of celestial women whose pairs of eyes are flooded with streams of tears,
for as long as the host of Gaṇas has not arrived like the hour of universal dissolution upon the seven worlds.
You behold [the goddess] who is skilled in shattering the established order of variegated forms, O Moon-crested Lord. ||89||

O lords of the Daityas, it is because you did not become moths in the fire of my wrath this very moment that my head has not attained the ornament of the garland of the circle of the command of Dhūrjaṭi. 90.
Having thus boldly challenged the lords of the Danavas with eyes reddened and parched by rage, he—
whose expansion of splendor at that moment was so heavy with weight as to obstruct the light of the sun,
and who crushed their rows of jeweled armlets whose saffron-like hue was fashioned from shaken, tawny dust— [proceeded].
With a glance like a burning coal from the corner of his eye, the messenger somehow managed to leave that assembly, though he was enraged.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth canto, titled "The Counter-Roar of the Messenger," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
Canto Thirty-Nine:
Then, having emerged from the Golden Mountain (Meru), the celestial river (Gaṅgā)...
His fatigue from the journey dispelled by the spray droplets of the waves, that preeminent attendant, plunging into the earth of immortality,
arrived at the capital of the moon-crested Lord.
Having offered salutations to him as he sat upon the floor of the assembly hall, he reported all those deeds of the enemy; then,
by his command, he reflected upon the matter of the impending battle.
Nandī is the joy of the lords of the Pramathas who inhabit the three worlds. ||2||
Then, displaying the hosts of the lords of the Gaṇas who had arrived from the netherworld, the mountains, the oceans, and the celestial abodes—
hosts who bore the crescent moon and were eager for the sight— [he approached].
With his head bowed in prostration before him, he spoke thus.
Behold, O Lord, these hosts of the Lord of the Ganas, whose mental dispositions are agitated by the desire for battle,
their various arts eager for the destruction of the entire army of the Daityas.
Their power and majesty are equal to yours alone. ||4||
Bearing matted locks, tawny like the tips of awns and ears of grain,
their binding knots loosened by the heavy speed of their celestial chariots,
they resemble the filaments at the edge of the lotus-navel of Viṣṇu.
Possessing great length, they appeared as if tawny from the dust that had settled upon them. ||5||
With one sprout-like hand, he seemed to mark the month of Āṣāḍha by displaying its joints as if it were a single month;
with the other, he was intent on crushing the lotus-seat.
He shone with a water-pot that resembled the foot of a swan.
He shone with a circular rosary of jewel-beads, beautiful with its massed, pure, and auspicious seeds,
and he bore a variegated deerskin draped over his shoulder.
It was like a region of the sky, with its upward-pointing stars clinging to it. ||7||
With a circle of rays from the emerald set in the beautiful necklace resting upon the peak of his finger-ring,
he was like a lotus pond with a white lotus serving as his seat.
Bearing that which is the cause for the production of another fragment. ||8||
The Creator himself, whose hair was turned tawny by the pollen from the tips of the lotuses on his seat as they were shaken off,
scattered [the flowers] amidst the celebration of the imminent destruction of the Daityas.
Like clouds of fragrant powder, it approaches the quarters of the sky, making a humming sound. (A group of five verses) The Śārṅga bow resounds,
its string blazing like the flames of the fire at the end of an aeon, fixed upon its firmly joined ends.
Licked by the luster of Śauri’s coral bracelets, it was like the surging orb of an agitated ocean. ||10||
Touched by the tips of the rays of the Kaustubha gem— which, resting upon the cloth on his chest, was clearly reddish-pink—
the face appeared as if it were a pond of blue lotuses that had spontaneously released its blossoms.
With impetuous haste, he draws his sword from its scabbard.
The arm of this [hero], possessing the luster of a garland of flax flowers, with its blade of a sword that is stainless yet formidable,
[attains] a terrifying state upon the battlefields of Kalinda—
He fell like a torrent of water upon the serpent Kāliya.
Bearing her face unveiled and eager for battle, its surface licked by the cresting rays of her slightly copper-hued Kaustubha gem,
she was engaged in a drinking bout of the wine-like blood of the lord of the Daityas.
O Lord of the Gods, his mace appears as if it were suited to him. ||13||
With his hand placed upon it, this [lotus] possesses the beauty of a slightly blossomed lily bud,
overspread by the moonlight of his teeth which has the luster of kunda flowers.
The moon-crested Lord bears the form of Pāñcajanya. ||14||
The discus resting upon his lotus-hand shines forth, being surpassed by the rays of the Kaustubha gem situated on his chest;
it appears as if its redness had been freshly released by the stroke of a sharp chisel.
It was like the orb of the sun made crimson by a downpour of rain. ||15||

Even the Lord of Puloma’s daughter did not release his thunderbolt, which possessed a crest of thousands of points as fierce as the flowing venom of the Daityas, and whose smoke blackened the faces of the quarters of the sky.
He has arrived, bearing a form like the interior of a dark blue cloud. ||16||
Mounting upon a conch-shell swan whose white luster rests upon the tips of the petals of his ears, which have been shaken by his playful movement,
the fire shines forth with radiant splendor.
Like the light of the sun upon a white lotus. ||17||

Behold this [elephant], whose high temples are like the peaks of the Añjana mountain, which— like the mountain itself— conceals the rays of the sun with a mass of darkness from the streams of ichor flowing from its powerful body.
Having ascended [the chariot] out of a passion for battle, he was joined by the wind.
Like a cloud, gleaming with the golden luster of lightning and possessing flames as dark as a mass of collyrium smoke from the dissolution of the world,
it swiftly moves away after having alighted upon the elephant.
Behold, O Lord of the Immortals, here is Yama, grasping his staff. ||19||
Bearing a formidable face with bristling whiskers and matted locks, and with tawny hair standing erect as if manifesting a desire to swallow the three worlds in a single mouthful—
like the terrifying countenance of the Primordial Boar (Ādivarāha).
Terrible, as it split the hollows of the earth with the impact of its snout. ||20||
Bearing a gaze as copper-red with blood as if it were the remaining *karavīra* flowers from all the people he had slaughtered without exception,
he mounted a wild boar fierce with its unbroken tusks.
Death approaches him from the front, hastening with joy.
(A pair of verses) Behold, they display the sky— connected with the twilight— as if by the flickering, tawny crests of lightning.
O Lord, the Yātudhānas approach, their bodies so dark with the luster of collyrium that they cause the spreading light of the sun to vanish. 22.
Like the noose of the Ender (Yama) touching its victim, the wielder of the noose (Varuṇa),
having mounted his elephant Supratīka, approaches;
he is drawn along by the force of the wind from the tips of his swaying ears.
A pearl necklace with its pearls scattered from the frontal globes of elephants.
Behold the Lord who seeks the welfare of others, who holds the conch and lotus,
whose foremost hand has crushed the heads of the hosts of Daityas with his mace,
and who wields the Śārṅga bow here like Garuḍa in his swift flight.
[He saw him] approaching the presence of the elephant Padmaprabha. ||24||
Upon their chests were fastened lion skins, which, by the way they were gripped as they cast aside their garments, seemed to have captured the stars themselves;
these skins clung to the broad frontal globes of scent-elephants that had been split open.
They shine with their nails as if they were pearls. ||25||
Upon their bodies, which are divested of garments,
the moon-like buds of their charming crests impetuously spread their own stainless luster across the sky, which is already bright with the light of moonbeams.
A letter whose dust of prosperity was doubted by his kinsmen. ||26||

O Lord of the Gods, these Rudras, with their hands adorned by serpent-bracelets, are rushing forward with their uplifted and formidable arms; having struck their own shoulders in a flash of fierce wrath against the enemy, they advance.
May the humps of you, the humped ones, together with their peaks, [protect us].
(Tilaka) May they protect us, scattering showers of ichor-water on all sides from their broad temples, which resemble the dense clouds of the doomsday storm.
Having ascended these elephants, whose weight upon their feet causes the earth to bend, the Vasus have arrived.
The lords of the Vidyādharas enter their camp, drawing their broad swords which act as smoke-pipes for the fire of universal destruction that consumes the entire forest of their enemies.
The regions were adorned with earrings that swayed like tossing water-birds.
Having fixed their arrows to their bows with swift movements of the fingers of their hands, producing loud twanging sounds, these warriors— ready for battle—
enter your camp, O treasure-house of auspiciousness.
The Viśvedevas, the Aśvins, and the Tuṣitas, together with the Siddhas and Sādhyas. ||30||

And whose shadow, consisting of the moon, shines forth, casting a variegated hue upon the interior of the solar disc— resembling the ocean connected to the city of the gods (Amarāvatī) that has been spat out.
Possessing the beauty of a cascading waterfall of flowing Yamunā waters. ||31||
Having mounted the back of the lord of the white quarter-elephants,
he approaches with the long and wide eyes of the women of his army, which, raining down nectar, are like this very moon.
Appearing as if his own hands had been applied with medicinal ointments;
(this pair of verses) [he was] cooled by the wind-like hissing sounds of intense pain from the tight binding of the multitude of serpents used as yokes.
Having drunk in the aggregates like winds and then vomiting them back out,
he established his station upon a chariot yoked with horses.
He was attended by circles of white chowries being shaken by the weight of his lofty eyelashes, which seemed to stain the surface of the sky;
he moved with grace, as if intent on avoiding the constriction of a formal posture.
O Lord, as if being thought of by the night-lilies. ||34||
Behold, this sun— possessing a body that has taken refuge in yoga, endowed with the fullness of mature majesty, and bearing seven green-hued leaves—
is approaching like the graceful manifestation of the autumn season.
They have emptied [the world], having surpassed the splendor of Indra’s day; (the *tilaka*).
Shaking off the waves that form bow-circles, with their fierce paths marked by deeply embedded arrows.
All these seven oceans have arrived, accompanied by their rivers, filling the atmosphere with a tumultuous roar. ||36||
Even the kings who had approached his camp— those who, upon the grounds of the army encampment, bore tents resembling new clouds as their prisons—
had their strength witnessed by him when their partisans were captured and destroyed.
And like young Vajras, or like rays of light recently entered into a womb. ||37||
Even the mass of clouds at the time of universal dissolution, with its continuous deep and terrible roar that deafens the seven worlds,
approaches you, desiring to assume the role of the war drum.
The beauty of these [clouds] is enhanced by the corners of the rays of lightning. ||38||
They rush forward, filling the sky with blossoming circles of hoods whose clusters of jewels act as sprouting shoots,
[reaching] the lotus-pools of the quarters which are blooming with pale-red and white lotuses.
They display their serpent-like strengths like fragments of [a broken] whole. ||39||
Possessing a majestic splendor through the mass of whisks as white as the rays of the risen moon,
and surpassing the speed of the wind,
the army of the king of the gods shines forth, variegated like a speckled mountain.
And the horse's bridle, jingling, was raised even higher. ||40||
With her body raised in beauty by the ornaments on her left side, appearing utterly like a foul donkey or a mule,
Caṇḍī was no different from the ground of the king’s camp.
A form with terrifying hands approaches with impetuosity. ||41||
Turning the circle of her jewel-beaded rosary like the starry mandala at night,
Brāhmī held the beauty of the staff and water-pot in her hands.
This auspicious line here is he who has established his presence in this camp. ||42||
It shines forth, surrounded by those possessing the luster of jasmine petals, who are intent on devouring rows of simple and charming lotus-stalks and tubers as clear as its own interior.
As if from the transformation of a spray of milk by the swans that are the clouds; (this pair of verses).
[The sword] whose sharp blade was stained with the blood spewed from the throat-pits of the haughty generals of the demon hosts.
Like the eastern quarter bearing the rising mass of the sun’s orb, this sinless Vaiṣṇavī [discus] bears a circle of blazing rays. 44.
The crooked-tipped ram of the Three-Eyed Lord approaches the Kaṭaka mountain,
bearing the crescent moon fashioned upon his crown,
while being driven away by the frown of his radiant third eye.
The splendor of her forehead-mark, which shone with the dust of ashes applied [thereon]. ||45||
O Lord, far away [is the place] where Cāmuṇḍā dwells, her body adorned with fragments of skulls and strewn with shards of bone, filled with the thick dust of coarse ashes.
[He entered] the army as if it were the household deity of the palace of the summit of Mount Meru. ||46||
And the reflection of the moon arrives, its rays white with the clarity of a heart whose passion has been broken, like nectar-beams,
and it bathes your clear [face] in a celestial luster.
By the flashes of her laughter, this ocean has been splashed upward. ||47||
O Śiva, this terrifying figure of Yama approaches your camp, his form marked by a garment of donkey-skin and a girdle of dangling skulls,
holding a child in his hand.
The beauty of her face was slightly bent by the weight of the ear-ornaments. ||48||

Having bound the remaining world-protectors with white [serpents], which were no different from the entirety of the principal mountain ranges reduced to ashes by the weapon of fire that devours all at once during the sudden dissolution; [The remainder of the verse: ...by those who, though white, were like the serpent Śeṣa. (Note: This is a fragment of a verse describing a cosmic battle or dissolution, likely from a work such as the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* or a similar epic/purāṇic text. The imagery involves the destruction of the world by fire, the binding of the world-protectors (Lokapālas), and the use of serpents.)
This [is placed] upon the head by the guardians of the quarters and the protectors of the world. ||49||
The mountain peak, whose forested thickets of matted hair belong to the Supreme Lord (Śiva) as he clings to his skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), the tip of which is rubbed by the waves of the Gaṅgā;
and [the mountain] containing the tusks of the trembling lord of the dead (Yama) upon his wings—
The splendor of whose blood-liquor from the seven worlds had been completely drunk.
Having mounted the lord of the assembly of donkeys with an army accompanied by fear due to her impetuous desire for the destruction of the three worlds,
she, whose face was radiant with fury and as pale-white as a broken lotus stalk—
The light of her teeth enters your camp; she is the Night of Doom.
(Tilaka) And Kālī, possessing the luster of a cuckoo’s melodious warbling and bearing sprouts of formidable fangs, arrives, agitated by the intense longing for battle.
He is the comet that destroys the stain of the dark age of Kali, like the Vidūra mountain with its sprouting sprouts of jewels. ||52||
Having heard these words uttered by Nandin in his presence,
the Enemy of Smara (Śiva), together with the entire circle of his army,
[directed] his own camp sites— the grounds for his encampment— to be saluted—
He sent [the message] with his face toward him, whose crown was loose and disarrayed. ||53||
Then, as the evening mud-flood of darkness— possessing the hue of powdered vaidūrya gems from the sky shattered by the hooves of the swift horses of the sun’s chariot— blackens the earth,
the birds, their vision obstructed, are filled with the joy of hastening to seize their nests amidst the continuous warbling of their wings.
In the night, the quarters of the sky, like female companions, seemed to engage in agitated conversation with one another.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth canto, titled "The Mobilization of the Army," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel [of its title], composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who bears the name Vāgīśvara and the secondary name Vidyādhipati, and who is a dependent of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
The Fortieth Canto:
Then, when the time of dawn had arrived, the moon-crested Lord...
Awakened by the cries of various bards and heralds,
and given his signal by the sound of hundreds of beaten drums, he beheld the ocean-like army filled with rivers of troops. ||1||
Then, as the circle of hoods of that serpent host, trembling in agitation,
was fixed upon the surface of the earth by the Lord,
his ears were paralyzed and his eyes rolled upward.
It was heard by the lords of the world-elephants, whose positions were shaken.
His form, vast as the expanse of the cosmic egg and appearing like a great elephant, was elongated by its heavy reflection across the quarters of space;
having gathered together upon the surface of the earth, it attained a state of dense mass.
As if splitting the netherworld once more with its excessive weight. ||3||

The sound of the departure-drum caused the hearts of the city matrons— the wives of the world-protectors— to tremble with agitation; it was like the roar of the drum of universal destruction at the time of the end of an aeon.
[She performed] the graceful sport of clapping her hands, which were as dark as the color of a bee. (The *tilaka* verse:
Then, out of a passion for battle, Gaurī emerged from that [Śiva], having joined herself to him by merging half of her body with his.
She bore a mind that seemed to have shaken off all fear and dejection regarding the beings within the scope of her thought. ||5||
As if being sprinkled by floods of honey-drops falling from the playful ear-ornaments of *pārijāta* flowers placed upon the tips of his alert ears,
[he was like] a mass of saffron-paste...
Bearing a clean cheek-mound marked with a line of writing.
With his sprout-like hand bent in playful grace, as if to wipe away the stainless beauty of her loveliness,
he reached toward the rays of the moon resting upon the crown of the swaying Pināka-wielder.
Desiring a complexion soiled by a scattering of dust.
A single-string necklace has been fashioned here upon this breast-mound that has attained loftiness through their mutual pressure;
