as if in rivalry with it, the three folds have acquired the state of being a triple-string necklace.
Even when grasped in a fist, they yield slightly; thus they are called "middling. //8//
With the tips of her fingers reddened by the shimmering glow of fresh lac-dye,
she— under the pretext of the radiance emanating from the multitude of rays from her bright moon-like nails—
seemed to offer a greeting of conciliation to the twilight, her resentment having dissolved.
She seemed to support those who had begun to fall at her feet. (A group of five verses) Then,
after a long time, the one who bears the crescent moon as his crest-jewel beheld her face, upon which the beloved’s gaze was impetuously fixed.
In his glances, he rejoiced in a triad of eyes that were free from the affliction of blinking.
Then, having emerged from his body after a long time,
she performed the auspicious rite for his departure, her skin bristling with horripilation born of the lingering flavor of that intense embrace she had finally attained.
He was brought forth by the host of Mothers who were intent upon the festival of service.
Even as he was about to strike, the leaders of the Gaṇa hosts somehow managed to bind his arm— already consecrated with mantras— at its very chest,
which shone variegated by the luster of their necks and was encased in iron armor.
The armor [is worn] by those whose intellects are deluded by the wandering [of bees] within a lattice.
Smeared with the smoke from the fire of his radiant third eye, which was being drenched by the spray of the Mandākinī’s waterfalls,
he [stood] above the crown of his head out of fear of the falling arrows of his assailants.
He was like the moon enveloped in a cloud. ||13||
The lord of serpents himself bound his mass of matted hair, which was loosened by the slackening of its knots as it was tossed about by the surging waves of the celestial ocean at that moment.
Furthermore, he was firmly encircled on every side by circles of hoods.
The splendor of the jewels on the hoods of the serpent kings, shimmering upon the broad neck-thrones darkened by shadows and gloom,
was like the beauty of fresh sapphires set for the auspicious occasion of his battle.
And the Kālakūṭa poison bore the beauty of a throbbing necklace upon his neck. ||15||
The trident, with its terrifying tongue difficult to discern amidst the rows of flame-crests issuing from the caves of its fang-like, formidable jaws,
was like a banquet for drinking the wine of the enemy’s blood in a fit of rage.
With his wide-lipped mouth quivering in fury, he yawned.
Then, as in the past during the occasion of churning the ocean, the lord of serpents made his middle body thin by rubbing it against the coils of Bhogīndra,
like Mount Mandara.
Having taken up the staff of his bow, whose tip was well-guarded.
Then, at his word, "Because of my longing for battle," the moon-crested Lord, clad in armor,
[was adorned] with ornaments whose brilliance was variegated by fragments of precious gems in response.
The Gaṇas donned armors fashioned from gold. ||18||
He bore a body clad in armor made of refined iron, wearing a garland of battle-ornaments upon his tawny form,
like a row of birds perched facing the setting mountain.
She possesses the playful grace of moving along the path of the sky, which is variegated by the circle of the constellations.
With his body clad in armor possessing the luster of dark blue clouds, the essence of which was the rays of red gems inlaid with gold, he stood tall,
like a cloud streaked by the brilliant flashes of lightning.
The son of Śilāda assumed the playful grace of a wandering cloud. ||20||
Like the night fallen upon another part of Mount Meru’s silver slopes, soiled by the smoke of universal dissolution,
she rests upon his chest which is smeared with the paste of fresh saffron.
Then the sturdy Māḍhī of Kālamusala shone forth. ||21||
With the binding of her armor rendered visible by its superior luster through the thousands of rays of emerging emerald light,
she was like a lotus plant with bits of moss clinging to it, [as it were] for a serpent.
The form of his face shone with the splendor of a full-blown lotus.
And the form of Agni, shimmering with armor and bound upon its great head with a helmet fashioned of blazing jewels,
shone like the peak of a many-fold, formidable mountain of sunrise.
It was like the sky at the end of an eon, with the solar disc appearing as a halo around the horizon. ||23||
Its surface was perforated by large drops of blood gushing from wounds burst open by the intense passion of unrestrained combat;
it was set with intensely radiant, fresh rubies.
The sight of Agnīka was exceedingly heavy on that day of the month. ||24||
Upon the broad chest of Caṇḍeśvara, his auspicious iron armor shone, its surface clearly marked by deep indentations from the wounds inflicted by hundreds of blows from weapons.
Like whirlpooling waters on the slopes of the snowy mountain. ||25||
The mace, resting upon the chest of Vīrabhadra— the hero who is an irresistible elephant among the foremost of enemies—
shone like the dark cloud of the cosmic dissolution (saṃvarta) amidst the onset of the Asuras.
The beauty of the veil covering the face of the bride Lakṣmī. ||26||
Bearing images that stain the surface of the sky with their banners and victory-flags fluttering high enough to scrape the clouds,
they possess a plaster of nectar-like new prosperity for the office of protection.
Possessing a pale luster, they were attended by throngs of gods who had gathered nearby.
The elephants, whose trumpeting resounded through the sky like the sound of conchs, bells,
and drums, possessed the lovely beauty of white yak-tail fans;
their rows of ivory tusks were clearly visible like ornamental archways.
With their armies, they engaged in battle, appearing like the very abodes of the gods.
(A pair of verses) Their long trunks moved with the grace of pythons intent on guarding fresh pearl canopies, treasure-pots, and jars.
The elephants roared, their backs formidable with swaying, trembling plantain trees that resembled the tips of blossoming kīcaka reeds. ||29||
The bees, settling upon the honey-thick mud dripping from the tips of the auspicious garlands placed on the water-pots (kumbhas),
and clinging to the smoke of the sacrificial fires rising from the peaks, bestowed beauty [upon the city].
They were like great family mountains covered with nets, or like rutting elephants. ||30||
Delightful with the scattering of clouds of vermilion dust from the frontal globes stirred by the wind of its raised ears and tail,
and being turned tawny by the pollen of tossed lotuses—
The entire circle of the quarters became as if illuminated by the dawn. ||31||
Then, a thousand [elephants], whose circles of white chowries swaying in play rendered all directions green,
and upon whose gold [trappings] hundreds of engraved leaf-patterns and sea-monsters were set—
Their backs were made formidable by the placement of the saddle-cloths.
The quarters of the sky were turned tawny by the rays of the golden palanquins, which were adorned with fragments of rubies;
and the gold [of the palanquins] was speckled with particles of gems emitting upward rays.
The parts of their mouths produced a clinking sound from their swinging bits. ||33||
Then, guided by those skilled in the arts of war,
the horses of the army moved through the streets with unabated speed;
their faces were dappled with drops of perspiration.
The splendors were like droplets clinging to the rising nectar of the moon.
(Tilaka) Even though they rendered [the world] full of joy, they lacked any point of comparison; though gentle, they yet dulled the force of the fierce winds.
The horses galloped forth with graceful gaits, their paces characterized by the placement of their legs as they drew up their curled hooves and extended them like staffs. ||35||
The form of those who had formerly risen from his fire-altar shone forth, rendered graceful by the crimson chowries being tossed about by the force of the wind.
It was as if covered by a mass of flames from the horses. ||36||
The horses, marked with auspicious white spots on their foreheads, repeatedly displayed beauty through their broad gaits and limbs that were lovely, pure, and well-proportioned;
they bore the splendor of their necks with the coverings of their saddle-cloths.
And with its quarters adorned by the splendor of divine jewels. ||37||
At that time, for those who delighted in the drama of battle,
they brought supreme joy by raising them up;
possessing the luster of clearly polished vessels, they were of exceedingly diverse forms.
The horses, favored by their trappings, bore Lakṣmī. ||38||
The instrumental music of the musical elements shone forth, possessing extensive breadth, its form and color fashioned by skilled artists,
with its beauty distributed through the rhythmic movements of the dancers, and following the sequence of the syllables.
He bore a troop of horses that was playful and free from agitation. ||39||

The horses of the enemy army, falling on all sides, made the effort of his leaping toward the sky appear even more intense, as their foreheads were curved and adorned by the tossing of their thick manes.
As if treading upon a worthy mate, with the tips of his hooves momentarily clinging to her.
Covering the earth with their vast extent, streaking the quarters of the sky with the fluttering fringes of their ensigns and banners,
and equipped with all necessary implements, they [prepared for] the ocean of battle.
The multitudes of chariots immediately took refuge in the splendor of the boat. ||41||
By her who was mounted upon a steady vehicle by the leader of the warriors, who possessed the delightful sounds of crying out and sighing,
and who displayed the beauty of her hips and the pair of her thighs;
In that regard, at the time of application, Śrī [is attained] by means of the chariot-procession. ||42||
And because they had assumed attire suited for the field of battle,
those radiant beings appeared to dispel that [darkness],
like the suns of dissolution appearing at the creation of all the worlds.
The tips of their circular blades were jagged with rays flashing as they were whirled about. ||42||
Even the moon-crested Lord ascended a chariot that was terrifying with a thousand coils of the serpent king bound as a yoke by a circle of lions,
and which was tawny like the crest of a flame of fire.
The splendor of assuming a costume appropriate for the battle of illusions. ||44||

The sun’s heat was warded off by his crown, which was white with the massed streams of the triple-pathed river (Ganges) driven upward by the wind from the hissing hoods of the serpents coiled upon it,
as they rested against his shoulder.
With its lofty golden staff inlaid with fragments of rubies. ||45||
Then, as it lay on his side, he shook his pair of water-jars, which were adorned with moon-like rays and emitted a continuous sound;
they rolled toward him of their own accord.
The Mandākinī and the Yamunā [flow] with impetuosity and devotion. ||46||
By him, with his circle of sharp claws, as he swiftly ascended to the heights of the sky shaking off his heavy mane,
the moon was forcibly driven from its face at night.
He was like one fleeing in all directions from the moon hanging over the reflection [of the sun]. ||47||

Upon hearing him, the temples of whose [elephants] were once adorned by swarms of bees dejected by the drying up of their rut, suddenly let out a piercing cry as they shrank within their own limbs under the weight of fear.
The elephants of the quarters desire to enter as if from afar. ||48||
His wrath aroused by the shaking of the mass of his long, flowing mane— terrible as the crescent moon upon the head of Śrīkaṇṭha—
he leaps up and truly desires to rend the thunderbolt.
He who [pierced] even the wind with needle-sharp nail-tips; ||49||
Upon that son of Siṃhī, who shone as white as a mass of snow, Kātyāyanī set her foot— her radiance dark as crushed collyrium— and attained supreme splendor.
[This is] like a fresh cloud-creeper upon the snowy mountain. (A *cakralaka* verse.
Even the wielder of the Śārṅga bow [Viṣṇu], seeing the circle of gods and asuras agitated by the fear that this was the fire at the time of the world's destruction, [acted].
He mounted Tārkṣya, whose wings were polished with streaks of refined gold, and whose middle was compressed by the weight of his own body. ||51||
And Tārkṣya, with his back reddened by the radiance of the jewels on the shining hoods of the serpents whose forms he grasped with his beak,
bore the weight of the body of Vasudeva’s son.
And he seized the heart of the excellent Dānava with great intensity. ||52||
Like the earth rising up with its mass of mountains tossed by the wind from his wings,
the body of that Indra bore a form bitten by the tips of [Indra's] sharp claws.
For a moment, the streaks of cloud resting upon the tips of his feet added to his splendor.
Possessing a tawny luster, as if by the power of the transformation of the fiery poison issuing from the circle of serpents he had swallowed,
he spread his golden wings across the sky.
Assuming its row [of feathers], it shone as it prepared for a swift flight.
Then, as Garuḍa ascended the path of the sky, his talons—
having firmly pierced the netherworld after its deep immersion—
drew up and released the earth, momentarily wearying him with the exertion of that obstruction.
The masses of mountains could with difficulty endure his roar. ||55||
The guardians of the world of the gods, whose faces were darkened by streams of ichor flowing from the peaks of their massive temples,
[traversed] the earth which was shattered by the heavy feet of the mountain they had set down.
Then the elephant-lords mounted their respective positions according to their rank. ||56||
While the circle of warriors, having utterly defeated their enemies, was filled with pride for the great festival of victory in the minds of those who witnessed it,
the young women fell into a state of intense agitation.
The beauty of her eyes, tremulous with agitation at that moment. ||57||
Yet, though paralyzed, the eyes of that timid man— his mind rendered vacant by despair as he feared the destruction of his auspicious fortune—
emerged, grey with washed-away soot.
Like bees from a blue lotus, so were the drops of her tears. ||58||
Even while the auspicious rites for his departure were being performed, the great hero perceived an obstacle through the trembling and drooping of her arm as she was overcome with extreme agitation.
His mental state was radiant with the impetuous passion of battle. ||59||
The sword-blade, held in the hand of a soldier and gazed upon with longing by his beloved,
attained an even greater blackness from the luster of her sidelong glance.
Shining brilliantly, she appeared as if washed at that very moment. ||60||
When her husband set forth for battle, she— overwhelmed by heavy grief and suddenly falling into a state of emaciation—
dropped from the tips of her hands a ruby-shaped bracelet onto the ground.
It shone like the halo surrounding the moon of beauty. ||61||
For a long time,
the bride, her heart deeply distressed and her auspicious *rocanā* unguent washed away, remained unable to look upon the face of her husband.
He applied white mustard seeds upon the surface of his forehead.
Then another woman, embracing her lover tightly as he was about to depart for battle, kissed his face;
by the heat of her very warm sighs, his [beard] was instantly dried.
He made his pair of lips resemble the juice of betel-leaf paste. ||63||

With a mind resting on two conflicting emotions, she first formed a bond of respectful regard for his concealed body, yet felt resentment at the interruption of the nectar of touch; such was her embrace.
The wife of her beloved beheld the armor fastened upon him.
Thus, those great warriors, filled with eagerness for the crushing of battle,
were somehow released from their homes by their beloved ones; then,
they departed from the city with impetuosity, roaring like lions.
On the jeweled peak, which was agitated by the crushing of chariots and horses.

Thus ends the fortieth canto, titled "The Mobilization of the Army," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked with the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
The forty-first canto begins:
Now, by some means, at the threshold of that narrow pass—
Being led swiftly by the most eminent hosts of the thirty gods,
the moon-crested Lord, hearing the shouts of "Victory to Hari! amidst the swelling sounds of musical instruments, emerged from the edge of the mountain ridges.
Having mounted his excellent chariot, whose top banner was adorned with a circle of bells jingling and resonant, and which bore fluttering flags,
he set forth himself with an attentive mind, desiring to provide for the auspiciousness of the journey.
They both impetuously struck his conch with their Vaiṣṇava weapons. ||2||
At that time,

the elephants— dense masses of clouds with white cranes— shone forth, their bodies draped in fresh white silk cloths that resembled the breaking waves of the milky ocean of the soldiers' fame, which was bright as the moon.
The Vaijayantī garlands, swaying with the strength of the wind, shone brilliantly. ||3||
With the beauty of its lotus clearly manifesting from the circumference of its radiant jewels, the orb of the sun,
being swiftly lifted up by the driver to strike it,
was situated not far above the peak of the Eastern Mountain.
The drum of the elephant produced a sound that surpassed the goddess Śrī herself in its resonance.
The trunk of the elephant, which had effortlessly cast aside the scent of the rut of rival elephants and bore clear lines impressed upon its quivering belly,
did not bring prosperity for ascending to heaven.
It was like a flight of stairs constructed for swift-moving warriors. ||5||
Having impetuously drunk the honey of great enchanting sweetness from the bellies of white lotuses in every direction,
[the bees] now taste the bitter ichor of the lordly elephants.
The bees repeatedly enter the interior of the mouths of those who have lost their passion.
Out of excessive anger toward each rival elephant,
you suddenly covered the faces of your own elephants with their face-cloths,
thereby putting an end to their incessant drinking bouts from the rut-fluid.
I consider even that which possesses many virtues to be sometimes a cause of fault.

The lordly elephant, with his broad temples shimmering like crags, suddenly spread his glory across the seven earths by means of the trickling ichor that was white with the application of protective *rakṣā* ashes.
Mount Arka, which serves as the gateway for the stream of the Gaṅgā from the city of the thirty gods. ||8||
The masses of yak-tail fans, dyed with fresh lac,
bestowed beauty upon the soldiers who moved with the speed of the wind;
while the entire earth was being pulverized by the falling impact of the tips of their hooves—
The horses appeared as if their forms were embraced by the mass of flames produced by the fire. ||9||

Śambhu experienced the immense weight of his vast army, which filled all directions and was so numerous that its count could not be determined; this burden was further intensified by the heavy, loud, and continuous sighs he let out as he struggled to maintain his composure.
The earth, the supporter of beings, was rocked upon the swing of the hoods of the Lord of Serpents. ||10||
He was pursued from below by the dust raised by the multitude of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, which caused him emaciation;
his mind was utterly distressed by the fear of being crushed by that light force, and he somehow—
The Lord of Serpents supports the earth with a thousand hoods that serve as fetters.
When the army, having passed beyond one *gavyūti*,
had reached the site of the royal camp,
it then assumed the appearance of the first measure of the followers of the Sugata.
The vast multitude of elephants was free from all conceptual construction. ||12||
Beholding Surabhi resting upon the edge of the forest,
birds with broad wings flew up swiftly from afar and settled in nests built upon the tips of the branches of the trees.
With their thirst directed toward their own offspring, they moved about in the very sky. ||13||

With his feet firmly planted upon the ground, which was agitated by violent tremors and swaying, he— resembling a moving lord of elephants— [stood] amidst the celestial trees whose branches were bound together in dense clusters. His army...
Even by the lords of elephants, there is no grace of a three-legged gait. ||14||

The bark of the forest trees fell away, shattered by the rubbing of the broad cheeks of elephants whose temples were streaming with rutting juice as they were bound to the trunks with firmly tightened ropes.
Whom do even the deluded not cause to be separated from their innate nature? ||15||
Possessing the fragrance of powdered camphor dripping from thick clouds, with the Mandākinī flowing gently with ripples stirred by jeweled banks,
they are cooled by the heat of the sun’s rays being intercepted by dense groves of trees.
The upward-moving [beings] took up residence upon the peaks and ridges of the earth. ||16||
With their expansive, fissured cheeks resounding with the humming of bees,
rich with forests of blooming and dense *elā*-candali plants, and abounding in blossoming *kośātaki* vines near the jewel-caves of the mountain;
Some, followed by young women, reached the broad expanses of the earth. ||17||
Then the soldiers of the one who bears the moon upon his crest, roaming in every direction across the mountain slopes with their arrayed cavalry forces,
were seen by herds of deer with eyes trembling in fear.
"Staying" means that they have long displayed a desire for purification. ||18||
Suddenly pierced by some rider with the intense flashes of dark rays from his [sword],
her eyes trembling with fear, she seemed to create a barrier.
The young doe, out of agitation, desired [to hide] her own form. ||19||
Even though she fled most swiftly, she perished there, having not seen her son who had gone elsewhere after crushing his own army; thereafter,
the female black antelope, indifferent to her life, [entered the fire].
Who here would not fall into ruin, or who could possibly have craving? ||20||
A hunter, swiftly piercing an innocent deer pursued by an archer whose glory was rendered most skillful by the discharge from a bow whose string was drawn back to his ear,
[fled].
As if in haste and feeling embarrassed, he departed unnoticed upon the earth.

At that time, as their beloveds were departing in haste, one man— with his neck clearly visible as it was being raised by an arrow whose shaft had struck the surface of the earth— stood with his neck upturned.
He beheld the path leading to the lives of the young fawns. ||22||
Indeed, there is nothing in this world that is not empty of its own essence,
since even a certain mountain, following after a young woman languid with the weight of her womb,
was struck by the impact of his rugged and curved peak.
On that ground of sandalwood trees, even a deer desired to strike him at will.
First,
the heads of the deer on the mountain slopes were violently struck down by the horns of the formidable lions; immediately thereafter, their bodies followed.
Those of swift intellect descended from the path of the sky with ease. ||24||
Like the peaks of Mount Mandara manifesting their formidable summits as they bear a deep affection for their dwelling place,
herds of deer leaped high into the sky and fell back down.
The feathered shafts of iron arrows became stuck, shattered by the teeth and hooves [of the horses].
Beholding the approaching army with disdain,
the lord of deer stood before it, having cast aside all agitation and disregarding the fear of his elders; for otherwise, those possessed of courage do not act in such a manner.
How indeed could there be a comparison for him by the power of his profound fortitude? ||26||
Then, as the army of the host of gods struck the lions, tigers, and other beasts dwelling on the slopes of Mount Mandara— which was devoid of pity—
their wrath rose up toward every quarter.
Thereafter, the excellent boars appeared, acting as adversaries. ||27||
The herds of *camara* deer,
with the radiance of their eyes and tails imitating the glances and tresses of their own female companions,
fled in various directions, avoiding the soldiers who pursued them.
The lion, the śarabha, the boar, and the leopard were to be slain. ||28||

As the deer, in their playful frolics, resemble lovers in the midst of amorous sport, they possess the beauty of form like that of a forest-queen who wears fragrant flowers and has eyes as tremulous as those of a doe; thus, on the other side, there appears a crescent moon.
With the falling of clear rays of light, he split open his cheek.
On the mountain peak, the peacock— his gait slowed by the excessive weight of his dancing plumage and pursued by the archer—
was unable to escape from us as we struck him with even greater speed.
In a two-line verse, a certain beauty of merit may take on the appearance of a fault. ||30||
Thus, having finished their hunting, the riders, with their saddle-cloths loosened and their reins drawn back,
whirled upon the surface of the earth;
their golden girths were embraced by a multitude of droplets of perspiration.
The horses had their limbs embraced by thick clouds of dust shaken up [by them]. ||31||
With the tips of their tawny manes smoothed by breezes cool from the agitation of the fourfold waves of the sun’s rays,
they descended upon the sands of the celestial river at the water’s edge to bathe, their trunks upraised.
The wheels of the pāṭhīna fish were crushed by the tips of the horse's hooves.
Leaving behind the masses of lotuses whose petals have opened wide, the bees,
their wings fluttering in excitement,
follow even the drops of rut-fluid from afar across the water upon the cardamom plants.
The scent of the flower-clusters was fragrant from the elephants as they plunged into it. ||33||
Before the hosts of immortals could hasten to the celestial river to bathe, their fatigue from the journey still visible,
you quickly sprinkled them with droplets from your own spray.
By the lordly elephants, whose hearts were gladdened by the fragrance of cloves held in their trunks. ||34||
With thousands of lordly elephants whose massive bodies— weighing down the mountains submerged within the river— rendered their faces and trunk-tips invisible,
[the waters] emerged from the many unrestrained wombs of the celestial river.
He was perceived from afar by the soldiers like Gaṇapati himself. ||35||
The sprays released from the trunks of the elephants dispelled the swarms of bees that had adorned the broad temples of those beasts intoxicated with rut;
or rather, what else could this be but the protection of those who have sought refuge from the waters?
Suddenly, from those [elephants] raised high by those blinded by the weight of rut... 36.
Having experienced the pleasure of swimming, the lordly elephants emerged from the interior of the ocean with their waves turned tawny by the scattering of abundant vermilion dust;
they appeared like mountains that had been shorn of their wings by the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Having again attained fearlessness, they shone as they rose upward. ||37||
With the tips of their heavy manes dripping with water, bearing broken roots,
and clinging golden algae-like vines to the points of their hooves,
the horses raised their snouts high as they reached the bank of the celestial river.
The horses crossed over the multitude of waves, which were made to tremble by their own panting.
With the dust of the army shaken up by the gusts of breath exhaled from throats slackened by fatigue,
the horses wandered across the plains with their straight tails flickering restlessly.
[He saw] patches of young grass as tender as needles made of emerald gems. ||39||
The ignorant, dwelling within the depths of impure waters, clearly manifest an arrogance toward their own faction;
for they cause the dust-clouds of the celestial armies to become turbid with stains.
Intoxicated in every direction, they were like fish in rivers. 40.
Then, having swiftly leaped far beyond the realm of the lords of mountains, the army— consisting of horses, elephants, infantry,
and chariots— having been arrayed, rushed even more rapidly toward the path of the celestial track, where the clouds were being struck away.
It rose up impetuously, pervading the entire universe of the enemy of Smara. ||41||
The sky was almost entirely filled as it rose toward every quarter until it reached its limit;
yet that other half which remained, desiring to rise high, stood still.
By him, the surface of the earth became established upon the ultimate foundation.
In every direction, the herds of celestial elephants, their streams of ichor dried up, leaped far away,
agitated by the affliction of the heat from the sun's rays.
Due to their proximity to the morning, the conch shells resounded loudly. ||43||

In every direction, the masses of clouds— charmingly mistaken for the streams of water trickling from the peaks of mountains that had been completely shattered as they flew up when the birds returned to them— were drunk by the elephants.
The ichor of rut falling from the broad temples of the elephants nearby.
The streaks of clouds in the sky, containing water as clear as crystal and dark as collyrium,
tossed by the winds and flickering for a moment, resemble the fresh ichor of elephants.
Clinging to his feet, they displayed the grace of tightly bound fetters. ||45||
The broad temples of the elephants, which imitate the expansive ridges of mountain peaks,
are adorned with shimmering garlands of large stars—
reflections of the streaks of flowing ichor.
The row of stars, shimmering nearby, extended its splendor.

Let not this mass of clouds, appearing like a forest of dark tamāla trees, burn the fly-whisks adorning the peaks of Mount Śravaṇa— whisks that have never known the seven-flamed fire of lightning’s fury; for it stands high and unassailable before us.
In every direction, by the winds from the fierce hissing of herds of elephants... ||47||
The celestial girdles of stars, flickering as they momentarily joined with the lofty frontal globes of the elephants, were struck by the swaying ears and scattered by the streaks of red lead-dust.
They seized the elephants, which were composed of nothing but illusory splendor. ||48||
Another herd of elephants, with girth-bands of massive golden chains flashing like lightning,
sat upon the earth;
they were such as once filled the expanse of the sky when the army of the Lord of the Gods marched forth.
It was like a mass of clouds dissolving away due to the heavy sorrow caused by their separation. ||49||
Reflected upon the temples of the elephants—
temples moist with trickling ichor—
the streaks of the moon were visible, as if being traversed by the shadow of the sun’s crimson crown.
In the sky, it possesses the splendor of golden elephant-goads slipping from massive frontal globes.
The path to heaven was playfully covered by lordly elephants rising up high— their trunks darkened by clouds of waterless, heavy smoke, and their tails flickering like uncurbed streaks of lightning.
In every direction, the light was obstructed by unbroken clouds.
The speed of the wind was exhausted in the sky by the tips of their hooves, which remained fixed upon the rear half of their bodies even as they were unsupported;
their nearby stars were driven away by the broad chests [of the horses] as they dashed along the mountain slopes.
He galloped along with his horses, the tips of his restless hooves striking the ground.
In the sky, the troop of horses, with their ears pricked up and nostrils flaring, leaping high without descending,
appeared like a herd of deer amidst shimmering, variegated jewels.
It was shining with molasses that were variegated by their intermingling.
The horses shone in the sky, tossed by the swift winds of their speed, with masses of yak-tail fans dyed in lacquered red flickering [around them],
as the interiors of clouds were rent asunder by the agitation caused by the tips of their formidable hooves.
As if their forms were embraced by flashes of lightning, flickering and stumbling. ||54||
Then, by the touch of the sun’s rays, the thousand-eyed Indra beheld the sky freed from thick mire,
with the white bellies of his eyes half-visible as they rolled rapidly.
It appeared like a lake with a multitude of saphara fish tossing about. ||55||
Clinging to the jagged peaks of the rows of banner-staffs, their variegated luster mottled by the shimmering reflections of various gems,
they resemble fragments of fresh rain-clouds beneath a canopy of peacock feathers.
They bestowed glory upon the soldiers who were descending below. ||56||
The orb of the moon, whose greatness was reflected within the interior of the knots of their crowns shimmering with jewels,
cast its mass of pure rays back toward the faces of the quarters in the sky.
At that time, its form appeared as if it were a helmet of molten gold that had not yet solidified. ||57||

At that time, the streaks of dust rising from the multitude of stars being crushed at every step by the tips of the hooves of the chariots and horses ahead spread forth like a bed of pearl-sand for the Goddess of Fortune.
Pervading the ends of the quarters from her abode in the makara of the sky. ||58||
The streaks of clouds, flashing with vast lightning and being tossed by the winds, assumed a dense, dark-blue luster;
they bore the submarine fire that had begun its sport of devouring [the ocean].
It possesses the playful grace of ocean waves with clearly manifest and most formidable flames. ||59||
And seeing a lion, full of fury, springing upon a cloud that was likewise roaring with harsh sounds, [the lion] cried out in the world: "In vain indeed is wisdom, utterly empty! of Caṇḍī.
The multitude of soldiers clearly lacked such splendor. ||60||
The Lord of the Pramathas proceeded, his conch Vaikuṇṭha and his bow Śārṅga appearing variegated with the reflections of jewels upon his temples moistened by the flow of rut;
and on the broad surface of his lofty summit was visible the bow of Vṛtrāri.
Bearing the grace of a lord of mountains, his splendor reached unto the clouds. ||61||
At that time, Gaṇapati, bearing Śrī before him, set out with great speed upon the path to heaven,
appearing like a second portion of the moon for the moon-crested Lord who already wears the crown.
The clouds were shattered by the intense flashing of the edge of his axe.
"Before this army can turbidize with its ichor-rivers the waters white as moonlight ahead of me," [the Ganges] retreated from the path as if in fear,
full of trepidation.
By the celestial river, which was agitated by the great speed of the Lord of Birds.
In this world, the stainless clarity of those who are pure is truly praiseworthy; indeed, any foreign substrate therein leads inevitably to blemish.
For, upon beholding it, the hosts of immortals mistook it for their own reflection.
Even the surface of the earth [is considered] a blemish upon the orb of the cool-rayed moon. 64.
Thus, having swiftly and far surpassed the path of the clouds, the army of the enemy of Smara halted for the distance of a *gavyūti* upon the slopes of the Jewel Peak (*Ratnasānu*),
where the host of the lord of Daityas stood, arrayed in various vast formations and prepared for the commencement of a great battle.
Looking toward liberation, there arose in every direction the sounds of various musical instruments resounding loudly. ||65||

Thus ends the forty-first canto, titled "The Departure of the Army," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who bore the name Vāgīśvarāṅka and was also known by the alias Vidyādhipati—and who was a dependent of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
Canto Forty-two:
The various weapons of the Lord of the Sons of Diti blazed intensely with the wrath of his assault upon him.
The armies, eager for battle, clashed together with their soldiers, their drums having been struck. ||1||
In the battle, bees, driven from the sky by the sharp arrows discharged from the palms of the powerful warriors,
fell upon the temples of the elephants out of thirst for rut-fluid, appearing like a thick mass of powder.
In that battle, the coats of mail— bringing about destruction, possessing a terrifying serpent-like splendor as they were instantly smeared with poison,
and shimmering with the brilliance of beautiful moonlight— shone intensely, resembling the majesty of Shiva.

The whirlpools of water in the jewel-treasury of the battlefield immediately imitated the enemies— those possessed of mighty arms— who were driven into confusion by the whirling blows delivered from the palms of his hands, as they moved in circular formations.
Struck by the cool spray from the hands of his enemy who had fainted on the battlefield, the lordly elephant revived the brave warrior;
for the conduct of the great is ever inclined toward the welfare of others.
In battle, the temples of elephants, struck by sharp swords and reddened with blood, bore the appearance of pomegranates with their fresh pearls and hundreds of bursting seeds clearly visible.
As the warriors, desiring battle, impetuously struck at the enemy's chariot-fences within the theater of war, their sword-blades—
interlaced with the petals of dark blue lotuses— shone like garlands that had slipped from their grasp.
He shone most brilliantly, bearing a jeweled crown and possessing powerful arms held high, resembling the mountain of sunrise as he bore the sun resting upon its peak. (8)

The elephants, possessing the beauty of sacred Vedic texts, shone with their bright masses of rays that followed them with impetuosity like fresh pearls from the source of the formidable Kumbha, resting upon their bellies. 9.
The battlefield shone with the trunks of elephants repeatedly coiled by their drivers,
appearing like the initial *praṇava* syllables first inscribed upon a collection of scripts bearing the names of great warriors.
As the enraged lord of elephants charged once more toward a rival elephant in battle,
the banner-cloth, its support suddenly shattered, fell upon his face and assumed the appearance of a broad eyelid.

With the pure, falling pearls from the elephants' temples and hundreds of threads from the whisks (cāmaras) resting upon the great warriors, that battlefield seemed to desire to quickly weave a marriage garland for the celestial damsels. ||12||

In the sacrifice of battle, the swift elephants, with their trunks raised and reaching toward the sky, fashioned altars upon the surface of the earth; those trunks, possessing the luster of blossoming lotus stalks, served as massive sacrificial posts set within the arena.
The water from the lordly elephant’s ears, shimmering with the brilliance of full-blown jasmine flowers,
imitated the flickering orb of the moon as it rested near the mouth of a mountain cave.
On the field of battle, the trunks of elephants shone with hundreds of conch shells fallen from their ears;
they clearly resembled hundreds of massive bamboo poles possessing straightness and adorned with clear pearls. ||15||

Seeing the great warrior reeling in battle before her, the celestial nymph, her body bristling with horripilation out of reverence for the memory of love, became exceedingly difficult for her own celestial chariot to support.

On the surface of the earth, the elephant—its two knees touching the ground, its trunk curled with pride, its three parts (the chest, head, and tail) raised high, and its eyes repeatedly veiled by the banner-cloth—bowed down during the battle of warriors. 17.
This battlefield shone with the jewel-bell that had fallen from a slain elephant as it was crushed under the wheels;
it resembled the lotus-seed vessel (karṇikā) that rests upon the Fortune of War who holds a lotus in her hand. ||18||

The celestial bride clearly laughed at the earth, which had lost its luster when the brave warriors were slain in battle, yet now appeared radiant with elephant pearls resembling rows of teeth. ||19||
Bearing a loftily unassailable splendor by his own brilliance, having utterly destroyed his enemies,
and veiled by the particles of dust from the battlefield, that great warrior then shone forth with perfect clarity.

With his mind filled with intense devotion, he scattered the dust of the earth profusely before Him— who stood firmly with His broad shoulders and was fanned by the breezes from His ears— just as an elephant in its fury scatters dust before one who stands with wide shoulders and is fanned by the wind from its ears.
The stainless sword-blade, resting upon the brave warriors and possessing the blue luster of the sky, shone forth;
it bore a resemblance to a streak of fresh Tamāla leaves upon the surface of the ocean of battle.
The thick dust, white as moonbeams, raised copiously from the tusks of the massed elephants as they trampled,
swiftly rose up and made the quarters of the sky variegated like the dense fame of that powerful king.
Like a crescent moon colored by a gem, slowly rising in a curve from the lord of the ocean of battle,

the dust— dense, dark as a cloud, and like potent poison— attained the splendor of resting upon the tips of the hands of the mighty warriors as they shattered their adversaries, appearing like a vast treasure-trove of jewels in the midst of the fray.

In battle, the excellent warrior, being praised by his fellow soldiers, rendered the pair of an elephant's tusks— struck by the thunderbolt-like grip of his fist— new and peerless, while he himself was likewise extolled.

Seeing the warrior in the sky, the celestial nymph displayed horripilation, shed tears of perspiration, trembled repeatedly, and yawned; indeed, there was no graceful charm consisting of love that she did not manifest.
The elephant tails, severed on the ground by the tips of arrows, drenched in blood, shone like the rays of the sun in battle, resembling fly-whisks dyed with fresh lac. ||28||
Having found their place upon the surface of the void—the seats of horses whose riders had been slain—they immediately took delight in drinking blood;
thus the hosts of hideous spirits roamed about in the battle.
In the battle, the arm of the hero, powerful and flashing with a sword that obscured the space with its mass of pure rays,
served as a jeweled mirror for the Goddess of Victory, who held it forth with the thought of offering a fresh and affectionate compliment.
Then, beholding Yudhiṣṭhira with a joyful soul as he performed his customary dance, that army—
as if by its white banners whose folds were fluttering in the wind— seemed to desire to cross over him swiftly.
Struck by the iron bar from the elephant's broad-tusked mouth, the fallen image of the revolving wheel as it wandered in battle shone, bearing its own luster like the beauty of a quiver.
With his severed trunks falling to the earth along with his inauspicious conchs, that demon of battle shone as if he were standing there with many mouths to swiftly devour the armies. ||33||
The camps of the great warriors attained splendor, protected by swords whose jeweled hilts sparkled like water-laden clouds, and adorned with shimmering auspicious jars (bhadraghaṭa). ||34||
The leader of the warriors, whose splendor was like that of a mendicant and whose restless movements were formidable,
forcibly drew together the circles of his household retainers and his artistic skills, just as a white-winged bird gradually contracts its vast circle of feathers.
The dust raised by the swords of the great warriors, thickened by their mutual blows in battle,
attained a splendor like that of fresh collyrium applied as a swift and natural charm for the celestial nymphs.
In battle, the tall elephants, with the masses of their frontal protuberances clearly split by the spikes hurled from the hands of warriors,
momentarily bore a resemblance to mountains upon whose peaks peacocks had settled.

The discus, having fallen from the hand due to the closing of the eyes caused by the luster of the ascetic’s matted hair, imitated the solar orb accompanied by a digit of the moon possessing a curved beauty. ||38||

Then, as he swiftly shattered the lord of mountains with his arrow-born roar in battle—as if splitting it apart—the wives of the enemies of the gods became utterly distressed, and the joy of the denizens of heaven increased. (39)

The formidable waves of the Lord of the Ocean, who is impartial toward all, attained a beauty like that of luxuriant tresses as they were impetuously whirled about by those possessed of powerful arms, with their fingers clearly visible. 40.

In battle, the sword-blade of Keśin, possessing the luster of the sky and set with pearls from the frontal globes of elephants, shone like the arm of Hari, variegated by the fragments of the jewel-like teeth of Keśin. 41.
In that battle, the lord of birds instantly tore apart the elephants' trunks— which had their tips severed in an instant by the sword—
as they lay scattered upon the earth like snakes huddled together in fear.

Whirling his slender sword-blade with speed, the warrior clearly perceived the enemy combatant standing below him on the shoulder of the rival elephant; leaping up with his teeth, he struck at the foe who had been targeted by hundreds of discharged weapons.

Seated upon an elephant on a mountain of crystal white with abundant wealth, like the Lord of Riches (Kubera), another great warrior, who had destroyed the wounds of his enemies, attained that dharma which is beyond the reach of mortals. ||44||
The warriors on the main roads shone upon the jeweled paths, their multitude of wheels gleaming;
they bore a resemblance to the clear waters of lakes that reflect the sun.
Likewise, the blood flowing from the tusks of the elephants in battle— thick with ichor and splashing across the quarters of the sky—
was suspected by the clouds to be mountain torrents falling from the heavens, and so they gathered it as if it were fashioned from the sky.

On the field of battle, with the uneven flames suddenly bursting forth from the blazing manes of elephants due to their mutual clashing of tusks, the mountain-like king appeared like a manifest forest fire. (47)

The horses, capable of long leaps, possessing the luster of water-laden clouds, and endowed with dense vigor, shone as they were driven in battle for the destruction of the enemy, bearing a resemblance to the dark paths of the wind.

The earth shone with the fallen heads of warriors, like water-pots placed in every direction for the sake of the arm-bearing king who desired to go to heaven, accompanied by the natural auspiciousness of his martial glory.
Having established their positions upon the lordly elephant, who was himself intoxicated with rut,
the sword-blades— reddened by the blood flowing from him— attained a beauty like that of lightning flashes amidst rain-clouds.

Thus, at that time, the armies of the gods and the Daityas, their wrath having been aroused and their compassion for the Jewel Peak [Ratnasānu] established, were divided in many ways as their minds became intent on each other’s victory.
They became inclined toward the flavor of the battle against the six internal adversaries. ||51||

Thus ends the forty-second canto, titled "The Description of the Commencement of Battle," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked with the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who bears the mark of Vāgīśvara and the alternative name Vidyādhipati, and who is a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
The forty-fourth canto:
Of those [heroes] whose actions were fruitful, at the forefront of the battle, success—
Then, for those who desired to act without restraint,
intoxicated elephants arose like hosts of Vināyakas, serving as an incomparable cause for their obstruction. ||1||
When a warrior leaped up to slay an enemy elephant that had raised its trunk like a staff and stood with its feet planted,
the assembly of Siddhas honored him with circles of lotus garlands.
And the celestial damsels with their long, intense side-glances. ||2||
A shower of arrows, ignited by the sparks arising from the friction of tusks as hard as diamonds, flew upward and,
striking firmly against the temples of the elephants' frontal globes, shone brilliantly.
Like a mass of forest fire upon the peak of the Añjana mountain.
The earth was stained with blood by the temples of lordly elephants, which were being struck in battle by the tips of tusks;
it was as if the earth itself had grown thin from the grief caused by heroes who had not yet attained death.
With the splendor of golden conch bracelets slipping from their trembling arms. ||4||
The flowing stream of blood issuing from the hands severed by the edge of the sword-staffs cast down by the leaping heroes is like a torrent of water made crimson by a mass of mineral ores.
The elephant experienced the delusion that the moving mountain had become fixed.
The lordly elephant, its temples made formidable by rows of golden iron arrows released from a bow drawn into a circle by the pull of the string,
bore the upward rays of the sun as they were partially obstructed by the edge of the bank.
It possesses the grace of a mountain whose peaks rise up, strewn with lines [of clouds]. ||6||
One [elephant], with his trunk raised like a massive iron bolt, was sniffing the scent of the ichor from another herd of elephants,
as he desired to descend from the sky to seize a brave [rival] beast.
Like divine women whose hands have slipped from the support of their girdles due to intoxication. ||7||
The lordly elephant spread his body across the path like the Vindhya mountain that has attained mobility;
with its long trunk as a hand and its upraised tusk as a staff—
The waters of the Narmadā, abounding with spray rising from its chasms. ||8||
Their chests bear the steady glow of the jewel, their necks are marked by three lines at the junction of the clearly visible hair-whorls,
and their broad palates are coppery-red like the large leaves of the *avagraha* tree.
Their eyes are tawny and small, their lips are like honey, and their teeth are well-aligned. ||9||

With bellies drooping like those of the kalaviṅka bird, their hands— acting as bolts— scattered with drops from fragrant sighs; they stood with a swastika posture, their feet firmly planted and well-distributed.
Their feet were broad, thick, and well-encased, like the finest water-jars.
Their coats are covered with very glossy spots;
they have well-defined dewlaps, long trunks, and bushy tails;
these brave ones have the haunches of boars and the finest pairs of bristles.
They have thick skin and hair that is sunken, long, and fine. ||11||
The autumn honey, rising from the crushed elephants of the gods and fragrant with blue lotuses, saptaparṇa, mango, and atimuktaka flowers,
brings harmony to the series of days by means of its dark hue.
The herds of elephants in the army discharged ichor. (A *cakralaka* [set of four verses]):
In the field of battle, that which was reddened by the radiance of the cresting rays of rubies and cast down by the palms of the hands of great warriors—
The discus fell upon the rounded surface of the elephant's forehead like the orb of the moon upon the peak of the western mountain. ||13||
The rows of clouds shimmered, turned tawny by the dust of siddhūraka from the frontal globes of elephants whose temples were struck by the wind from their flapping ears;
while blood flowed from the wounds inflicted by the brandished swords.
The sky appeared as if its surface were far away, like moist and loosened soil. ||14||
Approaching with flickering firebrands like creepers whose eyes were blood-red with envy,
they fought, causing Mount Meru to tremble;
yet their towering tusks were quelled by the falling rain of ichor.
The lordly elephants are masses of flame-tips from the fire of their mutual collision. ||15||

The lordly elephant made the path of the stars appear variegated with the clusters of spray-drops from his trunk, which were smeared with the red chalk dust from the slopes of his temples shaken by the broad flapping of his ears.
The evening was like the sky with its clusters of stars reddened by the twilight. ||16||
Another [elephant] bore the ornament of chowries on its ears, reddened by lac-like blood flowing from temples split by iron arrows;
it resembled a mountain whose cave-mouths emitted the fire of a forest conflagration.
Possessing the splendor of a formidable mountain of collyrium enveloped in masses of flames. ||17||
The elephants, smeared with red chalk-dust falling from their temples as they were shaken by the wind from their flapping ears,
were showered upon by the lotus-hands of the Siddha women.
The quarters of the sky were as if struck by the pollen of the filaments of mandāraka flowers. ||18||
He shone with rows of sword-blades like streaks of lightning,
with elephants dark as fresh mud like clouds,
and with [warriors] bearing crests of plumes like peacocks with their uplifted tails.
He suppressed the seasonal functions with his arrows, which were like beautiful ornaments. ||19||

At the head of the battle, the trunk of the elephant— its base severed by the brilliant and formidable swords of heroic warriors leaping up with their broad, club-like tusks— became like the dark palm tree of Death.
Karna fell, shorn of his splendor, like a flower dropped from its stalk. ||20||
The serpent raised up the head of the deceased hero like a great auspicious gem-vessel for his entry into heaven, marked by sprouts of hair as red as a mass of silk cloth. 21.
With the circle of its forest shimmering with trees that were spears— whose feathers were tossed by the hands of exultant heroes—
it resembled the peak of the western mountain from which half-moons were falling away.
The frontal globes of the elephants became garlands of stars. ||22||
The earth was struck on all sides by the thick trunks of the divine elephants as if it had fallen into the chasm of the underworld, its dust shaken off.
The entire earth and the quarters of the sky were shrouded in the darkness of his [the enemy's] net. ||23||
The elephant,
thrilled by the sound of the trumpets, bore upon its trunk— a bolt for the hand— whose rays were fierce with the anger of its tusks, and whose tip was held loose and curled like a string of flowers.
A lute for the stage of the battlefield where headless trunks were dancing.

They smelled the scent of the ichor from rival elephants, which revealed the base of their reddish-pale palates as they were uncovered, and whose formidable frontal globes were restrained by uplifted goads.
The multitudes of elephants in the army [beheld] me with my pair of eyes closed. ||25||
The ichor from their temples, made crimson by the dust of the vermilion from the frontal globes shaken against their ears,
was like clouds raining blood upon the Daityas whose wings remained unharmed.
The lordly elephants showered down [ichor] as an omen portending the destruction of the army.

At that time, the splendor of Hari— who bore the marks of the parted hair of Lakṣmī, who had taken refuge on the Golden Mountain (Meru), and whose circle of enemies was marked by the lines of severed heads— was stolen away by the horseman [Kṛṣṇa] as he stood upon the head of Smara.
The mind [was drawn] as if from a moment by the stream of Sudarśana. ||27||
Then, torn asunder by sharp-feathered arrows from the vast hollows of the earth and the sky, they fell,
being hacked by the swords of leaping foot-soldiers.
They were like the golden bowstrings of a great archer.
The light of the sun was turbid with the dust from the edges of swords shattered by falling upon various heads;
as if seized by fear, it fled in all directions during the battle.
He did not even notice the sky as it fled away. ||29||

Even the battlefield of war, though covered with forests of sword-leaves, became like the realm of the moon for those who were intoxicated with joy and whose complexions were as pale as the light of the cool-rayed one, owing to their extraordinary skill in action.
It was not the cause of the pleasure of enjoying celestial realms for those warriors. ||30||
Upon the auspicious battle-garlands resting upon the hard frontal globes of the herds of army elephants,
the winds from fluttering wings fell with great force.
Others, however, scattered the swarms of arrows. ||31||
With their foundations on the higher ground somehow severed,
and illuminated by a mass of shimmering rays,
they became like gold upon a touchstone of levelled earth.
The lines [on his body] were like the golden girth-bands of the elephants belonging to the hosts of gods. ||32||
The pair of frontal globes of the elephant, which constitute the pair of breasts of the Goddess of Victory in battle— torn open by sharp crescent-headed arrows and shafts,
lofty, plump, and unsullied by the stars of fear— [was struck by him].
With the saffron-like blood of a crimson hue, which had been prepared. ||33||
The banner-cloth of the standard, clinging to the stone shafts inlaid with coral and jewels, slipped away from the goddess of the battlefield,
as white as the rays of the morning sun, like a silk garment suddenly falling off.
The beauty of whose breasts was the site of high, full, elephant-like frontal globes. ||34||
The rows of stakes, possessing the terrifying splendor of the towering tusks of rutting elephants upon the roof-palace of battle,
bore a beauty like that of a circle of moon-disks inlaid within them.
The paths of the clouds were streaked with variegated colors by the arrows discharged by the great warriors. ||35||
Smeared with the saffron-paste of blood sighing forth from warriors being crushed by the furious trunks of intoxicated elephants,
they spread out as if desiring to honor [the battlefield] with great reverence.
The grounds of the battlefield became like the hubs of wheels for the multitude of chariot-poles. ||36||
Seeing the king of elephants fallen before him in battle,
yet raised up at the front of the fray by the bars of his tusks,
he was filled with grief and offered a handful of water from his trembling trunk as a cupped palm.
He was beheld by the great warriors as if he were a majestic elephant showing his regard. ||37||
Mounted upon an elephant on the sandy banks of the Sindhu river amidst a battle of royal swans whose ears were pale-white chowries,
he surpassed even Vaikuṇṭha with his many wheels.
The warrior, having severed the head from the host of enemies, attained glory.
With the beautiful splendor of their rows of teeth glistening as they hissed, and with networks of water-drops from their quivering, formidable lotus-like trunks,
these [elephants] were employed by warriors in battle for the slaughter of their enemies.
Swords and herds of elephants shone forth together. ||39||
With arms like sharp swords, leaping up, a certain man dealt a heavy blow to the enemy’s pair of frontal globes, which resembled the two footstools of Yama.
He was a great warrior who struck off the heads of the enemy host while they were in a state of swoon. ||40||
They did not lose their resolve in battle, nor did they yield out of pride; they neither retreated nor felt fear.
Likewise, they did not tremble before the flashing sword due to their valor.
He struck down the enemies of heaven with his very vital breaths in battle.
As they called out to one another and stumbled unrestrainedly due to their bonds of fortitude being strained by the uneven terrain,
the sun was obscured as the [battle] proceeded with great impetuosity.
The path of the stars was filled with oaths as the fierce clash of battle took place. ||42||
At that time, the warriors, agitated by an endless succession of one another through a continuous volley of arrows,
were utterly terrified by the fear of the impending conflict, which was both pitiable and trembling.
Those devoted to the Pārāyaṇa quickly completed their recitation.
Suddenly leaping up, the warrior on the battlefield of combat rushed toward the circle [of enemies] and stood there with a manifold array of diverse maneuvers. Grasping—
With his sword as his bow and his shield as his staff, he performed what was like a dance. ||44||
Devoid of the destruction of mental formations, they possess purity;
having reached the path of the sacred scriptures, their connections are clear;
like words that have formed a continuous composition, they yield abundant fruit.
They made those who enjoy great prosperity the ones who employ the arrows. ||45||
While the horses galloped, the chariots moved,
and the herds of elephants ran with great speed, the celestial river (Ganges) became like the dust from the slopes of Mount Meru being shaken and crushed.
Its marshy banks were formed from thickening golden sands.
Smeared with the dust raised by the black rocks of the Golden Mountain being split apart by the tips of the hooves of the army's horses,
they resembled the onset of the night at the time of the world's dissolution.
The quarters of the sky appeared as if turbid with a terrible darkness. ||47||
When the three worlds were covered in every direction by the mass of powdered sapphire crushed by the concealment of Sāvarṇī,
there appeared [the arrows] resting upon the lotus-like hands of the great heroes.
The swords have hilts adorned with formidable jewels. ||48||
With their entire bodies shrouded in the darkness of clouds of dust raised by the earth as it was crushed under the trampling of armies,
[the elephants] remained hidden within the temples, their scent being snatched away by the rut-fluid.
By means of bees that form clouds of doubt and delusion for elephants. ||49||
The path to heaven was covered by the dust raised from the white, black, red, and yellow gem-studded enclosures shattered and crushed by the army,
as if by heaps of mineral ores from a mountain.
It was intensely sprinkled with dust by those who had been traveling for months.
While that thick dust and darkness remained, having veiled the orb of the sun and all the quarters of space,
they challenged one another with the terrible sound of their neighing.
The throngs of warriors were inferred [to be present] by the loud neighing of horses and trumpeting of elephants. ||51||
The sea-monster of the ocean of space, the mass of mud from the gift of mountains and serpents, the auspicious lotus-garland for the bride that is the earth,
and the lovely, long [hair] joined with the straight locks of the women who are the quarters of the sky—
Her braided hair was like a row of clouds in the foul weather of battle. ||52||
A mass of smoke from the fires on the shoulders of the golden mountain, fierce with its tawny radiance and formidable weapons, rose up into the sky,
struck by the thunderbolt-like impact of the hooves of the army’s horses.
A streak of dust from the circles of crushed sapphire gems; (this pair of verses:
She rises up like a mass of powdered dust from crushed rubies, strewn with fragments of various jewel-powders.
Like the Vindhya mountain wishing to block the path of the hot-rayed sun, he was again permeated by hundreds of various minerals. ||54||
The splendor of the earth shone intensely, made formidable by the dust of rubies crushed by the impact of the tips of the hooves of galloping horses,
as if smeared with the glow of coral from the young women's lips.
The dust of crystal stones resembled the Ocean of Milk.
The sky, its brilliance obscured by the sun’s heat and shimmering rays, fell down like a watery creation, its splendor unperceived due to the concealment of Sāvarṇi.
It quickly displayed, as it were, a world composed of water.
A mass of beryl dust covered all directions. ||56||
The circle of the quarters was overtaken by masses of dust from heaps of fresh and ancient jewels, which turned the sky into deep darkness,
reaching as far as the hub, spokes, and rim of the sun’s chariot wheel.
[They were] like masses of atoms of the celestial realm (nāka) ground to powder. ||57||

How could the enemies of the gods have even managed to inflate themselves with the dust of the earth, crushed by the hooves of the army’s horses as they were driven by the wind of their own sighing breaths?
The warriors blew their conchs, which silenced all other sounds, for the sake of battle. ||58||
With the light obscured by the thick dust of the earth that had become dense, filling the entire space between the three worlds,
they called out to one another across the path of the sky.
Their names were distinguished by strings of enjoyments. ||59||
And rising from the surface of the earth, as if out of curiosity to see as far as the cosmic egg of the lotus-seated Brahmā,
the wind took its place high upon the shoulders, leaving no trace behind.
By the dust raised up, the splendor of the sun was eclipsed.

He took refuge [in that place] which was surrounded by smoke arising from the clouds of dust raised by the flapping of the tails of black antelopes, as they were deeply immersed in the golden bands of split black gems;
and by the white parasols turning grey on all sides—
The beauty of the lunar orb was eclipsed by fragments [of the mountain]. ||61||
Parasols fell down, their beautiful golden staffs broken by the impact of arrows with sharp points,
their backs now resting upon the surface of the battlefield.
As if from the heavy burden of the weight of a canopy of dust, [the mountain] rose high. ||62||
"May this flood of water from the gift, dripping down and concealing the beauty of the day, first bring me peace"—
thus [thinking], with the dust raised by the hooves of the horses, the cavities of the elephants' ears—
Having reflected deeply as if upon a future peril, he vanished.
On the path of battle, strewn with clouds of dust,
the chariot-pole— its wheels rendered motionless as its momentum was submerged—
struggled with great difficulty, yet remained steadfast as death itself.
You did not draw the mind with the senses as one draws horses with reins. ||64||
With their massive side-bells rendered motionless and mute by the unimpeded force of their fall that shook the earth,
they did not even look at one another in the darkness of dust.
He fought with lordly elephants that were brought down by the touch of his hands.

On the path of battle, the mass of dust from the heavy army— dark as the clouds at the time of universal dissolution— obstructed the sun’s orb, which possessed a splendor soiled by the clouds of the end of an aeon, just as a great wave of a planet obstructs the disk of the hot-rayed sun.
At that time, I swiftly quelled the army with the thick cloud of dust raised by the torrential streams of abundant gifts pouring forth from the mouths of the Saktakas as they were being sprinkled.
By means of showers of water released from the deep trunk of an elephant.
The ten directions, their bodies smeared by the ichor trickling from the temples of elephants and clothed in the spreading dust, were draped with the circles of divine rainbows.
With the feathers on the shafts of the harsh arrows spat out [from his bow]. ||68||
By the streams of ichor trickling from the temples of the elephants, by the wheels of their chariots falling upon the earth as they turned back,
and by the spray rising up and released from their trunks in the sky;
At that time, the mountain of jewels had its thick dust entirely cleared away.

Thus, in the battle where the floods of supreme exhaustion had ceased— their fierce splendor having subsided— by means of the sprinkling of water vomited from the tips of their distorted trunks, which was mixed with the continuous streams of ichor spat from the temples of scent-elephants blinded by pride; ...in that battle, [the elephants] were [seen].
Then, on the peaks of the Jewel Mountain, there was once again a battle among the warriors amidst the crumbling of the earth. ||70||

Thus ends the forty-fourth canto, titled "The Collision of Elephants and Horses," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
The forty-fifth canto begins:
Having observed that the leaders of the Dānava army had turned their backs from the battle, afflicted by the arrows of Giriśa, [he...]
With the circles of his cheeks quivering with the rays of a smile, the Lord of the Daityas spoke thus with great vigor.
As he, filled with fury, was inciting his enemies to the slaughter of the sons of Diti who were turned away from battle,
[the weapon] emerged from his mouth even though it had not been swallowed.
It was like a dense mass of nectar, a radiance of rays from his teeth. ||2||
O Daityas, how is it that you, though full of pride, having been shattered in the great battle, are fleeing so swiftly?
Do you not behold your own vast ancestral banner—your fame, which possesses a brilliant luster—snatched away by the enemy?
This army, though constantly attended by the trident-weapon, suddenly beholds you fleeing from the battlefield with averted faces and accompanied by laughter.
His glory is honored by the hosts of Māra and the heroic Aṅgirasas. ||4||

How was your power extinguished—like the flame of a lamp—as it sought to increase its intensity by means of the circles of arrows and spears from the enemy falling like a swarm of locusts with their wings spread wide? (5)
What need is there to praise these heavy-set jeweled armlets upon their circle of arms, with their shoulders marked by dark spots?
Let them be for the sake of the most formidable host of enemies in battle.
May she, whose brilliant ornaments crush the pride of the staff-like arms [of Māra], be for your protection. ||6||

O you who bear these maces—the very pathways to the city of the Lord of the Dead and the clashing jaws of the Night of Doom—why do you not feel shame at your terrified glances, and why do you turn your faces away? ||7||
O mallets, now that your enemies—shameless from even the slightest fear and fleeing—are situated in the palm of your hand, these do not shine like the pillars of the palace of Death. 8.
How could one fail to produce such distaste for this state, which is defiled by the insults and contemptuous ease with which the adverse elements are disregarded,
were it not for the mass of white, curved chowries being waved there?
Like the goddess Lakṣmī turned white by old age brought about by that sorrow. ||9||

How could a lion endure his own mane being violently pulled by the wind, when that mane has already destroyed the trunks of a compact herd of elephants struck down by his effortless blow? How much more so, then, [could he endure] those [actions] proceeding from deep and heavy wrath?
The mountain caves resounded with the roar of deep thunder.
May the act of healing the wounds inflicted by the weapons of enemies long bestow blessings upon you, O women;
for when their backs are scarred, your hearts will clearly become slow with the weight of blossoming modesty. (11)
Alas, how have your staff-like arms— once possessing shoulders so broad and formidable that they were empty of scars from the wounds of weapons—
come to serve as pillows for the cheeks of your beloved women?
They would now have become worthy of great honor. ||12||
Generally, those possessed of splendor accomplish their tasks by means of their own brilliance alone, without depending on many external instruments; thus,
the sun consumes the worlds with its seven rays alone.
The Fire-god, delighted at the time of universal dissolution, blazes with his crests of flame.

Now, for you whose vigor has been wounded by a formidable enemy and whose minds are intent on flight, these sword-blades—resting in your hands under the guise of their own rays—seem to vomit forth your fame. 14.
The noble declare that in this world, true ornamentation is sincerity— never stained by impurity, never bound by falsehood, free from barrenness, and possessing a desirable form.
For a man, glory alone is born from valor and majesty. ||15||
Great men possess weightiness only so long as they are seated upon the peaks of the Himalayas, white with snow;
once the blossoming flowers have been plucked from the tips of their summits, [they lose it].
Tell me, whose respect is it that has been shown? Speak of its origin.
There is no fear of lions for the elephants, even amidst the tumultuous clamor of the circles of rut-fluid-exuding *gaṇḍālī* bees, who are like honey-dripping, blossoming, and fragrant new mangoes.
It is possible that [this] may happen to your honors from your enemies. ||17||
The great warriors of the Asuras, who yawn with heavy blows while effortlessly dispersing the wind,
are surely bringing coolness to the battlefield as they advance with skill.
[May it be] for you, [the destroyer] of enemies who are consumed by the heat exhaled from their mouths as they hiss. 18.
For noble beings do not turn their backs even when being struck down at the front of battle against an enemy;
they are simply consumed by the submarine fire of the ocean.
And its breaking waves move toward him.

Even the trees of the bow and the palmyra palms, now serving as the resting places for various birds perched upon their branches that have not been severed by the bowstring, manifest this very clearly before your eyes.
That which is a source of great wonder for one's enemies is the fruit of prosperity.

With his joined palms folded as a weapon brandished, and his very horripilation serving as armor out of fear, surely for enemies in battle, prostration alone is the helmet that secures victory over you. 21.
Let it be observed by the soldiers with clapping hands: the very sword, out of fear, placed at the necks of hundreds of gods, has itself become their protective neck-garland.
With a circle of light from his gleaming teeth. ||22||
That earth, which was somehow lifted from the abode of the serpent by the one whose banner is the bird (Garuḍa) in the form of a boar,
has now its vast expanse balanced upon his forefinger.
It is possible for you, who possess exceeding strength, to perform this task. ||23||
Are you capable of making [the chariot] such that its unrestrained horses gallop toward the horizon with loosened, long coils of the serpent-king,
and with the traces and reins broken?
Even the form of the sun’s charioteer appeared reddened with fear.
By the drops of thick perspiration falling from the surface of their breasts, produced by the battle and lingering in the sky,
even the one who devours the abode of the sea-monsters [the moon] could, in an instant, be rendered visible.
May the submarine fire, though filled with flames, bring you peace. ||25||
The power of one who is truly radiant and exceedingly great is surely never obstructed, whether against the sharp or the mild;
having risen from the city of serpents like the submarine fire itself.
Together with him, the fire of destruction utterly consumes the Lord of Sindhu.
The noble ones say that the fire born from the thigh [of the sage Aurva] was indeed the submarine fire (maurva), which swallowed the tortoise-bannered ocean with its mass of flames;
but this [fire], having consumed the enemies, is the hero of the flood of battle.
Those of vast being [perceive] that which arises solely from the fire of anger. ||27||
He who now contemplates your fortitude— which is empty of calculation, transcends all reckoning, and functions as an undivided whole—
is surely digging up the sky without weariness.
The servant, with the tip of his nail-scraper, immediately [cleared it]. ||28||
In that [battle], where the tusks of elephants were split in two by the falling edge of the battle-axe held in an ear adorned with a blazing crescent moon,
and where the three types of obstacles were warded off by warriors who had made themselves their own weapons;
When the multitude of lances was cast down by the dragging of the lion.
In the circle of the bowman, who possesses the purity and excellence of specialized training in the conceptualization of a beautiful, curved, and distinct bow that captivates the heart,
[there are arrows] resembling various kinds of fruits, flowers, and leaves.
In which many beautiful bhindipāla missiles were prepared.
Upon a barbed arrow (digdhaśaṅku) whose shaft is adorned with beautiful peacock feathers, which is easy to grasp due to the firm placement of a well-knit fist,
and from which the excellence of its drawing has been perfectly extracted—
In which the circle of his bow was made to dance by the fierce quality of the sound "ṭāṃ". ||31||
There is no other suffering greater than the loss of manhood;
therefore, the gathering of your soldiers here for battle is in vain.
Is this not indeed the very path for you that leads to peace?
A confinement is being enacted as if for Rājyalakṣmī herself. (The *cakralaka* verse:
Indeed, no power whatsoever belonging to a person of splendor can ever suffer any impairment in the performance of its function here.
There is not even a single crest of fire from the submarine conflagration that does not incessantly consume the waters of the ocean. (33)
May the circle of warriors drink in your abundant fame, having formed a headless army for the Lord of the Gods, whose desires were fulfilled by the attainment of supreme mastery.
Unimpeded, it was as white as the milk of moonbeams. ||34||
These very same [heroes] stand before you now, their hair standing on end with the passion of battle, tawny like the mud of their own saffron;
they who even today cause the lotus of Brahmā to tremble.
His staff-like arms were like the tips of entangled stamens. ||35||
Upon the rows of tamāla creepers in the forest of battle,
upon the braided streams of the Kalinda’s daughter that are the armies,
and upon the terrifying nights of the world's dissolution—
How can you have such indifference toward these sword-blades? 36.
Indeed, due to the sudden onset of death and the resulting panic, you have all quickly become intent on flight;
and that [flight] was surely undertaken by those deprived of his warmth.
"By you"—thus, do this so that it is not redundant. ||37||
O demon warriors, why do you, overwhelmed by fear of the enemy in battle, turn your backs and shamelessly make this broad forehead-wall—the mere plaything of Death—uneven in vain? 38.
O soldiers of Śauri, why does your heart not ache at the sight of these [arrows] at the front of the battle, with their beautiful, darting movements,
resembling the sharp-pointed beaks of the lord of birds and the heron?
They were like the removal of the thorns of defeat caused by the demons who had been effortlessly uprooted [by him]. ||39||
With the playful grasp of a curved digit of the moon, she obstructed the flow of the world-elephants at the edge of the jars with the tips of *kuśa* grass;
shaking the three worlds by her swift movement, she— vihāra- [the remainder of the verse follows]
O gentle ones, you have been gazed upon by the gods with fear and wonder. ||40||
In this forest of battle, where the swarms of bees are agitated and distracted by the spreading branches of the *sumanas* flowers whose pollen has been shaken off with ease, you alone [must act].
The mace was quickly shattered like the branches, trunks, and creepers of a sandalwood tree.
