Rejoicing, it has attained a state of non-stumbling that extends farthest,
transcending all worldly obstacles and being free from impediments;
for indeed, it is praiseworthy for those endowed with strength of arm, as it is difficult to traverse.
First comes fame, and thereafter, splendor shines forth here.

May the grief over the loss of their husbands soon blossom into a state of amorous union for the wives of the enemies of the Asuras, whose pearl necklaces and jeweled girdles were crushed, and whose cheeks were split by the tips of his fingernails. (43)

Surely, when I have conquered Dhūrjaṭi at the head of the battlefield, crushing his attendants, this city appears like a woman with disheveled hair, her black chowries fluttering from the tip of his banner. 44.
When my anger was aroused, he beheld the pair of breasts of the enemy's wife— her complexion darkened and reddened by the blow of my sharp arrow—
and before long, her attendants bound them up.
With a wretched gaze fixed upon him, he was like a snake that has cast off its slough.
For those whose hearts have reached a state of joyless emptiness and whose minds are devoid of the possession of jealousy,
tears born of anguish flow incessantly.
O soldiers, [this is] the water of the hips of your enemies' wives. ||46||

This dark stain clinging to your precious jewel of valor—which causes the loss of your splendor and brings about the flight of the earth in battle—should be washed away by the waters of the flashing edges of your sword. 47.
Before this fierce one, resembling the thousand-rayed sun at the end of an eon of battle, sets by means of his sword-blade hands,
you must not be obstructed by the darkness of infamy.
Let the path of those who revel in battle be transgressed with extreme ease. ||48||
The pearls from the smiles of the spectators of the battle do not pierce the vital organs as much as this succession of arrows, fallen from fragments of bows twanging harshly;
nor does it praise infamy as much as the blinding darkness [caused] for the eyes.
Thus, [he heard] the sound of the dust raised from the earth of the battlefield, kicked up by the tips of the horses' hooves.
Just as the interruption of conversation spreads a faintness among the senses, so too a blow from a weapon, even when struck by a mighty warrior,
does not cause the bodies— though once dense with life— to fall into such extreme impurity when they are abandoned by their vital breaths.
Just as those who, being insignificant, transgress modesty—the mine of the jewels of virtue—[are rebuked]. (50)
Even now, as these rivers of ichor flow forth from the massive temples of the noble scent-elephants—
rivers that carry away in their entirety fragments of blue lotuses where bees have settled— may your swords, manifesting a fierce attachment to them, bring you prosperity.
May they mock the grand displays of the coiling movements of the host of arrogant black serpents.

Having heard these words of the Lord of the Daityas— words as lofty and weighty as the excellence of his own prowess, which were like the moonlight upon the shore of the ocean of the abundance of his energy, yet like the cataclysmic winds at the end of an aeon fanned by the fierce fire of his wrath;
Those Asuras, moreover, displayed their skill in the initiatory rites for the calamity of the battle with the gods.
With its elephants seized by disease, its fierce horses defeated, its ranks of foot-soldiers sinking, its slow-moving chariots scattered, and flooded by the surging rivers of blood;
with all the weapons of the celestial dwellers falling upon it like a fistful from a demon skilled in illusion—
A battle was waged by the warriors of the Lord of the Daityas, who were unacquainted with the taste of compassion. ||53||
Of those shouting amidst the roaring, who were the crushers and destroyers of the intoxicated lords of the Daityas;
whose Airāvaṇas had fled, and who, being without refuge, sought to seize the quarters of the world from Varuṇa;
whose planets were seized by exhaustion, and who were sky-rangers emerging from the depths of the earth in the thick of battle.
The army of the gods, rendered helpless by the host of Daityas, was incessantly subjected to wretchedness.
The river was strewn with the trunks of elephants, which were like *pīlu* fruits—mangled by swords and filled with many streams of blood;
it was covered with the limbs of horses whose bodies were scarred by the blows of weapons, resembling crocodiles;
and it was filled with the severed arms of warriors who had engaged in battle, appearing like large fish that had been caught and cast down upon the ground.
Then there arose a family of rivers of nectar, reaching up to the neck and flowing without obstruction. ||55||
Then, as the surges of blood issued forth from the hollows of the trunks of the headless torsos with such force that they rivaled the massive form of a mace made of rubies,
the rows of birds, bearing the appearance of whirling circles, formed great swarms.
In sport, he fashioned the vast form of a parasol out of the Night of Doom (Kālarātri). ||56||
The perfected ones (siddhas) were pierced by the emerging entrails of elephants whose bellies had been ripped open by flesh-eating beasts, sinking into pits within those bellies; meanwhile,
rivers of blood flowed from the warriors, reaching as high as the temples of the elephants of the quarters.
The path of battle, where gods were submerged in the womb [of the earth], came into being. ||57||

Thus, having utterly crushed the pride of the lord of the Daityas, who had caused the army of the gods to suffer a profound collapse under his many onsets, and having rendered the peaks of the mountains— whose jeweled summits were worn by the gods bowing down in distress—
useless; and when the host of Gaṇas, distressed by the fever of birth from that ill-born one, had become intensely desirous [of liberation]...
In that most fierce battle on the ground of Ugrālikā, Bhṛkuṭi bound him with a deceptive snare.

Thus ends the forty-fifth canto, titled "The Encouragement of Subhaṭa," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
The forty-sixth canto begins:
He who, as if bearing the Kālakūṭa poison, carries his throat together with the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā) and along with Āryā.
And he sent forth the waters of the Surasravantī together with those of the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā), accompanied by the Āryā.
Then,

at the front of the battle, for the destruction of his enemies, he drew his bow— which bore a beauty accentuated by a clear twang and which, like the orb of the sun, seemed to smear the sky with its emerging rays. (A pair of verses) That treasury of pride, with his bow fully extended, roamed through the battlefield on noble horses.
And by means of those arrows and noble horses, the mountain became the limit for the brilliance of the suns.
What comparison could there even be with the fire of destruction, the sun at the end of an eon, or the flames of Yama’s time when they are intent on the process of universal dissolution?
Even his own self could not serve as a standard for comparison in battle regarding the invincibility of the one who wears a garland of skulls.

The army of the enemies of the gods, filled with fear, sought protection from him in that assembly, as he was surrounded on all sides by his hosts who had swiftly advanced in every direction, bringing both destruction and the promise of safety.
Then, as the Lord of Himavat’s Daughter descended upon the path of battle with a desire for auspiciousness,
Rambhā— whose beauty was like that of the sacrifice of Indra— sang, as if she were the very abode of the gods.
Having obtained him— whose mind was not captivated by the charming Śaśilekhā bound to his head with a fillet—
that army of enemies perished, its horses neighing, their minds shattered, and their pride destroyed.
The heads of the Daityas, severed by his arrows from their bows and stained with the red hue of thick, trickling blood,
rolled upon the ground like fallen *gaṇḍa* stones.
They bear the splendor of mountains upon the peaks of golden mountains. ||8||
He whose desire to protect the world is equal to his own welfare, and who is ever honored by the virtuous;
he, possessing weapons, never tires in battle to strip his enemies of their power, for he is always equipped with arms and devoted to the good. (9)

Then the host of the enemies of the gods, rendered tawny by the masses of dust from the slopes of the mountain of the gods crushed by the impact of the tips of the horses' hooves, clearly resembled an army of Jāmbava monkeys. 10.
His wheel of enemies was incessantly shattered by white armies in the great assembly;
then, he who possessed a mass of fame attained splendor through those [fame-rays] which were incessantly sharpened in the great assembly. ||11||
There, a shower of arrows with variegated golden shafts was released by Andhaka and the other sons of Diti;
yet as it fell, it was turned back by Svayamprabha with the loud sounds of his "hum" roars.
As he crushed the hosts of gods and asuras together in the course of destroying them in battle,
he resembled an elephant in rut swiftly trampling a bed of lotuses.
He crushed them in the order of their arrival. ||13||
To protect him, Nandisena and other leaders unleashed showers of great missiles upon the lord of the Daityas on the battlefield;
his joints shattered by those weapons like the points of Indra’s thunderbolt hurled by Śṛṅgin, he then quickly fell into a state of collapse.
For he had been defeated by that infant Jaṭāsura, who shone in battle after slaying his enemies;
then, like Bhīma, he—having been conquered by Jaṭāsura along with Hiḍimba—rushed against them. ||15||

Then, at that moment, the lords of the hosts of Daityas, filled with the passion for battle, struck [the gods], filling the quarters of space with the thunderous roar of the circle of clouds of their bows, which resembled the clouds of the dissolution of the world. 16.

He struck down those destroyers of the three worlds because they failed to perceive the prowess of their enemies with focused attention; and he then conquered the thundering of the clouds because they failed to perceive it with focused attention amidst their own roaring.

Then, beheld by those stationed on the palace roofs during the battle, he attained a splendor like that of the moon— a beauty long served by the whiteness of ashes— standing clearly upon the surface of the palace.
He swiftly struck down the army of the Asuras, which had taken refuge in a battle that seemed interminable;
and fixing his spear—which possessed rays that appeared endless—he pierced their fortune, which likewise rested upon that protracted conflict.
"Is this the serpent Śeṣa? No, for his thousand hoods are not seen;
is this perhaps the Himalaya mountain? No, for it is not motionless. Thus spoke [the moon], the ornament of the crescent digit, facing [the mountain].
Seeing the end of the illusion, the Daitya warriors lay down to rest.
At the front of the battle, the Pramathas, fighting with impetuosity, scattered with various nets of weapons those attacking Dānava-slayers;
they scattered those Dānava-slayers out of fear as they fought with fury.
Then, with his equipment fastened and with his vast, dark-brown belly revealed by the hollows of his ribs,
he fell upon them in battle like the day falling with its circle of vultures, his body becoming their funeral shroud.
Tall and powerful, he strove to slay the demons; yet they did not vanish from his sight as he advanced.
In that battle, amidst the dust raised by the armies, he was not hidden from view as he strove and moved with fresh vigor.
By that force, he was not concealed from sight within the fray.

Then, though being struck by the arrows of the enemies of the gods, the moon-crested Lord did not tremble, just as a mountain on the shore does not shake from the breaking waves of the ocean agitated by fearsome serpents. 24.
Leaping about in battle with celestial maidens whose eyes were agitated and whose forms were like clouds, he was repeatedly seen by those women—
whose eyes were agitated and whose forms were like clouds— to be making the clouds variegated anew with his own splendor.
Then Andhaka, whirling upon the surface of the earth, scraped the stone of his chest with arrows,
just as [the mountain] with the tips of its peaks [scrapes] the pillar-like arms of Adhokṣaja.
Like Mount Mandara, the king of mountains, [churning] the wheel of the Mandāra tree. ||26||
The bow of that rider, who was intent upon discharging arrows in battle with jealous pride, broke with a loud crack as he bent it;
yet the bow of Śambhu, who was likewise intent upon discharging arrows in battle with jealous pride, did not break.

That Dānava, who appeared intoxicated with pride toward his enemy, was slain by her with a crescent-headed arrow released from her drawn bow; that arrow acted as the night for the forest of lotus-faces belonging to the women of the enemy.
With his mind established in fame, Bhāyaḍa, endowed with the glory of renown born of true yoga,
moved through the battle accompanied by his army.
Immediately, he [became] equal to the one who had struck down the demon Gaja.
Then, seeing the rout of the army in battle, the lords of the Daityas, headed by Prahlāda, quickly approached;
he was struck by a shower of trident-shaped swords and arrows, like a mountain peak by dark clouds rumbling with deep thunder.
Having descended to the battlefield with his own splendor, the unconquered one then displayed his capacity for crushing the enemy in combat;
even the mountain of the gods (Meru) then fell into exhaustion from the crushing of the army of the enemy of Smara (Śiva).

Then, in his wrath, he discharged an arrow whose straight feathers were like the spreading flames of fire—like the very hand of Yama—to the enemy of the gods; it reduced his body to the state of a headless trunk (kabandha). ||32||
Then, through his virtues, he attained fame even in battles;
he was full of passion for those who spoke softly, and being radiant, he caused the bow to resound against the enemy hosts that were devoid of softness and restraint.

On one side were the hosts of the thirty gods, and on the other, the forces of the Pramathas; for the Dānavas, who were fleeing from the entire battlefield by means of their fame alone, even the ten directions proved insufficient.

Then, the delighted host of the gods, having shattered the army of the enemies of heaven in battle— that host which had exhausted its efforts and possessed a destructive speed equal to that of Death itself— praised him.
He who brings an end to those honored in the assembly through illusion, laughing. ||35||
Hearing the loud, piercing clatter of swords as they struck the iron armor of the Daitya hosts,
the multitude of the gods recalled the cruel and harsh sounds of the mountain ranges when their wings were being severed.
He honored her with an incomparable glance,
she who was equal to the sun in battle, the peerless daughter of the mountain, and by whom he brought about the end of his separation from her.

Then, her pride destroyed by the leader of the assembly of Daityas in that dwelling-house of battle, she resembled the beloved of the enemy of the flower-arrowed god (Śiva), whose broad thighs were torn by the claws of the lion. 38.
Having inflicted mental anguish upon his enemies as far as the ocean’s boundary, he,
whose pure luster was like that of a radiant cheek, stood at Sahasraniveśa as if smiling.
Then the Lord of the Gaṇas repelled him with showers of arrows; by that incomparable feat, his fame, as if seized by embarrassment, turned pale along with the luster of his face. ||40||

The leader of the enemies, who had not performed battle and was not scorched by the forest-fire of shame, was abandoned by the celestial nymphs; she did not desire him, who was devoid of pride and deceived by his lack of distress. ||41||

With his navel possessing a beautiful depression as broad as the coils of the lord of serpents, he shone upon the ground of the battlefield like Mount Mandara, prepared for the exertion of churning the ocean of milk. 42.

Bearing the splendor of his face and possessing tusks equal to those of an elephant, he struck down the clouds in battle; having surpassed Svaru, he reached equality with him by means of that very tusker who tormented the sky.
The elephants, whose frontal globes possessed a beauty enhanced by a distinct rosy hue from the finely ground vermilion applied to them,
displayed their rut-fluid at the forefront of the battle, having been honored there.
The playful activity of the retinue of the Lord of the Gaṇas, who is possessed of all requisites. ||44||
Having somehow reached the battlefields where drums resounded, he— unassailable by his splendor—
covered the quarters of the sky and bore the face of Brahmā, whose cheeks were beautiful and free from blemish.
Then the six-faced one moved through the battle with speed, supported by his spear of dual form,
carrying clear garlands of blossomed *vaṣaṭ* sounds like sacrificial oblations of unequalled radiance.
There, among the celestial maidens, his skill in amorous dalliance was stainless amidst various fragrances;
and his white, fragrant, and vast glory, wandering in the heavens, was likewise stainless. 47.
Then, bearing swords as dark as the clouds at the end of an aeon and possessing an unyielding sharpness for piercing the enemy's ranks,
those demon warriors raised their blades.
And the princes, with their own armies, were accompanied by dense throngs of attendants.
Bearing the splendor of one who has caused the destruction of intoxicated elephants upon the earth of the battlefield,
that son of Bahula (Arjuna) repeatedly struck down the new warriors of the opposing side with his arrows, which were as fresh as those that had severed the Dānavas.
Having churned the vessel-like battlefield of his enemy until nothing remained— his arm, which was as beautiful as gold, a conch, and an eye,
its strength made manifest by its insults— the single staff-like arm suddenly became like a high Vaiśākha pillar.

He who was truly more formidable than the mountain of the Daityas, the destroyer of the fear of ascetics, and the subduer of the heart, he—who was the preceptor of supreme dharma—became the one whose delight was fixed upon battle in that conflict where the number of those seeking refuge was beyond counting. (51)
In that battle, the beauty of the faces of the enemy's horses was maintained by their ears, which were as sensitive as those of clever people at a great assembly,
and which seemed to drink in the poetry of excellent poets.
He, who was gentle toward the minds of the world and had conquered Vaśī, was then defeated by the army;
stumbling then, he—gentle toward his wrath—was conquered by Kayā.
Then, having swiftly struck down Vṛtra— who was already tormented by the blows of his teacher’s fists— the elephant-faced god rendered him faceless,
his chest bearing a formidable wound from the stroke of the axe, and sent him away for a thousand yojanas.

Who were able to conquer Hari—who was rending the world of his enemies with the ploughs of his arrows, who possessed a garland of teeth that seemed to laugh in his fury, who was intoxicated with battle, and who was dark as a tamāla tree? (55)
In that assembly of the foremost gods, where the wine was potent with its essence and flavor,
he— the best of gods, whose flow of nectar was unimpeded— roared loudly and discordantly in that moment of heroic glory for the destruction of his great enemies.
(Tryakṣara-vṛtti) He [Indra] [encountered] the gathering of the hosts of the Daityas amidst the assembly of women whose limbs were radiant like hundreds of sun-crystals.
And he, whose shoulders were broad and whose mind was pure, waged a great battle against the celestial damsels.
The younger brother, firm in his resolve, having heard of the fierce Vāyu-like forces of Vṛtrārāti, was delighted;
and there, Cāṇūra—who had previously caused suffering to the arrogant—was also tormented by distress.
On his body, dark as the sky, shone a garment with a close-fitting yellow hue;
he was the one who formerly adorned Dvārakā with various palaces and close-fitting yellow waves. (59)
By whom the enemy's vast army was humbled in battle, yet who, seeing them on the verge of slaughter, took pity upon them;
he, whose father praised him as being like Balarāma (Sīrin), who, laughing at the act of war, spared the cows that were near death.
"Now, having swiftly conquered the enemy hosts in battle, protect those who have arrived terrified!"—
by these words of the suppliants, he indeed abandoned those ranks.
The assembled armies were struck with terror in the battle against the heroic Tārakṣu. ||61||

He who, laughing, carried with his palm a blooming lotus (*tāmarasa*) that was stained red and whose petals were rustling—by him, the son of Maya, who had crushed hosts of gods (*amarasaṃcaya*) in battle, was slain along with his laughter. 62.
At that time, the armies of the inhabitants of heaven, whose creeper-like swords were being brandished,
were cut down by the arrows of the son of Danu as he pursued them with his force.
They were cut down by the creeper-like swords being brandished. ||63||
In every direction, being pursued from afar by those who pacified the rays of the sun with whisks, and being fanned by the rays of the sun as if by chowries,
the host of enemies in battle could not [withstand] the force of his great fury.
By day, he was fanned with yak-tail whisks by the rays of the sun. ||64||
While the Protector remained there like the sun to the lotus-lake of the celestial nymphs, the activities of the host of Daityas— though emboldened by many victories—
burned with fear and extreme uncontrollability at his towering rise.
He went forth to conquer those who were emboldened by numerous defeats.
Then the enemy of Mura, bearing arms that were like the sun and Rahu, caused the armies of the gods—
whose celestial flowers were being shaken by the new host— to breathe freely once more.
They were being shaken by the hosts of Dānavas led by Rāhu.
With a sudden tremor born of the onset of passion, she swiftly took hold of the chariot-warriors who were fixed upon the path to heaven; thus,
in that dense forest of battle, she shone with the splendor of a powerful woman.
He was brought by the charioteer Aṅgiras to the ocean with great speed.
Having entered the paths of the city gardens— the abodes of the splendor of celestial women,
where the bees have drunk the essence [of flowers] and the minds of the best of men are most purified—
she, longing for dalliance, enters a bower of fresh *tāla* creepers.
The most excellent ones, with their minds bowed low, quickly drank the honeyed drinks. ||68||
In battle, surpassing with his own luster the splendor of the winged birds (gods),
and displaying intense pride through his powerful arms as massive as Mount Mandara,
that haughty one brought agony upon the host of the Daityas as if by Death himself.
He brought together those whose pride was intensified by the flesh of the Nāmaṇdara mountain. ||69||

Having stationed the soldiers of his army in their appropriate positions in every direction, Vīrabhadra, the lord of the Pramathas, began to crush the vast host of the enemies of the gods; yet, as he struck down the mountain-dwellers, he felt a weariness born of impartiality toward both sides.
The enemy army, its impetuousness for combat dissipated, remained there in its immense size.
The enemy of the gods, like an elephant, caused distress to his own kin by trampling the very substance of their existence. 70.

Then that noble one— gentle by nature yet possessing majesty, having cut down his enemies through pride, and bearing the beautiful fame of his lineage— immediately cast down the glory of his foe who had been robbed of his fortune;
he, whose virtues were directed toward the path of policy, now offered the guest-offering (argha) for the sake of increasing his own power while bringing about the enemy's destruction.
The gods, with their palms joined in reverent salutation, offered service that dispelled all fear of enemies. ||71||
Thus, crushing the vast enemy host with his tree-like arms of unbearable pride,
he— possessing magnificent splendor like the sun accompanied by the moon at twilight—
shone in battle, his fame increased by the *ṭāṅkāra* sounds of his bowstring which distressed the multitude of his foes.
With his bowstring and arrow-tip carefully joined through effort, he indeed did not miss him.

(A pair of verses) This son of the Moon, Ratnākara—who is submissive to the venerable Durgadatta and who delights in the assembly of connoisseurs—has composed this poem, *Lalitāṅka*. (Thus ends the *utthāpyā*.)
In battle, the elephants were shattered; their tusks, once formidable, were broken off by those who had not abandoned their cowardice.
In that ocean of passion, where the wives of the gods rejoiced—
It was covered with lovely clusters of mandāra flower garlands. ||73||
Now, on the battlefield, with the hope of victory, he clings to his tree-like arms;

tearing apart his exceedingly powerful enemies, he is indeed not one whose impurity has blossomed through the fear arising from the agitation of combat, nor is he one who has abandoned delusion through the fear rooted in cowardice, which has blossomed into the ruin of his own faults. [Note: This verse is a palindrome (vṛttapratilomānuloma). When read backward, it yields the same meaning.]
"What indeed should one fear?"—this was as if proclaimed by the sounds of kettledrums struck with drumsticks, set forth for battle. (This *garbhayamaka* is composed in the *caṇḍavṛṣṭiprapāta* meter.
Thus, his celestial armies, whose warriors were delighted as they ascended to heaven, supported by the hands of the gods whose hosts had been slain by the hero, [proceeded].

He possesses the splendor of the world-elephants of the quarters, whose faces are veiled by dense shade, and who are like swarms of bees greedily drinking the nectar of his flowing gifts with impetuous haste. ||75||

In the act of variously casting away [obstacles], she shakes [the earth] with a movement impetuous with the weight of her speed; intent on her roar, she is devoted to the protection of the army whose dense clamor resounds through the forest;
ever-giving, she is attentive to the desire to bestow gifts upon the enemy cavalry that hastens toward her.
[The verse *nāhāsaktārirugbhīmudasarasadamugbhīruriktā sahānā* forms four wheels through its forward and reverse orders in the *Sragdharā* meter.
And meanwhile, the frown of Śambhu was like a single, preeminent,
and most terrifying *tāla* creeper in the forest of battle.
In the battle for the destruction of the Daityas, Cāmuṇḍā extolled an indescribable fury, like a wave in the ocean of her formidable prowess. ||77||
She waged a battle with Yama’s army, which was like a herd of wild elephants, causing the host of Dānavas to flee and the temples of the lordly elephants to dry up with fear,
while the forces of Andhaka were blinded.

With the midst of the army of the sons of Diti and Danu crowded together and sinking due to the activity of the continuous stream of weapons raised with impetuous force by the fierce outstretched arms of Caṇḍī,
she was, in that very moment, born as one whose fixed position was agitated by being submerged in the river of blood.
The earth of the battlefield, with its elephants, horses, and men prostrate, was the playground for the night of destruction. ||79||

The vast assembly of celestial maidens, filled with clamor as they rushed forward, their intense anger ignited by the lack of essence [in their opponents], heroes brandishing sharp spears, seizing them one by one in secret,
possessing great beauty like the majestic elephants of the forest, and joined by hosts of men who bowed down— this was the gathering.
When she appeared, her arrival was signaled by the falling rain of severed hundreds of syllables attached to the *sāman* chants— (this is the *ṣoḍaśadala-padma-bandha*).

And on the Jewel Mountain, the earth of battle resounded with the heavy clanging of the saw-like claws of Caṇḍikā’s hands, as they shattered the millions of watchtowers atop the temples of the fierce elephants' temples.

Then, the earth became bound by the succession of headless trunks that were bent over as they played at whirling their massive shoulders—forming a circle—as the heads of manifest warriors were severed by the tips of swords brandished in the air. 81.

Thus ends the forty-sixth canto, titled "The Incitement to Battle with Caṇḍikā," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara and was also known by the name Vidyādhipati, and who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
The forty-seventh canto:
At the forefront of the battle, having crushed the circle of Asuras—

Beholding her there, with their bodies covered in a multitude of bristling hairs, the Siddhas and Sādhyas, having composed an elaborate array of words within the range of their vision, praised the Blessed Lady as follows: ||1||

What wonder is there in this, O Mother, that you have violently shattered this entire circle of enemies at the front of the battle? It is no marvel that you, piercing the darkness of night dwelling within the house—
O abode of wonders, the flame of a lamp never [remains still]. ||2||
I consider that even the great warriors, whose minds are arrogant with the strength of their staff-like arms, are defeated at the front of battle by the enemy;
such is the power of his form, which possesses a faultless state... [saṃsthita].
...this manifestation of yours is [the result of] a sixteenth part of an atom. ||3||
In ancient times, when the hosts of the gods had been defeated by the Daityas, Śaṅkara— his power remaining unmanifested due to the necessity of protecting them—
meditated upon the eternal state.
You have been created so that your mode of existence is not bound by anything other than the conquest of life. ||4||
You now wield a sword that rivals the luster of the throat of the blue-throated Lord (Śiva), for the sake of [your] passion;
[you who are] surrounded by all the trembling enemies agitated by your roar of defiance.
Never again, out of a longing for battle, shall you [be] like wheels. ||5||
O Lord of Asuras, you were beheld in the battles by the entire circle of the gods as if [clinging] to the surface of a wide-spread mirror... clinging to the region of your belly.
She bore a solar disc that scraped the very heavens.

O Goddess, you have attained a transfer [of your qualities] from the Himalayan regions: harshness as if from a mass of stones in battles, a tenderness like a blade of young durva grass in every limb, and a coolness as if from the snowy peaks.
But your laughter is as white as the snow mountain. ||7||
In ancient times, it is said that the Vindhya mountain, whose course had been forbidden even by the sage Agastya when he was about to rise to obstruct the path of the thousand-rayed sun,
[now acts] while you reside within its cave-dwellings.
He attained a permanence and loftiness that surpassed the world. ||8||
Having intentionally assumed an incomparable form, O Puṣpaketu,
under the influence of the burning anguish of your own consumption,
you drew forth the hot breaths from the hollow of your throat, which were like the Kālakūṭa poison.
The moon-crested Lord released them like blazing fires. ||9||
The courtyard of your temple, where swarms of bees descend upon the offerings of flowers presented by the circle of sky-dwellers,
has severed the iron shackles of the bonds of worldly existence.
It shines like a forest strewn with nets upon the Mekalā mountain. ||10||
Like living beings who, having attained a good rebirth after being offered as sacrifices with their throats slit by the blows of swords,
shine brightly while dwelling in the caves of the Vindhya mountains, [they dispel] the darkness of the world.
The lamps placed near you shine forth, piercing through [the darkness]. ||11||
With the shell of the cosmic egg, its neck-opening fashioned by the throat region and its interior filled with the breath of your exhalation,
you fill this very [conch] during the nights of universal dissolution.
Having violently seized the form of Bhairava with both hands. ||12||
Within the vast and formidable cavities of the limbs of your form as the manifest Night of Destruction— difficult to restrain—
the seven worlds you have withdrawn find their full measure.
What is the use of even hundreds of accumulations of human bones as ornaments? 13.
With the beauty of the fleshless skull of Rāhu’s head,
white as a brass vessel, in which you have drunk the wine of the world’s blood,
you bestow upon us a small morsel of meat as a side-dish.
O Mother, whose teeth are tinged with a slight tinge [of red], who would not feel fear? 14.

O auspicious lady, you play [this instrument] during the nights of time, its sound— arising from the striking of the golden mountain as it serves as a cymbal— resonating through and overwhelming the seven worlds.
[He holds] a lotus-seat, a large egg-shaped vessel, a bell with an upward-pointing clapper. ||15||

You bear a form that encircles the seven continents, with the waters of the ocean of consumption flowing unimpeded from your throat, whose vessels have become parched and rough, swallowed by the sighs of your playful sport.
The island, the rays of the hot-rayed sun, the external mountains, and the circle [of the earth]. ||16||

O Mother, I do not think that even the mere sectarian mark (*puṇḍraka*) upon the surface of the forehead is born from the fuel of the seven worlds consumed by the comet that arises with fury at the time of universal dissolution.
Your heap of ash-dust attains completion [as a mountain]. ||17||
The fire within your belly is the Aurva fire, which reduced the waters of the ocean to ashes with its thousands of unrestrained and fierce flames;
and your very breaths are the winds at the onset of the cosmic dissolution.
They have playfully cast down the entire circle of the great mountain ranges. ||18||
You cause [the world] to hear the story of how the vessel of the gourd, shining like the crescent moon clinging to the staff of Mount Meru fixed upon the surface of your chest,
was shattered when your physical frame remained as a mere skeleton.
[She played] the stringed instrument with its strings and the lute made of a single bamboo tube during the nights of cosmic dissolution.
O Caṇḍī, by the mere force of your will, you suddenly create the very universe itself, its vast neck-region fashioned by imagination and filled with the waters of the seven oceans contained within.
This playful water-pot [is used] at the arrivals of the cosmic dissolutions.
O Blessed One, you wear upon your ear a single, enchanting lotus petal, its stalk fashioned from Vaikuṇṭha, its hollows concealed by a formidable, dangling noose.
And I consider Mount Manyu to be like the golden palm-leaf of the mountain of gold. ||21||
You wear as an ear-ornament a pale white lotus, whose stalk is a body with a mass of fresh eyelashes, and whose tongue is made formidable by hoods that serve as petals and are now expanding.
O Bhavānī, you are the splendor even of Ananta, the lord of serpents.
O Caṇḍī, with hands scattering the wide orbs of the sun and moon— like jeweled balls— as they were lowered and raised by the setting and rising mountains,
you played here in your childhood state.
Standing there, her form was a source of wonder to the world. ||23||
O Caṇḍī, delighted at the time of universal dissolution, you wander slowly upon the skulls of corpses, sounding the *tāraka* and *ḍamaruka* drums;
with a skull-topped staff (*viṭaṅka*) resting upon your shoulder—
The bell of Samavarti resounds with the sound of the divisions of time.
O Goddess, this row of skulls upon your head shines forth, its brilliance as white as split conch shells,
appearing like the fierce flames of the fire of universal destruction at the end of an aeon.
The splendor of the entire circle of the great boundary mountains has been reduced to ashes. ||25||
O Kālī, you shine with the slopes of your breasts covered by the skin of the king of elephants, mottled with streaks of blood,
like the eastern quarter of Indra when the rays of the young sun have not yet appeared.
The mountain of sunrise is veiled by the darkness of the intervening space that has been shattered. ||26||
Having playfully grasped with the shells of your fingernail-tips all the surging seven oceans, you fall into a state of trepidation; yet,
having made the thousand-rayed sun a mere armlet for your foot, you remain unshaken.
At the arrival of the times of dissolution, [the worlds] are situated within the abode upon the surface of the earth. ||27||
People meditating upon you— whose beautiful wheel, terrifying with its hub, is fixed upon the heart of Bhairava whose bones are bound therein—
are freed from the spikes of calamity and sorrow that had not been reckoned.
O moon-faced one, the conch shell attains the state of Śaṅkara (Śiva). ||28||
With an undisturbed mind, you sing the *sāman* chants that establish the distinctions within the manifold expansion of Brahman at the onset of the festival of cosmic dissolution;
and you play the *śarvāṇi* drum amidst the circle of your rays of light.
[She holds] a lute whose strings are adorned with the digits of the moon.
With fingers whose tips are variegated by the radiance of rubies resembling a profusion of clearly visible pale-red petals,
this [mountain] shines as it lifts up the lotus of the world.
Your hand alone is as long as the coils of the lord of serpents. ||30||
The sharp edge of the heavy axe for the dense forest of cyclic existence— where one has not yet entered the far shore due to the thicket of spreading afflictions—
is flashing forth, having surpassed the path of suffering.
Oh, how wonderful! In you alone resides devotion, which is a stream of the nectar of wisdom. 31.
O lotus-eyed one, if the lotus, being touched on all sides by a mass of frost, were not to abandon its beauty,
it would be as if licked by the radiance of the jewel-like nails shimmering upon it.
May this foot of yours attain its proper counterpart. ||32||
It shines, overwhelmed by the abundance of fragrance rising from the lotus-throne of her feet— whose toes have petals as red as the dawn—
as she perceives you to be the "night of Kṛṣṇa" (the dark fortnight) and has come to meet you.
Like the vast swarm of bees [attracted] by the essence of devotion. ||33||
O lady with a radiant conch-like neck, your pair of lips, crimson from the tint of betel and resembling a fruit that accords with its reflection,
shone like the sacrificial animal just consumed at that moment.
She seemed to bear [the earth] as if it were moistened by the flowing essence of blood. ||34||
Half of your body has been offered by him, whose mind is embraced by intense passion, to you who are adorned with the crescent of the moon;
yet your heart, O one free from guile, remains entirely his alone.
You have shown him the means for the destruction of pride. ||35||

O Blessed Kālī, you shine forth, adorned with black serpents whose hoods are marked by the crest-like rays of the jewels in their hoods, serving as your necklaces, bracelets, and girdles; you who have consumed the sacrificial offerings.
As if by the power of the transformation of the smoke arising from incense. ||36||

The flames of the fierce fire, rising from the hissing of the serpent Vāsuki whose broad hoods have blossomed as they are firmly pressed against the base of your throat by the binding of the *uṣṇīṣa*, bring you complete satisfaction.
Upon the head of the enemy of Smara (Śiva), he has dried up the clouds and rivers.
O Mother Night, you shine forth, bearing the orb of the moon with its deer-mark amidst the darkness, yet with its disc of nectar-rays incomplete,
while the paths of the sky remain turbid with clearly visible masses of mud-like clouds.
It resembled a shimmering skull lying crosswise in the forest. ||38||
O Blessed One, you bear a beauty like that of a woman whose full and swelling breasts are marked by the application of sandalwood water as tender as a dangling hibiscus flower,
while you are embraced by the twilight.
Through passion, you have become like the dark night of Kṛṣṇa.
Resorting to your radiant lotus-hands as a refuge,
as if to attain the status of an attendant by taking shelter there,
the shadows darken the inner recesses of the cave-dwellings.
The heroes, with their creeper-like formidable swords, bestow [their gifts]. ||40||
O Mother, the Śabaras dwelling in the caves of the Vindhya mountains bear a splendor like that of water-laden clouds, as if embraced by the rays of the sword-blades buried by heroes.
Your shadows, having performed the rite of offering water for honor, are now streaming forth. ||41||
O Mother, may those [beings] whose bodies bear the scars of Guha and the moon resting upon their laps, whose crests are disheveled by the offerings of your dance,
and who dwell within the cave-dwellings of the Vindhya mountain’s caverns— [protect us].
The peacocks bear the grace of an entourage. ||42||
The courtyard of your house, beautified by the splashing of streams of blood from the sacrificial animals cut down by the blows of your sword,
bears the likeness of the twilight seized by Śiva in his wrath when he was prostrating before him.
O Mother, [I behold] Lakṣmī as if she were constantly accompanied by hundreds of bards. 43.
O Mother, from you the sciences have obtained their incomparable birth— sciences honored for their power over the three worlds and which serve as the cause for the production of various fruits.
Like wish-fulfilling creepers following the slopes of Mount Hemādri. ||44||

The collection of phonemes that constitutes the entirety of the compositions of all speech, which establishes the eightfold divisions of the stages formed by the three principles (tattva), and which is the sole cause for the attainment of the fruits of heaven and liberation— Please note: The provided text appears to be a fragment of a verse from a Sanskrit work concerning grammar or philosophy (likely related to the *Śivasūtra* or a commentary thereon). The translation reflects the technical terminology used in such contexts.
Those who know the ancient lore desire you as the mother of the sacred tradition. ||45||
The activity of the Self, which is the supreme reality— tranquil, beyond the reach of all conceptual proliferation, immutable, and free from change—
is the Śikhā; it is the nature of the most subtle among the subtle and the profound.
Situated within the maṇḍala of deep sleep, you shine as the supreme light.
The Lord, desiring to create the worlds, constantly presides over you, who possess the nature of being the primal cause; by you,
through a succession of folds, he is established within the knot.
She had attained a state that was devoid of middle or end.
O Gaurī, you abide as the power that enjoys the fruits [of action], resting upon the Liṅga of the Lord, which clearly possesses the seventeen-fold state;
and you exist within all bodies as the essence of consciousness.
It is said that she has indeed attained the nature of consciousness within material elements. ||48||

Indeed, through the power of the practice of cultivation, you, O Mother of the Victors, have dispelled the dense darkness by means of the flames of the forest fire of meditation, which is unimpeded in its consumption of the fuel of the afflictions.
It has been declared by those abiding in the teaching of the Jina that darkness is not the cause of light. ||49||
For the Victor who has ascended to the pinnacle of enlightenment,
the stages beginning with *muditā* (joy) are declared to be a flight of stairs;
they consist of the clear twofold mode of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) directed toward resolute conviction.
O Upholder of the World, you are the Dhāraṇī who prevents one from falling into ruin. ||50||

O Mother, you alone are the motherhood of the Conqueror; you are Wisdom, whose delusion has been destroyed, while the fire of the path of outflows—which brings together the mass of fuel that is the afflictions—has its flames [extinguished] by him.
O Mother, you have destroyed his total darkness.
This, which is the cause for the destruction of worldly existence, has been repeatedly proclaimed by the Jains. ||51||

You are praised by those who have mounted the chariot of the path— the path that is unbroken, which has transcended the state of breaking the pair of paths (the dualistic extremes), and whose course is clearly manifest;
you are embraced by the fearlessness and selflessness proclaimed [by you].
O forms, you are the perfection of wisdom; thus it is understood by the Buddhas. (52)

This eightfold path was taught by you alone as the means for abandoning the stream of the aggregates— which is empty of the obstruction of the dense thicket of proliferating afflictions— for the sake of final nirvana.
The exceedingly profound path of the Sugata has been revealed. ||53||

And she was beheld upon the ground of Noble Avalokita, where the paths of travel had been rendered treacherous by the light of consciousness that had swallowed up the continuity of the blinding darkness of ignorance.
O Mother, you are called Tārā, born from the lotus family. ||54||
Having attained the state of supreme intentionality, it constantly abides in a secondary status adhering to conformity; through its preeminent whiteness,
it is known as "Vidyā," a name for all the manifold and complete perspectives.
Indeed, you are proclaimed as Saṃkarṣaṇī in the teaching.
Wherein the ascetics, having bound their bodies into a supreme posture suited for the highest yoga, attain the state of being the Lord’s own;
that [posture], though common to all, is the sole cause for the fruit of liberation.
She is described in the Bhagavatī as the path of the single way and as being without marks.
With heads [as many as] those of the thousand-headed Puruṣa, you are sung as the Sāman-chant, whose branches extend through the dense forest of manifold divisions;
you, who are pleasing to the ear, are sung with a beautiful manifestation.
His beautiful devotion is perfected in five ways. ||57||

By you alone, through the entire stream of nectar in the sky, which holds the leadership of the multitude of mantras numbering seventy million— the means for attaining the happiness of both worldly enjoyment and liberation— this whole [universe] is sustained.
The world, a manifold expansion of manifold qualities, is caused to be made worthy [of enjoyment]. ||58||
O Peaceful One, you are indeed the primordial digit (*kalā*), the supreme abode of the Śiva-scriptures and the sole cause of the triad of digits belonging to the Supreme Lord;
having transcended the [lower] principles (*tattva*) and attained your own state of being, you abide.
Those who are disciplined do not experience the long cycle of birth and death. ||59||
It is said that you have indeed emerged in five ways from the mouths of Brahmā;
from these five alone, you are the cause for the accomplishment of the three worlds,
through the various pure mantras manifested by knowledge.
He whose splendor is enhanced by a state that delights in the manifold expansion of hymns of praise. ||60||

That which is the mark of gnosis, in which the wheel of conceptual construction has ceased, which has transcended [all limits], and which is variegated with all objects for those of supreme intellect—
they call that the *udgītha*, having encompassed the universe on all sides.
One remains solitary, devoid of all means and dharmas. ||61||
He who abides pervading the world and all its speech, having indeed entered even those [words] of the Creator—
He who is to be praised by the Atharva-veda hymns as the cause, whose faces are turned in every direction.
Those of pure intellect declare that the root of all objects of perception is the ālayavijñāna. ||62||
It is said that in the beginning, for the sake of the emergence of the worlds, he arose from the slope of the cheek of the Self-born Brahmā;
he whose form assumes various distinctions through the transformations of its manifestations.
Those who know the higher and the lower maintain that Brahman exists in two ways. ||63||
That which the poets call the door of the hot-rayed sun, the solar, made of udumbara wood, and indeed named after the palate—
this [palate] attains a beauty through its threefold arrangement.
The state of those whose minds are intent on yoga is indeterminate.
That which is called the Pervasive, the Swan, the High Pitch, the Bright, and here the Vaidyuta, is said to be Ananta;
and they describe him as having the three locations and so forth as his sphere.
Those who are disciplined [attain] the stainless Brahman, which unfolds through threefold distinctions. ||65||
In ancient times, it is said that Brahmā and Maheśvara,
having assumed their respective forms like space and approached Prajāpati, both taught this very same Veda together with its auxiliary limbs.
He, too, was renowned upon the earth as "Mukha" (the Face). ||66||
He who is indeed pointed out in the world as being visible through the reality of sound, the nature of existence, names, excellent qualities, and meditative intent;
in whom those whose minds are dissolved perceive neither pleasure, pain, nor delusion—
And those who are disciplined become devoid of [ordinary] sensation. ||67||
He who is proclaimed in the Śrutis, the Upaniṣads, and all the branches of knowledge as the sole cause of the two-fold fruit;
and by whom the refined and excellent [Vedic] compositions were brought forth—
Indeed, it is said that the Vedas have come to be expressed by those [words]. ||68||
The foremost of the twice-born, desiring that supreme purifier consisting of Brahmā and the other deities, seek it as the means of purification through great austerity;
having ascended it, they immediately proceed upon its pole.
They were intent upon a path that was indeed extremely difficult to traverse and unimpeded. ||69||
That which they call the manifold consisting of consciousness and so forth, that which is designated as the "Person seen in the eye" (cakṣuṣaḥ puruṣa),
and that which the followers of the Taittirīya recension describe as the sheath of essence (rasa) and the rest—
He [perceived] the cause of the wheel and the treasury of those of pure intellect. ||70||

Having restrained the mind— the cause of the wheel of various transformations that are indistinct, manifest, or distinct— it shall never again fall into that same state; for it is difficult to bring [the mind] back from its dwelling within the hollow of the lotus of the navel and heart.
The Noble Ones, whose vision of meditative concentration is unimpaired, perceive this. ||71||
The wise, clearly devoted to the Self, relying upon a concentration free from conceptual construction, and having gathered all beings together,
indeed attain that which is beyond darkness and waveless.
One's own being, established as a counterpart to the ocean of destruction. ||72||
The sages desire that Lord of Sacrifice who bestows the unimpeded bliss of enjoyment in heaven and whose six limbs consist of the oblation properly cast into the mouth of the fire.
He approached the hot-rayed sun as it stood over the rain released from its belly. ||73||

If it were said that "eternal" refers to something not endowed with the nature of being non-eternal, then that would not be a valid reason; for [the opponent's position] is subject to a pair of objections that lack any subverting evidence.
He whose conduct toward his powers was constantly unremitting.
By the Supreme Lord, who is free from identity or difference with the earth, moon, sun,
self, wind, fire, ether, and water,
and who remains pervading the entire body;
By which [reason] the world's state of having no other creator was refuted. ||75||
Resting upon the pericarp of a lofty lotus, which has taken root within the womb of a body composed of atoms established by Brahmā,
like a lamp that has reached its end as the flame falls away.
It has the form of a lamp, yet it exists in a state beyond all forms.

It is devoid of sound, syllables, and phonemes; it is not produced by the throat or the palate; it is imperishable, not nasalized, and without support; its nature is free from movement, transition, and return.
Mounted upon a vast chariot that shattered the bodies [of his enemies]. ||77||
That supreme light, which is immortal, shines within the heart— a mass of wisdom, having attained the stability of four feet, a state of non-dual equilibrium, and a perfectly polished summit.
Though nearest at hand, it is farthest away for those from whom darkness has not departed. ||78||
That which, for the sake of the stability of this world, appears as if divided through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) though it is in truth indivisible;
and that which is the eternal reality established within the heart— [to that I bow].
Sages proclaim it to be the immortal essence whose nature is bliss. ||79||
That which does not grow weary before the sun or fire in any direction, by whose light all this world is illuminated,
and which the primordial nature (prakṛti) approaches as the true essence of knowledge— this is it.
And whose power is the Blessed One, the one with a lotus-navel. ||80||
When the phonemes (varṇa), which are devoid of denotative power, have ceased to exist, that reality of speech (vāktattva) which is sequentialless and free from differentiated forms—
what the grammarians call "sphoṭa"— is what they describe.
They possess the reality of things as they are, free from conceptual construction and direct perception. ||81||

And Kaṇāda, before Akṣapāda, explained [the system] on earth, divided by sixteen categories according to the aphorisms of the Pramāṇas, through the conceptualization of the distinctions of substance and so forth.
And whose foot the Blessed One placed upon his unshakable body. ||82||
Since this world, with its diverse forms, has arisen like a circle of bubbles from water,
having obtained its power from within the entire mass of seeds;
And Vāgīśvarī indeed desists from it, because of that. ||83||
From whose mind, it is said, the cool-rayed moon arose,
from the slope of whose hips the sun emerged, and from whose interior the sky was born—
that Blessed One, though himself unconditioned, manifests through ignorance.
And the person who [discovers] the knot placed within the cave.
These drops from the fire of knowledge, which indeed issue from his mouth, and that Imperishable One who for a moment has entered into flux—
through their union, the world shines forth according to the states of being.
That which is empty of form, yet possesses all forms combined. ||85||
Neither short nor long, nor even protracted; without gender, one, devoid of the distinction of case-endings and numbers;
it satiates the entire world with its supreme splendor.
And that which is devoid of existence and empty of the modifications of being. ||86||
There is no exclusion whatsoever here for that which,
being deluded by the persistence of non-substantial objects,
manifests as various effects caused by diverse states of existence.
All things are joined with the transformation of the manifold wheel. ||87||
Having attained the state of being the cause for accomplishing the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation, and possessing the power to sustain the world,
[the seven rivers] indeed emerged from the Bindu-lake as seven mantras.
Tens of millions [of them] went forth unimpeded, like clouds or rivers. ||88||
Just as there is the comprehension of another self, so too, when the triad is not perceived, that word which resides within the self— subtler than the subtle—
is for the manifestation of its own form.
Through his state of being, he has transformed the course of the world. ||89||
He who, though his form is eternally undifferentiated, has assumed all these modifications born of primordial nature (prakṛti), is the supreme ornament among those of various kinds in the deep,
flowing currents of the sacred fords (tīrtha).
That which they declare to be the cause of the diversity of views. ||90||
The unborn Brahmā, Hari, and Ātmabhū [are] endowed with the three abodes and so forth, devoid of beginning and end, the navel of the universe, and the unmoving center of that which moves.
They have emitted the entirety of speech.
Those of perfected intellect praise him as worthy of being upheld with great reverence. ||91||
*Tat sat*— that which is immeasurable and supreme, the realization of the wisdom of awakening through the dense scriptures that reflect upon the third body (*kāya*),
possessing a steadfastness that is not barren of the Vedas, and having shaken off the thick fetters.

O Mother, that *praṇava* is the Lord of Speech; it is Your mouth. (A group of thirty-two verses) Seated within the heart, it acts with skill in moving through the pathways situated within the interior of the sky of the thousand channels and veins.
You alone are Śakti, the secret protection consisting of the coming and going within the solar orb of Brahmā—the supreme and non-supreme reality of the Paramātman. ||93||

O you who are indeed some indescribable awakening of the son of Daśaratha, you alone have made your own the entire manifold of the path of reality, through the excellence of the treasury of space (Gaganagañja) becoming manifest.
The beings, the powers, the supreme lords, the deities, and so forth. ||94||
The tongues of those who dwell in the triple heaven, having offered clarified butter as a libation into the blazing fire for the sake of the path to immortality,
are the rays of the supreme Person, whose radiance is like that of the sun.
They lead him to that place; this is the manifestation of your power. 95.
[She who is] composed of light, consisting of the functions of the organs of sense and action, abiding in the primordial syllable *haṃsa*, offered with faultless *arghya*—
[to her who is] the sixteen heroic forms of the gurus headed by Śrīkaṇṭha...
She has attained the state of being seated upon a full-blown lotus of power. ||96||
I bow to you, who hold a trident manifested through the three powers in your hand, who illumines all the worlds with your splendor as Śivā,
and who are the abundance of supreme nectar agitated by waves.
Meditating upon the form of Bhairava, they indeed abide in the Kaula state. ||97||
With a sharp, broad, and formidable trident whose three points surpass the rays of the sun clinging to your limbs,
you are indeed subtle and the eternal body.
He is the sole cause for the shattering of the arts of illusion. ||98||
Having meditated here upon you, O Kaulika, seated upon the pericarp of the lotus situated at the tip of the trident resting on the wheel,
he attains the state of one fallen by grace (śaktipāta), embraced by the steady Bhairava.
This person [perceives] the function as possessing the distinction between the higher and the lower. ||99||

O Caṇḍī, for one who has taken his stand upon the wheel of the Mothers situated at the six limits, there occurs the activity of the gross and subtle bodies belonging to that wheel of the Mothers situated at the six limits.
You alone are renowned in the world as the Supreme Lord’s power, consisting of the imperishable syllable (akṣara), who has indeed assumed every form in the universe. 100.
Having occupied [the world],
obstructing the universe, and manifesting as all the primordial forms, those various activities of yours, which shine forth as unsurpassed, are performed for the benefit of living beings.
Indeed, you are the unimpeded power of the Supreme Lord. 101.

You, Bhavānī, are called the power (*śakti*) who gives birth to the cause; you are the entire seed-measure residing within the potency of the Self. Through your nature of gradual generation, the universe—variegated—
That [creation] is emitted by you with its course unimpeded. ||102||
Just as Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, ordained the path of the senses such as sight for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice— namely fire, wind, and the sun—
they desire you to be that very cause of the world.
O Mother, you who are born of a single desire, and who are red, white, and black.
You are indeed the unimpeded power of the mind;
you are proclaimed as Vāgīśvarī, variegated by the white drop (bindu).
They call you the navel, the immortal essence of the seven immortals.
But she who has taken refuge in a certain Kaumārika-cakra—104.

O Bhavānī, you are the supreme knowledge, possessing the distinction of being both transcendent and immanent; you are the unobstructed lamp that illuminates reality, revealing the entire range of objects within all the worlds.
It is the cause of the happiness of worldly enjoyment and liberation for the soul whose nature is unimpaired. ||105||
His splendor is honored by clusters of blossoming *śakti*-flowers with variegated colors distinct from their various modes of composition;
he is as delightful as a supreme *brahma*-tree entwined with pure creepers and a stainless lotus.
You are the one whose form is all-pervading and who bestows the fruit of liberation.
O Blessed Lady, you shine with a radiance that surpasses the sun— the very orb of the auspicious universe that fully illuminates the dense darkness of the night of illusion.
The thousand million radiant rays have dispelled the darkness.
O Mother, you alone are known as the eightfold cause for men who seek the means to enjoy the pleasures of heaven;
yet even the subtle distinction between Pradhāna and Puruṣa remains unperceived.
But you alone distinguish those who possess meditative concentration. 108.

O woman of excellent complexion, you are the pericarp of the Brahma-throne, established in the sixfold conduct, containing within you the seed-syllables of the unimpaired castes, having taken hold of the heart, and as fair as gold.
It is the center of the lotus of all speech. ||109||

O Goddess of the Jagatī meter, you are indeed said to be the presiding deity of those faultless scriptures for the wise, by whose mastery of the discernment of the world one swiftly attains residence in the same realm as the Divine.
You approached as the cause for the pacification of the flood of their sins. ||110||
Renowned as possessing the stainless nature of Maheśvara, you shine forth as the unimpeded one situated in the midst of those eight powers— Tārā and the others— who indeed exist in the world.
The primordial Śiva-śakti bestows the bliss of liberation for each individual. ||111||
O Bhavānī, those who know the higher and the lower maintain that this reality consists of Śiva and Śakti existing in a threefold manner; therein,
you have fully awakened to the sphere of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍamaṇḍala*).
Intoxication is a state of mind that follows after the desire for its cause. 112.
It is a ladder for those whose calamity of the threefold bondage has been severed by the excellence of the Lord’s grace,
for the attainment of the eternal state; it consists of six parts— ...
You are renowned as the path of the steps leading upward. ||113||

O Gaurī, whose nature is excellence, the reality of the word "Prakṛti" (Primordial Nature), which is the cause of all things, revolves through the worlds— beginningless and endless— in accordance with its true essence; that is the imperishable Brahman, consisting of Śiva.
It is said that you, O Mātṛkā, have emerged from the surface of his face.
Those skilled in the application of yoga, through their superior concentration,
utter the syllable "Om" as the *udgītha*, which is a long and piercing resonance arising from the deep humming sound produced by the steady flow of the vital breath.
But you alone are its unimpeded impeller. 115.
O Mother, because you manifest as the fivefold distinct agents in acts such as bestowing light upon the face [of the disciple],
the independent Brahman here appears as the sole non-agent.
Your action toward him is fruitful, for you possess unfailing power.
The earth is his feet, the sky his navel, the quarters of space his ears, the sun his eye, fire his mouth,
and the heavens indeed his head— of that all-pervading Lord you are...
He wore a brilliant garland of jasmine, sugar-cane, and clusters of *uḍu* flowers.
O Mother, you are indeed the Mātṛkā, whose inner cavern is filled with the fifty most graceful circles of phonemes;
those very same phonemes have become the foundation of all verbal expression.
O fair one, you shall soon bring forth fruits like a pod-bearing creeper. ||118||
O Supreme Goddess, you are indeed the power of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), abiding upon the path of the sixfold [mantras] and possessing the threefold state of division;
you are the unimpeded [source] for the sprouting of the entire host of flawless mantras.
The homage as the cause is said to begin with the syllable *praṇava* (OM). ||119||
O Bhavānī, the Brahmins here recite you as the *sāmidhenī* verse that utterly destroys the spreading darkness;
you are the cow who yields unimpeded desires and are free from all sin.
It is renowned as consisting entirely of the destruction of all [defilements], dripping with honey.
Having quickly drunk the divine nectar, those whose minds are intent on yoga become happy, their suffering dispelled; O Blessed One,
you are that very essence, having reached the state of cessation.
She alone constantly nourished the moon.
Indeed, by your own indestructible power, having extracted the multitudes of individual souls from the ocean of the bonds of existence for Śaṅkara,
you shattered the dense and most difficult nooses of initiation.
The Lord Ananta incessantly leads [the soul] upward from the wheel. ||122||
The power of the yoga of the support of the Blessed Lady, residing between the eyebrows— indeed, like a crystal, clearly manifesting various colors—
when meditated upon, bears manifold fruits for men according to reality.
Of that stainless state of Śiva, you alone are the crest-jewel. 123.
You alone are the Supreme Lord’s power, the progenitor of the canopy of knowledge, consisting of eighty-one throbbing syllables;
you are the bestower of the bliss of worldly enjoyment and liberation upon the three worlds.
In you alone do the collections of mantras find their honored and established foundation.
O Mother, that which is the thread of this world and its manifold traditional doctrines—
the reality (tattva) postulated by the Sāṃkhyas as beginningless— has indeed arisen from You,
the Supreme Cause, as the Self.
In the teaching of Śiva, you are declared to have gain as your sole motive. ||125||
That which is of the nature of bliss, immortal, beyond all description, transcending the fivefold path, resembling the waters of a motionless ocean,
and which is designated in the Upaniṣads as "not this, not this"— [that is Brahman].
It is representation-only, free from limiting adjuncts, and devoid of activity by others. 126.
Of that Lord, who has taken refuge in the indeterminate state and is devoid of all phenomenal attributes, there is one wondrous activity:
the faultless power of operation within the earth and other elements.
You alone remain as the sole controller of the pervasive universe. ||127||

O Gaurī, although Brahman is one and all-pervading, it exists in two ways: as the gross self and as the exceedingly subtle. O Mother, having penetrated its body which consists of light— The final line of the verse is incomplete in the source text; however, based on the context provided, the intended meaning is that one should contemplate the form of the Divine. Here is the complete translation of the available portion: "O Gaurī, although Brahman is one and all-pervading, it exists in two ways: as the gross self and as the exceedingly subtle. O Mother, having penetrated its body which consists of light—"
Whether external or internal, you attain prosperity through your power. ||128||
You are the subtle one, born from the nectar of the digit of the moon; you are visible through the yoga of abiding in the state reached by the single sense-faculty,
and you have arisen from the moon, the sun, and fire.
You shine forth with pure rays that dispel the blinding darkness.
O Mother Halahalā, you are indeed renowned as the Sarasvatī who presides over the Vedas and is celebrated as the supreme deity of the inner self;
yet another, the external one, possesses broad and full rounded hips.
Possessing a beauty as enchanting as hair, breasts, the pair of lips, and other such [features]. ||130||
Having reached the state of being the source of the Vedas, you possess a nature consisting of many distinct numbers of syllables, yet you are established beyond primordial matter;
you are composed of the splendor of Brahman and are the expansion of light.
She has indeed arrived, like a royal swan at the lotus-face of a brahmin. ||131||

O Lakṣmī, you alone shine forth, cherished by your affectionate embrace upon the chest of Kṛṣṇa— which is dark like the Kaustubha gem and possesses the brilliance of a thousand suns— while resting upon his sprout-like hand.
She whose lotus-face possesses the playful grace of a fresh white lotus while seated in the lotus posture. ||132||
O Mother, you alone have fashioned the circle of stars, shining like gems,
as the radiant orb for the great door-panel of the night.
Of the casket-like cosmic egg, which delights in the world of bondage. ||133||
Meditating upon you, who are established in the center of the lotus of the sky— the path of the stars— whose pericarp is the expansive orb of the moon,
[devotees] seem to shower down a rain of nectar.
Thinking thus, the practitioner suddenly meets with death. ||134||
Or those who drink from your fragrant breast,
which hangs down in the middle of the palate of the Supreme Goddess—
satiated by that nectar, they [attain] the path of liberation.
They enter [into that state], devoid of all feminine charms and emotional transformations. ||1365||
Having attained the state of lightning amidst the masses of clouds at the time of universal dissolution, you flash forth, fair as gold rubbed on a touchstone;
you alone are the flame of the fire in the mouth of the submarine mare.
You reduce even all the lords of the oceans to ashes. ||136||
Of those [lotuses] whose abundant filaments and fragrance emerge from the apertures of the petals— whose joints have been loosened by the power of contraction—
and which possess a dawn-like radiance capable of piercing the nocturnal darkness, at the awakening...
You alone are the kinsman of the mines of beautiful lotuses. ||137||
O moonlight, you alone are the splendor that causes the loosening of the continuous sleep of the circle of night-lotus groves for the sake of the moon;
you alone are the radiance variegated by the rays of the new Kaustubha gem.
She who was cherished by her affectionate embrace upon the chest of Murāri. 138.
The state of being Brahmī is attained by one whose form rests upon a seat of blooming lotuses, who is like a royal swan with a dwelling fashioned in a celestial chariot,
and who possesses four faces clearly arranged as a choir.
O Rāma, you shine like Nīti (Policy) through your beautiful virtues and skillful means. ||139||
O Gaurī, Śaṅkara bears within his heart an unceasing flow of passion, as if it were the red dye from the paste of betel leaves, fixed there by the imprint of his bimba-like lips.
And you, O Vaiṣṇavī, do not shine at the front of battles. ||140||

You are the consort of Maheśvara; with your three eyes copper-red with wrath, the flames expanding from them have numbed the fire at the tip of the Pināka bow, while the rays of the moon upon your crest—
Her matted locks were washed by the waters of the celestial river, which had been rendered turbid [by the dust raised by his chariot]. ||141||
O goddess whose vehicle is the peacock, you possess a splendor as you hold a spear with hands as tender as lotuses;
you are like the grace of the churning of the ocean by the coils of the serpent.
His body, like a mountain, had its waist thinned by the weight of his saffron robes. ||142||
Holding the thunderbolt itself, whose streams are as terrifying as fire from the blood of hundreds of Daitya armies swallowed by your formidable hands of flame-clusters,
you shine with your eyes.
Like the eastern quarter with blooming blue lotuses in autumn. ||143||
O Mother, with your hands joined in *añjali* by Cāmuṇḍā,
the moon upon your head is eclipsed by the mass of light from the nails on the fingers; you, O skeletal one covered in ashes, bow your head to her.
Śambhu was like a house-deity of a cremation ground accompanied by Bhājā. ||144||

O Blessed One, you whose splendor fills the quarters of the sky and the expanse of the heavens— where darkness has been pierced by the rays of your bared fangs, which expand like a wide-spread boat covering the sun— you have entered the ocean under the guise of your shadow.
In the midst [of them], you alone shine forth with the face of a boar. ||145||
O Sovereign Goddess, you are the face of the mass of the Vedas, which stands as the cause for achieving the fruits of heaven and liberation;
you are the Gāyatrī, the lotus-face of the twice-born people.
She is like a royal swan whose dwelling has been destroyed by the cessation of the fragments [of her body]. ||146||
Sāvitrī too, her lotus-like eyes closed by the shadow of the shimmering moon-face of her own countenance,
was turning the circle of her jewel-bead rosary.
O Mother, you shine like the night amidst a multitude of stars. ||147||
O Mother, having drunk again the smoke arising from the masses of incense burnt as offerings presented by the seven worlds, you seem to emit it once more,
veiling the rays of the sun.
The mass of soot from the rows of flame-tips of the fire [blazing] from the upward-gazing eyes.
O fierce goddess, when the Destroyer beholds the cruel slaughter of the enemy of Kāsarasa (the buffalo-demon) among the hosts of gods and demons,
he looks upon it as if out of fear for the destruction of his own buffalo.
Yama did not restrain those who were bowed down with devotion toward you. ||149||
O Bhavānī, your feet have been reached by those who have taken refuge in them, as their slender bodies are reflected in the mirror of your toenails;
they are like the Vālakhilyas who, through the merit of their prostrations, have instantly attained [the state of] the sun.
Like forms, they pay homage to beauty with their hands joined in reverence. ||150||
With the regions of your jar-like breasts bound by chains that are the flames of fire emitted from your hissing breath,
you bear a splendor that is the perfection of yoga through profound resolve.
You are the ground that serves as a treasure-trove for the jewels of the most excellent collection of mantras.
Beholding before you that greediness for raw flesh, wet with splashes of blood from the animal offerings slaughtered by the Śabaras,
your body became reduced to mere bones, its flesh entirely cast off.
This Revatī shines as if out of fear of the mechanical device. ||152||
O Mother, your face bears a beauty through the mass of rays emerging from your row of stainless teeth,
like a jasmine flower with its flesh-like petals playfully grasped as a morsel.
Like a staff of white bones, with a flickering and terrifying tongue. ||153||
Having heard the deep resonance of the drum struck at the tip of the foot of Vajrapāṇi at the front of the battle,
the sound of other drums turned away in despondency.
Surely, O Mother, this army is once again free from adversaries. (154)

They seem to leap across the peaks of the Vindhya mountains, which are like the dwellings of Kadamba trees, as if by means of the streams of blood flowing from their crests, shattered by the force of their mutual combat.
The cocks do not share in that teaching-method of yours. ||155||
O Sovereign Lady, this form of yours is terrifying, with its serpent necklace adorned by dangling skulls and garlands of flowers;
yet your heart remains tender with compassion for the seven worlds.
It is firmly resolved to achieve the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Sovereign Goddess, for those men whose souls are purified by the longing to remember the pair of your lotus feet,
the iron shackles quickly cast off their own form.
They assume the splendor of ruby foot-ornaments and bracelets. ||157||
With thousands of formidable masses of waves shattered by the impact of the rocks on its moving slopes at the shore,
may the ocean— the bridge that breaks upon the boat— protect you who meditate on it daily.
The ocean attains the state of a floor paved with sapphire. ||158||
For those who constantly remember the pair of your feet, may the [fire] with its flickering, fierce flames variegated by rows of terrifying smoke,
and which has attracted swarms of bees by its flowing, thick nectar— [May that fire burn away their sins.]
The fire attains the state of being beneath a grove of Mandāra trees. ||159||
O Mother, even in the forests, the elephants— whose temple-regions are drenched by the flow of rutting ichor and who are like dark storm-clouds—
flee at the mere remembrance of Your feet, as do lions.
As if they had become terrified by the fierce roar of the enemy's army. ||160||
With faces made terrible by fangs, with the luster of upward-pointing hair tawny like flickering flames, and with eyes red and fierce,
though your minds are utterly intent on violence toward those who do not bow to you—
O Gaurī, even those who roam at night bear friendship toward the world.
Dwelling within the recesses of mountain rivers and caves under your protection,
he surely does not harm those whose faces are well-adorned by the frontal globes of elephants with their profuse ichor.
Even a lion whose claws are worn down by the tips of the roof-beams. ||162||

Even the venomous serpents, though desiring to bite with flames emitted from their hissing and with the luster of eyes red with rage, become as harmless as the fierce appearance of quivering filaments before those devoted to You.
Their tongues bear the playful grace of garlands of blooming blue lotuses. ||163||
Though they desire to strike, with their creeper-like swords drawn and their formidable staff-like bows drawn wide,
they have come to kinship and rescue those who bow before you.
O Mother, those who have fallen into the wilderness or difficult terrain will certainly be plundered by robbers. ||164||

Homage to you, who have awakened the world— deluded by the greatness of your proclaimed lightness in thus transcending the objects of ordinary perception— and whose power is equal to that of the Lord of the Immortals.
Indeed, it was for the purpose of purifying one's vision that [it was offered] to Caṇḍikā. ||165||
Thus we have ceased our praise of you not because of a failure of desire for the Blessed One, but due to the deficiency of our own power;
we merely taste the rain of droplets from the spray of nectar.
Whose state of having a tongue devoid of relish does he not encounter? ||166||

Thus, O Mother, whatever collection of merit has been earned by us through these praises of your virtues—by that, may we have devotion toward you at every moment, which bears the fruit of delight in the worship of your feet. 167.
Quell the affliction of great delusion; grant me a vision that is ever more stainless; cast away the sin that has become a solid mass;
