and untie the firm knots of the snares that entangle one in worldly existence.
The remembrance of your lotus feet is never fruitless for those who have surrendered their souls. 168.
Thus, Caṇḍikā— whose auspicious beauty is purified by the grace arising from the mature sounds of the elaborate hymns offered by the hosts of gods bowing in prostration,
and who strikes terror into the inhabitants of the three worlds with her *huṃ* cries that consume pride like fire— is [the one].
With her weapons, she brought that host of lords of the Daityas and Dānavas to utter exhaustion. ||169||
Avoiding at that very time the fierce onset of the wrath of Kālarātri,
other heroic Daityas, who had not yet succumbed to despondency, approached Śauri on the Jewel Peak.

Thus ends the forty-seventh canto, titled "The Hymn to Caṇḍī," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel [ratna], composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara, who bore the title Vāgīśvara and was also known by the name Vidyādhipati, and who was a dependent of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati.
The Fiftieth Canto: When Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Indra had been defeated...
Then the Lord, together with all the world-protectors,
addressed the lord of the Daityas as "Five-Eyed," having angrily and harshly strung his bow of lofty tip. ||1||
Behold now this banner of the serpent-eater (Garuda), broken here by Andhaka, its passion for battle shattered;
upon it were once painted [the figures] as bright as moonbeams.
The quarters of the sky were clothed in his shared garments of glory. ||2||
Behold the body of the Self-born (Brahmā), reddened by the scattering of jewels from the Daitya-lord as he was struck by a multitude of arrows;
it resembles the navel-lotus of Madhusūdana when released from sleep.
Even now, it seems as if it were smeared with thick, motionless honey. ||3||
Behold the thunderbolt in the hand of Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, rendered blunt by the impact of the hard bones and stones of the *ātāyikas* whom he had conquered in battle;
it has become the source of fear for him because of the Daityas.
Like heat sprinkled with water, it does not spread its brilliance. ||4||
The wheel of the sharp-edged discus of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, whose fierce activity has ceased due to its familiarity with shame,
has fled away out of fear of Viṣṇu, leaving the fire-god behind.
Behold it smoking as it clings to your hand. ||5||
By the falling arrows from the circular bow drawn by the circle of arms of the Lord of the Daityas, who was bound in fury,
his middle was filled with hundreds of fractures and made manifest with gaping wounds.
The orb of the sun, its splendor spread wide, does not depart until it is full.
Behold him, whose heart is being occupied by a deer— his body mangled by iron arrows, his firm bond of courage broken after his habitual prowess in battle.
The moon was as if its own mind had become timid through transference [to her]. ||7||
Behold him before you, like Mount Asta veiled by a mass of dark clouds; having approached the leader of the Dānava host,
he is exceedingly distressed in this battle due to his intense heat.
The sun itself was shattered along with its own majestic splendor. ||8||
Wielding a heavy mace that had shattered the skulls of enemies,
with his conch and lotus held gracefully and languidly,
he who had employed hundreds of weapons against the showers of arrows from Andhaka—
The Lord of Orissa appears like the mangled Śauri [Kṛṣṇa] after his defeat by Jarāsaṃdha. ||9||
Behold this beauty of his face, which, as if out of shame, possesses the hue of a fresh heap of collyrium intensified by the shadows of the frowns formed in his conquests,
and is veiled by a clinging blue cloth.
Yama holds [him], avoiding the path of my sight. ||10||
Varuṇa, his trembling still unceasing, bears in his mouths a body reddened by the flames of the fire of the poison of his enemies—
[a body] clinging to his eternal dwelling in the ocean, the abode of makaras.
Like this very flame of the irresistible submarine fire. ||11||
Behold this [cloud], dense with bees falling from the masses of ichor-drops dripping from the temples of the elephants of the quarters as they are let loose,
which— due to its dullness caused by the delusion of being a forest of *kiṃśuka* flowers— [is mistaken for one].
The fire, its heat obstructed by the Asuras, rages within.
A mass of terrible darkness, like a cloud of stainless black swords, thickens and shrouds the sky;
it leaves those bewildered by their failing resolve, trembling with terror, utterly confounded.
With thousands of crests of smoke billowing forth from the intense wind. ||13||
Merely by the chanting of whose name the winds, trembling with fear, were made to quake within their own dwellings,
when they beheld him rising up at the front of the battle.
From where she had retreated, she was pursued by the host of gods who were filled with agitation.
Therefore, O you who ride upon a powerful lion, immediately urge that chariot toward the lord of the Daityas, who is deluded by pride;
now is the time for this heat that rains down arrows of calamity.
I shall cause him to be cast down here in battle, like a mountain. 15.
When the enemy of Smara had spoken thus, the charioteer swiftly released Andhaka as a counter-charioteer, causing Mount Meru to tremble;
yet even the chariot of the lord of the Daityas did not waver from its driver.
Urged on by some apprehension, as it were, he looked ahead.
Then, as if swiftly casting off the sovereign fortune of the three worlds from the groves of Mount Sumeru by the wind of its wings,
the vulture, like a messenger of the Lord of the Departed, [alighted] upon the tip of the banner.
He stood in the midst of it, fiercely inflaming the highest fires.
The clouds flowed forth, resembling the nectar-juice situated within the calyx of the lotus of the world,
while the joyful flocks of vultures and swarms of bees hovered about.
It is the unobstructed rain of missiles that fulfills all desires. ||18||
The earth reached a state of terrible upheaval through the clashing of sword-blades, the thundering of weapons, and the impact of dense masses;
and even the flesh-eaters [demons] experienced a harshness like the strike of a thunderbolt.
They let out a loud roar, foreboding the great dissolution of the world.
On the battlefield, the Lord of the Dānavas, whose terrifying signs were disregarded by his fortitude,
and Śambhu, who was unperturbed by the visible omens of victory.
Then those two great car-warriors likewise rushed at each other with speed.
The drums resounded with the striking of their skins;
the swarms of guñjā berries became noisy and discordant;
hundreds of gomukhas blared, and the paṇavas rang out.
Then, as that battle between those two was unfolding, ||21||
The quarters of the sky resounded with the noise of musical instruments such as kinkara, naka, and gomukha drums being beaten,
while the daityas [were accompanied by] sounds made long by the echoes from mountain caves.
The three terrible ones let out lion-like roars in the battle.
The warriors, their minds set on battle, leaped with impetuosity; their movement was fruitful, yielding a beautiful result that corresponded to their intent,
as they struck down their enemies with swords held firmly in hand, which were swallowed up by the blood of the slain.
[They were] intoxicated elephants, axes, swords, and cleavers. ||23||
Approaching the auspicious battle, they sang while striking the lute with fingertips trembling from fear; meanwhile,
Śambhu’s [face] expanded freely at the sight—
The Apsarases, bearing full breasts, held their lush banners aloft.

A rain of flowers from the celestial tree fell like a shower of pearls.
With hands whose fingers were long and red, their nails containing the reflections of jewels,
and with a crest that was as if inlaid with intensely blazing gems; the clear...
A mass of rays from the golden earring of Andhaka.
While that battle was shaking the very bonds of the courage of bowmen,
the mountains then roared like kettledrums along with the warriors of Kubera.
The hollows were made resonant by the sound of the bowstring. ||27||
The tip of his bow, joined with the string of the serpent king, contains within it the reflections of the multitude of jewels from his undulating hoods;
he resembles a crest-jewel of rubies set upon a fragment of the moon.
He wore it, which was fashioned with a terrifying crown. ||28||
With his arms raised unevenly like breaking waves,
he swiftly struck the lords of the Dānava ocean with fragments from his bow,
his face terrifying with flames.
The king of serpents shone, having made his dwelling upon the bowstring. ||29||
The Lord of Serpents, his circle of hoods expanded by the intense strain of the tight binding formed by the staff of Śiva’s bow,
drank the cool [drops] residing upon his head.
The breezes from the mass of waves on the waters of the Mandākinī.
From the center of his arms, which were adorned with the crescent moon, there issued forth arrows whose feathers hissed like wind and whose sharp points were flickering flames,
directed toward the son of Diti who resided on the Himalayas.
Like royal swans emerging from the depths of a dense forest thicket. ||31||
As he drew his beautiful bow into a circle up to his ear in battle, creating a shadow over the worlds like an untimely night at the end of a kalpa—
The floods of arrows released from his mouth pervaded the world.
Then, from that bow, the circle of the serpent’s hoods— its middle drawn by a hand in the *khaṭakāmukha* position with the bowstring fastened— was gradually [drawn],
while the flames of the fire of its hissing were released.
And multitudes of arrows, drawn into circles and other formations, fell down all at once. ||33||
Upon his chest, arrows released from the circle of the bow of the Daitya— feathered with the plumes of peacocks and clearly marked—
became rooted like celestial wish-fulfilling trees upon the slopes of a mountain.
Clusters of blossoming jewel-flowers fell down. ||34||
The chest of the Enemy of the Cities was beautified by the paths of battle created by the service of flowers— the jewels from the heads of the serpent lords serving as sacred threads—
resembling the bows of the lords of the Asuras.
He fell down swiftly, struck by hundreds of arrows discharged from the wheel. ||35||
The currents of the Mandākinī, turbid with masses of surging waves and bearing on their heads the interiors of turtles and skulls,
were drunk up by the falling flames of the arrows lodged there.
Like rivers [dried up] by the rays of the sun at the time of universal dissolution. ||36||
The lord of the Daityas, whose mass of arms became a circle of jeweled bows joined together in preparation for battle,
[resembled] many shimmering fragments of the moon.
He was like the orb of the sun in the path of the sky. ||37||
And I think that the life-breaths of the attacking hosts fell first before him, whose bow was drawn into a circle and whose fierce arms were hardened by the work of battle.
Afterwards, with vipāṭhas having the tips of their shafts sharpened to a keen edge. ||38||
Then, from between the staff-like arms of the Lord of the Daityas, who was bound in fury, arrows issued forth onto the path of battle,
like waves of the ocean struck by the winds of universal destruction.
The serpents have their mouths ablaze with fire from the wheel and other [weapons]. ||39||
The sharp-pointed arrows, having struck the fragments of skulls upon the garland on the head of the blue-throated Shiva— fragments from which fierce flames had been spat out—
shot forth like the rays of the sun against rough surfaces.
The arrows of the enemies of the gods [fell] upon the peaks of Mount Kailāsa.
Entering [the mouth], she whose eyes were obscured by the mass of smoke from the skull-cloth on her head, which had been crushed by the impact of that [skull].
Like one skilled in service, the serpent serving as the ear-ornament of the moon-crested Lord [Śiva] expelled him with his hissing breaths.
Upon the head of the Enemy of Smara is a crescent moon that serves as an ornament,
its curved tip turned inward by the fierce heat of the flames from the thousands of fire-tips of the arrows of the sovereign of the Daityas.
A stream of flowing nectar emerged, becoming particularly slender. ||42||
In that battle,

[the arrows] were shattered by the crescent-shaped head-feathers of his formidable plumage as they struck against the spikes, while the wheel of the bow of the Lord of the Daityas, provoked by intense rage—
The released arrows fell together like venomous serpents. ||43||
The lord of the Daityas, performing a wondrous feat as he expanded his form, was beheld by the circle of eyes of the motionless audience of joyful sky-dwellers who rushed forward.
The cāraṇa minstrels ceased their performance, the rhythmic beat of which had become disjointed. ||44||
As they advanced toward the enemy, casting off those who sought to steal their lives and crushing the pride of those who offered gifts, while facing those who had performed sacrifices,
all the warriors then struck one another in battle.
He densely covered the ten directions with arrows released from his firm bow. ||45||
With an arrow released from a jeweled bow that resembled the staff of Yama, coiled back to his ear,
he struck Śiva, the moon-crested one, in the chest.
Then, at the opportune moment, the enemy of the asuras (Indra) acted without any stinginess.
The god too, his wrath increased by the strike of the arrow, cried out, "Stay on the broad expanse of the chest of the lord of the Dānavas!
and discharged an arrow with its tip blazing like a flickering flame.
With its great feathers formed by a number of feathers equal to the number of the [nine] vital breaths (prāṇas). ||47||
On the path of battle, those two, whose arrows were exhausted as they grew increasingly weary from the ever-increasing difficulty of their struggle, sought each other's vulnerabilities.
May the intention to bind [the world] long remain fruitful and unimpeded. ||48||
The Lord of the Thunderbolt, with his dense, fierce, and tawny shafts resembling thick clouds and lightning, struck the chest of Andhaka—
[a chest] like the ridges and slopes of a mountain on a riverbank— with waves of arrows.
With its various divisions, it was like the god whose banner is a tortoise, accompanied by the Vasus and Śikhins.
Then, the mass of arrows released by Rāndhaka from his swaying bow-tips struck the head of the trident-bearing Śarāru;
yet it was met by the fire-weapon of the flames hissing from the hoods of the serpents upon his crest and its ornaments.
With the feathers of her wings scorched, she fell down unevenly. ||50||
With his wings scorched by the heat of the fire from the hissing breath of the serpent coiled as an ear-ornament, emitting sparks,
he fell from the sky onto the summit of the mountain, the lord of the sons of Diti.
The arrow of the bull-bannered god (Śiva) caused Saṃpāti to experience a state of delusion.

Spreading across the expanse of the sky, which was turned into a hunting ground by the deer and horses emerging from the mouths of his wide-reaching arrows, those shafts discharged from the circle of his bow spread forth, instilling fear.
The arrows [spread] in all directions like a multitude of meteors and piśācas. ||52||
"Drive poverty far away with fear; tear asunder the mountains;
slay, slay the enemies of men who are arrogant with pride"—thus did he whose ears were adorned with earrings proclaim as he wandered forth.
With his pair of eyes having red corners, he abandoned his distress.
Then, resounding with the deep twang of the bowstring mingled with the incessant humming of its string,
the flood of arrows reached from afar,
as if they were the circle of birds moving through the sky.
He bestowed upon him the joy resulting from the destruction of all his enemies. ||54||
Then, with shoulders shattered by the harsh blows spat out from the mouths of those who were like the halo of the moon of nectar,
he released the warriors who were longing for death at the front of the battle.
The wise strike at their enemies only through a vulnerability. ||55||
By the feathers of those gold-feathered arrows of the enemy of the gods, which were shattered in mid-air, the sky shone,
smeared with the abundant pollen-like dust falling from them.
Like mountain peaks variegated by the rays of the rising sun. ||56||

The rows of celestial chariots of thousands of sky-faring beings, moving upward and obstructing the path of the sun out of curiosity to witness the spectacle of the battle-play, [are being struck by] the fierce...
...he brought down the arrows discharged from the bow of the Enemy of Smara (Śiva). ||57||
And that [sky] became filled with clouds shattered by the impact of the wind from the wings of the multitudes of arrows discharged from that bow, which had been rendered incapable of movement;
it was further covered by the wounds inflicted by various weapons being brandished.
The sky appeared as if marked with the scars of deep, dark wounds. ||58||
The world-lotus was being drunk in by the buds of the sun’s orb, which were covered and yet possessed the beauty of petals blossoming in the morning heat and honey;
it was made resonant by the humming of bowstrings singing songs.
The womb was instantly [pierced] by the multitudes of arrows from the Daityas. ||59||
Then, stretching his bow which was like a flashing fire-weapon, the lord of the Daityas— whose storehouse of arrogance was filled with fearless "huṃ" cries—
displayed a contraction of his curved eyebrows.
"O you with the radiant forehead," he addressed Dhūrjaṭi.
"Stay right now, young brahmin! Where will you go from the path of my sight?
I am the one whose arrows are flowers; I am not of feeble power.
Furthermore, Time is no pitiless thing toward worms, insects, and living creatures."
Neither was Gajāsura skilled in taking away life. ||61||

For one is the ground of the ancestral temple, its surface garlanded by vetālas who have risen with the impetuosity of dance and struck the rhythmic beat; the other is the battlefield, where the fierce wheels of warriors— Please note that the provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available. If you provide the remainder of the verse, I would be happy to complete it.
The beauty of her arms was like a polished slab for testing the pride of the staff-like arms [of warriors]. ||62||
Having spoken thus, he, still smiling, pierced him with five arrows whose tips blazed like fire;
slightly shattered by the thunderbolt-like fall of those shafts—
And his chest, adorned with a crest-jewel shaped like the digit of the moon, trembled.
When he moved even slightly, his face— its lower lip trembling with shame at the sight of the slightest trace of distress seen by the eye of the Six-faced One—
Āmardaka swiftly rushed toward Andhaka.
It tore asunder and covered the peaks of Mount Sumeru and the sun. ||64||
Then, beholding him approaching head-on, the lord of the Daityas, overcome by rage, obstructed him with arrows;
he [the Daitya] hurled that mountain peak, its summit composed of the finest jewels—
This has ascended to a level of excellence that cannot be equaled by others. ||65||
To him, Murajit hurled a discus, Halī a great plow, and the son of Harita-sapta a staff;
then, having checked them with thousands of arrows, he [stood firm].
In the battle, he swiftly struck the moon-crested Lord with five arrows.
He severed the coils of Vāsuki as the archer discharged arrows, while the sky was made starry by sparks of fire hissing from the thousands of fruits situated upon the tips of his bow-staff.
Then, finding a vulnerability in him with his arrows, the enemy of the gods—
The bow of the moon-crested Lord [Śiva], its massive and lofty staff blended with the circular radiance of polished and blazing jewels,
and its serpent-string severed—
It bore within the sky the splendor of Indra’s rainbow. ||68||
With the coils of Vāsuki severed, his garment embraced the crest of his crown which was emitting sparks of flame— a sign of victory and attainment—
and with the knitting of his brows distorted by anger, he seized [the weapon].
A trident with a body difficult to behold, possessing a face and tawny eyes. ||69||
With his flickering, swaying weapon-tongue lashing out to swallow the entire world without remainder,
and springing forward with speed, he was like the Aurva fire rushing forth to greet him.
The fire of the syllable *huṃ* fell instantly into the ocean. ||70||
Then, by that [discus] rapidly whirled by the hand of Śaṅkara,
the triple-stranded [cord] of the sun’s thick path— flickering as it revolves— was quickly bound without being crushed.
The circle of the halo of flames from the fire of the three branches. ||71||
Dragging away the mountain peaks, causing the sun and moon to tremble, flooding the path of heaven with the waters of the ocean,
and heaping together the stars while shattering the surface of the earth’s foundation—
His orb was restless with the desire to wander through the months.
The roots and joints of the rocks were shattered by the heat of the fire from the tridents;
the celestial trees on the broken slopes quickly fell,
their distant forms made visible by the liberation [of the peaks].
The peaks of Mount Meru, established upon its back, reached toward the heavens. ||73||
And as that [churning rod] was whirled by Dhūrjaṭi, the surface of heaven was inundated by a mass of waves from the agitated ocean; then,
a thick shower of sparks from that fire burst forth—
The orb of the sun, whose greatness is manifested through its distinct rays. ||74||
The waters of Sumeru were carried forth, flowing from the broad peaks of golden rock that had melted by the heat of the tip of the Pināka bow,
their currents broken as they struck against jeweled stones.
The mountain streams, eroding their banks, flow through the terrains of the foothills.
Then, by means of his hands, which were formidable with clusters of fire-flames flickering as they shifted between the gaps in the branches,
he was raised up by that continuous whirling motion.
Like the celestial river when its ten courses have become difficult to restrain. ||76||
He discharged a fierce fire from his mouth, which swallowed the seven oceans with its mass of flames,
produced a terrifying roar like that of a mountain peak,
and blazed with intense power.
Like Śambhu at the time of universal dissolution with the palm of his mouth. ||77||
Therefore, the arrows released from the circle of Andhaka’s formidable, upraised bow, falling so as to shroud the horizons,
pierced through the firm [host] with hundreds of aged weapons.
Like the ripples on the waves of the ocean by the fire of the submarine flame. ||78||
Having struck down that son of the Daityas with spears, javelins, clubs, thunderbolts, sharp-edged spears, swords, and scimitars,
the Conqueror of Cities (Śiva) struck Dandaka as well with terrible showers of weapons.
Furthermore, he grew even more distinguished than Agni in that [battle];
for in combat, the wielder of the crescent moon (Śiva), having violently struck down the mass of his arrows issuing from the circle of his bow—
He rushed impetuously toward the chariot; the lord of the Daityas also struck him, who held a heavy spear in his hand, with a mace.
Then the fire from the mouth of Dhūrjaṭi blazed forth and scorched, its jagged flames drenched by the thick blood spurting from the head of the lord of the Daityas as it was shattered by the mace.
That chariot, complete with its horses, banner, driver, and wheels, [was destroyed]. ||81||
When his chariot was then consumed by that fire— which turned the ten directions tawny with its flames and weapons— just as Tripura had been,
the lord of the Daityas, wearing the moon as his crown, desired to seize him.
Then, out of pride, he suddenly leapt into the air.
With his cheeks blooming with a smile,
the wielder of the trident simultaneously pierced with his three-pointed spear that [demon] who was rushing toward him with great speed, as well as the hearts of all the wives of the Daityas.

His chest, with the tip of the spear blazing like a flickering fire and deafening the atmosphere with its whirring sound, flowed with blood until it resembled a circle of clouds streaked by the rays of the sun, copper-red at twilight. (84)
The solar disc, darkened by the smoke produced from the flames of the trident’s tip drenched in the streams of blood of the Daityas,
appears like a mountain peak whose brilliance has vanished due to the blow of a chisel and whose base is firmly rooted.
At that moment, it shone in the sky like blood. ||85||

When the flood of blood gushed from the slope of the chest-armlet of the enemy of the gods, which had been split by the three-pronged [spear], it alone brought peace to all the worlds that had been scorched by the fire of his majesty. (86)
Being crushed at the boundary of the sky, he— possessing the hue of a heap of powdered collyrium due to the splitting of his three-peaked face— fell to the earth;
and he was beheld in the expanse of the heavens by the armies of the enemies of the stars.
He was a portentous cloud heralding the destruction of the prosperity of the lineage of the sons of Aditi. ||87||
Having drunk that thick blood fallen from her bracelets into the hollow of her skull-cup, she bears a body that is copper-red as if turned crimson by its digestion;
and from the touch of the tip of Cāmuṇḍā’s finger, [she bears] the sprouts of the seeds of that vital energy.
He did not hastily create counter-images of those whose entire lineages had been severed. ||88||
Then, as his entire body was instantly reduced to ashes by the heat of the blazing flames of the three-pointed fire, which boiled the thick blood [from him],
he was beheld by the hosts of gods and demons with their eyes fixed in a trance.
Then his body entered the light of the one whose crest is the digit of the moon. ||89||
The Andhaka and Kālakūṭa [poisons], which had entered the ocean of battle where the circles of gods and asuras were swallowed and crushed,
were fanned upon his shoulders by the wind from the waving yak-tail whisks.
Then, on the throne, he bestowed the royal fortune upon Hari. ||90||

Then, by his command, as if they were the guardians of the celestial realms, the protectors of the quarters swiftly uprooted all opposing forces and established their defenses in due order throughout the directions.
For this reason, they fixed their gaze—eyes blossoming with passion—upon her.
He [made] the battlefield, which had fallen [in ruin] and was struck by the enemy forces, free from wounds caused by blows through the touch of his own hand—
the flowing nectar-water from the crescent moon upon his crown.
Having sprinkled water from the stream, he restored the army to life. ||92||
In every direction, bees intoxicated by the flowing nectar made the paths fragrant; scattering showers of flowers,
they produced the sounds of many musical instruments with ever-fresh melodies.
Delighted by the destruction of their enemy, the Siddhas and Sādhyas offered hymns of praise;
the celestial maidens sang auspicious songs,
their thick breasts heaving as their pearl necklaces trembled in the rhythmic cadence of high and low notes.
On the path to heaven, their intense latent impressions (vāsanā) of the heavy heart were clearly discernible through incessant and various contractions of the eyebrows. 94.

Then, having honored those lords of the hosts of the thirty-three gods— who had displayed their devotion by bowing with heads bent low before him in battle, their crest-jewels loosened— as they were granted their desired boons by the Goddess;
Experiencing happiness together with him, he resided in his own city. ||95||

Thus ends the fiftieth canto, titled "The Installation of the God of Gods," in the great poem *Haravijaya*, marked by the jewel, composed by the great poet Rājānaka Śrī Ratnākara—who was a servant of the illustrious Bālabṛhaspati, who bore the mark of Vāgīśvara, and whose other name was Vidyādhipati.
This work is complete.
(The author's eulogy.)

Ratnākara— the son of the moon-like Amṛtabhānu, who took refuge in the lake of the Gaṅgā on the peak of the Himalayas that is his own lineage, [the mountain] bestowed by the illustrious Durga— composed this work of graceful composition.
A poem charming by its reliance on the life-story of him whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon. ||1||

That poet, it is said, spoke thus: "Verses that are playful and sweet, adorned with ornaments, delightful through their clarity, and unrestrained by the constraints of complex *yamakas*, *śleṣas*, and elaborate compositions."
O King, as I utter words concerning diverse destinies on this manifold path, my mind does not indeed tremble, even before Vācaspati himself.
In the expression of the reality of things by our words— which possess excellence and flow with the vibration of the essence of the nectar of intense bliss—
[there arises] that which serves as an ear-ornament for the women of the quarters, blossoming white like the full moonlight.
He is an indescribable chisel of the sound *ṭāṅkāra*, whose fame is like a cluster of blossoms upon the pillar of Brahmā. ||3||

His supreme devotion was fixed upon the composition of poetic works in continuous streams; his speech, worthy of being drunk by the ears of poets, never incurred the weightiness of a burden even when employed within the six languages.
His wealth of knowledge attained a splendor of most stainless acquisition, having reached the very limit of all that is to be known.
O King, I am Ratnākara, who has taken my place in your assembly, marked by the Lord of Speech.
Know that King [Rāma], at whose rising the oceans of speech swallowed by darkness are constantly purified as they burn away their blinding gloom.
Then he [beheld] the sun, the mine of jewels, as well as Agastya and Aurva.
There is nothing in this world that has not been woven by poets of true wisdom; once a subject has been traversed, there is no concern for it being traversed again—let alone its depth of meaning.
Among those whose speech is heavy with the flow of both gentle and bold expression, Bāṇa alone is the foremost.
And Rājanratnākara, like a fire, blazes intensely upon the earth as the second. ||6||
Listen to the vow of Haravijaya, the great poet, who has formed an affectionate attachment to my work:
"Even a child who is not a poet becomes a poet through influence, and a poet gradually becomes a great poet. (7)
